It calls Osceola's brief but heroic struggle equal, if not superior, to any of Reid's former works. The reader's patriotism will be gratified at the result, it says, while sympathy wakes for the gallant spirit who fought for his red brethren and their hunting-grounds. The first chapter salutes Florida, Linda Florida, fair land of flowers, much as Ponce de Leon found it. Readers get frontier romance on history's ground.
35642-the-bible-in-spain-vol-1-of-2-or-t:
George Borrow recounts the journeys, adventures, and imprisonments of an Englishman sent to circulate the Scriptures in Spain. In his preface he explains that the Bible Society sent him to print and spread the Bible. The errand threw him among people of every rank and into many strange situations.

This is volume one of the 1896 edition, with notes and a glossary by Ulick Ralph Burke. Borrow insists he is no mere tourist. He claims his is the only book on mission work in Spain. Readers get a vivid travel narrative of the Peninsula, Portugal included, from a man adrift in a land of wonder.
35676-the-bible-in-spain-vol-2-of-2-or-t:
The Bible in Spain, volume 2 of 2, carries George Borrow's journeys through Spain. Borrow travelled as an agent selling Bibles for a British society. This new edition of 1896 adds notes and a glossary by Ulick Ralph Burke. The second volume opens at chapter XXIX. The road leads into Galicia and the Asturias.

Borrow rides among gypsies, muleteers, priests, and officials. Arrests and prison chapters come toward the end of the narrative. His ear for speech fills the pages with talk as much as travel. His taste for odd company does the same. The book made Borrow's name when it first appeared. Burke's edition served a later generation of readers. They still took Spain as a half-known country of romance, danger, and stubborn local custom.
35783-mornings-at-bow-street-a-selection:
Wight, the Morning Herald's reporter at Bow Street court, gathered these police reports into a book. Routledge printed this edition in London and New York in 1875. George Cruikshank drew its twenty-one plates, full of low London life.

The volume draws on reports run in the Herald across three years, the front note says. Public praise moved the author to pick the most graphic and droll of them. Drunks, thieves, sharpers, and wives crowd the dock at Bow Street. The magistrate's dry wit meets street talk at its richest. A bird quote heads the title page: sweet birds that love the noise of folly, most musical, most sad. Rich period reporting, half court record, half stage play.
35808-the-boy-scouts-of-the-air-in-india:
Gordon Stuart wrote The Boy Scouts of the Air in Indian Land, issued at Chicago with a copyright of 1912 and pictures by Norman Hall. Carl and his fellow scouts are shown in the front matter creeping through smoke and darkness to reach a machine. Their teacher Hawke promises to show them the model of the Thunder Bird Aeroplane, named from a legend told early in the book.

Nineteen chapters run from a ride and a runaway to winning an aeroplane, work on the plane, and the first flight. A storm in the mountains, a strange meeting, and a fire in the hangar raise the stakes. The patrol becomes a fact along the way. Stuart mixes early flying with scout camping and the West of its day.
35835-history-of-prince-edward-island:
Duncan Campbell wrote a History of Prince Edward Island, issued at Charlottetown in 1875. Campbell had writ a History of Nova Scotia. The front note sets his aims in plain words. He sought a brief, true, and fair tale from the time the island became British to its union with the Dominion.

Campbell read all books and tracts on the island that he could find. He tested their claims with care. He then read a vast mass of state papers not yet in print. Leave to read those papers came through Lord Dufferin and the lieutenant governor. Campbell notes that more lies in French stores at Paris. The small book rests on large work, he warns.
36040-george-sand:
George Sand is an essay by Justin McCarthy on the French novelist. The piece reprints from The Galaxy magazine for May of 1870. McCarthy speculates on what might have been in her life story. If Cleopatra's nose had differed by an inch, the old chain runs. If Hannibal had not lingered at Capua, if Cromwell had emigrated.

What if George Sand had married happily in her youth, he asks. Would she ever have taken to literature at all in that case? Loving fields, flowers, and brooks as Frenchwomen rarely do, he notes. Might she have lived a peaceful, obscure life in a country place? Home and love might have contented her. Or would her books have lost their passionate purpose in that life? Books a Podsnap might approve for his daughter stand as the joke. A different early life might have changed all her writing, he muses.
36065-the-life-of-saint-columba-apostle-:
The Life of Saint Columba is a saint life by Forbes in a faith flag set. A Washbourne house of London brought out this second print in nineteen nineteen. Church leave marks of nineteen thirteen stand at its front in Latin form. More than a score of centuries have gone since Columba death, the front says. Yet his name lives strong as few saints names do, it claims.

Adamnan, ninth abbot of Iona, wrote his life at great length in old days. He was born a bare span of years past the saint death in that count. Men who knew Columba face to face gave him his tale stuff. Carlyle held that life man could tell no lie in his work. Stone cup and birth room floor stone of the saint still stand in Ireland.
3612-john-bull-s-other-island:
George Bernard Shaw sets this play in Ireland in 1904, opening on a summer afternoon in the London rooms of Doyle and Broadbent, civil engineers. The partners, Lawrence Doyle and Thomas Broadbent, are bachelors and close friends who live above their office. Broadbent, a cheerful Englishman, decides to buy land and improve Ireland, while Doyle, an Irishman, knows the country far better and dreads the result.

Shaw turns the Irish question into comedy and argument. Broadbent's plans for progress collide with Irish priests, farmers, and local politics, and Doyle watches his friend blunder with affection and despair. The play suits readers interested in Shaw on empire, Home Rule, and the gap between English good intentions and Irish reality.
36193-the-viceroys-of-ireland:
Charles O'Mahony wrote a history of the viceroys of Ireland, published at London in 1912 with thirty three portraits. Its subtitle tells the story of the long line of noblemen who ruled Ireland for over seven hundred years. Their wives, who led Irish society, share the story. A photogravure of the Earl of Aberdeen fronts the book. O'Mahony dedicates it to his wife, dating his preface from London in June 1912.

Contents run by numbered chapters without names, inviting the reader into the sequence. The viceroys, or lords lieutenant, embodied English rule in Dublin Castle. Their wives led its society. O'Mahony's gallery mixes politics with court life. John Long issued the handsome volume from the Haymarket.
36259-the-corner-house-girls-on-palm-isl:
The Corner House Girls on Palm Island, by Grace Brooks Hill, is a girls' adventure in the Corner House Girls series, published in New York in 1922. Thelma Gooch drew the pictures.

The Kenway sisters and their friends sail into tropic climes, and a sea adventure leaves them cast away on Palm Island. Chapters cover the island refuge, the adventures of the castaways, and a night of despair. The girls build a raft, set a flag on a tree top, and catch turtles on the shore. Tess and Dot have an odyssey of their own, and an old turtle called Mr Methuselah plays a part. A frontispiece shows deep scratches on a great shell. The last chapter ties all the threads and brings the party home.
36375-fifty-years-in-the-northwest-with-:
Folsom wrote Fifty Years in the Northwest, published in 1888 and edited by Edwards. Folsom dedicated the book to the old settlers of Wisconsin and Minnesota who laid the foundations of two states amid privations later generations never knew. His preface says he landed at nineteen on the Upper Mississippi, pitching his tent at Prairie du Chien, then the military post of Fort Crawford, in 1836.

He kept memoranda of events as they passed, never meaning to publish until 1876, when fifty years of settlement seemed worth handing on. An account of his first nineteen years gives the work a life-history frame. The sketches reach back to the Jesuit explorers and the French, English, and American traders, then trace the turn from wilderness to farms, cities, and railways. Readers get a pioneer's own chronicle of the upper river country, by a man who watched the change for half a century.
36376-the-life-of-benjamin-franklin-with: The Life of Benjamin Franklin, with many choice anecdotes and admirable sayings of this great man, never before published by any of his biographers, is the popular biography by Weems. Street and Smith of New York issued it as number fourteen of their Historical Series. Weems was famous as the author of The Life of Washington. The title page carries verses on Franklin: sage Franklin next arose in cheerful mien, a wreath of palm for all the arts upon his locks of age.
36540-myths-and-folk-tales-of-ireland:
Jeremiah Curtin gathered this set of Irish myths and folk tales, drawn from the mouths of the Irish folk themselves. Giants, kings, and clever sons crowd the contents. The Son of the King of Erin and the Giant of Loch Léin leads off, and The Three Daughters of King O'Hara follows. Fair, Brown, and Trembling gives the Irish Cinderella.

Fin MacCumhail stands at the heart of the book: his birth, the rise of the Fenians, the Castle of Fear Dubh, and the Knight of the Full Axe. Cúculin and Oisin in Tir na n-Og close the hero tales. Notes at the back back up the tellings. Curtin keeps the voice of the fireside, with its turns, tests, and wonders.
36565-the-welsh-pony-described-in-two-le:
The Welsh Pony is described in two letters to a friend by Olive Tilford Dargan. Charles Stone had the book printed privately at Boston in 1913. Pinkham Press did the printing for that small private edition run. Dargan gives the book to Anne Whitney at its opening page. A herd of Welsh mountain ponies grazing fronts the picture list.

My Lord Pembroke, a famed Welsh stallion, stars in many plates here. He won first prize at Brockton Fair in 1912 under saddle. Searchlight, Greylight, and Longmynd Eclipse stand among the pictured ponies. Rainbow, an imported Welsh stallion, and a full brother of Daylight appear. Brecon, the Beacons, and Forest Lodge pastures show the ponies' home ground. Mare and foal pictures soften the long list of proud stallions. The letters praise the breed for American friends of the pony.
36631-king-eric-and-the-outlaws-vol-1-or:
Ingemann's King Eric and the Outlaws, turned from the Danish by Jane Frances Chapman, was published in London in 1843 in three volumes. The subtitle names its ground: the throne, the church, and the people in the thirteenth century. A stern notice at the front warns sellers and circulating libraries against foreign copies of the copyright text.

Chapman's preface mourns that Danish books, old and new, stay near unknown to English readers while German, Swedish, and Italian works find translators at once. She notes how Denmark's old lore is woven tight with the lore of Anglo-Saxon England. Volume one opens the tale of a king, his church, and the men cast out by both.
36632-king-eric-and-the-outlaws-vol-2-or:
Ingemann writes a Danish tale in King Eric and the Outlaws, volume 2, printed in London in 1843. Longman made the book, in three volumes. Chapman renders it from the Danish. Its subtitle names the stakes: the throne, the church, and the people, in the thirteenth century.

The first chapter opens before a shut gate at Kallundborg castle. The drawbridge stands raised, and the castle holds itself ready for defence. The king's face flushes with anger, and his hand grips his sword hilt. Count Henrik waits on his war horse for the warder's answer to the king's demand, and the king marvels at the delay.
36633-king-eric-and-the-outlaws-vol-3-or:
The hosted text is the third volume of King Eric and the Outlaws, a Danish historical novel by Ingemann. Its full title sets the tale among throne, church, and people in the thirteenth century. Jane Frances Chapman turned it into English. The London issue is from Longman and partners, dated 1843.

The volume opens on a quay. Sir Helmer comes up from a Rostock vessel with wounds bound and clothes torn. He spots a man in the dress of a German grocer's lad leaping ashore. He is sure it is the outlaw Kaggé. Helmer and a squire hurry off in search of him through the crowd. The scene sets the tone of chase, disguise, and feud that drives the last volume.
3679-getting-gold-a-practical-treatise-f:
J C F Johnson writes a practical treatise for prospectors, miners, and others interested in gold mining, in a second edition revised in 1898. Johnson, a fellow of the Geological Society and member of the Australian Institute of Mining Engineers, draws on thirty years of experience. His preface says the information, original or compiled, will be found useful by men in every branch of the gold industry.

The book covers finding gold, testing ore, crushing, washing, and working claims, with drawings and diagrams in the print edition, omitted here. Johnson writes plainly for working miners rather than for scholars. The treatise suits readers interested in gold rush history and in the practical science of prospecting.
36799-the-history-of-the-last-trial-by-j:
The History of the Last Trial by Jury for Atheism in England is a fragment of autobiography by George Jacob Holyoake. It was published in London by James Watson in 1850. Holyoake addresses it to the perusal of the Attorney General and the British clergy. A quote from Richard Carlile heads the book: he would rather be found guilty with Holyoake than cleared on a cheap ground. The dedication thanks a friend who first helped the freethinkers when they were unknown and struggling.

The book tells of a history of six months imprisonment, as its dedication says. Holyoake had been tried for words spoken on religion and found guilty. He writes in hope this trial may stand the last of its kind. Doubt of the old saying that atheism is a bloody system runs through the pages. The tone is sober, wounded, and proud.
37113-the-sixty-first-second:
The Sixty-First Second is a mystery novel by Owen Johnson, printed at New York by Stokes in 1913. Johnson also wrote Stover at Yale. Wenzell drew the illustrations. The frontispiece has a host promising detectives, a man and a woman, within half an hour: there is nothing to do but wait.

The plates sketch the puzzle. In a gay party one person was a thief, but which one? A match sputters, a cry of amazement and horror rises, and the table is absolutely bare. Rita is asked whether she cannot help out somehow, and a garden talk is begged in whispers. The story opens in the ominous, grumbling days of October, with the air full of confusing rumours. Johnson sets his jewel theft inside high society and keeps the company guessing to the named second.
3722-a-daughter-of-the-land:
Gene Stratton-Porter follows Kate Bates, a farm girl who takes the minister's text about the wings of the morning as a personal call. Kate grows up on an Indiana farm, fights for schooling, and sets out to teach, determined to earn her own way rather than marry for shelter. Her grit carries her into a schoolhouse at Walden, where she cleans the rooms herself and readies the winter term with her own hands.

Love complicates the plan, since John Jardine courts her and then crosses her, and Kate answers with a telegram ending the affair and a long walk to clear her head. Stratton-Porter fills the novel with cornfields, country schools, and family quarrels. Readers who like heroines who work for their freedom will find Kate a sturdy companion across a long and eventful story.
37264-yankee-girls-in-zulu-land:
Louise Vescelius-Sheldon wrote Yankee Girls in Zulu Land, with pictures by G E Graves, in an 1888 New York edition from Worthington Company. Chapter One is a letter from a mother in New York City to her children. She asks what has set them thinking of South Africa, where there are only Zulus and missionaries, in the phrase of the day.

Chapter Two tells of six months of rain, snow, and fog in London. The sun was seen on just ten days in that stretch, the teller says. A doctor ordered a change of climate for Frank's health. Heat and sunshine were the need, and South Africa was advised. An African lady in the same house had just come home to see the wonders of the civilised world. The girls weigh a health trip to the far side of the globe as the tale starts.
37277-chaucer-and-his-england:
Coulton wrote a study of the poet Chaucer and the England he lived in, first published by Methuen in 1908. Thirty two pictures go with the text. One shows Chaucer as his pupil Hoccleve had him painted, grey haired, with a rosary in his hand. The first six chapters tell the poet's life in plain stages.

They run from boyhood through his years as the king's squire, envoy, and man of business, to his last days. The rest of the book opens out into the land itself. Coulton treats the London custom house, town and country, and the laws of London. Three chapters walk through the Canterbury Tales day by day. Others treat kings, knights, husbands, the great war with France, the poor, and the priests. The aim is to let the reader see the age whole, with the poet at its heart.
37278-fly-fishing-in-wonderland:
Fly Fishing in Wonderland is an angling book by Barnes about the Yellowstone country. Barnes took the copyright in 1910. He dedicated the book to a fishing companion named Gill. Their days together ran along streams and woods. A poem about a hill vagabond opens the volume.

The foreword bounds the wonderland precisely. It runs from the Montana line to the Teton mountains. Idaho's edge and the Absaroka range frame it east and west. Streams there drain to three different seas. Congress reserved most of the region as a public pleasure ground. Chapters treat native and planted trout. A chapter on trout flies gives practical counsel. Grizzly Lake, Iron Creek, and the Firehole supply the fishing scenes.
37313-the-standard-galleries-holland:
The Standard Galleries: Holland, by Esther Singleton, author of Dutch and Flemish Furniture, was published in Chicago in 1908 by McClurg, with forty-six pictures. A plate of Vermeer's View of Delft attends the title. Singleton wrote the book for the traveler with two or three days in a city, whose first question is always what must be seen.

Her preface lists the order of sights: the city itself first, its streets, bridges, canals, parks, and drives. Then famous churches, city halls, and old buildings, perhaps a palace, and most certainly the museums of art and antiquities. The volume walks the Dutch galleries in that spirit, room by room, naming the pictures a short visit cannot skip. It is a Baedeker-minded guide to painting, for tourists rather than scholars.
37418-palm-tree-island:
Palm Tree Island tells how Harry Brent and William Bobbin of Limehouse were left on an island in the southern hemisphere, and what befell them there. Herbert Strang wrote the tale, and Henry Frowde with Hodder and Stoughton published it in London in 1910. Archibald Webb and Alan Wright drew the pictures.

The chapter heads promise a full castaway course. The boys sail in the Lovey Susan, meet mutiny and shipwreck, cheat Neptune, and live on clams and cocoa-nuts while they hunt for food and shelter. Wild dogs raid their stores, a fleet of canoes threatens a siege, and an underground adventure costs them dear. The book is a hearty specimen of the boys' island adventure, told in the old faithful manner.
37426-whirlpools-a-novel-of-modern-polan:
Henryk Sienkiewicz writes of his own land in Whirlpools, a novel of modern Poland, printed at Boston in 1910. Little, Brown made the book, published in June of that year. Drezmal translates from the Polish. Sienkiewicz had writ Quo Vadis, With Fire and Sword, and The Deluge.

Part first opens at a manor house at midnight. Gronski arrived at the Jastrzeb manor house about midnight, the tale starts. In the house all were asleep except an old servant and the young heir, Ladislaus Krzycki. The heir awaited his guest with supper, and greeted him with great cordiality. Notwithstanding the disparity in their ages, they were bound by ties of an old intimacy. It ran back to the days when Gronski, as a university student, surrounded the youthful Krzycki with a tutelary friendship at the gymnasium.
3750-letters-of-franz-liszt-volume-2-fro:
Franz Liszt's later letters, collected by La Mara and translated by Constance Bache, cover his years in Rome through to the end of his life. The composer writes to friends, pupils, and fellow musicians about scores, church music, concerts, and the daily business of an artist who has also taken holy orders. One long letter weighs a Mass movement bar by bar, praising its fire while asking whether a celebrant standing still at the altar can survive three hundred slow bars.

The letters show Liszt as teacher, critic, and friend, placing a new work between Bach and Beethoven with easy confidence. They also record an old man's faith, travel, and failing strength without self pity. Music lovers will find the volume a close view of a great career winding down, told in the composer's own busy and generous voice.
37651-the-new-paul-and-virginia-or-posit:
W H Mallock wrote The New Paul and Virginia, a satire. Chatto and Windus issued it at London in 1890. Its subtitle reads Positivism on an Island. Mallock had written The New Republic before. Frederic Harrison's dark line heads the book. Pessimism marks man's enervated age, it claims.

Professor Clifford reads man's kingdom at hand, a second motto says. A Swinburne-like hymn cries glory to man. Man is the master of things, it sings. Eighteen chapters and notes fill the book. The steamship Australasian opens chapter one at sea. She sails home from Melbourne with the mails. Ninety-eight first-class passengers ride her in comfort. Skies stand cloudless and the sea like glass. No sickness sounds aboard her that day. A shipwreck of two creeds, the tale strands faith and positivism together to argue man's worth.
37705-popery-as-it-was-and-as-it-is-also:
Popery As It Was and As It Is is an anti-Catholic polemic by William Hogan, published in 1854. Hogan writes as a former Roman Catholic priest. The volume also treats auricular confession and what its title calls popish nunneries, and it carries several illustrations.

The preface states the author's motive plainly. He says he aims to serve the free institutions of his adopted country, the United States. The book is dedicated to American republicans. Hogan expects hostility from the church he left, and he describes its custom of defaming those who go out from it. His argument rests on his standing as an insider turned critic. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg, and it preserves the heated tone of its decade.
37858-leaves-in-the-wind:
Leaves in the Wind is a gathering of essays by A. G. Gardiner, who wrote as Alpha of the Plough. The book came out in the Wayfarers Library from J. M. Dent and E. P. Dutton. A note at the front states that the essays were written in the war years. They first came out in book form in that same span of time.

Gardiner calls the essays the play of his pen in a time of great public strain and heavy tasks of his own. The writing of them was, he says, a glad break from sad things. Now that the great wind has passed, the fallen leaves are gathered in book form once more. He leaves them as they fell. The contents open with pieces such as A Fellow Traveller.
37891-bygone-cumberland-and-westmorland:
Bygone Cumberland and Westmorland is a work of local history by Daniel Scott. Andrews of London issued it in 1899. Scott gathered its matter over twenty years. Old registers and papers fed many of its pages. The preface notes how well the two counties had been worked. Their local societies had dug deep for thirty years. His contents open with an unmatched sheriffwick.

For six centuries Westmorland's sheriff held his post by birth. Watch and ward, fighting bishops, and walled churches follow. Church oddities and manor customs fill the middle. Old punishments and legends come next. Scott writes for lovers of the northern past. The book is thick with small, strange facts.
3799-landholding-in-england:
Joseph Fisher expanded a paper read to the Royal Historical Society in 1875 into this history of English landholding. He begins from the principle that tillage is the most useful art, since a nation draws its food and its surest riches from the soil. From there he follows that thread through centuries of tenure, law, and custom. The book quotes Vattel on the duties of government toward the soil and Proverbs on food in the tillage of the poor.

Later passages trace statutes of Edward the Third that freed buyers of land from royal seizure, and De Lolme's remark that such laws stripped the king of power over alienation. Fisher writes for readers shut out from the costly Transactions of the Society. Students of English history will find a compact guide to how land passed, who held it, and why it mattered.
37993-climbing-in-the-british-isles-vol-:
Climbing in the British Isles is a guide to the climb of rocks and hills, by Haskett Smith, a man of a great climb club. The host text is the first of three parts, on England. Two more parts, on Wales and on the north land, were in the works at its print. It was put out at London and New York in eighteen ninety four. Three and twenty plates and five plans stand in the book.

The list of parts gives the plan of the guide. First come the shires and tracts of note to the hill man. Then come the towns fit as climb posts for the hills. Then the hills and rocks that give climbs are set out. Climbs of fame come next, with words on how to find and do them.
38134-beyond:
Beyond, by Henry Seward Hubbard, came out from the Arena Publishing Company in Boston in 1896. Hubbard argues for the reality of what he calls the immaterial world, the part of existence that mortal eyes cannot be made to see.

He limits himself mostly to the borderland of that world, the part that adjoins earthly life and bears on whether the dead return. His readers are those who cannot perceive such a world yet honestly wish to be convinced. He insists that the truths of the higher life do not clash with common sense, even where they rise past its full grasp. The book belongs to the wide spiritual inquiry of its decade.
38241-uncle-s-dream-and-the-permanent-hu:
Uncle's Dream and The Permanent Husband brings together two shorter works of fiction by Fedor Dostoievsky. They appear here in Fred Whishaw's English translation, in the series called Vizetelly's Russian novels. The publisher's pages around them praise Dostoievsky beside Turgenieff and Tolstoi as giants of the Russian novel. The Idiot and Crime and Punishment are quoted from the press with warm words.

Dostoievsky was famed as one of the keenest watchers of human nature among modern novelists. These two tales show his lighter and his darker sides. One plays with a provincial scheme built around a doting old uncle. The other turns on a husband, a wife's memory, and the man who loved her. Both were early read in English through Whishaw's versions. The volume preserves how Russian fiction first reached a broad British public, wrapped in reviews and lists of its fellows.
38446-outlines-of-a-philosophy-of-religi:
Outlines of a Philosophy of Religion is a study by Auguste Sabatier of France. Sabatier also wrote a noted work on the Apostle Paul. Pott published the English text in New York in the year 1910. Its two books treat religion in general, then Christianity in turn. Book one opens on the origin and nature of religion itself.

First reflections and a contradiction of consciousness start that inquiry. Religion as the prayer of the heart forms its third head there. Religion and revelation, miracle and inspiration, follow in chapters two and three. The religious development of humanity closes the first book in survey. Prayer through the ages stands as Sabatier's thread of proof.
38597-martha-or-the-fair-at-richmond:
Martha, or The Fair at Richmond, is an opera libretto with text by Friedrich and music by Friedrich von Flotow. This Boston edition came out in 1913 in the Laurel Octavo line. Louise Baum edited the English text, and Glen Carle edited the music. The editors aimed the version first at schools. It can be sung in concert form or staged with scenery and costume.

Dull numbers and needless repeats were cut out. The best music was kept and joined into a smooth whole. The words were revised and, where needed, rewritten for clear singing. The libretto gives dialogue, stage directions, and all that singers need in words. Front pages carry ads for other school music from the same house.
38606-poultry-a-practical-guide-to-the-c:
Hugh Piper wrote Poultry, a practical guide to the choice, breeding, rearing, and management of fowls, turkeys, guinea-fowls, ducks, and geese. The fourth edition was published by Groombridge and Sons in London in 1877, with eight coloured plates. Piper had earlier written a book on pigeons and their diseases.

The preface states the aim plainly. The guide serves beginners starting a poultry yard and old hands seeking the best recent practice. Piper compiled his matter from the best authorities of all ages, not from his own experience alone. He thanks Tegetmeier for knowledge of poultry diseases and Wright for his practical treatise. The book treats profit and exhibition together, for the Victorian keeper who wanted eggs, meat, and show prizes from one yard.
38649-early-days-in-north-queensland:
Early Days in North Queensland records the pioneering of Australia's far north. Edward Palmer wrote the account before his death. Angus and Robertson published it at Sydney in 1903. A signed portrait of Palmer fronts the book. A long poem to the north-west opens it. That poem is dated from Cloncurry in 1897.

The preface traces Palmer's own road. He reached Queensland two years before its separation. In 1864 he rode west from Bowen toward the Flinders River. He stayed with the outside settlement work until 1899. Many original explorers were known to him personally. Few of them remained alive, he notes. The book claims no literary style. It simply preserves names and incidents of the pastoral frontier.
38700-chambers-s-twentieth-century-dicti:
Part four of four in Chambers's Twentieth Century Dictionary covers the letters S to Z and the back matter. The Reverend Thomas Davidson edited the 1908 London and Edinburgh edition.

Davidson explains the plan plainly at the front. Words stand in letter order, with offshoots grouped under their roots. Odd plurals and verb forms are shown where they break the rule. A word left bare takes its sense from the word above it, plus the sense of its ending. Speech sounds are spelled out afresh after each word so any reader can say it. The part closes the set that aimed to give sound, sense, and word history in one cheap volume for home and school use.
38732-the-old-testament-in-the-light-of-:
Old Testament in the Light of the Historical Records of Assyria and Babylonia is a study. Theophilus Pinches wrote it for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. The third edition, revised with appendices and notes, came in nineteen o eight. A Hammurabi relief plate fronts the volume as its first pictured stone.

Hammurabi is generally taken as the Biblical Amraphel of Genesis, the plate notes. An Andrew Lang line on old writings and common humanity fronts the text. A Babylonian dragon hymn in translation opens the records quoted here. Ansar sends his messenger Gaga in the ancient creation combat song. Pinches reads Hebrew scripture beside the clay records of the two rivers.
38790-england:
England is a descriptive book by Frank Fox, issued at London in nineteen fourteen with thirty two full page pictures in colour. Fox is billed as author of works on the British Empire and on Australia. In his preface he says a full account of England in one volume is impossible. He aims instead at an impression of the land's most English features.

Origins of the English people come first in his plan. Fields, flowers, trees, homes, and schools then get far more space than cities or manufactures. Those things are more peculiar to the land, he argues. England stands apart, in his view, as a land of green trees and meadows, of noble schools and sweet homes. A front picture shows Saint Paul's from the Thames.
38841-the-commercial-restraints-of-irela:
John Hely Hutchinson, provost of Trinity College, wrote these letters on Irish trade, first printed at Dublin in 1779. Carroll re-edited the book with a life of the author, an introduction, notes and an index. A portrait from a painting by Reynolds stands at the front of the new edition.

Froude called the work the best account of the poisonous forces long working in Ireland, the title page quotes. Blackburne called it perhaps the best book ever written on Irish trade and its restrictions by England, in a second quote. Hutchinson argues in letters to a noble lord that England's laws crippled Irish commerce.
39064-hegel-s-philosophy-of-mind:
Hegel's Philosophy of Mind is a translation by William Wallace of the third part of Hegel's Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences. Wallace, a fellow of Merton College and professor of moral philosophy at Oxford, added five introductory essays. The Clarendon Press printed the book in 1894.

Wallace says the volume stands complete in itself, though it may also serve as a sequel to his version of Hegel's Logic. The contents divide mind into subjective, objective, and absolute. Subjective mind runs from anthropology through phenomenology to psychology. Objective mind covers law, the morality of conscience, and social ethics. Absolute mind ends with art, revealed religion, and philosophy. Wallace has reproduced only Hegel's own paragraphs, leaving out the editors' addenda drawn from lecture notes. The book is a standard English door into Hegel's system.
39120-salvation-syrup-or-light-on-darkes:
Salvation Syrup is a sharp print blow at the Salvation Army by the free thought writer Foote. Its full name adds Light on Darkest England, a jab at a famed Booth book. The tract came out in eighteen ninety one as a reply to General Booth. Foote grants the Army grew more prim in late years of that age. Its first years, he says, were coarse past what a ripe age would bear.

Street shows, rowdy meets, and dolt words drew his scorn in full. Odd rank names in its own sheet struck him as proof of folly. Hallelujah fish men and devil dodgers crowd his list of such names. He grants their acts ape the crude Methodist ways of old days. All night meets at Whitechapel get a close, sour look in the tract.
39159-sky-island-being-the-further-excit:
L Frank Baum wrote a children's fantasy copyrighted in 1912, drawn by John R Neill, as a sequel to The Sea Fairies. Baum tells readers that many liked Trot almost as well as Dorothy. Cap'n Bill, the old sailor, returns with her. Button Bright joins them, bringing his magic umbrella.

Baum says the story could never have been written without that umbrella. Polychrome, the Rainbow's Daughter, lives in the sky, so a meeting is natural. The book is the second in the Trot and Cap'n Bill series. Baum dedicated it to his sister Mary Louise Brewster. The tale takes its young heroes from the sea to an island in the sky.
39176-delusion-or-the-witch-of-new-engla:
Delusion, or the Witch of New England, is a tale by Eliza Buckminster Lee. Hilliard Gray of Boston issued the novel in eighteen forty. Lee states in her preface that scenes and persons are wholly made up. The tragic weight of the year sixteen ninety two is much softened here.

Lee aim was not a tale of witchcraft as such, she explains. She sought to show how events can unfold strength in a timid woman. Such a woman may choose death over yielding to a life saving lie. Lee notes that many of those truly accused of witchcraft were young. Firm hearts in that deluge of fear held a rare inner beauty.
39195-legends-of-gods-and-ghosts-hawaiia:
W D Westervelt gathered Legends of Gods and Ghosts from Hawaiian tales and Englished them for this book. George H Ellis printed it in Boston in nineteen hundred fifteen. Constable sold it in London the same year. Westervelt had written books on old Honolulu and on Maui.

A guide at the front tells how to sound the long names. No word part ends in a hard sound, it notes. The ghost of Wahaula Temple leads the set of tales. A shark god of Molokai and a shark man come next. Milu, king of ghosts, rules the world below in two tales. A poison god and a maid of the gold cloud add more. A word list at the back helps new readers.
39375-christmas-tree-land:
Molesworth wrote Christmas-Tree Land, published by Macmillan in London in 1884 with illustrations by Walter Crane. She was already known for Carrots and The Cuckoo Clock. The story follows two children, Rollo and Maia, who find their way into a strange country of fir woods. A white castle opens the tale, and a mysterious cottage follows.

Inside the cottage the children think they have found the house of the three bears. Fairy housekeeping, a squirrel family, and a committee of birds fill the middle chapters. The children hear the story of a king's daughter and sail through the air in a queer ship. An eagles' eyrie and a vision of Christmas trees close the adventure. Molesworth wrote gentle fantasy for the nursery, in which the marvels grow out of woods and winter. Crane's pictures, among them the white castle and the flying ship, made the book a gift-book favourite.
39621-the-jenolan-caves-an-excursion-in-:
The Jenolan Caves: An Excursion in Australian Wonderland, by Samuel Cook, was printed in London in 1889 by Eyre and Spottiswoode, with twenty-four plates and a map. A front plate shows the Coral Grotto. The account first ran in the Sydney Morning Herald, and Cook republishes it by the proprietors' leave, at the request of many correspondents. The caves were formerly called the Fish River caves.

Cook owns in his preface that neither tongue, nor pen, nor pictorial art can match the caves themselves. Their galleries are dressed with myriads of graceful and fantastic forms, purest white alternating with rich colour and delicate tints. Of all the caves in New South Wales, he says, Jenolan's are the most beautiful. Well-travelled men, he adds, call them unrivalled in any part of the world. Photographs carry the proof his words disclaim.
39651-switzerland:
Switzerland is a country book by Frank Fox, published by Black in London in 1914. It holds thirty two full page illustrations in colour for its subject. Sister volumes in the same series treat Austria Hungary, England, France, and Italy in its list. Fox is named as author of Ramparts of Empire and of a volume on Australia.

Contents open with The Spirit of the Mountains and the earliest Swiss of the lake dwellers. The Swiss in the Middle Ages and modern Switzerland follow in the chapters of the book. The Swiss People Today, alpine climbing, and the natural beauties of Switzerland come after in order. Fox writes the tour of a nation in the last summer of the old Europe, when the Alps were the playground of the continent and the hotels were full.
39728-in-far-bolivia-a-story-of-a-strang:
Gordon Stables, a naval doctor, wrote this adventure story of Bolivia, published by Blackie and Son in 1901 with pictures by J Finnemore. The contents promise forest adventure from the first page: chapters open on the banks of the great Amazon, move through Burnley Hall, and plunge into lost wanderers, fierce fights, and savage revels.

Later chapters bring a cannibal queen, a marvellous lake, La Paz, a fight at the fort, and the cry of Eastward Ho for Merrie England. The book opens with the roar of a great sawmill deep in the forest by the Amazon. Readers get a hearty boy's tale of a strange, wild land.
39732-budd-boyd-s-triumph-or-the-boy-fir:
William Pendleton Chipman wrote this boys' business tale, copyrighted in 1890 by Burt of New York. Chipman had earlier written 'Roy Gilbert's Search' and 'The Mill-Boy of the Genesee' for young readers. Budd Boyd seeks employment in chapter one, and a slight misunderstanding follows at once.

Against wind and tide, Budd finds a new friend and faces Benton's wrath in the contents. A new firm forms, business booms, and an ox-cart goes missing on Fox Island. Three intruders, a trial, entrapment and an escape keep the boy firm in peril before its triumph, promised by the title, arrives.
39866-terrestrial-and-celestial-globes-v:
Terrestrial and Celestial Globes, volume one, by Edward Luther Stevenson of the Hispanic Society of America, treats the history and making of globes. It weighs their value as aids in the study of the earth and the stars. Yale University Press published it at New Haven in 1921, for the Hispanic Society. A second volume completes the work.

Chapter one opens with globes in the ancient world. The first steps of star lore and earth lore come first. Early map making is seen in the Babylonian plan of the world. Anaximander was probably the first true map maker. A note at the front explains the stand-ins used for marks the plain text cannot carry: lines over letters, tildes, and raised figures. Spellings in joined, hyphenated, and spaced forms were left as printed, to stay true to the original.
39867-terrestrial-and-celestial-globes-v:
Terrestrial and Celestial Globes, volume two, by Edward Luther Stevenson, traces globe making. Yale University Press issued it in 1921 for the Hispanic Society of America. Stevenson belonged to that society; his first volume covers the earlier centuries. Chapter ten opens with Dutch masters taking the lead in globe craft.

At the close of the sixteenth century the craft shifted to northwest Europe. The Van Langrens lead, then Jodocus Hondius and his son Henricus in turn. Willem Jansz Blaeu and his sons John and Cornelius follow as great makers. Plancius globes, Habrecht spheres, and Greuter work reproduced by Rossi fill the chapter. Value of globes for geography and astronomy study frames the whole.
40554-journal-of-a-horticultural-tour-th:
James Forbes kept a journal of a plant tour through Germany, Belgium, and part of France in the autumn of 1835. The book was printed in London in 1837. A list of cactus kinds grown at Woburn Abbey is added at the end.

In his preface Forbes says the Duke of Bedford sent him abroad for eight weeks. British plant men had rarely seen the great gardens of the mainland. Forbes went to view their stock, their glass houses, and their ways of growth. He thanks Otto of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Berlin in the front pages. Gardeners and plant fans get a close, dated tour record.
40555-no-man-s-island:
Herbert Strang wrote a boys' tale of war at home called No Man's Island, issued in London in 1921 with art by Brock. Strang's long list of tales at the front runs from air scouts and flying boats to Drake on the Spanish Main. A color front plate shows men saving what they can from a wreck.

Twenty five parts and an epilogue tell the tale. Odd part titles hint the plot: tin tacks, pin pricks, queer fish, watermarks, and a topmost room. A scrap of paper, a face in a thicket, and word received drive the hunt. Reprisals, a trapped band, a parley, and a levy en masse build to the squaring of accounts. The tone is brisk schoolboy war fare.
40620-hilda-s-mascot-a-tale-of-maryland-:
Hilda's Mascot, subtitled A Tale of Maryland, My Maryland, is a girls' novel by Mary Ireland. The Saalfield Publishing Company issued it in 1902, with halftones by Donald Gardner. Ireland dedicated the story to her young friend Mary Louise Graham, and called it a companion to her Timothy and His Friends.

The chapters open with an ebony box, then introduce Hilda's Aunt Ashley and a place called My Lady's Manor, with its mystery. Hilda proves a literal follower of Bunyan, visits a gypsy encampment, and receives an offer of marriage. Letters bring her a trial, and Archie finds a package before the homecoming of the last chapter. The first scene is set many years before: a man walks a Baltimore street at evening, leading a girl and a boy toward an orphan asylum. Grief sits in his fine eyes, and his right hand grips a bulky package.
40970-exploiter-s-end:
Exploiter's End is a short tale of work on a far world. James Causey wrote it for a pulp book of the year 1953. Its work force is a race of great bugs with four arms each. Men time the bugs at their tasks with a stop watch in hand.

The bugs fit studs and screws at a wild pace on the line. Their feelers glow with the strain of the pace set for them. One bug's rate falls as the watch hand runs past his mark. Great hulls rise in blue smoke as the bugs swarm the frames. The side note at the head gives the theme of the tale in one line. Folk or bugs, there is a mark past which none can be driven.
41015-shaun-o-day-of-ireland:
Madeline Brandeis wrote Shaun O'Day of Ireland, for Grosset and Dunlap in 1929. Flanagan held the rights, and Grosset printed by arrangement with them. Photographs made in Ireland by Brandeis herself fill the book. She produced motion pictures of child life in many lands, the title notes. Her dedication runs to every child of every land.

Little sister, little brother, may you learn to love each other, it says. The contents fall in two parts of five chapters each. Isn't it a great wonder, and Shauneen and the leprechaun, open the tale. Come away, the strange land, and the frightened giant follow. John, the girl fairy, and over the green land fill part two. Kit Wain, a real Irish boy, posed for Shaun in the photographs. He played on stage and screen, and on the piano too, she adds.
41058-the-wizard-of-west-penwith-a-tale-:
William Bentinck Forfar wrote The Wizard of West Penwith, a tale of the Land's End printed at Penzance in 1871. Forfar had earlier written Pentowan, Pengersick Castle, and Kynance Cove, all Cornish tales. His preface says he always tried to show the Cornish character in its native wit and humor.

Most of his scenes, he claims, rest on incidents that really happened near the Land's End, with names changed. A horse's fall over the cliff is still remembered, and guides point out the hoof marks in the grass. The wizard, or conjuror, was a notorious character at St. Just some fifty years before. A horrid murder and a case of mistaken identity are also, Forfar says, true facts. The tale mixes local legend, crime, and west-country talk.
41102-the-king-s-threshold-and-on-baile-:
Two plays by W B Yeats, published at London in 1904. A H Bullen issued the volume. It forms volume three of Plays for an Irish Theatre. Both plays were written for Fay's Irish National Theatre. The King's Threshold played in Dublin in October 1903. On Baile's Strand was set for the following spring. Old Irish prose romances supplied both stories.

The first play centres on Seanchan, chief poet of Ireland. King Guaire heads its cast list. Princesses, cripples, a mayor, and the poet's pupils surround them. A comic prologue survives in print here. The small company could not spare a speaker for it on stage. Yeats borrowed arrangement ideas from Edwin Ellis's Sancan the Bard. The plays mark the Abbey movement's heroic early phase.
41110-arabian-society-in-the-middle-ages:
Edward William Lane turned the Thousand and One Nights into English and filled the margins with notes on the life shown in the tales. His grandnephew gathered the chief notes into one volume, and Chatto and Windus published it in 1883.

Lane was not content with a bare rendering. The manners and ideas of the tales called for a commentary. He set essays at the end of each chapter. Scholars of the East have long held them the most complete picture in existence of Arabian society. Scattered through three large volumes, they were hard to consult. The editor has cut the notes that live only by the tales, and set the rest in a natural order by subject.
41153-the-spell-of-switzerland:
Nathan Haskell Dole's The Spell of Switzerland was published at Boston in 1913 by Page and Company, first impression October of that year. Photographs and original paintings by Woldemar Ritter illustrate it. The book belongs to the publisher's Spell series, boxed volumes at two dollars fifty, net, beside companion spells of Italy, France, England, and Holland.

The series box at the front lists the set and names Dole for Switzerland. Inside, a colour plate, Evening near Saas-Fee, stands before the title page, and the list of illustrations begins with a map of Switzerland and a view in the Engadine Valley. Dole had ground to cover: the travel spell books promised a country rendered through its scenery, its towns, and its people, in text and picture together.
41166-trails-and-tramps-in-alaska-and-ne:
William Thomas wrote of trails and tramps in Alaska and Newfoundland, printed at New York and London in 1913 with one hundred forty seven photographs. Thomas had written Hunting Big Game with Gun and Kodak. He gives the book to his wife, who shared none of the pleasures of the trail and bore all the anxieties for his return. A mother possum and her family front the volume.

Cruising and hunting in southeastern Alaska opens the road. Kodiak Island, big game on the Kenai Peninsula, and a trip to Newfoundland follow. Hunting with a ferret, a night hunt, and in the springtime fill the middle. A plea for protection closes the tale. Ketchikan, myriads of salmon, Metlakatla and Father Duncan's church stand in the pictures. The mate's loud clear voice rings over the pier bustle in the evening twilight as the tale starts.
41623-the-spell-of-scotland:
The Spell of Scotland is a travel book by Keith Clark, in the Spell series of illustrated volumes. Each volume of the series came boxed, with coloured plates and many illustrations, at two dollars and a half. Clark's sisters in the series include the Spell of Belgium, Japan, France, and Egypt by other hands. The books promised a country through its charm.

Clark's own subject needs no selling. His Scotland is the land of glen and castle, of Edinburgh stone and Highland water. The Spell books were gift books for the armchair traveller, written in a warm, pictorial manner and dressed by their publishers to match. This volume stands in that row as the Scottish panel: a tour in prose and pictures meant to cast, and to prove, the spell of the north.
41723-the-duck-footed-hound:
The Duck-Footed Hound is Jim Kjelgaard's story of coon hunting for young readers, illustrated by Marc Simont. Thomas Y Crowell Company of New York published it, copyrighted in 1960 by Eddy Kjelgaard. The Creeping Hills hold one coon no one has ever caught.

Old Joe is the biggest, fightingest, craftiest coon in the hills, denning in a hollow sycamore by a slough. Precious Sue, a bluetick hound peerless at tracking coons, has never caught him. But Sue has a pup, Duckfoot, whose webbed paws make him skillful in water and whose nose beats every other hound hollow. The boy Harky feels this autumn will be different. His own troubles are school, where Miss Cathby calls Old Joe a raccoon and says he is mortal, and Melinda, the bossiest young lady for miles, who wants to hunt.
41785-archaic-england:
Archaic England, an essay in reading prehistory by Harold Bayley, was published by Chapman and Hall of London in 1919. Bayley also wrote The Lost Language of Symbolism. His tools, named in the subtitle, are megalithic monuments, earthworks, customs, coins, place names, and faerie superstitions. A quote at the front speaks of folk memory surviving in tiny fragments of proof.

Chapters treat the magic of words, a tale of Troy, and the name Albion. Gog and Magog, Puck, and Oberon get long studies. The scouring of the White Horse and a set of English Edens follow. Bayley holds that of the thousands of earthworks in England, few are truly known, and each hides a new problem in history. Five short appendices close the book, on Ireland, Glastonbury, and the Druids among them.
41803-joan-of-the-sword-hand:
S R Crockett wrote Joan of the Sword Hand, a romance. Ward, Lock and Company issued it at London in 1900. Frank Richards drew the plates for this edition. Crockett's many books line the front pages. The Stickit Minister and The Raiders stand there. The Red Axe and The Black Douglas join them.

The Hall of the Guard opens the tale. The Baiting of the Sparhawk follows it fast. Joan Draws First Blood heads the third chapter. The Cozening of the Ambassador comes at four. Johann the Secretary enters at chapter five. A princess called Impetuosity appears at seven. The Rose Garden and Prince Wasp fill the middle. Joan Forswears the Sword at chapter twelve. At the High Altar stands the fourteenth. The Chief Captain's Treachery darkens the late tale. A sword girl at a German court gave readers a fresh Joan to cheer.
41830-the-spell-of-flanders-an-outline-o:
The Spell of Flanders is a travel and tale book of the low land by the north sea, by Vose. It stands in a set of spell books of lands. Each book in that set has plates in colour. Each has a wealth of prints as well. Its kin in that set are told of at its front.

Those kin take Italy, France, and the south shores of America. England stands in the set as well. Each book is bound in a rich cover with gilt top, in a box. A set price is told on the page. This part weds the past of the land to its lore tales: its old towns, its belfries, and its paint men.
42030-the-rocky-mountain-wonderland:
The Rocky Mountain Wonderland, published in 1915, is Enos Mills's book of essays on the high Colorado country. Mills dedicated it to George Horace Lorimer. Photographs, most of them his own, fill the volume. The first essay guides seven football players, hiding their names, up Long's Peak.

Chapters take up wild mountain sheep, the forest frontier and the chinook wind. Mills writes of snow-slides, glacier lakes, a mountain pony and the grizzly bear. Beavers in drought and chipmunks at his door get tender pages. The book closes with the Rocky Mountain National Park and a plea for the conservation of scenery, written the year the park was new.
42085-a-bachelor-husband:
Ruby Ayres wrote A Bachelor Husband, a novel issued in New York in 1920 with a front plate by Paul Stahr. The tale opens on Marie Chester, a girl who has adored Christopher Lawless from the day he came to her house as a big schoolboy. She waited on him hand and foot and took his bullying as proof of his worth.

The two are not kin by blood. Their fathers were lifelong friends, and when Christopher was orphaned, George Chester took him in as a son. An aunt who kept the house warned that the boy would spoil the shy girl. In a fortnight Marie was climbing trees and riding bareback at his word, a tomboy made by love and daring.
42093-morag-a-tale-of-the-highlands-of-s:
Morag is a tale of the Highlands of Scotland, published in New York by Robert Carter and Brothers in 1875. The story is set in a glen and its village, among cottars and kirk folk. Chapter titles map its world from the first morning in the glen onward.

Morag's home, the fir wood, and a discovery carry the early chapters. Kirsty Macpherson enters as a leading figure, and Morag's visit to her is told at length. The gypsies arrive at last, a stock excitement of Highland tales. Vanity Fair, the kirk in the village, and the loch follow in turn. The book belongs to the evangelical Scots fiction sold widely in America. Its Highland scenery frames lessons of faith, humility, and village duty for young readers of the seventies.
42147-louise-chandler-moulton-poet-and-f:
Lilian Whiting wrote the life of Louise Chandler Moulton, poet and friend. The book came out in Boston in September 1910. A front plate shows Moulton at age twenty in old photo form. Her girl home, Elmwood Cottage at Pomfret, shows in a plate. Parts run by year blocks from 1835 to her last days.

Girl years in Pomfret and first verse fill the front parts. Boston rooms, famed friends, and books crowd her mid life. Her watch bears a carve from her mother's own hand. Whiting tells the life through notes, notes, and tales of friends. Verse fans get a loved name's full, warm road. The tone stays fond and grave.
42150-with-sully-into-the-sioux-land:
With Sully into the Sioux Land is a frontier history by Joseph Mills Hanson. McClurg of Chicago published it in November of the year 1910. John Norton drew the illustrations for the Among the Sioux Series. Hanson also wrote The Conquest of the Missouri and Frontier Ballads. He dedicates it to his father, who lived the old Dakota frontier.

That father, as boy and young man, lived more adventures than a volume holds. Contents open with The Scourge of the Border and a flight through darkness. Besieged in Fort Ridgely and refugees fill the early chapter list. Hope deferred and later campaigns against the Sioux fill the rest. General Sully's expeditions after the 1862 outbreak anchor the history here.
42210-bancroft-s-tourist-s-guide-yosemit:
Bancroft Tourist Guide to Yosemite, San Francisco and Around the Bay was issued at San Francisco in 1871. Bancroft and Company published the guide for travellers in California. The full title covers the valley, the city, and the bay shore to the south. A steam printing and engraving house of the firm made the book.

California tourism was young when rail links first brought crowds west in number. A guide of this kind told visitors routes, sights, and lodgings for the trip. Yosemite drew wonder seekers, while San Francisco served as the base and port. Towns around the south bay filled out the circuit for a tour. The volume now reads as a record of how the West was first sold to tourists.
42278-toy-making-at-home-how-to-make-a-h:
Morley Adams's Toy-Making at Home, how to make a hundred toys from odds and ends, was published in New York by Frederick Stokes, and printed in Great Britain. Adams writes to boys and girls. His opening claim is that every household throws away the makings of toys, without seeing what they could become.

Cotton-reels head his list: strongly made, and fit for furniture and playthings once the cotton is wound off. Match boxes, broken clothes pegs, cocoa tins, egg shells, cigar boxes, nut shells, and corks follow, with old broom handles besides. The toys given are samples, meant to set a patient maker devising more. The first lesson is the paper windmill the rag-and-bone man gives for an old bottle. It takes a six-inch square of stiff paper and two small cards, cut down the diagonals nearly to the centre.
4245-a-history-of-the-early-part-of-the-:
Charles James Fox, the eighteenth-century statesman, began this history late in life. He left it unfinished at his death in 1806, and it first appeared in 1808. The narrative opens with the reign of Charles II. It carries the story into the early years of James II. It breaks off at the execution of Monmouth.

Fox worked from papers he had gathered in Paris after the Peace of Amiens. The book reads as a statesman's view of a monarchy sliding toward crisis. An introductory section traces the Fox family itself. It runs from a royalist grandfather under Charles I to the author's own birth in 1749.
42486-the-two-magics-the-turn-of-the-scr:
Henry James bound two tales together in a volume Macmillan published in 1898. One is a play called Covering End. The other, far longer, is the ghost tale that opens the book. A company sits round the fire in an old house on Christmas Eve.

Some one remarks that this was the one case he has met where a visitation fell on a child. A child, he says, gives the effect another turn of the screw. Two nights later Douglas brings out what is in his mind. If one child gives one turn, what do two children give? They give two turns, cries the company, and call for the tale. Nobody but Douglas has ever heard it, and it is, he says, quite too horrible.
42571-travels-in-south-kensington-with-n:
Travels in South Kensington, with notes on decorative art and architecture in England, by Moncure Daniel Conway, was published in London in 1882 by Trubner. Conway also wrote The Sacred Anthology, The Wandering Jew, and a life of Carlyle. Three essays make the book: the South Kensington Museum, decorative art and architecture in England, and Bedford Park.

A front plate shows Foley's statue of the Prince Consort. The picture list reads like a tour of the museum courts. Casts of the Vatican biga and Pisano's pulpit from Pisa cathedral appear. Chinese potters at work, Italian majolica, an Arabian mosque lamp, and Sevres porcelain follow. Conway walks the reader through the great teaching museum of Victorian design, then out to the new garden suburb of Bedford Park.
42583-a-history-of-banks-for-savings-in-:
A History of Banks for Savings in Great Britain and Ireland is a work by William Lewins. Sampson Low published it in London. Lewins had earlier written a book on Her Majesty's mails. The volume is dedicated, by permission, to William Ewart Gladstone.

Its full title promises more than the rise of savings banks alone. Lewins gives a full account of Gladstone's financial measures for the people. Post office banks stand first among those measures in his account. Government annuities and government life insurance follow in the same plan. In his preface he calls the book a gift to the history of provident schemes. Such schemes, he notes, had worked quietly for years without a chronicler. They touched the lives of great masses of the people, he argues. An earlier treatise on the subject served actuaries, not general readers.
42585-the-ballads-songs-of-derbyshire-wi:
The Ballads and Songs of Derbyshire, edited by Llewellynn Jewitt, was printed in 1867 at London and Derby. Jewitt gives the book to the Duke of Devonshire, lord-lieutenant of the county. The volume adds notes to the songs and gives samples of the old tunes.

In his intro Jewitt finds it strange that no one had gathered these songs before. Derbyshire, he says, is rich in ballads and folk song beyond dispute. Yet its ballads, traditions, and lyrics had lain uncollected and, he fears, uncared for. His book claims to be the first such gathering for the county. Singing Sam of Derbyshire serves as a frontispiece. The songs keep the speech, trades, and tales of the shire alive on the page.
42874-in-the-grip-of-the-mullah-a-tale-o:
Captain Brereton wrote a tale of adventure in Somaliland, printed at New York in 1903 with pictures by Charles Sheldon. Brereton had written One of the Fighting Scouts, The Dragon of Pekin, and With Rifle and Bayonet. The leading man fell to the deck, the frontispiece shows. The castaway opens the tale, then off to Aden and the gun runners.

In disguise, a desperate encounter, and on African shores lead to the mad Mullah himself. Preparing to advance, against heavy odds, and fighting the tribesmen fill the middle. A march into the desert, the white prisoner, and hemmed in by the enemy raise the stakes. A clever ruse, the last daring attempt, a dash for liberty, and in the gold mine close the road back to the coast. Boys of the empire age get desert war at full gallop.
43237-the-spirit-land:
The Spirit Land, by S B Emmons, came out at Philadelphia from John E Potter and Company. The work was entered for copyright in 1857. A note to the reader calls the book a cure for a sort of error ripe in each age of the church.

Emmons says men have run mad in an age of isms, chasing ghosts. They claim words from heaven that are no more than dreams of their own minds. Such craze leads some, he warns, to dire crimes and self death. He bids readers cling to the Bible of their fathers as the sole safe guide. His pages draw on books on witchcraft, false prophets, and spirit knockings. Scores of works feed the whole. Church readers get a stern brief against the spirit craze of the day.
4333-studies-from-court-and-cloister-bei:
J. M. Stone gathered these historical and literary essays under the title Studies from Court and Cloister. The first part treats Margaret Tudor, a notable Englishman, the Catholic Reformation in Germany, Jesuits at court, Giordano Bruno in England, and Charles I and the Popish Plot. The second part turns to runic crosses, a missing page of the Idylls of the King, and Foxe's Book of Errors.

Later essays cover the spoils of the monasteries, the royal library, and the Harleian manuscripts. Stone writes as a Catholic historian with an eye for archives and for the human detail inside great events. The book appeals to readers of Tudor and Stuart history, and of the history of books.
4356-sky-island-being-the-further-exciti:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Oz-related fantasy as a sequel to The Sea Fairies. It follows Trot and Cap'n Bill to an island in the sky. A magic umbrella lifts them to a strange place divided between the Blues and the Pinks. The place holds a Boolooroo, six snub-nosed princesses, and a blue city.

A pink country ruled by Queen Mayre completes the map. Later chapters bring Button-Bright and the blue wolf. They bring the sunrise and sunset tribes, Rosalie the witch, and a war of Pinks and Blues. Baum's invention is cheerful and crowded, with new creatures on every page. Young readers who know Oz will enjoy this separate adventure.
43584-the-mystery-of-the-secret-band:
Edith Lavell wrote a mystery for girls in the Mary Lou set of tales. The Saalfield Publishing Company issued it from Akron and New York. Rights are marked with the Roman year MCMXXXV on the title page. A plate shows Max crying out to Mary Lou in alarm.

Eighteen chapters run from A Real Detective to two captures at the close. A book club, a midnight guest, fresh thefts, and a lone house stir the plot. Detective Gay arrives mid-tale, and Christmas morning brings a turn. Young readers of the time got brisk sleuth work with a bright girl lead.
43667-extracts-relating-to-mediaeval-mar:
Extracts Relating to Mediaeval Markets and Fairs in England is a school source book. Helen Douglas Irvine chose the cuts for a set led by Vickers. A Macdonald house of London brought it out in nineteen twelve. That set aims to put first hand past in the hands of class kids. Low price is its key, since past class work needs cheap true texts.

Heads run from Saxon marts through the Conquest change and new grants. Mart plots, Smithfield in Henry Second days, and odd rights fill ranks. Dust foot courts, gains, first take rights, and mart homes stand mid heads. Sale watch, far trade men, and fair rot close the head scheme. Worcester mart rights from a bishop plea text open the cuts shown.
43934-harbor-jim-of-newfoundland:
Harbor Jim of Newfoundland is a religious story book by Bartlett, a minister, published by the Revell company in 1922. Bartlett dedicates it to the Newfoundlanders who gather harvests from the sea for the world's hungry. The chapters follow a fisherman called Harbor Jim through his conversion, his engagement, his miracles and his Christmas.

The opening is a St John's morning of fog. The narrator watches Bob McCartney spreading cod on the flakes and coaxing monosyllables out of him. Bob, a Newfoundlander who left the gift of blarney in Ireland with his ancestors, finally speaks a whole sentence: the fog will lift, for there goes Harbor Jim. Through the mist a little boat appears, Jim standing at the bow as erect as the mast, looking straight out to sea. The sketch sets the book's method: doctrine carried by harbour talk and the daily work of the fishery.
44019-a-course-of-mechanical-magnetical-:
Course of Experiments is a syllabus of lectures in natural philosophy. Francis Hauksbee performed the experiments for paying audiences in London. William Whiston read the explanatory lectures that went with the shows. The course spans mechanical, magnetical, optical, and hydrostatical trials in turn. Pneumatical experiments with air complete the promised range of wonders.

Day one demonstrates Newton's three laws of motion by experiments in view. The velocity of falling bodies and their lines of descent come next. An instrument to measure the force of falling bodies stands described there. Sliding, rolling, and falling of bodies fill the first day's work. Day two turns to the balance and steelyard and their uses.
44066-wanderings-in-ireland:
Michael Myers Shoemaker wrote a travel book on Ireland with seventy two illustrations, issued by Putnam's in New York and London. Shoemaker had written on the islands of the southern seas and on France. A frontispiece reproduces The Harp of Erin, a painting by T Buchanan Read in the author's possession. The volume is a large octavo with gilt top.

Shoemaker's other travel books are listed at the front: quaint corners of ancient empires, the great Siberian railway, and the heart of the Orient. Winged Wheels in France shows his motoring interests. The Irish volume follows the same model of literate wandering. Such books sold scenery, history, and anecdote to American readers planning or imagining travel.
44073-the-aquarian-gospel-of-jesus-the-c:
The Aquarian Gospel of Jesus the Christ was put out in 1911 by Levi, with an opening by Eva S Dowling. Levi claims the text was transcribed from the book of God remembrances, known as the Akashic Records. A map of Palestine from the exploration fund surveys stands at the front.

The full claim is that this is the gospel of the Aquarian Age, the age now dawning, for the Church Universal. Sections treat the birth and early life of Mary, the mother of Jesus, and the birth of John the Harbinger and of Jesus. Later sections treat the schooling of Mary and Elizabeth in Zoan, and the childhood schooling of John and of Jesus. The book fills the silent years of the Bible tale with travels and teaching. Curious readers get an occult gospel in full.
44121-history-of-scotland:
History of Scotland is a school past by Margaret Macarthur, led by Freeman. A Holt house of New York brought out this state side form in eighteen seventy four. It stands in Freeman school course for past study in that age. Gael years open the eight part scheme of the book in rank. A year list pins invasions, fights, and king deaths by their dates.

Agricola's invasion of the year 80 heads that date list. Union of Picts and Scots in eight forty three stands mid list. English years run from ten ninety seven to twelve eighty six in scheme. Fight for free rule runs to Bannockburn in thirteen fourteen next. James kings, faith change, and crown join fill the late scheme parts.
44129-fair-haven-and-foul-strand:
Fair Haven and Foul Strand, by August Strindberg, was issued in New York by McBride, Nast and Company in nineteen fourteen, as the date MCMXIV shows. The book holds the title tale plus The Doctor First Story and The Doctor Second Story. A fourth piece is called Herr Bengt Wife. All are tales of life, love, and strain.

The title tale starts with a quarantine doctor of sixty five years. He is short, slim, and brisk, with a soldier air from his time in the Army Medical Corps. His stern home as a boy made him wary of all folk. He trusts few and keeps his guard up at all times. Strindberg traces how such a youth shapes a hard, lone manhood.
44167-the-royal-observatory-greenwich-a-:
The Royal Observatory Greenwich is a glance at the history and work of the great observatory by Walter Maunder, printed at London in 1900. Portraits and pictures from old prints and new photographs fill the book. A portrait of Flamsteed, the first Astronomer Royal, stands at the front, and the contents run to thirteen chapters.

Maunder begins with Flamsteed and Halley, then turns to Airy and the buildings themselves. The later chapters walk through the departments one by one: time, transit, magnetic and weather work, the sun, and the stars. For its first century, he notes, the place was so small that the Astronomer Royal and one helper did all the work.
44278-from-the-earth-to-the-moon-direct-:
From the Earth to the Moon, by Jules Verne, is a tale of a moon shot. Scribner Armstrong of New York issued the English version in eighteen seventy four. Louis Mercier and Eleanor King rendered the French book into English. Eighty full page pictures fill the volume for its readers.

Contents join From the Earth to the Moon with a Trip Round It. Early chapters set the Gun Club and President Barbicane bold plan out. The romance of the moon, the hymn of the cannon ball, and powder questions follow. Florida and Texas fight for the launch site in the tale. Stones Hill, the casting feast, and the great Columbiad gun come next.
44382-old-country-inns-of-england:
Old Country Inns of England, by Henry P Maskell and Edward W Gregory, came out at Boston in 1911, with pictures by the authors. A front plate shows the Chequers at Loose. Long lists name inns in shot after shot, from the Bull at Sudbury to the Falstaff at Canterbury.

Nineteen chapters trace the inn from its roots. First come inns of lords, monks, and rest houses for the poor. Then come town inns, guild inns, and church inns. Coach inns and wayside alehouses follow, with signs, sports, and ghosts. Last parts treat inn build, goods, and the innkeeper, and urge reform of the public house. Travel fans get a warm past of rest, ale, and road in old England.
44397-haunted-places-in-england:
Haunted Places in England is a set of ghost tales by Elliot O'Donnell. Sands and Company published it in London in the year 1919. O'Donnell bills himself as a ghost hunter of twenty years. Past books by him treat haunted houses of England and Wales. Chapters bear short, stark titles: The Chair, The Head, The Cupboard.

Later chapters cover the Syderstone hauntings and a green vapour case. Stepping stones, pines, a cough, and a trunk fill out the list. The first case turns on a haunted house in Red Lion Square. O'Donnell denies that he is much of a psychometrist in that tale. Still, he says, strange things are shown him through objects at times.
44805-a-little-tour-in-ireland:
Little Tour in Ireland is a travel book by S Reynolds Hole, dean of Rochester. John Leech drew its pictures. The hosted copy is a new edition dated eighteen ninety two. It is dedicated to the memory of Leech. He was a true artist, a true friend, and a true gentleman, the dedication says. The book, which he made a success, is offered to his memory.

In his preface Hole says he was often asked to republish the tour. He wrote it as an Oxonian many years before, at Leech's request, he explains. Only one edition had been issued, and it was long exhausted. The scenes Leech drew and he described show little change, he says. Friends insist that gaiety becomes an undergraduate as much as gaiters a dean, he jokes.
44822-ask-mamma-or-the-richest-commoner-:
Ask Mamma, or The Richest Commoner in England, is a comic sporting novel by Surtees. John Leech drew the pictures for it. The long chapter list runs to hunts, meets, and country-house scenes. Titles promise cub-hunting, a hunt breakfast, and the opening day of the season.

The publisher's own preface, quoted in the front matter, disarms the reader at once. The story, it says, has no complication of plot to unravel. It is a plain running tale of everyday life, heightened for comic effect. Sporting scenes carry much of the book's energy throughout. Leech's drawings match the text as a second comic voice. Readers of Surtees will know the world on offer here. Foxes, horses, hunting men, and match-making fill its pages. The title hints at the marriage game played alongside the sport.
44860-the-comic-history-of-england:
The Comic History of England is a humorous history by Gilbert Abbott A'Beckett, with reproductions of the two hundred engravings by John Leech. Routledge printed this edition at London. In his preface A'Beckett states his object: to blend amusement with instruction, by serving up the facts of English history in as palatable a shape as he could.

He pledges himself not to sacrifice the substance to the seasoning. Though he has been a little free with his sauce, he hopes he has not produced a mere hash. The book is meant to take its place as a standing dish at the library table, light but not devoid of nutriment. Some readers who see history as a pageant may think it a desecration to present it in homely shape. A'Beckett answers that truth has rather gained than lost by the treatment.
45041-mental-philosophy-including-the-in:
Mental Philosophy is a college textbook by Joseph Haven, here in an improved edition from Sheldon and Company of New York in 1881. Haven had taught philosophy at Amherst College and theology in Chicago. The title names his three fields: the intellect, the sensibilities, and the will.

Haven first defines mental science and argues its importance. He then divides the mental powers and traces how others divided them. Consciousness, attention, and conception open the study of the intellect. Perception by the senses follows, with the organs and their trustworthiness examined. Memory and imagination come under the representative power. The book's plan promises the same care for feeling and will. Such texts trained American students to map the mind as a set of faculties. Haven's clear order kept his book in classrooms for decades.
4508-south-wind:
Norman Douglas published South Wind in 1917, opening with a bishop travelling by sea and feeling wretchedly sick. The bishop, who serves in equatorial Africa, hates inefficiency and ill health, and he prides himself on getting through any task in a businesslike way. His arrival on an island resort throws him among a mixed company of exiles, artists, and talkers, far from his ordered African duties.

Douglas uses that clash for satire, letting long conversations test morals, religion, art, and English respectability. The island air loosens rules that seemed fixed at home, and the bishop must judge people he would rather dismiss. Readers get a witty, talkative novel of ideas, where character shows itself in argument, and where a holiday island becomes a stage for serious questions about how to live.
45097-letters-from-switzerland:
Letters from Switzerland is a travel book in letter form by Samuel Irenaeus Prime, printed in eighteen sixty. Sheldon published it in New York, with Gould and Lincoln in Boston. Prime had written travels in Europe and the East before this Swiss tour. Fourteen chapters of letters carry the reader from Basle to the high Alps.

Basle and the Rhine open the letters, with the old council and the Dance of Death. Constance brings the lake, the Kaufhaus, and the dungeon of John Huss. Zurich offers Zwingli's town, Lavater's grave, and a sunset from the garden. Mountain tops, lakes, and land slips follow as the tour climbs southward. Agassiz and the glaciers enter the later letters from the high valleys. Interlaken and the Jungfrau face the reader in the front picture plate.
45155-the-overall-boys-in-switzerland:
The Overall Boys in Switzerland is a children's travel book by Eulalie Osgood Grover. Rand McNally published it in 1916. Bertha Corbett Melcher illustrated this volume. Grover also wrote the Sunbonnet Babies books for young readers. She is called the mother of those series on the title page. The contents list seventeen short chapters of Swiss travel.
