Three Cheers for Europe opens the journey. On the River Rhine and The Bear City follow. Above the Clouds and On Mount Rigi climb the mountains.

Shopping in Lucerne and an evening on its lake come next. A birthday party and William Tell's story fill the middle. Exploring a glacier and a summer blizzard give Alpine adventure. A letter and a list of difficult words close the book. A map shows the places the boys visited in Switzerland. The book teaches geography through two small travellers.
45238-wyeth-s-oregon-or-a-short-history-:
Volume Twenty One of Early Western Travels, 1748 to 1846, holds Wyeth's Oregon and Townsend's Narrative, edited by Reuben Gold Thwaites and issued at Cleveland in 1905. Thwaites had edited the Jesuit Relations and the Lewis and Clark journals. The series reprints rare first hand travel books with notes.

Wyeth's part is a short history of a long journey in 1832. It was drawn from the notes and talk of John B Wyeth. John left Nathaniel J Wyeth four days past the Rocky ridge on July 28, 1832. He was the sole man of the party to return to New England. Townsend's tale of a Rocky Mountain trip in 1834 fills the rest. Notes and an index aid the reader.
4527-the-story-of-the-soil-from-the-basi:
Cyril G. Hopkins wrote The Story of the Soil to teach soil science through farm life, joining exact science with real work on the land. Rather than a dry textbook, the book follows farming practice through the year, showing how soil, crops, and feeding of the land fit together. Its full subtitle promises a story built from absolute science on one side and lived experience on the other.

Readers learn why fertility falls when land is cropped without return, and how careful management of plant food, rotation, and care can rebuild it. Hopkins speaks to farmers, students, and country readers who want reasons they can test in their own fields. The book pairs well with his Farm That Won't Wear Out, and it gives a clear, early twentieth-century account of why good soil is a farm's true capital.
45324-the-young-o-briens-being-an-accoun:
Margaret Westrup wrote this tale of an Irish family in London, printed by John Lane in 1906. Westrup wrote as the author of Elizabeth's Children and Helen Alliston, and the title page names her so. The O'Briens arrive on a rough night, packed in a hired omnibus with rain lashing the panes.

Molly sniffles in her corner while Denis keeps a superlatively cheerful voice. Nell laughs with a queer catch, and Sheila Pat sits stiff and silent, clutching a bag and a box till her arms ache. Mr O'Brien at last names what all are thinking: the year ahead and what it holds. The book follows the young O'Briens through their sojourn in the great city, by turns gay and sore.
45328-summer-days-in-shakespeare-land:
Summer Days in Shakespeare Land is a travel and biography book by Charles Harper, published by Chapman and Hall in London and James Pott in New York in 1913. Harper illustrated most of the book with his own pen. The subtitle promises the delights of Stratford-upon-Avon and the country round about.

The contents mix town history with the poet's life. Chapters trace John Shakespeare, glover and wool merchant, and the birth and early marriage of his son William. Anne Hathaway, the hasty marriage, and the wild young days follow. The death of Hamnet, Shakespeare's only son, is recorded. Harper's long title page also promises that certain fanatics are handsomely confuted along the way. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
45387-morality-without-god-a-lecture-del:
Morality Without God is a lecture by Mangasarian, printed in 1905. It was delivered before the Independent Religious Society at Orchestra Hall in Chicago on a Sunday morning. The pamphlet also holds a letter to Bishop Anderson of the Episcopal Church. The letter tells how the pamphlet came to be.

The churches of Chicago had arranged a run of meetings at Orchestra Hall to stir a revival of interest in church work at home and abroad. Mangasarian wrote to the bishop with an offer. Mangasarian would sit on the platform, introduce the guest, and give his own thoughts on the same subject. There would be no debate and no interruptions. In the letter he states his own side plainly in advance.
45567-on-old-world-highways-a-book-of-mo:
Thomas Murphy wrote this book of motor rambles in France and Germany, published at Boston in 1914, with color reproductions from paintings and dozens of photographs. It also records a pilgrimage from Land's End to John o' Groats in Britain.

Murphy had made his name with motoring books: British Highways and Byways from a Motor Car and In Unfamiliar England with a Motor Car, alongside Three Wonderlands of the American West. The frontispiece shows the mountain meadows of the Bavarian Tyrol. Writing from Red Oak, Iowa, in January 1914, he offers the old-world highways to American motorists on the eve of the war that would close them. Travelers get the grand tour remade for the automobile age.
45671-myth-land:
Myth-Land is a book on fabulous beasts by Edward Hulme, published in London by Sampson Low in 1886. A verse from Whittier stands at its head, on dragons and griffins of the twilight time. Hulme's preface tells the book's birth. Its core was two short papers read to a public school natural history society. The subject, he says, falls in two parts. One treats creatures of pure fancy that never lived. The other treats the strange beliefs that cling to real beasts.

This volume keeps to the first part, the impossible creatures. The unicorn leads the contents, in Bible, heraldry, and medieval legend. Its horn as a test for poison gets its tale. The rompo or man-eater, the manticora, and the lamia stand in the run. A wolf that causes dumbness is among the wonders. Hulme writes with a naturalist's care for the tales men told.
45712-a-leisurely-tour-in-england:
James John Hissey wrote a leisurely tour in England, printed at London and New York by Macmillan with thirty full page illustrations. Hissey had written The Charm of the Road, On the Box Seat, An English Holiday, and Over Fen and Wold. A drive through England, a tour in a phaeton, and across England in a dog cart stand in his long shelf of road books.

Hissey tours at a gentle pace, by horse and wheel, through towns and lanes the railways pass by. Inns, churches, old houses, and road folk fill his pages. The charm of the road was his life subject, and each book returns to it with fresh miles. English readers who loved the slow road before motors took it get their fill here. His tours now read as a record of a vanishing England.
45810-over-periscope-pond:
Esther Sayles Root and Marjorie Crocker wrote Over Periscope Pond. Houghton Mifflin Company issued it at Boston in 1918. Their letters run from October 1916 to January 1918. Two American girls in Paris wrote them home. Photos of the pair front the book. Number 6 Place Denfert-Rochereau stands pictured there.

A women's and a men's vestiaire stand in plates. Doctor and Mrs Shurtleff fill an office plate. Marjorie poses with a leopard skin in one. Esther and Marjorie ride a Ford truck in another. Rootie stands in a park at Saint-Germain. A cedar at Saint-Germain fills a late plate. The contents shown open at letter thirty here. Relief work in wartime Paris fills these bright letters, where two young Americans learned war through canteens, refugees, and a pond nicknamed for danger.
4586-danger-or-wounded-in-the-house-of-a:
T. S. Arthur published Danger, or Wounded in the House of a Friend, at Philadelphia in 1875, as a temperance novel about drinking that begins at home. His preface argues that bars and saloons are less the cause of intemperance than its effect, since the appetite is first formed in the home. It is easier, he says, to kill a weed an inch high than after it has set a hundred rootlets in the soil.

Arthur had already exposed the liquor traffic in Three Years in a Man-Trap, and here he follows the harm done inside families and friendships, where a host's glass can wound a guest. The book preaches plainly, and it aims to warn parents and hosts before ruin starts. Readers get an earnest nineteenth-century moral tale, useful for temperance history, and for seeing how reformers argued to ordinary households.
45862-through-arctic-lapland:
Cutcliffe Hyne wrote Through Arctic Lapland, a tale of hard travel in the far north. Adam and Charles Black issued the book in London in eighteen hundred ninety eight. Hyne gave the book to Mrs Alfred Harmsworth, a friend of the house. A map and many plates trace the long route he took.

His road runs from London to Vardo, then across the Varanger shore. Finner whale boats and their crews fill the first wild days. Canoes bear him to the Neiden and the Russian Lapps’ feast at Boris Gleb. Enare lake is crossed in a square sail craft of Viking build. Nomad Lapps, their deer herds, and their hoards take a full span. Old sorcery fades among them, Hyne notes with plain regret. Raft, swamp, and rapid tax the last marches to Kittila town. Bear tracks ringed in snow front the whole brave account.
45922-the-voyage-of-the-deutschland:
Paul König, captain of the submarine merchant ship Deutschland, tells her crossing in The Voyage of the Deutschland, turned into English by Vivien Ellis and published in London in 1917. König calls his ship the plain sign of a German will to beat the English blockade. The boat was built for trade, not war, and made her run to the United States.

Chapters follow the trial trip, the first days at sea, a U-boat trap, and a somersault in the North Sea. Then comes the Atlantic run, the stay at Baltimore, and the dash home past the blockade. The book ends with the welcome the crew met in Germany, told in full at the Bremen Town Hall.
45973-trackers-of-the-fog-pack-or-jack-r:
Trackers of the Fog Pack, or Jack Ralston Flying Blind, is a boys' aviation novel by Ambrose Newcomb, author of The Sky Detectives. The Goldsmith Publishing Company of New York issued it in 1931. Its thirty chapters open with Perk sighing for action and getting his wish. Echoes of the past, a special delivery letter, and the cat out of the bag set the plot.

Laying plans and ready for anything lead to the winged messenger and a heading for trouble. Battling with the fog, the mystery airship, and a clever landing fill the middle. A silver-tip bear, circling buzzards, and the Tom Sawyer cavern raise the hazards. The end of Robbers' Roost concludes the chase. A passage preserved in the copy introduces the comic partner.
46058-two-tragedies-of-seneca-medea-and-:
Ella Isabel Harris rendered Two Tragedies of Seneca into English verse: Medea and The Daughters of Troy. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published the volume at Boston and New York in 1899. An introduction treats the sources of Senecan influence on English drama. The tendencies of that influence and direct borrowings follow. Harris states her purpose at the start.

English students care for Seneca because of his powerful influence on the rise of English drama, she writes. The translations were made to serve those students. Not all the tragedies under Seneca's name are by one hand, she owns. In France, Senecan influence was overmastering and tyrannical, she argues. In England the native spirit resisted more strongly. The English drama at its best stayed distinctively English, with Seneca formative rather than dominant.
4606-it-is-never-too-late-to-mend:
Charles Reade dedicated It Is Never Too Late to Mend to the president, fellows, and demies of St. Mary Magdalen College, Oxford. He signs as a grateful son of that ancient house. He calls the book an attempt at solid fiction. It opens with George Fielding, who cultivates a small farm in Berkshire. Farming, Reade says, is less enviable than it was, and a farmer must now be as sharp as his neighbours, or, like them, he will break.

Some soils and situations, Reade adds, break even the intelligent and sober, just as shops in a great street change names wave upon wave, however lively, severe, industrious, or lazy their keepers. From Fielding's farm grows a novel of crime, punishment, prison reform, and second chances. Readers get a vigorous Victorian reform novel, with a title that states its hope: it is never too late for a life to mend.
46078-the-senses-and-the-mind:
The Senses and the Mind is a book for family and general reading. The American Sunday School Union printed it in Philadelphia at 146 Chestnut Street, with the Religious Tract Society of London. A note explains the joint plan of the two houses.

The Union had arranged with the London society to print, at the same time, such of their valued works as best suited American circulation. The books would hold a distinct place on the Union catalogue. As they would be, in substance, reprints of the London edition, the credit of their general character belongs to the English brethren. The text opens on questions few thinking folk have not asked, whether the sun, the moon, the planets, and the stars are what they seem. Church readers get a plain study of sense, mind, and the heavens.
46132-the-wars-of-the-roses-or-stories-o:
The Wars of the Roses, by Edgar, retells the fight of York and Lancaster for young readers. Edgar wrote other books for boys, and this one is given to his godson. In his preface he calls the thirty years of war the richest stretch of old English tale.

Edgar holds the war was no mere clash of proud chiefs, but a fight against harsh rule. He blames the men around Henry the Sixth and Edward the Fourth for trampling old rights. The tale runs from the plucking of the roses in the Temple Gardens to the fall of Richard the Third. It ends with Henry Tudor crowned on Bosworth Field. A first part traces the Plantagenet line from its roots.
46151-india-under-british-rule-from-the-:
India Under British Rule is a history by James Talboys Wheeler, a former officer of the government of India. The subtitle promises the story from the founding of the East India Company. Wheeler had written a five volume history of India from the earliest ages. A page of his earlier works lists travels, records, and tales from Indian history.

Wheeler served as an assistant secretary in the foreign department at Delhi. He also served as secretary to the government of British Burma. His earlier books covered Madras in old times and the first English voyages to India. This work gathers his knowledge into one account of British power in the East. It treats the company years and the rule that followed. The book served readers who wanted the whole arc of the British in India in a single volume.
4623-the-son-of-my-friend:
T. S. Arthur published The Son of My Friend as the first of his New Temperance Tales, identifying himself as the author of Ten Nights in a Bar-Room. The tale opens in a household planning a party, after the couple have accepted many winter invitations and feel they should return social entertainment. The wife suggests hiring a professional caterer, who will supply the table and furnish waiters, leaving the hosts only to receive their guests.

From that easy, fashionable start grows a temperance story about drink at social gatherings, and about a young man, the son of a friend, whose path crosses the party world. Arthur writes to warn parents and hosts, in the plain moral style of his day, that hospitality can become a trap. Readers get a short, earnest tale about social drinking, friendship, and responsibility, useful for the history of temperance fiction.
46238-mazes-and-labyrinths-a-general-acc:
W H Matthews wrote Mazes and Labyrinths, a full account of these old forms, in a London book of 1922. Matthews starts by asking what counts as a maze and what counts as a twin path form. He notes that some fine old turf mazes in Britain had been lost or left to rot.

The book then walks through the great maze of Egypt as told by Herodotus and Strabo. Next comes Crete, with Theseus, the bull man, and the thread that led him out. Later parts trace church floors, garden mazes, and hedge mazes in great homes. Photos and plans fill the book. It gives fans of old places a clear guide to a strange and long-lived form.
46320-wulnoth-the-wanderer-a-story-of-ki:
H Escott Inman wrote Wulnoth the Wanderer, a story of King Alfred of England, issued by A C McClurg and Company in Chicago in nineteen oh eight. Troy and Margaret West Kinney made decorations and a front plate. A plate shows Princess Edgiva lifting her face to Wulnoth with eyes that speak unuttered words. Chapter heads all start with How or Of, in saga style.

Chapter one tells how Wyborga the Wise spoke with King Hardacnute. Chapter two tells how Wulnoth saved Edgiva from a bear. Later chapters bring Hungwar and Hubba, Wulnoth schooling, and strange wrestling in a place of desolation. Wulnoth comes to Danish sea kings, sails for East Anglia, and sees the slaying of Edmund, king of the East Saxons. Young readers get Viking peril, Saxon faith, and Alfred age in bright tale form.
4637-angel-island:
Inez Haynes Gillmore opens Angel Island the morning after a shipwreck, with five men lying where they slept, bruised, bloodless, and almost corpse-like in their stillness. A long time passes without speech or movement, until Frank Merrill breaks the silence in a level, metallic voice. He cannot forget the scream of the Norton child on seeing the great wave, nor the way the child's mother pressed the boy's head to her breast.

The men have reached an island inhabited by winged women, and their story turns on what shipwrecked men do when they meet beings freer than themselves. Gillmore uses the fantasy to probe power, love, and the treatment of women, with wit and feeling. Readers get an early feminist fantasy, strange and readable, about captivity, wings, and the price of trying to tame what was made to fly.
46399-the-story-of-mankind:
Hendrik van Loon wrote and drew The Story of Mankind, published in New York by Boni and Liveright in 1921. The title page boasts eight pages in three colors, more than a hundred pictures, and maps by the author. Printing followed printing, 20 of them inside a year.

The dedication is to Jimmie, and a line from Alice stands under it: what is the use of a book without pictures? The contents open with The Setting of the Stage, then Our Earliest Ancestors. The Egyptians invent the art of writing. Chapter by chapter the tale runs from the cave to the modern world, in a storyteller's voice. The book made van Loon famous. Parents and children got the whole human story in one fat, pictured volume.
46450-manual-of-the-trees-of-north-ameri:
Manual of the Trees of North America is a handbook of the trees of that continent north of Mexico, by Charles Sprague Sargent. Sargent was director of the Arnold Arboretum of Harvard and the author of The Silva of North America. This second edition came out in Boston and New York in 1922 from Houghton Mifflin Company. It holds 783 pictures from drawings by Charles Edward Faxon and Mary W. Gill.

A map at the front sets out the chief tree regions of the continent. The north eastern and north western regions stand first in its key, with the south eastern next. Tropical Florida, the Texas-Mexican boundary, and the Rocky Mountains stand in the key as well. Oregon and California and the New Mexico and Arizona border close the list. The work is a full field guide to the trees of a continent.
46536-the-gospel-an-exposition-of-its-fi:
Elder B H Roberts sets out first principles in The Gospel, an exposition issued by George Q Cannon and Sons of Salt Lake City in 1893 in a revised and enlarged edition. Roberts also wrote a life of John Taylor and Outlines of Ecclesiastical History. A line from Burns heads the book: religion is a simple business, concerning ignorant and learned alike.

The preface says the work was written to instruct the youth of Zion. Their parents examined the faith closely before joining, but the young, raised inside it, too often grow up ignorant of even its first principles. Clear teaching is the remedy.
46559-travels-in-the-central-parts-of-in:
Travels in the Central Parts of Indo-China records the journeys of Henri Mouhot, a French naturalist, in 1858, 1859, and 1860. Murray published the two volumes at London in 1864, after Mouhot's death. This is volume one. A frontispiece drawn from a photograph shows the king and queen of Siam.

Mouhot's brother presents the journal to the learned societies of England. He thanks them for backing a traveller France had neglected. Mouhot died in the flower of his age amid his finds, the letter says. His notes cover Siam, Cambodia, and Laos at first hand. He described ruined Khmer temples that Europe had barely heard of. The book made his name and carried his discoveries to the world.
46560-travels-in-the-central-parts-of-in:
Travels in the Central Parts of Indo-China is the next part of a two part set by Henri Mouhot, a French man of wild lore. It came out at London in eighteen sixty-four, past the mans death. The trips span the years past eighteen fifty-eight to eighteen sixty. Drawn plates from the mans own hand and a friends fill the book.

Parts of this book treat a great old town of ruins, with its wall and arch of triumph. Notes on that land and its ruins come next. A come back to the chief town, a fresh trip to the north east, and a chain of towns fill the mid parts. The last part gives the end of the day book and the death of the man on his road. Back parts list new kinds of beast and fish he found.
46592-center-rush-rowland:
Ralph Barbour wrote this school football tale of Center Rush Rowland. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in New York, copyright 1917. Caswell drew the plates, Ira blushing on his feet up front. Contents open with Rowland arrives and a chance acquaintance made.

Getting settled, a found roommate, and school begins fill early chapters. The enemy calls, a fight, and Ira declining an invitation follow. On the fourth squad, in the line up, and hard knocks come. Parkinson change of heart and a coach apology close the tale. Left End Edwards and Left Tackle Thayer stand as his past school tales listed.
46630-the-supernatural-in-the-new-testam:
The Supernatural in the New Testament, by the Reverend Charles A. Row, asks whether the miracles of the Gospels can be believed, and it was issued at London by Frederic Norgate in 1875. Row was a prebendary of St Paul’s and the author of kindred works on the Gospels. His subtitle states the aim, possible, credible, and historical. The book tests new attacks on Christianity as a divine revelation.

An opening chapter sets out the state of the controversy. A second chapter defines the terms in dispute. Row then asks what the supernatural elements in the New Testament consist of. He asks what view its own writers take of those elements. A chapter on miracles follows in the same close manner. The work is a Victorian defence of faith by argument, step by step.
46635-gospel-philosophy-showing-the-absu:
J H Ward, a Mormon elder, wrote a gospel philosophy printed at the Juvenile Instructor Office in Salt Lake City in 1884, with many engravings. Its title promises to show the absurdities of infidelity and the harmony of the gospel with science and history. The preface opens boldly: sectarians dread meeting a Mormon elder in discussion. Hundreds of such meetings, Ward says, ended in humiliating defeat for them.

Another class, though, brings stronger arguments: learned skeptics disgusted with so called Christianity. Ward addresses their research and intelligence with respect. The book belongs to the nineteenth century Mormon defense literature, answering infidel objections point by point for ordinary readers in Utah.
46757-fighting-the-boche-underground:
Captain Trounce's Fighting the Boche Underground was published in New York in October 1918 by Charles Scribner's Sons, with illustrations and diagrams. Trounce had served in the Royal Engineers and was by then a captain of engineers in the United States Army. His own portrait fronts the book.

Fourteen chapters cover the miners' war. To the front and underground lead into crater fighting and tunnelling in the Vimy Ridge trenches. Chalk caverns and trench mortars, the Somme show, the battle of the Ancre, and the two battles round Arras follow, ending at the Hindenburg line. A chapter on the psychology of fear and one on principles of mining close the text. The plates show breathing apparatus for gassy galleries, a mine exploding, and a German machine-gun post.
46853-le-morte-darthur-sir-thomas-malory:
Sir Thomas Malory's book of King Arthur and his noble knights of the Round Table, in the text of Caxton. Sir Edward Strachey edited it, with an introduction, for Macmillan in 1893. Strachey notes that his introduction was re-written with his daughter's help.

The introduction treats the authorship and matter of the book, its epic plan, Malory's use of the old romances, Camelot, Glastonbury, and the Sangreal. A second section traces the text through Caxton's edition of 1485 and Wynkyn de Worde. It ends with Southey and Sommer. An essay on chivalry follows, from the chevalier's education to the decay of the order. Strachey calls the book a poem in prose. Readers get the great Arthurian romance in its first printed English.
47122-agnes-strickland-s-queens-of-engla:
Agnes Strickland's Queens of England, Volume Two, is Rosalie Kaufman's abridgement of Strickland's famous lives, printed at Boston by Estes and Lauriat in 1882. The set runs to three volumes, fully illustrated. Kaufman prepared the abridgement for young readers. Her first care, the preface says, was to prepare a narrative which should interest young people. She endeavoured also to make it a source not only of pleasure but of profit.

The preface explains the method and its limits. Up to Queen Anne, the work is based upon Agnes Strickland's Queens of England. After that period many authorities have been consulted, and only such matter used as would seem appropriate. Politics could be introduced only when requisite for understanding the events that depended on them.
47123-agnes-strickland-s-queens-of-engla:
Rosalie Kaufman abridged Agnes Strickland's great Lives of the Queens of England for this three-volume edition, published by Estes and Lauriat at Boston in 1882. The set carries the story from the Conquest to the present day, and this third volume covers the Hanoverian court. Its illustrations tell the range: Sophia Dorothea of Zell, George the First, Caroline of Anspach, Sir Robert Walpole, George the Second, and Kensington Palace.

Later lives take in Queen Charlotte, George the Third, the Pitts, father and son, and Caroline of Brunswick. The editors own that some eminent names and events were sacrificed to the abridgment, but claim nothing needful to the story was left out. Strickland's queens were Victorian favorites, and this shortened set put them into many parlors.
47150-a-book-of-burlesque-sketches-of-en:
A Book of Burlesque, a study by William Davenport Adams, was published in London in 1891 in the Whitefriars Library of Wit and Humour. Portraits of F C Burnand, W S Gilbert, and G R Sims go with the text. The subject is English stage travestie and parody.

Adams says in his preface that he does not try to give a full history of the form. He offers an introduction, with sketches of the groups that stage burlesques fall into. Extracts show the methods of single writers at work. His stress falls on the literary side of burlesque, its wit and humour, more than on stage craft. Dates and casts fill out the record for readers.
47228-indian-myth-and-legend:
Donald Mackenzie wrote Indian Myth and Legend for the Gresham Publishing Company of London. It belongs to a series on myth and legend in literature and art, next to volumes on Egypt, Babylon, and the Celts. Warwick Goble painted the color pictures, and one shows Sita finding Rama among lotus blooms.

The chapters start with Indra, king of the gods, and the great Vedic deities. Yama, the first man and king of the dead, follows, with demons, giants, and fairies. Middle chapters treat the making of the world, the ages of the world, and the wandering of souls. Then come the new faiths: Vishnu religion, Buddhism, and Jainism. The book ends in the epic age, with the Pandavas and Kauravas, their gambling match, and their exiles. Readers get India's old stories in one clear survey.
47253-sport-in-vancouver-and-newfoundlan:
Sport in Vancouver and Newfoundland is a sporting travel book by Sir John Rogers. Chapman and Hall published it in London in 1912. Illustrations and maps by the author accompany photographs. The dedication names his wife as companion of many wanderings. The contents divide into two books of travel. Book one journeys to Vancouver Island and the Campbell River. The fish at the Campbell River get two chapters of sport. A chapter on fishing tackle interrupts the narrative practically.

To Alert Bay, the forest, and the wapiti country follow. After goat on the mainland closes the first book. Book two crosses to Newfoundland for its sport. Long Harbour, hunting grounds, and ponds mark that journey. Sport on Kepskaig and the Shoe Hill country follow there. A morning's catch and two good fish appear in the photographs. Rogers writes the gentleman sportsman's Canada.
4747-the-river-s-end:
James Oliver Curwood opens The River's End with a striking resemblance between Conniston, of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and Keith, the outlaw he has hunted. Both have observed it, and it gives them a sort of confidence in each other. It hovers as a subtle presence, tempting Conniston toward a line of action that would make him a traitor to his oath. For nearly a month he has crushed down those whisperings.

Conniston represents the law, and for twenty-seven months he has followed Keith, under orders not to return until he gets his man, dead or alive. A racking cough splits his thoughts, and at a gasping cry of pain, with blood on his lips, Keith goes to him and supports his shoulder with a strong arm. Readers get a northern tale of law, loyalty, and likeness, where hunter and hunted must reckon with each other as men.
47483-hesper-the-home-spirit-a-simple-st:
A domestic story by Elizabeth Doten, published at Boston in 1859. Abel Tompkins and partners issued the small volume. Its subtitle calls it a simple story of household labor and love. Charity never faileth stands as its motto. The preface states one leading idea. True merit in humble life deserves its due honour.

The world celebrates conquering heroes, Doten writes. Patient heroism in quiet homes passes unnoticed instead. Such sufferers bear their crosses in silence to the grave. Petty daily vexations, not great sorrows, test the soul most severely. Love that seeks another's good is the one thing needful. Angels in the house, her phrase runs, must be known before heaven's angels walk with man. The tale embodies that creed in a servant's life.
47492-old-fort-garland:
James Forrest made a brief past of Fort Garland in a made soldier's voice. The State Historical Society of Colorado put the book out in 1954. Paul Rossi made its drawn work. It is kept in mind of Edgar McMechen in its front. Forrest grants the soldier and his journal are not real men.

The facts in the tale are true in the main, he says. Digging in the fort's files grounds each part he tells. Made bits add color, but no great fact is faked. The first note dates to July 29, 1860, at the fort. A troop's come kicks off the post's long tale. West fans get a fort's life year by year.
4769-young-folks-history-of-england:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote Young Folks' History of England as a history for young readers, moving through the island's story. It opens with Julius Caesar in 55 B.C., the Romans in Britain from A.D. 41 to 418, the Angle children in 597, and the Northmen from 858 to 958. The Danish conquest, the Norman conquest, and William the Conqueror follow, with William II, called Rufus, and Henry I, Beau-Clerc.

Stephen, Henry II, Richard I, and John carry the story through the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Henry III of Winchester, Edward I, called Longshanks, Edward II of Caernarvon, and Edward III follow. Richard II, Henry IV, Henry V of Monmouth, Henry VI of Windsor, Edward IV, Edward V, Richard III, and Henry VII come next. Later chapters continue the line of kings and queens in the same clear, short form. Readers get Yonge's history, written for young folks but useful to any beginner.
47753-a-history-of-england:
Charles Oman wrote this history of England in one survey volume. Arnold printed the eleventh edition in London in 1904. Oman taught modern history at Oxford, a fellow of All Souls. Chapter one treats Celtic and Roman Britain at the start.

The coming of the English and conversion of England follow next. Danish invasions and the great kings of Wessex fill chapter four. Cnut and Edward the Confessor days precede the Norman Conquest here. William the Red, Henry the First, and Stephen take chapter seven. Henry the Second and Richard and John take the two chapters that follow in turn.
47793-sparky-ames-of-the-ferry-command:
Roy Snell wrote Sparky Ames of the Ferry Command, a wartime boys' novel published by Whitman at Racine in 1943, with pictures by Erwin Darwin. The copyright page declares every name, character, place, and event entirely fictitious. Twenty chapters ferry Sparky and Mary across the war's air routes. The flight of the Lone Star over Brazil, savages and the night, and battling a spy open the run. A lady in black, desert battles, and a roll of papyrus follow.

Sealed orders, a snake charmer, a Burma detour, and Saint Elmo's fire carry the run to Deep Secrets Revealed. The opening puts a formation of four-motored planes over the Rio Branco, watched by two natives in a dugout canoe. Ferry Command pilots delivered aircraft worldwide in 1943, and Snell turns their routes into a spy-and-cargo adventure for young readers, with Mary creating sensations at secret airfields along the way.
47907-mr-punch-s-animal-land:
Punch's Animal Land is a comic picture book drawn and written by Reed, maker of Prehistoric Peeps, and published at London by Bradbury, Agnew and Company. Its preface is written in the voice of a child author, in wilful bad spelling. There are two kinds of prefaces, the child explains: your own, or one by a swell writer. Reed does his own, since the talk under the pictures is his.

He owns that he is at the opening of his career and asks allowances for style and penmanship, to be put down to youth. He learned to draw, he says, off the Venus of Milo, which does not help much with animals. The pages give mock natural history in pictures and jesting notes, in the Punch manner, on the most notable beasts.
47948-the-arch-ology-and-prehistoric-ann:
A founding work of Scottish archaeology by Daniel Wilson. Sutherland and Knox published it at Edinburgh in 1851. Wilson was honorary secretary of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland. He dedicates the book to the Marquess of Breadalbane. The marquess presided over the society and enriched its collections. A runic brooch from Hunterston forms the frontispiece.

Wilson builds a system in two great periods. The primeval or stone period comes first. Chapters treat graves, dwellings, temples, weapons, and ornaments. Skulls from the burial mounds get a chapter of their own. The archaic or bronze period follows, opening with the introduction of metals. Wilson helped give English the very word prehistoric. His annals made Scotland's deep past a science.
47955-the-nursery-book-a-complete-guide-:
Bailey's Nursery-Book, a complete guide to the multiplication and pollination of plants, was published by the Rural Publishing Company in 1891. The preface calls it a handbook of the methods commonly used in propagation and crossing. Questions of ultimate results, bud formation, and the interplay of cion and stock are left outside its province. The whole text was read by skilled propagators before printing. Watson of the Bussey Institution at Harvard passed the volume and added to its value.

The articles on orchids were contributed by Bean of the Royal Gardens, Kew, a known orchid specialist. Bailey drew on Nicholson's Illustrated Dictionary of Gardening and on French and German garden manuals. The Nursery List aims to cover every plant commonly grown in America for food or ornament. An ordinal index lets the reader find the treatment for anything omitted.
47991-erchie-my-droll-friend:
Hugh Foulis, Neil Munro, wrote these sketches of Erchie, his droll friend. Blackwood printed the book at Edinburgh and London in 1904. Most chapters ran first in the Glasgow Evening News pages. Erchie is beadle of the church on Sundays, a waiter else.

In church he is Mr MacPherson, with solemn dignity of bearing. At city banquets, passing fruit, he is simply Erchie to all. No Mr MacPhersons here, he reproves, or wages would not pay starch. A flat foot motto stands as his proud Glasgow saying. Some sketches in the book appear in print for the first time, the preface notes.
48105-dictionary-of-quotations-from-anci:
A Dictionary of Quotations, selected and compiled by James Wood, gathers sayings from ancient and modern, English and foreign sources. Warne printed it in London and New York in 1893. Wood also edited Nuttall's Standard Dictionary. Two mottoes head his work: aphorisms are portable wisdom, and a proverb is much matter decocted into few words.

Phrases, mottoes, maxims, proverbs, definitions, aphorisms, and sayings of wise men fill the pages, bearing on life, literature, science, art, religion, and morals. The arrangement is alphabetical by the first word of each quotation, with a topical index behind it. Wood calls the book the pleasant labour of more than three years.
48119-hulme-s-journal-1818-19-flower-s-l:
Early Western Travels, volume ten, reprints four rare accounts of the early West. Reuben Gold Thwaites edited the series, issued at Cleveland in 1904 by Clark. Hulme Journal of 1818 and 1819 leads the volume in full. Thomas Hulme toured the western countries from autumn 1818 into 1819 there.

Richard Flower letters from Lexington and the Illinois follow, dated 1819 on. Flower defends the English settlement against Cobbett charges in print here. His 1820 and 1821 letters from Albion carry the tale further on. A Birkbeck letter and Benjamin Flower notes join that section in full. John Woods two years on the English Prairie closes the volume.
48146-on-adventure-island:
On Adventure Island, by Bess Moyer, is a girls' flying adventure in the Girl Flyer Series, published in Chicago in 1932.

Terry Mapes, a young pilot, loops her little blue and gold monoplane Skybird high over the hills for the joy of it. Her twin sister Prim, riding in the rear seat, scolds her through the earphones and tells her to save her strength. The sisters are bound for South America on a secret errand to Peru. Their father, an old airmail pilot, taught both girls to fly. Chapters promise a hazardous flight, pursuit by a flying foe, a tropic storm, a cave of wonder, and a crash. The twins end as island prisoners before the final jump.
48223-the-history-of-gambling-in-england:
John Ashton, who wrote Social Life in the Reign of Queen Anne, traced the long tale of gambling in England. Duckworth printed this history in London in 1898. Ashton had written a history of English lotteries before it.

Gaming and gambling split at the start, then the vice's age and spread. Egypt's gods and dice, China, India, and the Jews open the wide view. Greeks, Romans, and followers of Mahomet share the vice. Dicing in England runs from the 1200s to the great gamblers of the 1700s. Cards take the first chapter: Latimer's words, the soldier's prayer book, and royal play fill it.
48622-grettir-the-outlaw-a-story-of-icel:
Grettir the Outlaw, a story of Iceland by Baring-Gould, retells the Saga of Grettir the Strong for young readers. Published by Blackie in 1889 with illustrations by Zeno Diemer, the book grew out of Baring-Gould's schoolroom. He had learned Danish, then Icelandic, to read the saga, and his pupils begged him for a version of their own.

Baring-Gould tells the tale in his own words, following Grettir's feats, feuds, and long outlawry among the farms and wastes of Iceland. He had walked much of the saga's ground himself in 1861, and the places are real. The retelling helped carry the Icelandic sagas to English boys and girls. It still shows the strength of the original: a hero both mighty and doomed.
48626-mollie-s-substitute-husband:
Max McConn wrote Mollie's Substitute Husband, for the Ryerson Press at Toronto in 1920. Dodd, Mead held the rights, and Caswell drew a front plate now lost from this copy. Chapter one is called The Professor on a Spree. John Merriam, principal of the high school at Riceville, Illinois, is the Professor to all in town. He is wickedly, gladly happy, on a rare spree as the tale opens.

The narrator owns that readers may be shocked at such an act by such a man. Contents promise the prettiest girl, friendly strangers, and an unscrupulous reformer. Passages with Mayor Black, a missing senator, and the confessions of a waiter add intrigue. A senatorial dinner, a code telegram, and the business of being an impostor drive the plot. McConn gives a brisk small-town tale of reform, fraud, and love.
48810-a-magnificent-fight-marines-in-the:
Robert Cressman wrote a history of the Marines who fought for Wake Island, issued in a series marking the Second World War. Wake is a small atoll in the Pacific between Hawaii and Guam. The story begins on Monday, December 8, 1941, as word of war reaches the island.

Marines of the First Defense Battalion had spent weeks on hard work to ready the atoll. Major Devereux led the Wake detachment, while Commander Cunningham held charge of naval work on the atoll. When news came that Hawaii had been raided, Devereux called his men to arms at once. Sidebars profile the leaders and the guns they relied on, from antiaircraft guns to five-inch guns. Readers get a close account of a small force bracing for attack far from help.
48813-the-black-diamond:
Francis Brett Young wrote The Black Diamond, a novel of life in a coal town. Collins issued the book in London and Glasgow, first in February nineteen hundred twenty one. Five more printings came in two years. Young gave the book to M Compton Mackenzie with thanks and love.

Abner Fellows is born in Hackett’s Cottages, a row of brick homes near Halesby. Coal dust and smoke have eaten the brick faces for fifty years. The ground sags over the Great Mawne Colliery far below. A crack splits the plaque on the Fellows house itself. His father John, a miner, lodges near the pit by choice. The pit pays the wage and the pub takes it back. Football at the Mawne ground pulls John as hard as drink does.
48874-a-brief-history-of-forestry-in-eur:
A Brief History of Forestry in Europe, the United States and Other Countries was written by Bernhard Fernow, dean of the Faculty of Forestry at the University of Toronto. The University Press at Toronto issued this revised and enlarged edition in 1911. Fernow dedicated the book to Rossiter Raymond, whose interest had inspired his labours for forestry in the United States.

The history begins with the forest of the ancients: its conditions, the growth of forest property, forest use and early literature. Germany then fills long sections, from the earliest times through the first shaping of forestry methods between 1500 and 1800, and into the nineteenth century. Fernow treats property law, forest treatment, restrictions on use, policy, administration, schools and literature country by country, as a working manual for a young profession.
48908-legends-of-norseland:
Mara Pratt edited these legends for young readers, copyrighted at Boston in 1894. Chase illustrated the volume for the Young Folks' Library of Choice Literature. A Valkyrie frontispiece stands at page six, before the beginning of the world in the first tale.

Ygdrasil, the great tree, follows the beginning in the contents list. Odin at the well of wisdom, Odin and the all-wise giant and the stolen wine come in turn. The theft of Thor's hammer, the apples of life, Loke's wolf and the dying of Baldur carry the Norse gods through theft, laughter and doom for young readers meeting them first here.
48953-the-invasions-of-england:
The Invasions of England is a military history by Edward Foord and Gordon Home, published by Black at London in 1915. It first appeared in 1913 as England Invaded. The frontispiece shows Admiral de Ruyter, the great Dutch commander whose fleet's guns were heard at Whitehall in 1667. Publisher's notices at the front list companion picture books on England.

The chapters march through two thousand years of attack. Caesar's invasions and the Claudian conquest open the story, with the Roman province and the first Teutonic landings after. The English conquest, the Viking ravages, and Alfred's saving of Wessex follow. The invasions of 1066, mainland and Scottish attacks, and the Spanish Armada fill out the roll of England's dangers.
48973-three-apostles-of-quakerism-popula:
Three Apostles of Quakerism is a book of popular sketches of George Fox, William Penn, and Robert Barclay, written by Rhodes. Henry Longstreth of Philadelphia published it in 1886. Stoughton, a historian of the English church, supplied the introduction. Its motto, from Gurney's memoirs, says the three pleaded only for broad, unfettered, spiritual Christianity.

Stoughton testifies to the diligence, care, and ability of the work, and finds its conclusions in general the same as his own. He warns readers not to assume the small book merely copies the larger biographies. He finds in it numerous signs of original research and an independent judgment of the questions before it. A note preserved with the text adds that Rhodes plainly has much sympathy with the life and labours of the early Quakers.
48992-from-pekin-to-calais-by-land:
De Windt wrote From Pekin to Calais by Land, printed in London in 1889 with illustrations and a map. A front picture shows the author's caravan at dawn in the Gobi Desert. The book is given to the Raja of Sarawak, in memory of pleasant hours of travel in his lands in Borneo. A preface owns that two Englishmen in Shanghai, who had made the overland trip, are pestered with letters asking about the journey.

That flood of questions, De Windt says, is the main reason these pages appear. The general reader, he fears, will find little to interest him in a monotonous pilgrimage through Europe and Asia. The book does not aspire to be a book of travel, only a record of impressions in the less settled parts of China and in Siberia. A glimpse of Urga and Irkoutsk, he holds, hardly repays the hardship of the caravan route.
49067-historic-towns-of-new-england:
Lyman Powell edited this set of town histories for Putnam in New York and London in 1898. A frontispiece shows Plymouth in 1622, from a copyrighted drawing at the front. George Perry Morris supplies an introduction to the American Historic Towns series volume.

Portland, by Pickard, opens the contents, and Rutland, Massachusetts, by Mead follows. Salem, Boston, Cambridge, Concord and Plymouth each get a chapter by a local writer. Higginson and Hale share Boston between them in the list. Cape Cod towns, Deerfield, Newport, Providence, Hartford and New Haven round out a portrait of old New England.
4910-the-magic-pudding-being-the-adventu:
Norman Lindsay's comic fantasy follows Bunyip Bluegum, a koala who leaves his tree-top home after a quarrel over his uncle's whiskers, and soon meets a pudding that never runs out. The magic pudding regrows as fast as it is eaten, which makes it a prize for every thief and scoundrel on the road.

Bunyip joins Bill Barnacle the sailor and Sam Sawnoff the penguin, and the three defend their pudding through a string of absurd adventures, courtroom farces, and songs. Lindsay's verse and prose keep the tone mischievous throughout. Young readers get a tall tale about friendship and appetite, told with Australian humor and nonsense logic.
49131-wings-over-england:
Roy Snell wrote this war tale for boys, with eight full-page plates by Glen Sheffer. Goldsmith printed Wings over England at Chicago in 1941. Cherry, a girl of the tale, gives the first chapter her name.

Catbirds and Hawk and Dolls and Nazis show the book's strange mix in its early list. Hans Schlitz, a young lord, and lady spies enter the cast. Enemy sighted, first blood, and a dungeon night raise the pitch. Dave's strange craft and a sky drama mark the late chapters. The Lark defends his home town, and victory and a rescue close the tale. Plates show a dog finding a fugitive and shots tearing a wall.
49220-leila-at-home-a-continuation-of-le:
Leila at Home, by Ann Fraser Tytler, continues the story of Leila for young readers. Francis published it at New York in 1853, with engravings by Orr. Leila had first appeared as Leila, or The Island, then in Leila in England. In her preface Tytler says she had meant to bid a last farewell to Leila, but her young readers said no.

She feels too grateful for their kindness not to try to meet their wish, she writes. The tale resumes with Leila in all the joy of her cousin Selina Stanley having recovered her speech. Selina's sister Matilda goes on making good resolutions, and too often breaking them again. Their little brother Alfred is little Alfred still, and not over wise. Tytler's Leila books taught by way of a shipwrecked child's gentle story. They were beloved in nurseries on both sides of the Atlantic,.
49291-beadle-s-dime-national-speaker-emb:
Beadle and Company of William Street, New York, issued a dime speaker as number two of a speaker series, embodying gems of oratory for school and public use. The front matter advertises the house's hand books for popular use. A dime letter writer leads the list, called a perfect guide to all kinds of correspondence. Its chapters teach composition, punctuation, and style.

Such speaker volumes gathered recitation pieces, dialogues, and addresses for elocution practice. Beadle built its name on cheap, useful books for ordinary readers. The national speaker aimed at school exhibitions and lyceum evenings. Pupils memorized its gems for Friday afternoon programs across the country.
49496-the-scouts-of-seal-island:
The Scouts of Seal Island is a boys' adventure novel by Percy Westerman, first published in 1913 and reprinted many times into 1930. Black of London issued this edition with eight illustrations in colour by Ernest Prater. Westerman had written The Sea Scouts of the Petrel and The Sea Monarch. The contents open with Sir Silas Disapproves, then Dick Atherton's Good Turn and the patrol leader's dilemma.

Off to Seal Island and the arrival follow. A spoilt breakfast and the mysterious footprints deepen the camp's puzzles. A passage preserved in the copy shows the scoutmaster addressing the Otter and Wolf patrols. He pauses to note the effect of his words, and practically every boy knows what is coming. One and all give no sign of disgust at the shattering of their hopes. Some purse their lips tightly, others set their jaws grimly.
49572-observations-of-a-naturalist-in-th:
Observations of a Naturalist in the Pacific Between 1896 and 1899, volume 1, by Guppy, was published in London and New York in 1903. The volume treats Vanua Levu, Fiji, and describes its chief physical and rock features. Guppy dedicates the book to the Fijian people. Front plates show high acid peaks such as Na Raro, at 2,420 feet.

Guppy lists the main past works on Fiji, from Dana in 1849 to Horne's A Year in Fiji. His own field notes rest on three years of travel and study in the islands. Maps, rock notes, and accounts of rivers, coasts, and plants serve scientists who need a firm base for later Pacific work.
49829-the-geological-history-of-fossil-b:
Paul O McGrew and Michael Casilliano of the University of Wyoming geology department wrote a study of Fossil Butte National Monument and Fossil Basin. It appeared as National Park Service occasional paper number three. Contents cover location, the history of research, and stratigraphy. Named rock units include the Thaynes Limestone and the Evanston and Wasatch formations.

The authors trace a chain of old lakes in basins formed as the Rocky Mountains rose. Lake Flagstaff came first, then Lakes Gosiute, Uinta, and Fossil. Together they made the Green River lake system, which grew and shrank over a long span. Fossil Lake left the rich fossil beds the monument protects.
49957-mary-jane-in-new-england:
Clara Ingram Judson wrote Mary Jane in New England, issued at New York by Grosset and Dunlap with a copyright of 1921 and pictures by Thelma Gooch. Judson had told Mary Jane's home life, her visit, her kindergarten, and her time down South in earlier books. Here the Merrill family plans a journey east: Mary Jane and Alice are to see Boston, Harvard, and Uncle Hal's Class Day.

A day of wetness, first glimpses of Boston, and a visit at Wellesley open the trip. Class day fun, a game won, an adventure by the lagoon, and commencement in the stadium fill the middle. A day in Plymouth, cousin Louise, a lost Mary Jane, and tea on the terrace end the stay. Judson dedicated the book to her brother, with memories of his commencement week.
50050-the-sea-girt-fortress-a-story-of-h:
Percy Westerman wrote The Sea-Girt Fortress, a story of Heligoland issued by a London house known for boys' adventure books. Reviewers quoted on the opening pages praise Westerman for breathless excitement that no boy could read with a steady pulse. The tale puts two young sailors on a yacht near a German island fortress as war looms.

The first chapter, Man Overboard, finds Oswald Detroit and Jack Hamerton aboard the Diomeda in fog, taking soundings and unsure of their place. The contents speed ahead: an arrest, a discovery, a sentence, and nights in a prison cell. A Zeppelin experiment, a tunnel under the island, and an errant airship follow, and the book ends with the Battle of the Galloper Sands and the fall of the island fortress. Wigfull drew the pictures, including spies facing armed men. Readers get a full-throttle spy and sea adventure.
50475-the-young-ship-builders-of-elm-isl:
The Reverend Elijah Kellogg wrote The Young Ship-Builders of Elm Island for boys. Lee and Shepard issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred seventy one. It stands fifth in the Elm Island Stories of his pen. Lion Ben and Charlie Bell head the set of Maine coast tales.

Home tasks give way to hard trade work in this part of the set. The boys now serve stern masters and the public for their bread. Rules bind them, and blame falls fast when their hands slip. Fear of God shields a lad in the hour of trial, Kellogg holds. He who serves his master best serves himself best in the end. Learning a trade and gunning on the far reefs open the tale. The West Wind’s wreck at sea marks one dark high point here. Charlie in Boston gains new thoughts, and learns a new tongue.
50490-legendary-heroes-of-ireland:
Legendary Heroes of Ireland is a story book for young readers by Harold Hughes, issued at San Francisco in 1922. Hughes dedicates it to his father, whose tales of the Irish heroes first opened the wonderland of Celtic folk lore to him. A teacher's preface then states the book's aim in the classroom. The stories hope to promote a love of reading in boys and girls.

Our duty in teaching reading lies not in the subject matter but in the desire, the preface argues. If a child sees that reading is a golden key, it will unlock the storehouse of books for itself. The Irish heroes of legend are the bait chosen here. Their deeds, told plainly for school readers, carry the old Celtic tales into an American classroom of the nineteen twenties.
505-history-of-the-warfare-of-science-wi:
Andrew Dickson White traces the long clash between science and church dogma in this two-volume history, combined here. From creation to evolution, from comets to medicine, White shows how literal readings of scripture blocked inquiry, then slowly gave way. Ezra Cornell, co-founder of Cornell University, receives the dedication.

White writes as a historian and university builder, marshaling cases with calm, learned force. His ice-barrier image opens the book: truth presses like spring water till old walls break. The work endures as a landmark plea for free inquiry, and for a faith that need not fear fact.
50501-the-medi-val-hospitals-of-england:
The Mediaeval Hospitals of England is a past of the old sick houses of that land by Rotha Mary Clay. It first came out in nineteen nine, with past seventy plates. A church chief of a west town wrote its front words. Its first part stands in past fifteen heads, from houses for way folk and the sick to the fall of the houses.

Heads treat homes for the weak and the poor, homes for the mad, and the lazar house. The leper of that land, the founders and givers, and the folk in the houses take heads. House build, the rule of the house, care of the soul, and care of the flesh fill the mid list. A next part treats the saints of the houses, and back lists give a rite and a table of founds.
50509-baby-land:
Baby Land is a book of cradle verse by Almira Corey Frink, whose pen name is Wild Bird. Olive Bacon Frink shaped the book at Denver with a right claim of nineteen eleven. Its scheme runs to more than a score of short songs and tales. Lull songs of the moon, the sea ice, the woods, and the sea start the set. Baby bed, baby Noah, and warm feet songs stand in that first row.

Cradle songs of the Nile, of the mines, and of the farm fill mid ranks. Snow birds, a kit, and a small fawn get verse of their own. Songs of loss stand by the glad ones, as with its first born grief part. The front give leaf sends the notes out like wing seed on the wind. Each song flies to rich house and poor hut alike in that wish.
50575-firemen-and-their-exploits-with-so:
Holmes wrote a plain, fact filled history of fire work, printed in London in 1899 by the Partridge firm. The full title promises an account of the rise of fire brigades and of tools for saving life at fires. Holmes had written like books on engineers and miners, and this one forms part of that set.

Early pages trace fire engines from ancient Egypt and Hero of Alexandria to the London work of Newsham by 1726. Later parts cover steam engines, the joint London brigade formed in 1833 under James Braidwood, fire escapes, water towers, and town brigades. Big fires, such as the Great Fire of 1666, give the tale its drama.
50614-walter-crane-s-painting-book-conta:
Walter Crane made this painting book for children, printed by Edmund Evans. Routledge issued the book in London, Glasgow, Manchester, and New York. Twelve colored plates stand beside twelve outline plates for painting. Each outline page lets a child copy the color model near it.

Rhymes pair with the plates, like The Peacock Complaint on pride. Jack and Jill, I Saw Three Ships, and garden rhymes appear. Short morals, like do not quarrel with nature, tag the short verses. Crane other rhyme books for babies are listed at the end.
50662-peeps-at-many-lands-england:
England is a volume of the Peeps at Many Lands series by John Finnemore, printed at London in 1908 with twelve full-page pictures in colour. It opens in London town, which Finnemore calls the greatest city in the world. Three chapters walk the reader through the capital and two more follow Old Father Thames.

The tour then goes to a cathedral city, through Wessex, and round the tors of the west. It visits the land of saints, Shakespeare's country, an old English house, fen and broad, and dale and fell. The last chapters call the Lake District the playground of England and end with heroes of the storm, the lifeboat men. The book was made to show young readers their own country, its towns, rivers, and famous places. Its colour plates show guards, cathedrals, lanes, and cottages.
50666-songs-of-the-sea-and-lays-of-the-l:
Charles Leland gathered these songs of the sea and lays of the land. Black printed the verse book in London in 1895. The Old Tavern opens the sea songs, El Capitan General second. Uncle Sam, Mother Carey, and the Bird Crew follow in the list.

Davy Jones, the Devil Pot, and La Bella Strega fill the middle. The Mermaid, the Merman, and the Wizard Finn stand among them. Lays of the land open with the rise and fall of Gloryville. A tale of Idaho and a Californian romance close that half.
50698-my-uncle-florimond:
My Uncle Florimond is a novel by Sidney Luska, the pen name of Henry Harland. D Lothrop Company published it in Boston in 1888. Harland dedicated the book to his grandmother, in remembrance of old Norwich days. The narrator, Gregory, lost both parents as a baby. He grew up in Norwich Town, Connecticut, in his grandmother's house. She was a French lady born a de la Bourbonnaye, daughter of a marquis.

Gregory's father was shot at the Battle of Bull Run in July 1861. The man of the house is Uncle Peter, a lawyer the neighbours call Square or Jedge. Gregory fears him deeply and loves him not at all. The stern uncle growls that children should be seen and not heard. Meals with him are an agony for the boy. The novel's title points to another uncle, Florimond, whose story the orphan's memories slowly uncover.
5086-rainbow-s-end:
Rex Beach's Rainbow's End opens with a first view of the Yumuri valley, probably from the Hermitage of Montserrate, where coach drivers take visitors to look over the valley of delight. Chapters follow with a world run backward, capitulation, a woman with a mission, filibusters, a city among leaves, and a city of beggars.

Food, a sick man from San Antonio, El Demonio's child, treasure, the trocha, and a city of death carry the Cuban adventure forward, toward a haunted garden and three travelers coming home. Beach writes the island's wars and beauties with adventure-story energy. Readers get a romance of Cuba in revolt, colorful, crowded, and fast-moving.
50876-earthbound:
Earthbound is a science fiction story by Lester del Rey. It first appeared in Galaxy Magazine in August 1963. The hero, Clifton, is a deep space captain back on Earth.

A company has paid Clifton to grace its hundredth anniversary party. He slips onto a balcony and meets an old boot maker. The old man won a prize for fifty years of making space boots. Yet he has never once left Earth himself. The meeting turns Clifton's pride into pity. Del Rey often wrote about longing for space. This story gives that longing to a man who never flew.
50925-a-visit-to-newfoundland:
A Visit to Newfoundland is a travel sketch by Mary L B Branch. It was printed for the Lucretia Shaw Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution. Branch recalls the island in a chain of small portraits. Old Mrs Pike keeps a poppy-bed by a broken fence. She can neither read nor write, yet commands respect. Jim Savery's wife rears children in a one-roomed cottage.

Another fisherman once drifted three days among ice floes in fog. The man with him froze to death in the boat's bottom. All night the survivor clasped the dying man, trying to keep the vital spark. A wooden cross marks a clergyman drowned returning from a sick visit. Branch reached the island by the steamer Bruce from North Sydney. A hundred miles of ocean ended at white rocks and a winding harbour.
50973-about-my-father-s-business-work-am:
Thomas Archer wrote of Christian work among the sick, the sad, and the sorrowing, printed in London in 1876. Archer had written The Terrible Sights of London and The Pauper, the Thief, and the Convict. His title takes Christ's words about being about his father's business. Chapters open with the rarity of Christian charity.

Archer goes with the children of the stranger, with those left desolate, and with them that go down to the sea in ships. He writes of the feeble, the little ones, lost lambs, and those with nowhere to lay their heads. He asks if advancing civilization makes men lose sight of their neighbour in a long vista of charity by subscription. First hand visits give the book its force.
50993-lion-ben-of-elm-island:
Lion Ben of Elm Island is a boys' novel by Elijah Kellogg, published in Boston by Lee and Shepard in 1869. It opens the Elm Island Stories series. Kellogg also wrote Spartacus to the Gladiators and Good Old Times.

The preface explains the series' aim. Kellogg wants to stir boys to manly effort, and to inspire respect for labor, integrity, and every noble sentiment. His stories show the home life of the families American youth sprang from. The scene is the rugged coast of eastern Maine, with its perils and enjoyments by sea and land. Charlie Bell, the waif of Elm Island, is announced as the next volume. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
51-anne-of-the-island:
Anne Shirley leaves Green Gables for college in this third Anne book. Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of the Island follows Anne to Redmond College with friends old and new. Letters from home, Patty's Place, and first proposals fill her terms.

Gilbert Blythe waits in the background while other suitors press their cases. Anne learns what she wants in work, friendship, and love. The novel closes with spring and a return to the island. It bridges Anne's schoolgirl years and her adult life. Montgomery balances college comedy with quiet scenes of home, loss, and growing resolve.
51059-mrs-pendleton-s-four-in-hand:
Pendleton's Four-in-Hand is a short novel by Gertrude Atherton, author of The Conqueror, published by Macmillan at New York in 1903. It belongs to the Little Novels by Favourite Authors line. A portrait of Atherton fronts the book. The tale opens at Newport, where Jessica stands with clenched hands and set teeth over a heap of letters on the floor.

Sun blazes through the open window, and the ocean's deep voice rises to the sands, seeming to repeat one word: contempt. Tall and faultless in dress, with the air of a New York woman of fashion, Jessica shows more anger than shame, though her pride lies in the dust. Two pictures mark scenes of insult and challenge in the brief, sharp tale.
51114-plays-written-by-sir-john-vanbrugh:
Sir John Vanbrugh's plays fill a second volume printed in London in 1776. The book holds The Confederacy, The Mistake, and The Country House. It also holds A Journey to London and The Provok'd Husband. A prologue spoken by a shabby poet opens the volume, mocking the poor pay of poets.

The poet shows his ragged coat and laurel crown and asks where he is to eat. That tone fits Vanbrugh, who worked in both theatre and building. Readers get five stage works in old spelling and print style. The volume is a useful record of how his plays were read long after his death.
51173-the-stately-homes-of-england:
Llewellynn Jewitt and Hall compiled this tour of England's great houses, illustrated with three hundred eighty engravings on wood. The introduction argues that England is richer than any country under the sun in homes, from palace to cottage. It adds that the love of home is the nation's main source of greatness.

The title itself is borrowed from a poem by Hemans: the stately homes of England, standing beautiful amid their tall ancestral trees. Jewitt, an antiquary, and Hall, a veteran art editor, chose houses not for stateliness alone but for owners who let visitors enjoy their art and grounds. The descriptions mix architecture, family history, and pictures of parks and halls. Books of this kind fed the Victorian taste for country house visiting, and this one, complete in two series, was among the most handsome of them.
51213-the-art-of-bookbinding-a-practical:
Joseph W Zaehnsdorf wrote a practical treatise on bookbinding, in a second edition revised and enlarged in 1890. It belongs to a series of technological handbooks covering dyeing, glass making, cotton spinning, and printing. Zaehnsdorf dedicated the book to Hugh Owen, in admiration of his knowledge of binding. A plate shows a Florentine binding in small folio.

The preface says the first edition was written for amateurs. Trade binders bought it heavily, and the edition soon sold out. Zaehnsdorf kept the old arrangement but added much fresh matter. Plates and diagrams throughout show tools, styles, and steps of the craft. The book remains a record of hand binding practice.
51247-dead-end:
Dead End is a science fiction story by Wallace Macfarlane. It first appeared in Galaxy Science Fiction in January 1952. The opening scene follows a scientist named William Manning Norcross.

Norcross eats dinner while watching a staged swimming show on television. He studies his own messy appearance in a mirror with cold curiosity. The story opens on a future where feeling is treated as a burden. It suggests that sparing feelings can erase them. Magazine science fiction of this era often hid its ideas inside odd daily scenes. This tale uses a quiet evening to raise a bleak question.
51319-woodcraft-boys-at-sunset-island:
Woodcraft Boys at Sunset Island is a boys' novel by Lillian Elizabeth Roy and M F Hoisington, printed at New York in 1919. The frontispiece shows Billy's prize fish. The first chapter, The Sports of Sunset Island, opens on the water. Billy Remington cries out at a fin sticking out of the water near the Cove, toggle-iron in hand.

He stands in the bow of a large rowboat manned by three other boys. The chapters run through what the trawl brought forth, foggy days and woodcraft ways, and a council. The boys win the degree of Shingebis, picnic at Spruce Island, and cruise to Castine. A night of the masked ball and the pirates of Scilly Ledge raise the adventure. Thieves in the night and the twenty-fourth feather close the tale. Pictures show lobster traps, a string of cunners, and the war bonnet of the sagamore.
51393-toadstools-mushrooms-fungi-edible-:
Charles McIlvaine wrote this vast guide to American fungi, in a revised edition printed at Indianapolis with copyrights of 1900 and 1902. McIlvaine led the Philadelphia Mycological Center. Robert K MacAdam added the part on toadstool poisons and their treatment. The title promises one thousand American fungi, with full botanic accounts of each.

The book teaches how to pick and cook the edible kinds and how to know and shun the poisonous ones. Students get guidance, cooks get recipes, and the sick get treatment notes. Plates show the gifts of forest and field. Indexes of genera, species, and recipes close a work built for use in hand, not on a shelf.
51411-the-campaign-in-russian-poland:
Percy Cross Standing wrote on the campaign in Russian Poland in the great war. Hodder and Stoughton issued the book in London in the Roman year MCMXIV. The work stands in the Daily Telegraph War Books set, sold for a shilling. Eight chapters run from Lemberg to the German retreat.

The fall of Lemberg, capital of Galicia, to the Tsar's forces leads the tale. Standing calls that gain in early September a turning mark in the east. The Vistula defense, the siege of Przemysl, and fights on the San follow. British readers at home gain swift news of huge armies in the east.
51718-what-i-saw-in-kaffir-land:
What I Saw in Kaffir-Land is a war memoir by Sir Stephen Lakeman, who also bore the Turkish title Mazhar Pacha, published by Blackwood in 1880. Lakeman had served at the Cape during the frontier war of the early 1850s. His book prints extracts from his daily record, with, he insists, very little omitted and nothing added.

His preface warns that he has said little good of anyone because he perceived little. The contents show a volunteer corps raised amid red tape and damaged stores. Then come mutiny, marches to Graham's Town and Fort Beaufort, and the first trial of the Minié rifle. The title uses the period's name for the Xhosa frontier; the book is a soldier's unvarnished diary of a colonial war.
51885-the-trade-signs-of-essex-a-popular:
The Trade Signs of Essex, by Miller Christy, is a popular account of inn and shop signs in that county. Durrant printed the book at Chelmsford in 1887, with a London house as co-publisher. A view of Chelmsford High Street in 1762 fronts the volume.

Christy came to the theme through heraldry, where charges, crests, and badges fill the eye. He saw a clear kinship between those devices and the painted boards over roadside inns. From about 1879 he followed the lead through his native county sign by sign. Only three set treatises on signs had ever been printed, he found. The chief was the History of Sign-boards by Larwood and Hotten, to which he owns a large debt. His preface quotes a learned wit: prefaces are to books what signs are to public houses.
51908-in-indian-tents-stories-told-by-pe:
In Indian Tents, published in Boston in 1897, gathers stories told by Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, and Micmac tellers to Abby Alger. Alger inscribed the book to Charles Godfrey Leland, saying it owed its start to his urging. The tales come from the Native peoples of the northeast woodlands and were set down in English for a wide readership.

The contents run from The Creation and Grandfather Thunder to witches, spirits of the woods and air, and animal tales. One story explains why the rabbit's nose is split; another tells why the raven's feathers are black. The opening tale has the culture hero Glus-kabe shaping the world beside God, ruling that rivers run one way and that the sea must rise and fall. Readers get a shelf of traditional tales told in the tellers' own turns of speech, kept close to the way they were heard.
52025-motor-matt-s-make-and-break-or-adv:
Street and Smith sent out this Motor Matt tale as number 26 of Motor Stories, on August 21, 1909. The price was five cents, and the line's head cries thrilling adventure motor fiction. A plate shows Matt in an aeroplane over a river, crying catch the rope.

The Skeleton in the Closet opens the tale, then What Next and Bringing the Skeleton Out. The Start, a shot across the bows, and the man hunters crowd the list. Fooling the cowboys and the trailing rope mark the chase. A bolt from the blue and advancing the spark, a pun on engines and friendship both, close the part shown here. Matt's speed and grit carry all.
52047-a-little-maid-in-toyland:
A Little Maid in Toyland is a tale for the young by Adah Sutton. Russell drew its plates, and it came out in the year 1908. Sutton had writ of a bunny and of teddy bears for the young. The tale opens on a doll's house in a wide play room.

The house will not sit still in the room of the two young ones. Bob and Sally push and pull it from nook to nook for days. Each stick of the room's goods is moved to clear its path in turn. At last it rests where it first stood, in a sun spot by two panes. Four bright bulbs light it from a bar on the wall at night. A plate shows a sleigh at a sheet of glass strewn with snow dust. From the house the maid steps out to the land of the toys.
52087-a-history-of-inland-transport-and-:
A History of Inland Transport and Communication in England, by Edwin A Pratt, came out in London in 1912. Pratt had written books on railways, canals, and trade. His book leads a set on the chief trades of the nation. A front note sets out its wide sweep in full.

Pratt tracks travel from the first times to his own day. He treats roads, rivers, canals, and toll roads in turn. He then treats railways, tramways, and wire-free power cars. For news and rides he runs from packhorses and stage coaches to cabs, cycles, motors, and planes. He shows how each step changed trade and town life. Readers get one clear tale of how England learned to move.
52103-lays-of-ancient-babyland:
Lays of Ancient Babyland is a book of tales in verse for small children, printed in London by Basil Pickering in 1857. It is dedicated, with much respect but without permission, to the babies of England. The tales were written for the amusement of one child, Augusta Mary.

Four long tales stand first. Whittington and his Cat is told as it is sung in the streets of London on Lord Mayor's Day. The Three Wishes, Little Red-Riding-Hood, and Jack the Giant-Killer follow. A set of small histories then turns to beasts. A vain mouse, a proud eagle, and an oyster and a muscle learn their lessons in turn. Cock Robin and Jenny Wren close the bird tales. The verse is simple, and each tale carries its moral on its face.
52120-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science and Arts for the year 1877 is a bound run of a weekly paper from Edinburgh. Issues number 680 to 731 cover the full year, each of sixteen pages. A cross list at the front ties each issue to its page span and date for quick use.

An index at the front sorts the year's pieces by kind, such as familiar sketches and essays. Named items deal with air and water pollution, the boarding out system, costers and their donkeys, and Christmas time. The volume shows what a wide home readership took in each week: tales, facts, verse, and notes on daily life.
52307-the-life-of-a-foxhound:
John Mills first published this hound's autobiography in 1848. The fifth edition, with illustrations by John Leech, came from Philip Allan at London in 1921, and its editor dedicated it to the Prince of Wales. The preface explains the conceit: an old and sagacious hound told the story of his life long ago. He spoke of men and foxes as he found them, severe on the faults of the first and ready to show his teeth to the second.

The tale begins at walk, in a farm-house where every animal is treated with universal kindness. Sweet milk, meal, and broth are the puppy's provisions, with a clean, dry, warm bed. He basks in the sun and plays with the shepherd's dog before the serious schooling of the kennel begins. Mills made the book a sporting classic: a hound's-eye view of the chase, its men, and its country.
52423-the-white-slaves-of-england:
John C Cobden compiled The White Slaves of England from Official Documents, with twelve spirited illustrations, issued at Auburn and Buffalo in 1854 in its fifth thousand. A front note calls the system shown here abhorrent to justice and humanity. The abuses are hard to believe for their enormity, it warns. Yet impartial proof backs them, it holds.

England prides itself on a free constitution held up as a model, the note says. The book faults that pride as vain and false. Want, misery, and starvation mark her people, it charges. Slavish toil and low rank touch nineteen twentieths of her folk, it claims. Miners, mill hands, workhouse tenants, and sailors are called to witness. Ireland and India are named as sufferers too. Church, state, and law are blamed for the results.
52434-deadly-adulteration-and-slow-poiso:
Deadly Adulteration and Slow Poisoning Unmasked is an exposé of fraud in food and drink, signed only by an Enemy to Fraud and Villany. Its subtitle promises disease and death in the pot and the bottle. The new edition lays open the adulterations of wines, spirits, and beer.

Bread, flour, tea, sugar, spices, pastry, confectionery, and medicines get the same treatment. Tests and methods are given for detecting the frauds and for telling good articles from bad. The book also attacks medical quackery, regular and irregular, and the malpractices of pawnbrokers and madhouse keepers. A quoted line calls the distillery workshop the laboratory of disease and early death. The work is a furious piece of early consumer protection, naming the poisons in the daily loaf and cup.
5248-the-dock-rats-of-new-york-or-the-sm:
