Old Sleuth's Dock Rats of New York, published in 1908 as Adventure Series number seventy-six, is an early pulp tale of smugglers on the New York waterfront. It opens with a cry of Hold, Stranger, as a young man seizes a boat's tiller rope on a shore of white drift sand, and the chase is on.

Old Sleuth was the pen name of Harlan Page Halsey, a pioneer of American dime-novel detective fiction. The novel offers readers a fast, sensational story of a smuggler band's last stand, with disguises, dangers. Dockside intrigue fills the tale, in the breathless style of the pulp era.
52524-clara-barton-national-historic-sit:
Park Service staff wrote this handbook on Clara Barton site in Maryland. Handbook 110 came out in Washington in 1981. The site at Glen Echo honors Barton, who founded the American Red Cross. More than one hundred handbook titles were then in print.

Part one gives a chronology of Barton and her times in brief. Part two holds a life essay called The Professional Angel. Part three guides the park and other sites tied to her career. The series aims to aid visits before, during, and after a park trip. The Park Service issued it as Handbook 110 in 1981.
5254-four-little-blossoms-on-apple-tree-:
Mabel C. Hawley's children's book follows the four little Blossoms on a summer adventure that begins with a new car and Bobby's plan. Chapters move from Twaddles' grasshopper and errands in town to a journey, old Brookside friends. The story reaches Apple Tree Island itself, where a damp adventure, sunny days, a signal for help, and a rescue follow.

Hawley writes gentle, old-fashioned family stories for young readers, with illustrations by Walter F. Rodgers. The book offers simple pleasures — siblings, pets, picnics, and small dangers safely overcome — in a world where children are resourceful and kind.
52545-the-princess-nobody-a-tale-of-fair:
Andrew Lang wrote a tale of fairy land after the drawings of Richard Doyle, printed in colours by Edmund Evans and published by Longmans. A ballade of dedication addresses the babes at Branxholm Park. This book I dedicate, Lang sings, a book for winter evenings dark, too dark to ride or skate. He made it up out of his own head, he says, wasting midnight oil.

Each cut and plate he interprets, the works of Dicky Doyle. When winter comes and the Teviot roars in spate, he asks the children to think of the prince and his mate. Doyle's fairy drawings came first; Lang's verses followed them. The book is a Victorian picture book classic.
52557-rex-kingdon-on-storm-island:
Rex Kingdon on Storm Island is a boys' adventure by Gordon Braddock, printed at New York by the Burt Company with copyright of 1917 by Hurst and Company. Braddock also wrote Rex Kingdon of Ridgewood High, Rex Kingdon in the North Woods and Rex Kingdon Behind the Bat. The frontispiece shows a ballplayer trying to steal home, to everybody's amazement. Thirty-two chapters carry Rex and his chums through a summer on the coast of Maine.

The author's foreword states the premise as a question. Such a vacation would provide plenty of good fun, as well as some troubles and annoyances. No vigorous, high spirited American boy, the foreword insists, would mind a few inconveniences on a camping trip. Enos Quibb makes trouble more than once. The eight-oared shell and Kingdon's surprising move bring the season to its climax.
52599-miss-fairfax-of-virginia-a-romance:
St George Rathborne wrote Miss Fairfax of Virginia, a romance of love and adventure under the palmettos. Street and Smith published it at New York in 1899. Rathborne was the author of Doctor Jack and A Chase for a Bride. The tale opens in Dublin, under Nelson's column in Sackville street. Roderic Owen has come that day from Liverpool on the Holyhead steamer.

The chapters promise a sword duel in an East Indian bungalow and millions that may not purchase love. A chase to a yacht and the invasion of San Juan follow. Julio declares for war, and a strange meeting in a dungeon comes late. The last chapter shows the Spanish flag leaving Porto Rico forever. Rathborne wrote brisk dime-novel romance, and the war in the Caribbean gave his heroine's story its closing stakes.
52798-essays-from-the-chap-book-being-a-:
Essays from the Chap-Book fill these pages, printed at Chicago in 1896. The title page calls the set a mixed bag of tales and lore, new made by many famed pens and sweet to read. The list of parts shows the range of the bag. H. H. Boyesen writes on the new play of Ibsen. John Burroughs gives bits of critique. Mrs. Reginald de Koven writes on Verlaine from the view of a woman.

More names fill the list. Alice Morse Earle writes on the rot of the age, on the joys of the tale of times past, and on an office of letters. Lewis E. Gates takes up Meredith and his Aminta. Edmund Gosse writes on how much the crowd loves verse. Louise Imogen Guiney writes on Trilby and on the town.
52838-creation-of-the-teton-landscape-th:
Creation of the Teton Landscape, a geology guide by J D Love and John C Reed of the United States Geological Survey, tells the story of Grand Teton National Park. The first edition came out in 1968, with a revised edition in 1971. The book is dedicated to Fritiof M Fryxell, the park's first ranger naturalist. Photographs from the park service fill the pages.

The opening chapters view the range as astronaut, pilot, motorist, and climber see it. Then the book shows how the peaks were carved by rock decay, running water, and glaciers. Mountain uplift, faults, and the scale of geologic time come next. Deep chapters treat the ancient core rocks of the Tetons and the seas that once covered the ground.
52845-the-girl-in-his-mind:
The Girl in His Mind is a tale of the far days by Robert Young. It first ran in a press sheet of star tales in April of nineteen sixty-three. A front line says that each mans mind is a world with a score of hid spots, where he can hide from his own self. The tale is set on a far world of twin suns.

It opens in a dance den where a girl does a rite dance of the maid folk of that world, in a cut form. A man named Blake watches her with thick voice and asks if she is free. He pays her price with no haggle and takes a flask for the wait at her hut. What his mind holds, and what hers does, is the knot the tale works loose.
53002-a-legend-of-goat-island:
A Legend of Goat Island is a poem by Peter Porter, printed at Niagara Falls, New York, in 1900, with sketches by Breckinridge Porter. The tale is ascribed to Father Louis Hennepin, who visited Niagara in 1678. Goat Island splits the tumultuous tides of the river at the brink of the great Fall.

Porter tells, in verse, an Indian tradition of how many a warrior's heart was stirred to belief by a priest's holy mission. The stranger is a giant of a man in a long loose robe of reddish brown, with a rosary at his waist. He is the first of his race the Neuter tribe has met face to face, and his coming to their village by the rapids sets the legend in motion.
53189-the-history-of-parliamentary-taxat:
The History of Parliamentary Taxation in England is a scholarly essay by Shepard Ashman Morgan. It is number two of the Williams College David Wells Prize Essays. Moffat, Yard and Company printed it in New York in 1911 for the college's department of political science. Morgan dedicates the book to his late teacher, Henry Loomis Nelson.

The work grew out of Nelson's course in English constitutional history, and some readings of events are the teacher's own. Nelson died before the second draft, and the revision went on without him. Morgan traces how Parliament gained control of taxation, from medieval grants to the modern budget. The essay is a compact study in constitutional history.
53230-ancient-streets-and-homesteads-of-:
Alfred Rimmer drew and wrote a book of old streets and homes of England. Howson, Dean of Chester, wrote its first words. The book came out in London in 1877. One hundred and fifty plates from Rimmer's hand fill it. Cooper cut those plates for the press with care.

Rimmer grants that great ruins draw warm crowds in his day. The Arch of Titus and the Pont du Gard prove his point. Homes and streets of less fame are his true theme here. Small towns keep the past in their walls more than courts do. Each walk pairs a drawn view with a told tale. Past fans get England's old face town by town.
53363-glue-gelatine-animal-charcoal-phos:
A technical handbook by F Dawidowsky, edited by William T Brannt. Henry Carey Baird published the second edition at Philadelphia in 1905. Dawidowsky was a technical chemist, and Brannt edited from the German. Extensive additions describe the most recent processes. Fifty-nine engravings illustrate apparatus and methods. The first edition had long been out of print.

Two parts divide the subject. Part one covers glue, gelatine, and allied products. Skin and bone glue, animal charcoal, and phosphorus come from the same raw trade. Isinglass and fish glue also get treatment, with testing methods. Part two turns to cements, pastes, and mucilages. Workshop, laboratory, and office uses guide the recipes. The book served manufacturers who turned slaughterhouse waste into industry.
53537-the-heart-of-scotland:
Hope Moncrieff described this heart of Scotland, painted by Sutton Palmer. Black printed the book in London in 1909 with colour plates. The Pass of Killiecrankie fronts the volume as first picture. Contents open with Perthshire and Tayside in first chapters.

Atholl, Breadalbane, and Strathearn follow across the highland heart. The Macgregors and Rob Roy and his sons take two chapters. Menteith closes the eight chapter tour of the region. Plates list Dunkeld, the Trossachs, Loch Tay, and the Falls of Tummel. Bonnie Scotland and the Highlands and Islands stand as her sister colour books listed.
53643-two-voyages-to-new-south-wales-and:
Two Voyages to New South Wales and Van Diemen's Land, by Thomas Reid, was printed in London in 1822. Reid was a surgeon in the Royal Navy and a member of the Royal College of Surgeons. The book is given to Elizabeth Fry, the prison reformer.

Reid says his late voyage in the Morley, a female convict ship, was made chiefly at her urging. The title page promises a picture of the colony as it then stood. Facts on the state and handling of convicts of both sexes fill much of the book. Reid adds reflections on seduction and its broad effects, a theme tied to the women's fate. His aim is reform: to show how the exiles were shipped, kept, and set to work.
53810-the-mysterious-basket-or-the-found:
The Mysterious Basket, or The Foundling is a story for boys and girls, published in London and Edinburgh by Gall and Inglis. Its fourteen chapters promise discovery, punishment, and reunion in the old tale manner. A second story, The Wood-Gatherer, shares the volume.

The first chapter is called The Unwelcome Discovery. It opens in a village where two inns compete, one merry and one sulky. Hicup, landlord of the lower inn, grumbles to his wife over her almanac. The village musician, the bird catcher, and the new fashioned nurse enter in turn. A journey on the ice, a sick bed, and a mistake build toward the unexpected discovery. The bad reception and the reunion close the foundling's arc. Such tales taught children that lost infants are restored and kindness repaid.
53843-oaths-of-allegiance-in-colonial-ne:
Oaths of Allegiance in Colonial New England, a study by Charles Evans, was reprinted from the Proceedings of the American Antiquarian Society for October 1921. The Society published it at Worcester, Massachusetts, in 1922. Evans collects the oath forms by which colonists bound themselves to king and colony.

The book first gives the English oaths: of supremacy, of allegiance for recusants, and of abjuration. It then prints the forms colony by colony. Plymouth gives the Mayflower Compact and the oaths of freemen and residents. Massachusetts Bay, Connecticut, and New Haven follow with their own freeman and fidelity oaths. Spelling and superscriptions are kept as the records left them.
53879-the-witches-dream-book-and-fortune:
The Witches' Dream Book and Fortune Teller was published in New York in eighteen eighty-five by Henry J Wehman. It stands as Universal Handbook number two. The title page promises full and correct rules of divination concerning dreams and visions. It also offers the foretelling of future events.

The rules apply, the title adds, to physiognomy, palmistry, moles, and cards. Talismans, charms, spells, and incantations are treated as well. The dream dictionary runs in alphabetical order from the start. To fight with an acquaintance in a dream signifies distraction. Almonds seen or eaten mean difficulties and trouble. The preface defends dreams with sacred and profane history alike. Wehman's cheap handbook put a gypsy's whole stock-in-trade into print for a few cents.
53899-eva-s-adventures-in-shadow-land:
Adventures in Shadow-Land binds two tales in one volume, printed at Philadelphia in 1874. Eva's Adventures in Shadow-Land, by Mary Nauman, fills the first part. The Merman and the Figure-Head, by Clara Guernsey, fills the second. A front plate shows a toad woman who stops fanning to look at her guest.

Eva, a girl who loves fairy tales, sits by an old mill pond after dinner and makes a tale for herself. Chapters follow her first adventure, a fountain gift, a magic boat, an enchanted river, and a green frog. Aster's fortunes and a door in a wall add wonder. The tales close with the last of Shadow-Land, in a gentle moral style for young readers.
5406-afoot-in-england:
W. H. Hudson records his walks across the English countryside in this travel book. The contents run from guide books and the pleasures of walking to Salisbury and its doves, Stonehenge, Bath and Wells, and summer days along the River Otter. Hudson moves on foot, stopping to watch birds, study old roads, and talk with people he meets.

Chapters on Roman Calleva, a cold day at Silchester, and an old road leading nowhere show his mix of natural history and quiet reflection. He writes with patience and close attention, finding interest in a cow, a hill, or a ruined wall. Readers get an unhurried walking companion and a portrait of rural England before modern roads changed it.
54222-blood-and-sand:
Blood and Sand, Blasco Ibanez's novel of the bullring, is kept here in Mrs Gillespie's translation from the Spanish, issued by Grosset and Dunlap under Dutton copyrights of 1919 and 1922. An opening essay on the author and Sangre y Arena sets the book in his shelf. The regional novels like La Barraca stand there, and the novels of purpose like La Catedral and this one. The inward studies and the war books complete the range.

The essay makes its case plainly. The style, and the book, is the man; his works are literary projections of a dynamic nature. The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse made his name in English. Fearless in denouncing evil, the essay says, he has lived his ideas as well as fashioned them. He reveals not only a new Spain but a new world. The novel of the torero follows the essay.
54260-the-spiritual-guidance-of-man-and-:
Rudolf Steiner lectured on the spiritual guidance of man and of mankind, in an authorized English translation edited by Collison in 1915. A man who reflects on his own nature, Steiner says, soon finds a second and more powerful self within him. At first that self feels lower than the conscious soul, bent to the good and true, and a man strives to overcome it.

Closer self examination may reveal something else about the second self. A survey of a life's acts and experiences brings a singular discovery. The older a man is, the more significant he finds it. Steiner builds his lectures on that hidden guide, and on great guiding beings behind human history as his teaching presents them.
54402-a-broken-journey-wanderings-from-t:
A Broken Journey is a travel book by Mary Gaunt, issued at London in 1919. Its subtitle traces the route from the Hoang Ho to the island of Saghalien and the upper reaches of the Amur river. Gaunt had written of West Africa and of a woman in China before this book. She dedicates it to her sister and brothers, in memory of days before they wandered.

Her first chapter, on the lure of the unknown, asks why she travels at all. The wander fever was born in her blood, she answers, and in her siblings' blood too. They were raised in an inland town in Victoria, Australia, and have roamed the world since. None has gone nearer the poles than set points she names. In many lands between, though, they have all wandered widely.
54474-new-zealand:
New Zealand, by Reginald Horsley, belongs to the Romance of Empire series edited by John Lang, with twelve color pictures by McCormick. A frontispiece shows Heke felling the flagstaff at Kororareka. Thirty chapters in three parts carry the islands from the coming of the Maori race to the Dominion.

Part one tells the old Maori world, its voyages, daily life, and wars. Part two brings the Dutch and then the British, Hongi Hika, and the signing at Waitangi. Part three fights through the wars of Heke, Kawiti, and Te Rauparaha to the sun of peace. It is imperial history told as romance for young readers.
54648-frank-reade-jr-and-his-engine-of-t:
Frank Reade Junior and His Engine of the Clouds, or Chased Around the World in the Sky, filled number 16 of the Frank Reade Weekly Magazine. Frank Tousey issued it at New York on February 13, 1903, at five cents. The tale is signed Noname. A detective orders a prisoner up a ladder to the airship on the cover line. The contents promise a stowaway, a light from the sky, and an oasis in the desert.

A tiger's jaws, the loss of a wheel, and a bombshell come before the conclusion. The story opens on a bitter March night in Chicago. A poor little boy in rags slinks along an aristocratic avenue, his face showing poverty and privation. The Reade weeklies fed boys a hero inventor, a wonderful machine, and a chase in every number.
54696-happy-england:
Happy England presents the watercolor art of Helen Allingham, with text by Marcus Huish. This Royal Canadian edition was limited to one thousand sets, issued at Montreal with Black of London. A portrait of the artist fronts the volume. Ten chapters run from the title theme through paintresses past and present, the artist's early work, and her Surrey home, to the influence of Witley and Tennyson's homes.

The picture list names the owners of the originals, a roll of collectors of the day. Subjects are pure Allingham: the market cross at Hagbourne, Milton's house at Chalfont, the Waller oak, apple and pear blossom, clothes-lines and clothes-baskets, a donkey ride and a goat carriage. Huish's text frames the cottages, gardens, and lanes that made her the painter of a vanishing rural England.
54767-the-hard-scrabble-of-elm-island:
The Hard-Scrabble of Elm Island is one of the Elm Island Stories by Elijah Kellogg. Lee and Shepard of Boston brought the book out in the year 1871. Kellogg had writ Lion Ben, Charlie Bell, and the Ark of Elm Island. John Andrew's picture of Ben junior trying his goad fronts the tale. This volume finds the boys entering upon manhood at its start.

Isaac at sea, John at the anvil, Fred in trade, Charlie in the shipyard. Integrity and energy have won them respect in their community by now. Fired by Lion Ben's success, they resolve to build a vessel together. Severe toil and make-shifts complete the hull, then their means fail. They weave canvas for sails on household looms to save the ship. A winter hunting and trapping in the forest depths follows that. Spring finds them fitting out for a voyage to Martinique.
54889-observations-of-a-naturalist-in-th:
Observations of a Naturalist in the Pacific, volume two, by Guppy, came out in London in 1906. The volume is subtitled Plant Dispersal. Guppy worked in Hawaii and Fiji between 1896 and 1899. He gives the book to those who helped him on his stay. A long list of papers on island plant life stands at the front. Plates show mangrove fruits and seedlings from Vanua Levu in Fiji.

The subject is how plants cross seas and stock far islands. Guppy draws on his own field notes and on other writers' studies. Tonga, Rarotonga, and French Polynesia all figure in his sources. The work suits readers of botany and island science. It shows patient field work turned into a general account of seed travel.
54896-my-adventure-in-the-flying-scotsma:
My Adventure in the Flying Scotsman is a railway romance by Eden Phillpotts. Hogg published it in London in 1888. Its subtitle promises a romance of railway shares. An introduction frames the tale. The meek little man at its centre told Phillpotts the story. Phillpotts made him narrate it in the first person.

The narrator is John Lott, a small banking clerk. His home waits in Kilburn with wife, daughter, and tea-cake. A sudden death has shaken his orderly existence. The first chapter calls it a dangerous legacy. Lott walks from Richmond to Petersham through a lurid sunset. The wet branches seem to drip with blood. Honour and duty, he warns, hang on the death beside his own interests.
54969-sound:
John Tyndall, the Irish physicist, wrote Sound, his classic set of lectures on how sound travels and how we hear it. The hosted edition is a New York printing by Collier and Son from 1902. Tyndall dedicated the book to the memory of his friend Richard Dawes, late Dean of Hereford.

The first chapter treats the birth and spread of sound. It covers tests with sounding bodies in a vacuum, the deadening effect of hydrogen, echoes, and the bending of sound through air of uneven heat. Tyndall works through Newton's count of the speed of sound and the fix Laplace gave it. Later pages turn to pitch, the tuning fork, and the siren. Students of physics get the science of music built up from plain trials.
55152-whale-fishery-of-new-england:
Whale Fishery of New England is an illustrated account printed at Boston in 1915. The State Street Trust Company published it. Its subtitle tells of the rise and fall of the trade. That trade made New England famous through the world, it says. A title vignette shows the ship Maria of New Bedford. She was built as a privateer in the Revolution. William Rotch of Nantucket bought her in 1783.

The Maria earned her owners a quarter of a million dollars. She made twenty-five voyages with full cargoes. The contents move from the whale itself to old whaling. Nantucket and New Bedford get their own chapters. Life aboard a blubber hunter is described next. Implements and whaleboats are treated in turn. Rare prints from local societies illustrate the pages. The book is a bank's gift to local history.
55320-the-voyage-of-the-arrow-to-the-chi:
The Voyage of the Arrow to the China Seas is a sea novel by T Jenkins Hains, published at Boston in nineteen hundred six. Six illustrations by H C Edwards appear in the book. The tale is set down by William Gore, chief mate of the Arrow, as its title states. Its adventures and perils include capture by sea vultures from a countess's ship.

A frontispiece shows the mate drawing a woman to him for a kiss, pointing to a love thread in the yarn. Hains was a steady writer of windjammer tales, and two sister books are listed at set prices. Storm, piracy, and shipboard honour carry the plot. Square rig romance for boys and men is the aim.
55413-antietam-national-battlefield-mary:
Antietam National Battlefield, Maryland, by Frederick Tilberg, is Historical Handbook number thirty one of the National Park Service, printed at Washington in 1960 and revised in 1961. The handbook series explains the historic and archeological areas of the park system in short, plain volumes for visitors.

The text walks the 1862 Maryland campaign step by step: the lost order, South Mountain, Harpers Ferry, the sunken road, and Burnside's bridge. It closes with Clara Barton at Antietam and a guide to the battlefield and cemetery. Photographs, including the Dunker Church, anchor the story to ground a visitor can still walk.
55564-lustra-of-ezra-pound:
Lustra, by Ezra Pound, was published in London in 1916. Elkin Mathews issued the poems from Cork Street. A photograph portrait by Coburn fronts the book. The title page defines its word: a lustrum was an offering for the sins of the whole people. Some poems had appeared in Poetry, Blast, and other magazines. Contents open with Tenzone and The Condolence. The Garret, The Garden, and A Pact follow. In a Station of the Metro stands at page 45, among longer pieces.

A full section named Cathay gathers versions from the Chinese. The River Merchant's Wife: A Letter is the best known of them. Song of the Bowmen of Shu and Lament of the Frontier Guard keep it company. Provincia Deserta and Near Perigord close the book in Provence.
55628-dealings-with-the-inquisition-or-p:
Dealings with the Inquisition is a work by the Rev. Giacinto Achilli. Its full title runs on: Papal Rome, Her Priests, and Her Jesuits, with weighty disclosures. Achilli states his past posts on the title page. He had been a prior and visitor of the Dominican Order and a head professor of theology. He had also been vicar of a high officer of the Sacred Apostolic Palace.

A line from the Psalms stands as the motto of the book: our soul has got free as a bird out of the net of the fowlers. The title page thus sets the frame of the work. It is an account by a man who had held high place in the Roman system and now writes of his dealings with its court of faith. The text was made from page pictures held by the Internet Archive.
55665-clergymen-of-the-church-of-england:
Anthony Trollope wrote Clergymen of the Church of England, ten keen essays. Each takes one rank of the cloth in turn for its theme. The Modern English Archbishop leads the sharp, kind array. Trollope knew that world from desk, hunt, and kin alike.

The old archbishop was a prince; the new is a prince no more. Canterbury still stands first peer of the realm in Parliament’s house. Yet wealth, reserve, and barred doors made the old awe, he shows. Becket and Wolsey held sway no churchman can hold in this age. Bishops old and new, the dean, and the archdeacon follow in turn. Parish parson and town incumbent take their own close studies. The college fellow in orders and the curate share the next pages. An Irish beneficed man and a Colenso backer close the set.
55862-the-industrial-history-of-england:
The Industrial History of England is a textbook by Gibbins, sometime scholar of Wadham College, Oxford. Methuen of London printed it, first in July 1890. This file holds the twenty-seventh edition of 1920. Five maps and a plan serve the text. Gibbins also won the Cobden prize in political economy at Oxford.

The contents divide England's working past into periods. The first covers England before the Norman Conquest. Gibbins grants that industrial history does not properly begin until the settlement the Conquest made. Still, he holds, some reference to the earlier centuries cannot be omitted. Edition after edition, the book carried school and university readers from guild and manor to mill and mine. Its thirty-year run of printings marks it as the standard short history of English industry.
55958-the-holy-land:
The Holy Land is a picture book of Palestine, painted by John Fulleylove and described by John Kelman. The house of Black published it in London. The first edition, with ninety-three illustrations, appeared in October 1902. A revised second edition, with thirty-two plates, followed in 1923.

The publishers warn that no attempt was made to describe changes after the war. The author revised and slightly abridged the text for the reissue. The book falls into three parts, of land, invaders, and spirit. The land part treats its colour, its desert, and its waters. Brown villages, white towns, and a grey city close that survey. The invaders part marches five conquerors across the same ground. Israelite, Graeco-Roman, Christian, Moslem, and Crusader follow in turn. The spirit of Syria, in lighter and darker moods, fills the final part.
56009-marjorie-in-command:
Marjorie in Command is a girls tale by Carolyn Wells, of the Patty books fame. The book stands in a line of tales of a bright young host at home. A print shows Marjorie at work on her own birth day cake. Rights date the work to the year nineteen ten.

A home confab opens the tale as a guest of rank is set to come. Flower greetings, card games, and a jinks party fill the bright first half. Willing aides, a home on Spruce Street, and a grand house mark the rise. A birth day plan swells to a fine feast and a plant box prize. Tree day rites and a spring walk close the gay school year tale.
56041-the-inevitable-crimes-of-celibacy-:
The Inevitable Crimes of Celibacy is a polemic by Thomas Watson of Georgia. Watson had written popular lives of Napoleon, Jackson, and Jefferson. His own Jeffersonian press printed the work at Thomson, Georgia, in 1916. The full title charges convents, monasteries, priests, and nuns with vice bred by enforced celibacy.

The first chapter argues that wrongdoing in the dress of righteousness is the hardest kind to punish. Watson then ranges far beyond his title. He claims that robbery dressed as law has ruined more peoples than any highwayman. Bank laws and tariff laws, he writes, beat down more victims than armies. Pirates never beggared provinces as law backed greed has done. The book joins his attacks on Rome to his wider populist case against money power.
56061-in-tamal-land:
In Tamal Land is an illustrated book of place by Helen Bingham, copyrighted in 1906 and published in San Francisco. Its subject is the Marin shore across the bay, the land under Mount Tamalpais. A dedication to the author's mother, the chum of her childhood and the friend of her youth, opens the volume.

The list of illustrations reads like a tour. It begins with the approach to Marin's shores and the ferry boats and landing. Main Street in Sausalito and its houses and club house come next. Then the road runs out past fishing boats and a wharf to the lighthouse at Point Bonita, with fog signals and views over the fog. Angel Island, hillside roads and gardens, and the great mountain seen from Mill Valley fill the plates. The book sells its home ground as a place of beauty at the city's gate.
56141-the-british-interned-in-switzerlan:
Picot, late British military attaché at Berne, ran the care of British prisoners of war held in Switzerland in the First World War. His book came out in London in 1919. Early chapters tell how Switzerland stood at the outbreak of war and how talks began on sending sick and wounded men there.

Later chapters give the full working of the scheme. They cover the Red Cross bureaus at Berne, the first train loads of men from Germany, and Swiss rules for the camps. Picot treats hospitals, surgery, work, trade schools, church care, sport, and visits from kin. He also notes the strain that long waiting laid on men's minds. The book stands as the record of the man in charge.
56364-the-flight-of-georgiana-a-story-of:
Robert Neilson Stephens's The Flight of Georgiana, a story of love and peril in England in 1746, was published by Page and Company of Boston in August 1905, with pictures by Edwards. Stephens's historical romances stand listed at the front, An Enemy to the King and Philip Winwood among them. An old ballad gives the motto: death itself cannot stop a lover on his way.

The sixteen chapters carry one-word heads, a plot in miniature: Enemies, Friends, Knaves, Fugitives, Risks, Thanks, Kisses, Threats, Swords, Wagers, Proposals, Tears, Surprises, Roads, Pistols, Horses. The frontispiece catches a rustic voice asking what the county would say to a bit of writing shown about. The year 1746 sets the flight in the aftermath of the Jacobite rising, with the road as the place of peril.
56429-gray-days-and-gold-in-england-and-:
William Winter, the American critic, gathered his British travel pieces in this volume. Macmillan published a new edition, revised and illustrated, at New York in 1896. He dedicated the book to Augustin Daly, remembering a friendship of many years. The preface is dated July 15, 1896, and opens in the country of Burns and Scott. Winter pleads an irresistible impulse of reverence and affection for the ancestral home.

His hope is that American travellers in Britain will bring home more than sights. The supreme need of the age in America, he argues, is a conviction that progress is not material prosperity but spiritual advancement. Utility has long been exclusively worshipped; the future lies in the worship of beauty. York Cathedral stands among the illustrations. The essays muse over relics of a storied past, in the line of Washington Irving, whom Winter salutes as having done it before him.
56441-analysis-of-the-phenomena-of-the-h:
Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind is a work of philosophy by James Mill. Longmans published this second edition in London in 1878. John Stuart Mill edited it with added notes.

Alexander Bain, Andrew Findlater, and George Grote supply critical notes. The book breaks mental life into simple parts and laws. It argues that complex feelings and thoughts grow from basic ones. This method is called association, since ideas link by habit. James Mill helped found a school of British thought. His son's edition kept the work in debate for decades.
56619-general-history-of-connecticut-fro:
A General History of Connecticut is Samuel Peters' account of the colony, first printed at London in 1781. Appleton reissued it at New York in 1877 with notes by McCormick. Peters was a clergyman of the province, though the title page says only a gentleman of it. His history runs from the first settlement under George Fenwick. It ends with the last period of amity with Britain before the Revolution.

The preface complains that Connecticut had found no writer of its own. Other provinces and general histories gave it only slight mention. Peters adds a description of the country and many curious anecdotes. An appendix points out the causes of the rebellion in America. It also sets out the part Connecticut's people took in promoting it. The 1877 editor added letters verifying many of the author's statements.
5675-the-holiday-round:
A. A. Milne's Holiday Round, published in London in 1912, gathers light pieces about holidays, housewarmings, games, and small accidents of leisure. Its contents run from Holiday Time and The House-Warming through At Play, Two Stories, An Odd Lot, and Little Plays for Amateurs, ending with an epilogue. The opening piece finds the narrator woken from a pleasant dream by a voice insisting that everyone must bathe at once.

The charm lies in Milne's gentle comedy of friends at ease: plans go slightly wrong, meals loom large, and a simple outing becomes a small drama. Readers who know Milne only from children's books will meet the same wit turned on grown-up holidays, with dialogue that carries most of the fun. It is an easy, companionable book, best read a piece at a time, like a holiday itself.
5678-heroic-romances-of-ireland-translat:
Leahy presents early Irish heroic tales in English, with a preface, introductions, and notes that argue for their place beside the literatures of Greece and Rome. He insists these old legends are not mere curiosities for scholars. They carry some of the oldest stories of modern Europe. They were written in a land outside Roman rule, by a people who kept Celtic legend alive. The volume draws on old manuscripts, including the Book of Leinster version of the great cattle raid, the Tain bo Cuailnge.

Readers meet heroes, queens, cattle raids, and fierce loyalties, told in prose with verse renderings nearby. The notes explain where each tale came from and how its manuscripts differ, so a newcomer can follow the story while a careful reader can see the sources. For anyone curious about Irish myth before modern retellings, this is a direct route to the tales themselves.
5679-heroic-romances-of-ireland-translat:
Volume two of Leahy's Heroic Romances of Ireland gathers five shorter tales that lead up to the great Tain: the Tain bo Dartada, Flidais, Fraich, Regamon, and Regamna. Each tale is given in verse with a literal prose rendering set beside it, and a short introduction explains its manuscript source. The last four are called remscela, or preludes, to the Tain, while the longer Fraich tale stands well on its own.

Readers meet Queen Maev and King Ailill planning a raid, young princes sent to harry Regamon, and the cattle, daughters, and honor at stake in Cualnge's war. One ending even differs from the main Tain account, claiming Cuchulain was defeated and Connaught gained ground, which shows how freely these tales varied. The volume suits readers who want the Irish cycle in its early, many-voiced form.
5680-heroic-romances-of-ireland-translat:
Leahy's translation of early Irish heroic romance returns in this companion portion of the first volume, again pairing verse renderings with literal prose so readers can compare the two. Its manuscript notes give weight to the Book of Lecan. That fourteenth-century source stands beside the older Book of Leinster. The text is arranged in parts, so the great Tain material and its related tales stand in clear order. Introductions before each tale explain the manuscripts behind it.

The tales themselves concern cattle raids, champions, and kings, with Cuchulain at the center of the Cualnge war. Reading them in this form shows both the story and the scholarship. The verse carries the drama, while the prose keeps the meaning plain. The notes mark where manuscripts agree or part ways. It suits readers who want Irish myth in its early shape, not smoothed into a single modern novel.
56940-mycen-a-narrative-of-researches-an:
Mycenae is a tale of digs and finds at two old Greek sites by Doctor Henry Schliemann. A fresh form with new plates came out in eighteen eighty, past the first of three years past. A prime head of the realm wrote the front note. Maps, plans, and past seven hundred plates fill the book.

Schliemann was known for past books on Troy and on the far east. The front plate shows a great vault tomb by the famed Lions Gate, dug out by his wife. The book is given to an emperor of a far land with deep thanks. Lines of the old Greek poets head the work, on the gold rich town of the tale and its kings. The digs sought the world of those poems in the earth.
57045-the-knights-of-england-france-and-:
The Knights of England, France, and Scotland by Henry William Herbert, published by Redfield in New York in 1852, gathers tales under the heading Legends of Love and Chivalry. Groups cover the Norman conquerors, the crusaders, feudal days, and Scotland, ending with passages in the life of Mary Stuart: Chastelar, Rizzio, the Kirk of Field, Bothwell, and the captivity. The first tale, The Saxon's Oath, opens with Harold, son of Godwin, flower of the Saxon race.

Harold seeks Edward the Confessor's leave to cross the Channel and free the Saxon hostages held by William of Normandy. Herbert also wrote The Cavaliers of England and The Roman Traitor.
57188-beautiful-lakeland:
Beautiful Lakeland is a guide to the English Lake District by Ashley Abraham. Abraham of Keswick published it in the year 1912 for walkers. Thirty two full page monogravure plates show the lakes and fells. His brother of Keswick took those photographs across the district in seasons. A motto from Wordsworth fronts it: who comes not hither knows not beauty.

Contents open with an appreciation: the cause and history of Lakeland. Windermere and Ambleside, Grasmere and Rydal, fill the next chapters in turn. Thirlmere, Derwentwater, and Bassenthwaite follow in the northern lake round. The Buttermere round and Ullswater with Helvellyn come after in order. Kirkstone Pass closes the high ground of Abraham's loving survey.
57254-good-morning-rosamond:
Constance Lindsay Skinner published this novel with Doubleday, Page of Garden City in 1917, with illustrations by Thomas Fogarty: Good-Morning, Rosamond! Its heroine is Rosamond Mearely, the richest and fairest woman in the village of Roseborough, and a widow whose dead husband's name is still spoken with pride.

Roseborough is a formal place: negligees are unknown there, and even at seven in the morning the ladies dress fully rather than appear in kimonos. Rosamond rules her house over the formidable Frigget sisters, Amanda and Jemima, her maids. A coloured frontispiece carries the book's keynote, that when one is to have perhaps only one wonderful day, deciding how to spend each moment of it is important. The illustrations promise knitting neighbours, a man crawling through an orchard, and a weather-tanned stranger.
57268-oliver-cromwell-and-the-rule-of-th:
Oliver Cromwell and the Rule of the Puritans in England is Charles Firth's biography of the Lord Protector. G P Putnam's Sons of New York and London published it in 1900. It belongs to the Heroes of the Nations series, edited by Evelyn Abbott of Balliol College, Oxford. A portrait from the National Portrait Gallery illustrates the volume.

Firth opens with Cromwell's own words to one of his Parliaments: he was by birth a gentleman, living neither in any considerable height nor yet in obscurity. The family was one of many that rose to wealth and importance at the Reformation. It owed its name and fortune to Thomas Cromwell, Earl of Essex, Henry the Eighth's minister and the destroyer of the monasteries. Firth, the leading Cromwell scholar of his day, compressed a lifetime's study into this series volume.
57544-history-of-texas-land:
History of Texas Land came out at Austin in 1958. Bill Allcorn wrote its preface as land commissioner. The book treats the state's General Land Office. A photo shows the old office building about 1890. That house stands by the Capitol grounds' southeast corner. It is among Austin's oldest houses still up.

Doctor C C Stremme drew its plans in 1854. He had held a title at the Russian emperor's court. German Romance shapes the stone house, built 1856 to 1857. William S Porter worked there as a draftsman thirty years on. Readers know him as the tale writer O Henry. He set one story in that very building. Land history and a famed clerk meet in this state-published record of Texas ground.
57562-painting-by-immersion-and-by-compr:
Arthur Seymour Jennings, editor of The Decorator, wrote this practical handbook on painting by dipping and by compressed air, published by Spon at London and New York in 1915 with 150 illustrations. The frontispiece shows a piano being lowered on its carrier into a varnish tank. Jennings argues that dipping, spraying, and flowing-on save enormous time over the brush, and give coats more durable and thorough.

A complete coat of enamel, he says, can be given to the body of a four-seated touring car in an almost incredibly short time by the flowing-on process. The book was written for manufacturers whose paint bill was a serious item, and for the painters and engineers who served them. It marks the moment when the spray gun began to displace the brush in industry.
57588-index-for-the-project-gutenberg-se:
Volunteers compiled this index for the Abbott American pioneers series. Twelve volumes of John Abbott lives stand listed in order here. Christopher Columbus heads the set, Ferdinand De Soto second. Chevalier de La Salle and Miles Standish follow in the list.

Captain William Kidd, Peter Stuyvesant, and Benjamin Franklin come next. George Washington, Daniel Boone, and Christopher Carson fill the middle. Admiral John Paul Jones and David Crockett close the dozen lives. A Filson Young Columbus life fills the first volume slot here. Linked tables of contents for each volume stand ready in the index for readers.
57597-the-last-million-how-they-invaded-:
Ian Hay wrote The Last Million, How They Invaded France and England, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in nineteen nineteen. Hay gave the book to the American Doughboy, whom he calls a born fighter and modern crusader. Sixteen chapters fill the book, from The Argonauts to Gallia Victrix. Hay had earlier written The First Hundred Thousand and Pip, a Romance of Youth.

Early chapters show the ship company, the lower deck, and the danger zone at sea. Later chapters treat strange isles, three musketeers in London, and the promised land. The line, the Forest of the Argonne, and the eleventh hour bring the tale to the front. Hay writes with wit and warmth of the last vast draft of American troops in the Great War. Soldiers and home folk alike will find pride and humour in the tale.
57599-the-heart-of-england:
The Heart of England, by Edward Thomas, was published in London in 1909 and dedicated to Henry Nevinson. Front matter for the series calls Thomas a curious and keen explorer of the English countryside, and the heir, as a prose writer, of Richard Jefferies, whose life he wrote. The book first came out in a limited edition at a guinea.

Parts move from Leaving Town into the lowland, with chapters named Faunus, Not Here O Apollo, and Walking with Good Company. No Man's Garden and March Doubts show Thomas's mix of close nature notes and quiet doubt. He walks the southern counties in all seasons, turning paths, farms, and weather into a prose poem of rural England on the edge of change.
57715-footsteps-of-dr-johnson-scotland:
George Birkbeck Hill wrote Footsteps of Dr Johnson, the Scotland volume. Sampson Low and partners issued the book in London in eighteen hundred ninety. Lancelot Speed drew the views that crowd its bright pages. Hill gives the work to the Johnson Club of Fleet Street fame.

Johnson’s Scots tour of seventeen hundred seventy three grounds the whole book. Three tales of that tour stand in print for Hill to walk by. Johnson’s own Journey and his letters to Mrs Thrale make two. Boswell’s Journal of the Hebrides tour makes the third account. Each was penned apart, and Hill keeps them apart in his plan. No weave of the three would suit his taste, he owns in print. Place by place, he tracks the great man’s road through the north. A mate book for England and Wales waits on this one’s fate.
57753-the-flower-fields-of-alpine-switze:
G Flemwell painted and wrote The Flower Fields of Alpine Switzerland, part love song and part plea. Hutchinson and Company issued the book in London in nineteen hundred eleven. Twenty six prints of his water colours fill the pages. Flemwell had written Alpine Flowers and Gardens before this.

Champex and its high fields star in most of the views. May fields bloom with marsh marigold and bird’s eye primrose. The spring gentian gets a chapter of close praise. June meadows, haymaking, and pink bistort evenings follow in turn. A rhododendron chapter and the fall crocus close part one. Part two pleads for alpine fields in England itself. Flemwell wants such bloom saved here and grown at home. Loves of the high meadows thus turns into plain work for them.
57921-the-man-with-the-iron-hand:
John Carl Parish wrote this true tale of the Great Valley, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1913. Shambaugh edited the series, True Tales of the Great Valley, for young readers. A plate shows La Salle taking possession of land in the name of the King of France.

Parish asks readers to picture the history of the Mississippi valley as a splendid drama. Its giant stage reaches from the Alleghanies to the Rockies, he writes in the opening. It runs from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico, with the Father of Waters flowing through, and La Salle, the man with the iron hand, at its center.
57975-excavating-a-husband:
Ella Bell Wallis's Excavating a Husband was published at Baltimore by the McLean Company under a copyright of 1916. The story opens at home. Katherine Boulby has reached her fiftieth year, all of it spent single, and the narrator finds her blessed among women for it.

Miss Katherine lives with her brother Joseph, a quiet, fairly pliant man who rarely crosses her plans. Mental culture is her chief aim in life, and not a selfish one: she gives her knowledge freely, and works to correct and purify the tastes of her friends. Versatile as the great geniuses, she strays from path to path in the labyrinth of learning, in all likelihood lost in it, and happy there. The narrator insists she is no blue-stocking, but a most charming person.
58016-peeps-at-many-lands-newfoundland:
Ford Fairford wrote the Newfoundland volume of the Peeps at Many Lands series for young readers. The book came out in London in 1912. Twelve full page plates in colour, by Lowther, show the land and its coasts.

Fairford calls Newfoundland the oldest British colony at the start. He then sketches the folk who live there and their traits. Chapters cover the perils of the sea and home life in the outports. The great fisheries get a full chapter of their own. Timber and minerals point to wealth on land. The book gives a clear first portrait of the island. A trip across the island rounds out the tour.
58081-the-french-in-algiers-the-soldier-:
Two first hand accounts of French Algeria are joined in this volume, translated from the German and French by Lady Duff Gordon. John Murray published it in London in eighteen fifty five. The larger share belongs to Clemens Lamping, a young Oldenburg lieutenant. He resigned his commission in eighteen thirty nine, missed the Spanish war, and sailed to Algiers to join the Foreign Legion.

Lamping's chapters mix barracks life with notes on Arab coffee houses, courts, marriages, and towns from Coleah to Blidah. Hard fighting against the Kabyles and a shipwreck fill out his two years of service. The second narrative comes from a French naval lieutenant named de France. It tells of five months as a prisoner among the Arabs under Abd-el-Kader. Together the pieces show France's conquest of Algeria in its rough early years, from inside the ranks.
58308-a-description-of-greenland:
Hans Egede, who was a missionary in Greenland for twenty five years, wrote A Description of Greenland. A new second edition with a historical intro and a life of the author was printed in London in eighteen eighteen. T and J Allman and others sold the book. A map of Greenland and many wood engravings aid the text. A plate shows old Greenland in its eastern and western parts.

Chapter one treats the place and extent of Greenland and the chance that it forms part of America. Chapter two treats the first settlement and the loss of the old Norwegian colonies. Later chapters treat soil, plants, minerals, and climate. Land beasts, birds, and how folk hunt and kill them follow in order. Readers get an early, close account of a hard northern land and its people.
58310-john-lackland:
Kate Norgate wrote John Lackland, a life of King John, issued by Macmillan and Company in London and New York in nineteen oh two, with maps. Sidenotes giving years stand at the starts of paragraphs. Footnotes stand at the ends of chapters. Maps carry keys in their plate descriptions. Norgate keeps old spellings of names, with a few plain printer errors mended.

John, called Lackland, ruled England in a time of loss, tax, and revolt. Norgate traces his reign from his youth and quarrels to the loss of lands in France and strife with barons and church. Her method is close and sourced, with dates pinned to each event in the margin. Students of medieval England value Norgate for care and for a fair mind on a much blamed king. Readers get a full life in measured, learned prose.
58370-the-boy-from-green-ginger-land:
E Vaughan-Smith wrote this tale for the young, printed by Wells Gardner, Darton and Company of London. She had written Crags of Duty. A plate shows a crowd gathered to watch Micky. Three children and a dog open the book at Fir-Tree Cottage, and a feudal castle follows.

Micky, eight years old and full of dignity, argues over which story to act out, urging Swiss Family Robinson. Diamond Jubilee Jones joins the cast, with trials of philanthropy and an omnibus of nuts. Bad news, a spare room of blankets, and a trip to the fair fill the middle. Green Ginger Land itself waits for chapter fourteen. The tale ends with Diamond Jubilee adopted for the second time.
586-religio-medici-hydriotaphia-and-the-:
Thomas Browne meditates on faith, death, and friendship in this volume of three seventeenth-century works, edited by J. W. Willis Bund. Religio Medici sets out Browne's personal religion with learned wit; Hydriotaphia, or Urn Burial, reflects on Roman urns dug in Norfolk; a Letter to a Friend counsels a sick man.

Browne writes in vigorous, rugged prose, a tissue of many tongues, as Johnson later put it. His style strikes more than it soothes, yet it rewards slow reading. The book serves as a classic of English meditation, where a physician-philosopher weighs belief against the grave.
58894-witchcraft-second-sight-in-the-hig:
John Gregorson Campbell, minister of Tiree, collected tales of witchcraft and second sight in the Highlands and Islands of Scotland entirely from oral sources. Press opinions at the front praise his earlier book on Highland superstitions. The border line of fairyland once crossed is a bourne from which few antiquaries return, one critic jokes.

Campbell is said to stand in the innermost secrets of the elfin folk. His Popular Tales of the West Highlands are full, yet critics hold this plainer work richer still. Misty legend, wayward romance, and quaint realism mark the Celtic supernatural in his pages. Some tales appear in other versions elsewhere, but most are printed here for the first time, a rich mine for the folklorist.
58914-the-white-eagle-of-poland:
Benson's The White Eagle of Poland was copyrighted in 1919 by Doran at New York. Benson also wrote Crescent and Iron Cross. The book falls in two parts: the reconstruction of Poland, and the German occupation. Part one treats Poland and Mittel-Europa, Poland under the partitions, Poland and the Entente, and Poland's place in the new Europe. Part two covers the Russian proclamation, the first year of German occupation, attempted solutions, and the Polish Legions.

The first chapter admits that few educated English readers in 1914 could place Poland on the map, beyond knowing the Tsar was also its king. Benson argues that the settlement of the Polish question will show which side truly won the war. Even a peace restoring Belgium and Alsace-Lorraine, he says, leaves Germany the winner if Poland is arranged to her eastward design. The book is a wartime brief for a real Polish state.
5897-castle-richmond:
Anthony Trollope sets Castle Richmond in Ireland, opening with a direct address to novel readers. He wonders whether readers will be offended if he lays his plot in Ireland, noting a strong feeling against things Irish that cannot be denied. Irish servants need not apply, he observes, and Irish acquaintances are treated with limited confidence, yet he proceeds to tell an Irish story anyway.

Readers follow the barony of Desmond through famine, landlords, and family secrets, with Trollope's steady attention to character and society. The novel favors domestic drama over political tract, letting Irish life speak through its people. It suits readers of Trollope, Irish historical fiction, and novels that face prejudice while telling a compelling family tale.
59180-rubble-and-roseleaves-and-things-o:
Boreham, a much loved essayist, gathered these short pieces under the title Rubble and Roseleaves and Things of That Kind. The Abingdon Press printed the book in 1923. Three parts hold twenty-one essays in all, each built on some small, homely thing.

Old envelopes, a front-door bell, a green chair, and new brooms start the set. Boreham says he has a gift for a snug chair, a bright fire, and good company. Odd volumes, old photographs, a box of blocks, and piecrust fill later parts. One piece takes its text from the tale of a good wife and a brave ship. Plain things turn, in his hands, into thoughts on how to live.
59253-attack-of-fortified-places-includi:
James Mercur, who taught civil and army works at West Point, wrote Attack of Fortified Places for cadets of the United States Military Academy. John Wiley and Sons issued the book in New York in 1894. It deals with how an army takes a strong place by storm, surprise, blockade, or siege.

Mercur gives standard forms for trenches, gun pits, stores, and mines, drawn from schools at Chatham, Fontainebleau, Vienna, and Berlin. Old sieges such as Vicksburg, Paris, and Plevna show why such work still counts in an age of fast field wars. Notes on shells and mines by General Abbot add test based detail to the text.
59363-ecology-on-rollins-island:
Varley Lang wrote this short story, printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in August 1955. Earth strips every resource to feed its millions, and George is a throwback and a poacher whose punishment must fit his crime. The teller spends his days in a run-down library near Charles Neck on Murdock Sound, reading old stiff-backed books left on the shelves.

Since the WFI took over the Sound, he has had little to do by day. From his reading he has built himself into a one-man resistance, a thing he grants is pitiful and foolish. He tried to be forward and found himself hard to live with, and he lives mostly with himself. Backwardness, he knows, will not be forgiven in a world that wastes nothing.
59714-blacks-and-bushrangers-adventures-:
Blacks and Bushrangers is a book of adventures in Queensland, Australia. Kennedy wrote it, having also written Four Years in Queensland before. Sampson Low published it in London in the year 1889. Stanley Berkeley drew the illustrations for the adventure record. A front plate names a place called Dromoora in the wild interior.

Kennedy recounts travel, hunting, and peril in a raw colonial frontier. Encounters with Aboriginal people and with bushrangers frame the title's promise. Queensland in those years was a land of cattle, gold, and distance. London readers craved true tales from that far, rough edge of empire. Kennedy served them hardship and narrow escapes from his own years there.
59746-historic-ornament-vol-1-of-2-treat:
A great work on old ornament treats the art of dress for stone and wall. Volume one holds the first half of that wide theme. A plate shows the choragic stone of Lysikrates at its front. Full plates crowd the book, moved here to sit by their text. The work is a treatise, as its sub-title in full says.

Greek, Roman, and east forms of carve and hue fill its scope. Each age's mark is drawn, named, and set in its line. Build men and art men share its worth in their trades. Rules grow from true old work, not from mere taste. Such books taught a whole age to dress its halls well. Plates do half the work of the text.
59874-around-the-end:
Around the End, by Ralph Henry Barbour, was published in New York in 1913. Appleton issued the school story that year. Twenty six chapters make the book. Chapter one is called The First Scrimmage. Coach Payson calls the squad together with his small blue megaphone. Veterans, second team men, and new boys pant in from all parts of the gridiron. Cotton tries football in chapter three. A launch rescue in fog and a wager fill the early middle.

Gerald maps a campaign, and Harry scents a mystery. A spy and a foiled Broadwood raise the stakes. A fumble, a remembered clue, and two sheets of buff paper turn the plot. The title play, around the end, wins its chapter near the close. Barbour writes prep school football with a mystery threaded through the season.
5992-station-amusements-in-new-zealand:
Lady Barker continues her account of settler life in New Zealand, turning from practical matters to the idler hours. Her earlier Station Life had pleased readers with a simple, true picture of everyday days, and this sequel answers friends who kept asking how she amused herself up at the station.

The book opens with a bush picnic in a valley of the Malvern Hills of Canterbury, where picnics ranked among favorite amusements. Barker writes for readers with friends and relations in those distant islands, eager to know what sort of life their absent dear ones led. The tone is cheerful and unforced.
59930-walled-in-a-true-story-of-randall-:
Walled In, a True Story of Randall's Island, is a boys' book by William Stoddard. The Revell Company published it in New York, Chicago, and Toronto. Copyright was taken in 1897, and the printing followed two years later. Stoddard had written Dab Kinzer and other tales for boys before it.

The high stone wall of the title opens the contents at once. Supper time, evening visitors, and life behind bolts and bars follow. A boy named Jim forms a plot for liberty in the fifth chapter. One plan fails, new ideas come, and the wall is crossed at last. Stolen money gives the closing chapters their final complication. The opening chapter surveys the islands scattered at the Hudson's mouth. Randall's Island, with its walled institution for children, is the scene throughout.
59971-historic-ornament-vol-2-of-2-treat:
Historic Ornament, volume two, is a treatise on decorative art by James Ward. Chapman and Hall issued it in London in 1897. It carries 317 illustrations. Ward also wrote The Principles of Ornament. The preface says this volume continues the former one. The first treated ornament in its broad history. This one turns to the minor arts in detail.

Pottery, enamels, and ivories are named on the title page. Metal work, furniture, and textile fabrics follow. Mosaics, glass, and book decoration complete the list. Goldsmiths', silversmiths', and jewellers' work are covered. A Venetian book border of 1470 serves as a specimen. Ward tells students to read both volumes together. Some minor arts are only touched in the first. This volume gives them their full treatment. It served art schools of the late Victorian age.
59985-cuba-and-her-people-of-to-day-an-a:
Cuba and Her People of To Day is a survey book by Forbes Lindsay. Page of Boston issued it in a uniform peoples of to day series. Panama, Brazil, Guatemala, Mexico, and Argentina volumes stand beside it there. Each sold at three dollars, pictured from original and selected photographs.

Lindsay gives the island history and progress before its independence first. Physical features of Cuba follow, then a study of its people in depth. Present politics, industries, natural resources, and prospects get close treatment after. Facts and hints aim to aid the would be investor or settler there. A Cuban courtship plate is listed among the book pictures within.
60102-wanderer-of-the-wasteland:
Zane Grey's Wanderer of the Wasteland was printed in Canada in 1923 by the Musson Book Company, with Harper & Brothers in New York and drawings by Herbert Dunton. Grey gave the book to his wife, Lina Elise Grey, in words of love and thanks. Thirty chapters carry the tale, and the frontispiece shows a girl whose red lips curl in scorn.

Grey was by then the best-known western writer in America, with Riders of the Purple Sage and The Man of the Forest on the same list page. The desert of the title is his ground: lone men, hard travel, and love tested far from towns. Readers who know his earlier books will find the same wide, dry stage here.
60153-winter-sports-in-switzerland:
Winter Sports in Switzerland is E F Benson's guide to the Alpine winter season. George Allen and Company published it in London in 1913. Twelve full-page colour illustrations by C Fleming Williams accompany it. Mrs Aubrey Le Blond contributed forty-seven photographs. The Eiger, from Fleming Williams's drawing, fronts the book. Eight chapters cover the sports in turn.

The Sun-Seeker opens with the resorts themselves. Rinks and Skaters treats English and Continental skating styles. Tees and Crampits is the curling chapter, named for its gear. Tobogganing follows, dominated by the Cresta Run at St Moritz. Its Church Leap and Battledore Corner are illustrated repeatedly. Ice-hockey gets a short chapter, then ski-ing a long one. The Telemark turn and the jump appear in colour plates. Notes on winter resorts give practical guidance by place. A closing chapter addresses parents and guardians.
60247-a-tour-of-historic-richmond:
Whittet and Shepperson of Richmond published this tour of the historic city, its illustrations copyrighted in 1940, under the heading Richmond, Her Story and Her Spirit. The opening survey calls Richmond capital of the Cavaliers, mellow and yet modern, where the rustle of the past is heard amid the bustle of the present.

Richmond was founded in 1737 by William Byrd the Second of Westover, on the James. The site mattered earlier, though. Weeks after the Jamestown landing of May 13, 1607, Captain Newport pushed up the river and found his way to the Indies blocked by the falls of the James. The survey recalls Patrick Henry's liberty-or-death speech at Saint John's Church in 1775, Benedict Arnold's raid of 1781, and Jefferson's flight from capture. Hotels William Byrd, John Marshall, Richmond, and King Carter are named for visitors, with Broad Street Station and Capitol Square pictured.
6039-stories-by-english-authors-england:
Seven English tales open with Charles Reade's Box Tunnel, where the 10:15 train glides from Paddington on 7 May 1847. In a first-class carriage sit four passengers, two worth description, including a lady with a smooth white brow, strongly marked eyebrows, and eyes that seem to change color.

The volume adds F. W. Robinson's Minions of the Moon, Amelia Edwards's Four-Fifteen Express, Angelo Lewis's Wrong Black Bag, Thomas Hardy's Three Strangers, Wilkie Collins on Mr. Lismore and the widow, and Anthony Hope's philosopher in the apple orchard. Each story offers a compact English scene, from railways to country houses.
6040-stories-by-english-authors-ireland:
Irish tales open with Samuel Lover's Gridiron, where an old gentleman in the west of Ireland loves the ridiculous as much as claret and fox-hunting. On festive occasions he draws out a servant fond of his travels, a trusty domestic who will correct his master, saying plainly, throth you won't, sir, when a rash dismissal is threatened.

George Jessop's Emergency Men, Jane Barlow's Lost Recruit, John Banim's Rival Dreamers, William Carleton's Neal Malone, and the anonymous Banshee follow. The collection favors humor, talk, and country character, with servants and squires trading wit across the Irish countryside.
6045-the-hollow-of-her-hand:
George Barr McCutcheon opens in March, as a train roars through a withering gale of sleet up from New York and halts with ear-splitting sighs beside a little station. A reluctant porter steps down, and the chapters that follow promise Hetty Castleton, a mob waiting, a faithful crayon point, and Hetty weighed.

Later come Hawkwright's model, the ghost at the feast, a man named Smith, Mr. Wrandall's perjury, and Sara Wrandall finding the truth. The hollow of her hand gives the book its title and its central image. McCutcheon mixes society drama with mystery, letting a woman's hand hold the clue.
60645-new-zealand:
New Zealand is a large illustrated volume published by Adam and Charles Black in London in 1908. The pictures are by the painters Wright, and the text is by William Pember Reeves. Reeves was then High Commissioner for New Zealand in London. The title page carries a Latin line meant for an epic that was never written.

The chapters survey the islands and their cities first. They then take up country life, sport and athletics, the forest, and fire and water. A chapter on alps, fiords, and sanctuaries follows, and one on the outlying islands. An appendix offers a word to the tourist. The plates show lakes Wakatipu and Te-Anau, Maori villages, tree ferns, and harbor towns. The book is an official-age portrait of the young dominion, handsome enough to recruit visitors and settlers alike.
60658-old-houses-in-holland:
Old Houses in Holland, with text and drawings by Sydney R Jones, was edited by Charles Holme and issued by The Studio in London, Paris, and New York in MCMXIII. Colour plates after other artists add to Jones own work. The front plate shows a Dutch house interior by Pieter de Hooch. A plate after Johannes Vermeer shows a woman reading a letter.

Inside, Jones tours old Dutch homes town by town, from Breda in North Brabant onward. He notes thanks to museum staff in Amsterdam, Leeuwarden, Dordrecht, and Middelburg for their help. Plates show tiled rooms, Delft dishes, and snug Hindeloopen rooms. Readers who love old homes, Dutch art, and fine rooms will find a rich store of views and facts.
60694-virgin-ground:
Rosel George Brown wrote this short story, printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in February 1959. Annie has signed on a bride ship for Mars. Forty brides sail, and the hook of the tale is plain: when they land, only thirty-nine men wait. The pilot hands out oxygen masks as the women step down, since the air, though fit to breathe for fifteen years, runs thin for new throats.

Annie goes first, big, plain, and brave, with a grin set hard for the rest. She had led girls at summer camps and knows how to steady a crowd. Light gravity lifts her heavy suitcase. Then she spots the men counting the women, and prays the short count will not fall on her.
60914-prometheus-illbound:
Prometheus Illbound is a tale by Andre Gide, turned to English by Lilian Rothermere. A Chatto and Windus house of London brought it out in nineteen nineteen. Its front tag asks, eagle, vulture, or dove, in the words of Victor Hugo. In May of an eighteen nine year, a fat gent drops a cloth on a Paris walk. A thin gent picks it up and pens a note cover at his ask.

Then the fat man slaps his face in thanks and flees by cab at once. That fat man was Zeus the bank man, the tale voice learns in time. Prometheus, bored by chains and qualms on his crag, walks that same walk. A tale of lone morals is the next name the book gives that stroll. Street chance, free acts, and their costs drive the scheme from there.
60959-john-chinaman-on-the-rand:
John Chinaman on the Rand is an eye witness charge against Chinese labor on South African gold fields. R A Everett and Son issued the book in London in nineteen hundred five. John Clifford wrote its front note with grief and heat. A front plate shows a new form of torture, it says.

The writer saw the import of Chinese coolies with his own eyes. Clifford calls the tale one of the foulest woes in British annals. Sifted proof, he says, fills page after page of the book. Parliament let the wrong stand, the charge runs on. Four plates show scenes from the Rand compounds and mines. Hotel ads for Port Elizabeth and Cape Town crowd the front leaves. Those gay leaves jar hard against the tale of wrong that follows.
6104-station-life-in-new-zealand:
Lady Barker writes Station Life in New Zealand as letters from the wife of a sheep-farmer, aware they incur reproach for egotism and triviality. She insists the fault could not be avoided without lessening their value as an exact account of a lady's experience of the brighter, less practical side of colonization.

The letters are no guide for the intending emigrant, who already has his own literature and will find scarcely a statistic here. They record expeditions, adventures, and emergencies of daily life, written while novelty stayed fresh. Barker gives England a picture of delight and freedom far from highly wrought civilization.
61052-spawning-ground:
Lester del Rey strands a crew in Spawning Ground, from the September 1961 issue of Worlds of If. The head tag warns that they were not human. They were something more, and something less: in short, humanity's hopes for survival.

The tale opens on a hard landing. The starship Pandora creaks and groans as her pads settle unevenly in the muck of an ugly world. She seems restless to end her fool's errand here, two hundred light years from the waiting hordes on Earth. Captain Gwayne curses and rolls over, reaching for his boots. He is a big, rawboned man, barely forty. Ten years of responsibility have pressed down his shoulders. Lieutenant Jane Corey greets him by the ever waiting pot of murky coffee: morning, Bob, you need a shave.
61416-orkney-and-shetland:
J G F Moodie Heddle and T Mainland wrote Orkney and Shetland, issued by Cambridge University Press in 1920. Mainland was headmaster of Bressay Public School. The book forms part of the Cambridge County Geographies for Scotland. Maps list all parishes in both island groups at the front.

Shetland parishes run from Unst and Fetlar to Dunrossness. Orkney parishes run from Papa Westray to South Ronaldshay. Maps, diagrams, and pictures aid the text. The series aimed to give a clear account of each county's land and life. Readers get the lay of the isles, their towns, and their past in brief form. The book suits schools and home readers who want sound facts.
61530-outland:
Outland is a novel of the wild west by Mary Austin. The book came out in New York in the year nineteen nineteen. Its tale is told in the first person by a woman on a trail. A hawk nest at a broke tree marks the start of that trail.

Fifteen chapters track outliers, a hid camp, and a tale of lost rubies. A man named Herman shares the quest and shapes a plan of his own. A tall woman in the wood and a smith with a past cross the path. Love, loss, and a kings desire drive the turns of the plot. The close brings the pair back to the broke tree where they began.
61588-a-treatise-of-taxes-and-contributi:
A Treatise of Taxes and Contributions is a work on public finance printed in London in 1662. Brooke at the Angel in Cornhill published it. Its title promises to show the nature and measures of many levies. Crown lands, assessments, customs, and poll moneys head that list. Lotteries, benevolence, penalties, monopolies, and offices follow. Tithes, raising of coins, hearth money, and excise are also treated. Discourses on wars, the church, and universities are interspersed.

The whole is frequently applied to the state and affairs of Ireland. A preface explains that the sheets began as the author's private musings. Their birth coincided with the Duke of Ormond's going to Ireland as lord lieutenant. Ireland must keep a great army, the preface argues. That army occasions heavy levies on a poor and wasted country. So Ireland should understand the nature of taxes, the author holds.
61597-eleanor-ormerod-ll-d-economic-ento:
Eleanor Ormerod is an autobiography with correspondence of the English entomologist Eleanor Anne Ormerod, edited by Robert Wallace, professor of agriculture at Edinburgh. Dutton published it in New York in 1904, with a portrait and illustrations. Ormerod was the leading economic entomologist of her age: the science of insects as pests of farm and garden.

The book is dedicated to all her correspondents in the field. Its first chapter covers her birth at Sedbury Park in 1828, her childhood, and her first insect observation. She was educated at home by her mother, among a family's estates and Roman remains. The second chapter traces her parentage and the Ormerod family back to the year 1311. From that rooted beginning she built a life of unpaid public science, advising farmers across Britain on the insects that ate their crops.
61813-folklore-of-wells-being-a-study-of:
Masani studies water worship in Folklore of Wells, a study of water worship in East and West, printed at Bombay in 1918. Taraporevala made the book. A front plate shows the floating of lamps during the Kartik Bath.

Part one treats the wells of Bombay. One head treats the sanctity of water, the origin of fevers, and the wrath of Shiva. It treats rites that call for water drawn from seven wells and lamps lit in well niches. One head treats water saints, spirits pent in wells who bring disaster. Tales of a sacred well and an oracular well stand in the run. A head on the penalty for defilement closes the part shown.
61992-nor-urfari-or-rambles-in-iceland:
Nordurfari, or Rambles in Iceland, by Pliny Miles, was published at New York in 1854. Charles Norton issued the travel book in that year. Verses in Icelandic by Brinjulfsson stand at the front as a motto. The dedication praises Philip James Bailey, author of Festus, for his genius.

Miles writes as a northern traveller, which is what the Icelandic title means in his framing. Iceland in the eighteen fifties was a remote and little visited land for American readers. A ramble narrative could mix roads, farms, sagas, and scenery in one tour. Such books fed a growing taste for the far north in the United States press. The volume stands as an early American account of Iceland and its people.
62123-the-sworn-brothers-a-tale-of-the-e:
The Sworn Brothers, by Gunnar Gunnarsson, was published in 1921. Knopf issued the Icelandic tale at New York. Field and Emme translated it from the Danish. The book stands in a Borzoi-Gyldendal line of northern works. Three books make the single volume. Book one opens in a fire-lit hall. Carved images of the gods stand on the high-seat pillars. Their grotesque shapes shift as the fire blazes and sinks. Orn sits between those pillars, a broad grey-haired warrior. His fingers are buried in his thick white beard. A great carved drinking horn stands at his side.

Orn seldom drinks much in the evening, the tale notes. His men sit across the fire in near silence. Uneasy glances pass toward the high seat. The early days of Iceland are the book's ground.
62229-the-story-without-an-end:
The Story Without an End was written in German by Carové and translated into English by Sarah Austin. Effingham Wilson published it in London in 1834, with illustrations by William Harvey. Austin dedicated the translation to her daughter, at whose wish she made it so that other children might share its delight.

In her dedication letter Austin answers the child's regret that the story stops so soon. The continuation, she says, lies in a wide and magnificent book holding more wonderful things than all fairy tales together. To read that book well takes pure, clear eyes and a humble, loving heart. The tale itself begins in a green meadow at sunrise, when finches wake a child with their morning songs. Story and letter together form a small classic of early children's literature in translation.
62568-stories-from-switzerland:
Stories from Switzerland is a children's story book translated from the French, published in London by the Religious Tract Society in 1837. The author is named only as the writer of The Two Old Men. The tales were meant for juvenile readers.

The contents list short moral pieces. Maurice learns that the way of the slothful is a hedge of thorns. Other tales treat idle Dick, a lost child, real charity, and a lesson of mercy. Mountain John and the bear supplies the adventure piece, and hymns for children close the set. The first story praises the pleasure of being able to read, since readers can share the Bible with the old and the blind. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
62580-quest-s-end:
Basil Wells wrote this short story, printed in Planet Stories in the spring of 1944. Thig curses himself for a fool at the eyepiece of his etherscope, watching the eastern horizon from his boathouse. He should have known the men of Ortha would send a second ship to Earth. By day he writes western sagas as Lewis Terry, a name known to millions.

In truth he is an alien who deserted an Orthan expedition. His gift of curiosity, unknown to his kind for thousands of years, led him to build the scope from odds and ends and trace his old ship. The Hordes of Ortha send patrolmen who report and then destroy themselves. Only Thig can halt Earth's destruction, with a weapon that is but a thought.
62734-the-daughter-of-a-soldier-a-collee:
