Meade, author of A Wild Irish Girl and a shelf of school stories, wrote The Daughter of a Soldier, a colleen of south Ireland, published in New York by Hurst in 1915. Charles Wrenn drew its four pictures. The contents run past 23 chapters, and their titles mix the sea, school, and sorrows.

Periwinkles and eavesdropping open the tale at Kingsala by the sea. The O'Shee enters, then the major and his child, and Colonel Herbert comes to the rescue. Step-daughters arrive, and the scene moves to Templemore and a grand Blüthner piano. Then the titles darken: Miss Pinchin, the power of hatred, the home of silence. One chapter stands on the peak of desolation where God was. Girls of 1915 got Ireland as a home for a soldier's motherless daughter.
62784-oration-the-american-mind:
The American Mind is a Fourth of July oration by Father Charles Lyons. It was delivered before the city government and citizens of Boston. Faneuil Hall hosted the address on July the Fourth, 1923. That day was the one hundred forty seventh anniversary of independence. The oration opens with a reflection on pausing in life. At times it is fitting to turn from the whirl of activities, he says. The mind may run lovingly over a treasured past at such times.

Today our beloved country turns to her children of a later generation, he says. She pleads that they tarry while she lives over her past again. Her thoughts, emotions, and heroic sacrifices gave her birth. Lyons speaks as a Jesuit orator on a civic altar. The address is patriotic oratory in the Faneuil Hall tradition.
62830-the-young-section-hand:
The Young Section Hand is a boys' tale of the rail road from 1905. Burton Stevenson wrote it, fresh from a case tale of note. The hero is Allan, a lad who starts at the foot of the road. A plate shows him snatch a child from the wheels of a train.

Allan proves his grit and meets a foe on the track gangs. A mate named Reddy stands by him in fix after fix. Night calls, a clear track, and a shot from the rear crowd the plot. A sign in the night and a fresh risk test the lad's nerve. The road's thanks close the tale of the young hand. The book is given to the boys of yard, shop, and desk. It calls back the days when the writer told rail news for a press.
62887-the-highlands-and-islands-of-scotl:
The Highlands and Islands of Scotland is a picture travel book, painted by Smith the younger and described in words by Hope Moncrieff. It was published in London by A and C Black in 1907, a year after its first issue. The plates show the north in colour, from Inverness to Staffa.

The chapters march across the region. One treats tartans, one the land of Lorne, and one the holy isles of Iona and its neighbours. Pibrochs and coronachs get a chapter on Highland music and lament. Tourists get a chapter to themselves. The book then sails to the Outer Hebrides and to Thule, the far north. A last chapter is named Children of the Mist. Views of Glencoe, Ben Nevis, and Loch Ness fill the list of plates.
6336-the-misuse-of-mind:
Karin Stephen, formerly fellow of Newnham College, Cambridge, writes a study of Bergson's attack on intellectualism, with a prefatory letter from Bergson himself. She argues that no prior philosophy is needed to understand Bergson, and indeed the less a reader knows of current metaphysics, the easier the required mental attitude may come. Bergson holds that philosophical tradition is all wrong and must be broken with, by a reversal of the intellect's usual work.

That usual work is analysis and classification, asking what a thing is and fitting it to a known class, as one stumbles in a dark room and feels for texture. Stephen follows Bergson through explanation, fact, and matter and memory, showing how qualities, once distinguished, crowd out the whole fact. The 1922 book is a clear guide to a hard thinker, respectful, critical, and plain in its examples.
63376-the-sweating-sickness-in-england:
Francis Webb, a London doctor, sketched the old sweating sickness in England. The piece was reprinted from a health journal of July 1857. Webb draws chiefly on the German scholar Hecker and his work. He aims to make those scarce researches plain to English readers.

The sickness was unknown before the year 1485, Webb notes at the start. It struck five times in a hundred years, then vanished in 1551. Once it spread to German lands on the continent as well. The sketch sets up a later talk on the nature of the plague.
63566-jack-manly-his-adventures-by-sea-a:
James Grant wrote this tale of a sailor's adventures by sea and land, one of his many military romances published by George Routledge and Sons. The contents alone map a hard life: why he went to sea, an adventure in a cask, Kidd the pirate, a chase, combat with a sea-horse, and long ordeals on an iceberg.

Later chapters bring a death-ship, graves on the starboard bow, a shark, a whale, the loss of the Leda, and land adventures in Africa, ending in pursuit and escape. The story opens one March evening, six months after the narrator left his father's snug villa. Readers get incident piled on incident in the old hearty style.
63577-love-potions-through-the-ages-a-st:
Harry Wedeck, a lecturer in classics at Brooklyn College, wrote Love Potions Through the Ages, a study of amatory devices and mores under copyright in 1963. Wedeck surveys how people across history have tried to stir, win, or keep love by charms, foods, spells, and drinks. His chapters move by era and by land.

The opening chapter on antiquity ranges over erotic cults, rites, and symbols in Greece, Egypt, Asia Minor, and the Bible lands, with love songs, spells, and tales from Herodotus. Later chapters treat the Greeks, the Romans with Ovid as chief witness, the Orient, and India with its erotic manuals. A chapter sorts the varieties and occasions of potions, and another gives ingredients, recipes, and anecdotes from legend and history. The survey runs through the Middle Ages and beyond. Readers get a wide, plain-spoken catalogue of love magic across cultures.
63683-color-blind:
Color Blind is a science fiction story by Charles Stearns, printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1954. Its heroine is Sukey Kireina Jones, whose blood mixes South Asia with the Celtic strain. Her eyes are dark and a little sad, her hair black as the Rim. She stands barely five feet in heels.

The narrator found her broke and alone near the Surface Transit offices. He got her a job as counter girl in the Company hash house on the edge of the space-port. The fashion of the day drives the plot: Earth women flock to Venus to bleach their skin to a green-white glamour. Olive-skinned Sukey is the ad men's blind spot. Stearns plays the pulp romance against a sly point about beauty and race.
63876-milly-at-love-s-extremes-a-romance:
Milly: At Loves Extremes is a romance of the south land by Thompson, author of a famed tale of an old town of the west. Prints fill its form, struck and bound at New York in the first year of the last age. Its rights were held that year by its house.

A front print sets its tone with a line in the tongue of the hills: I guess the lad is not on his way, Dad. Its first parts take hill dew, the girl her self, and a proud man of the place. A game hand at the card talk, a meet at the gate, and an old great house of a farm fill the next run. Dog and gun, a meal in the open air, and the girls asks lead on.
64032-return-of-a-legend:
Raymond Z Gallun wrote Return of a Legend, a tale of a lost Mars tramp. Planet Stories ran the story in March nineteen hundred fifty two. Port Laribee, a shabby Earth drop on Mars, frames the tale. Dave Kort, the first wild tramp of that port, is its lost man.

Sealed Nissen huts guard the port from the thin, cold air. Kort plodded in each warm season with a pack no Earth man could lift. Two fifths gravity let his frame bear that vast load of gear. Carved stones and odd finds bought his tobacco and chocolate there. Frost bites bound in dry Mars leaves marked his craggy frame. Three summers he came back, thin as a scarecrow, grinning still. The fourth winter’s end brought no Kort through the red dust. His tale lived on at the port when the man was dust and bone.
64112-kaipara-or-experiences-of-a-settle:
Kaipara, or Experiences of a Settler in North New Zealand, written and illustrated by Barlow, was published at London by Sampson Low in a second edition dated 1889. The narrator inscribes the book to his uncle at High Combe, Old Charlton, with deep respect, gratitude, and affection.

The preface states his excuse for troubling the public: nothing had yet been published about life in this part of New Zealand from the pen of a genuine settler. He disclaims literary talent and aims only to lay a true narrative of his experiences before readers in readable form. Earlier colonial books, he argues, were written by visitors who identified themselves with their characters rather than by men who had actually settled.
64155-crosby-lockwood-son-s-catalogue-of:
Crosby Lockwood and Son's Catalogue is a trade list of books of lore, craft, and trade works. It was made at London for the first month of nineteen hundred and one. The house stood in a small court of the town. Its list falls in set heaps by theme. Each heap names its books with their size, their price, and their praise.

The heaps run from the works of gears to the works of the farm. Gear craft, town craft, sea craft, mine craft, and the craft of the pit stand first. The new force of wires, the build craft, clean health and wa ter, and the work of wood and paint fill the mid run.
64163-legends-of-switzerland:
Legends of Switzerland retells the folk tales of the Swiss cantons, written by Guerber. Dodd, Mead published the book at New York in 1899, with pictures. Guerber had written matching volumes on the Rhine, the Virgin and Christ, and the middle ages. The author dedicates the book to Switzerland itself, in thanks for happy summers.

The tales are sorted by canton, from Geneva to the Grisons. Lake Geneva opens the book, praised as the largest and bluest of Swiss lakes. Pictures show Tell defying Gessler, the oath on the Rutli meadow, and the Devil's Bridge. Alpine fays, the wild hunt, and a mist nymph fill other pages. Guerber writes plain, warm retellings for young readers. The book rounds its survey with tales from every corner of the small republic.
64344-history-of-king-charles-the-first-:
History of King Charles the First of England is a historical narrative by Jacob Abbott, printed at New York in 1848 with engravings. A plate shows John Hampden, and another the Tower of London. In his preface Abbott explains why so many accounts of the same life exist. Each one, he says, is intended for a different set of readers.

Among the twenty millions of people in the United States, he reckons, there are perhaps two millions between the ages of fifteen and twenty-five. They wish to know the leading events in the history of the Old World. But their ideas differ so widely from those of other nations and times that a mere republication of existing accounts is not what they require. The story must be told expressly for them. Abbott's series of historical narratives was made for those young American readers.
64348-travels-in-turkey-and-back-to-engl:
Travels in Turkey and Back to England is the journal of Edmund Chishull, printed at London in 1747. Chishull had been chaplain to the Turkey Company factory at Smyrna. His son brought the journal to the publisher after his father's death. The preface praises travel journals above other travel books. A reader of a journal fancies himself in the traveller's company, it argues. Busbequius and Maundrell are named as the models of the kind.

Chishull's learning and diligence are vouched for by long acquaintance. His book on Asian antiquities had already won celebration. The journal keeps the day by day form the preface commends. Customs and manners of the nations on the route supply its matter. The road home from Smyrna gives the book its shape. It stands among the classic English accounts of the Levant.
64351-earthbound:
Earthbound is a science fiction tale by Henry Guth, first printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1947. Its blurb promises a daring spaceflight. Virgil and Lanya seek what all their age has given up in despair. The tale opens in the Martian Museum of Science. Lanya Greggor, ten years old, holds her brother Virgil's hand. Virgil is twelve, and this is her first visit. Guards watch as the children walk the great halls in awe.

In one hall stands the first rocket that flew to Mars. Its huge bulk is near all engine and fuel tanks. The small cabin in its nose could hold three men at most. Beside the sleek atomic craft of later days it looks grotesque. Lanya, from her school books, knows how that flight changed Mars. Trade with Earth turned a farm world into a world of science.
64540-the-greatest-heiress-in-england:
Mrs Oliphant wrote this novel, issued at New York in George Munro's Seaside Library. It sold for twenty cents alongside dozens of her other works, from Salem Chapel to The Perpetual Curate.

Chapter one settles into a quiet country town in frost. A river lies stilled with cold, red houses line the streets, and few people are about, brightening at the thought of skating tomorrow. The town's grandest dwellings are the Terrace, twelve houses built to look like one Elizabethan mansion, facing the common and its sunsets. Number six in the Terrace is the chapter's heading, and the proud occupants of these houses are its subject. Oliphant opens with her practiced survey of provincial respectability. Readers get a late novel from the indefatigable Scots storyteller.
64608-from-the-land-of-the-snow-pearls-t:
From the Land of the Snow-Pearls: Tales from Puget Sound, by Ella Higginson, was issued by the Macmillan Company in New York in 1902, first printed in 1896. The book had earlier appeared under the title The Flower That Grew in the Sand, and two stories are added in this edition. Its title comes from the snow covered mountains that ring Puget Sound like pearls.

Twelve tales fill the volume, among them Esther's Fourth, The Blow-Out at Jenkins's Grocery, Zarelda, and Mrs. Risley's Christmas Dinner. Several first ran in magazines such as McClure's and Lippincott's. The opening story brings Demaris to a rose garden to beg pink roses, and the talk turns on kindness, pride, and want. Higginson's tales give the speech and daily life of the Sound country a local voice.
64609-a-west-point-treasure-or-mark-mall:
Frederick Garrison wrote A West Point Treasure; or, Mark Mallory’s Strange Find. David McKay issued the boys’ book at Philadelphia in nineteen hundred three. Garrison, an army lieutenant, knew cadet life at first hand. Mark Mallory, a plebe in grey, leads the seven lads of the tale.

A letter from Wicks Merritt, a second class man, opens the fun. The old cadets mark the bold tricks of the new plebe band. A walk leads the seven to a strange find of hid wealth. Loss found, thief found: the plot knots through the mid acts. Seven burglars fall in a trap the cadets set and watch by night. Mark is caught and the yearlings rack him to make him yield. Coward is the taunt thrown at Mark in the test to come. He finds the nerve to seem a coward, and wins his laurels so.
64761-the-humour-of-holland:
The Humour of Holland is an anthology of Dutch comic writing in English translation, published in London in 1893. It belongs to a humour series that had already issued volumes of French, German, Italian, and American humour. Werner translated the pieces and wrote the introduction, and Dudley Hardy drew illustrations.

The contents open with a piece by Frederick van Eeden and a tale of a dominie, or Dutch parson. The bulk of the volume belongs to Multatuli, the great Dutch satirist. His pieces include a rascally valet, sketches of the dry merchant Droogstoppel, aphorisms, parables, and essays on education and self-depreciation. Newspaper humour, fiction at sea, and a half-hour at the hairdresser's fill out the set. The book offers English readers a taste of Dutch wit through its sharpest pen.
64773-the-history-of-the-london-burkers-:
The History of the London Burkers is a true crime pamphlet printed in London in 1832. Kelly sold it at Paternoster Row for the proprietors. Its title promises a faithful account of noted resurrectionists. Bishop, Williams, and May are the men named there. Their trial and condemnation at the Old Bailey are reported. They were condemned for the wilful murder of Carlo Ferrari. The criminals' confessions after trial are included in the pages. Portraits of the three men face the title page.

The life and behaviour of Eliza Ross are also included. She was the murderer of Mrs Walsh in a like trade. Engravings show Bishop's cottage and the entrance of King's College. The burkers killed to sell bodies to anatomy schools. Their case horrified London in the winter of the trial. The pamphlet is gallows literature rushed out for the crowd.
649-ancient-poems-ballads-and-songs-of-t:
Robert Bell edits this collection of old English poems, ballads, and songs of the peasantry, gathered from broadsides and oral tradition. The Plain-Dealing Man, The Vanities of Life, and The Life and Age of Man lead the poems. Ballads follow, like The Three Knights, The Blind Beggar of Bednall Green, and The Bold Pedlar and Robin Hood.

Bell's notes place each piece in its folk setting, from harvest to highway to churchyard. The verses speak of work, love, death, and jest in plain, sturdy lines. The volume serves as a treasury of English folk verse, where the voice of common people survives in song.
65284-massasoit-s-town-sowams-in-pokanok:
Massasoit's Town Sowams in Pokanoket is a local history book by Virginia Baker, printed at Warren, Rhode Island, in 1904. Baker had earlier written a history of Warren in the War of the Revolution. Her subject here is Sowams, the chief town of Massasoit, the Wampanoag sachem, in the land called Pokanoket.

The opening voice sets the tone. A verse by Hezekiah Butterworth praises Warren and its storied past, and the text speaks of the keen interest that clings to all that touches Massasoit. Baker grants him a life-long loyalty to the early settlers and virtues few kings have matched. Yet, she notes, readers know little of his town itself. Her book fills that gap with the history, legends, and traditions of Sowams and the ground it stood on.
65837-on-the-borderland:
On the Borderland gathers short stories by Britten Austin, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1923. Austin also wrote According to Orders and In Action. The stories first ran in magazines between 1919 and 1920. Twelve titles fill the contents, from Buried Treasure to Yellow Magic.

The opening tale sets men talking after dinner in a liner's smoking-room. The talk has revelled in the uncanny for twenty minutes, one yarn capping another. A story-teller turns to a doctor who has listened in silence. As a specialist in mental disorders, he must know delusions of every kind. Is there any truth in spiritualism? Austin's tales all walk that border.
65860-the-old-miracle-plays-of-england:
The Old Miracle Plays of England retells the old church plays for the young. Netta Syrett wrote it, out in London in the year 1911. Two plates from hand tint draws dress the book for its readers. A frame tale sets two young ones at the feast of the host.

The plays start with the fall of the bright fiend from the skies. The making of sun, moon, beasts, and man fills the next play in turn. The ark of Noah and the tale of the sire and his son come next. The herd men's play and the wise men's trip fill the midst of the set. The cruel king and the slain babes close the run of the old plays. Syrett tells each play as a tale, in words the young can hold.
6599-the-letters-of-norah-on-her-tour-th:
Norah, writing as special correspondent to the Montreal Witness, sends home letters from a tour through Ireland. The volume opens with a long list of subscribers who paid to print the letters, from Montreal, Toronto, Belleville, and even Paris. That roll of names shows how keen Canadian readers were to hear news from Ireland.

The letters that follow report towns, people, and Irish life as Norah saw them on the road. Her voice is that of a traveler writing for a paper, keen, personal, and close to daily fact. The Letters of Norah give a lively, first-hand Irish tour through Canadian eyes, in the form of news from abroad.
66010-anecdotes-of-painters-engravers-sc:
Shearjashub Spooner published the first volume of his Anecdotes of Painters, Engravers, Sculptors and Architects, and Curiosities of Art in New York in 1853, through Putnam. The work runs to three volumes, companion to his biographical dictionary of artists.

His preface insists the book is no mere compilation: it holds original matter and much of the most interesting history of art. Spooner also tells his own story. For years his great labour was restoring and publishing Napoleon's grand plate books, the Musée Français and the Musée Royal. In five years spent on those and on Boydell's Shakespeare illustrations he allowed himself but one evening out of his study. He admits the sums sunk in such ventures may never come back, and calls the work a labour of love to awaken American interest in art.
66131-the-bride-of-huitzil-an-aztec-lege:
Hervey Allen's The Bride of Huitzil, an Aztec legend in verse, was published in New York in nineteen twenty-two by James Drake and dedicated to a dead child. The poem opens its first scroll under the sign of a bundle of reeds tied with string, the symbol of fifty-two years. In Anahuac there reigned a king of some fifty summers, the bloody darling of his gods, rich in gold and captives from a thousand fights.

Age saps the king's trust, and the priests harvest his fear. Tribute rolls bring bales of cloth, cloaks of fine feather-work, opals, pearl strings, quetzal skins, and keen obsidian knives. Young slaves die on Huitzil's altars while the priests grow rich on doubt. Their last demand sharpens the tale: bring beauty, they tell the king.
66190-the-antelope-boy-or-smoholler-the-:
The Antelope Boy, or Smoholler the Medicine-Man is a dime tale by George Aiken, out at New York in the rights year of eighteen seventy-three. Its name page calls it a tale of red man risk and riddle. Parts run past a camp of chain men, a note sent by shaft, and the fiend and the grace of the herb man. A scout band, a tree stair, and a chiefs bride take parts.

The tale opens at a camp on the banks of a great west stream, near the mouth of its mate. The band holds two chain men, a Scot and a Yank, past ten troops sent to guard them. An old hunt man guides them and keeps them in fresh meat. Two boy chain hands, kin and both of one first name, are marked as the true leads of the deeds to come.
66191-barren-ground:
Barren Ground is a novel of farm life by Ellen Glasgow. Three parts name three growths: broom sedge, pine, and a long life bloom. The tale opens on a girl in an orange shawl at a store glass. Snow falls on a lone road as the last train of the day rolls past.

The girl stands still as flight caught short, as if she ran toward life. Bare, starved land shuts in round her small town and kin home. Long parts in each stage track her rise through work and loss. Land, love, and will form the stakes of the famed south tale. Glasgow won high praise for this strong book of a womans life.
66251-is-tomorrow-hitler-s-200-questions:
The journalist Knickerbocker poses the title question in Is Tomorrow Hitler's?, a book of questions and answers published by Reynal and Hitchcock in New York in 1941. Its subtitle promises two hundred questions on the battle of mankind. A note warns that the contents list gives only a sampling of the provocative questions discussed.

The first chapter, on Germany, asks whether the reader has ever met Hitler, and what impression he makes at close quarters. It asks whether Hitler is personally brave, what kind of public speaker he is, and what the secret of his power might be. Did Hitler direct his battles like Napoleon, and why did he not attack England after Dunkirk? Later questions ask whether the Nazi atrocity stories are exaggerated, and what should be done with Hitler after he is defeated. Written before America entered the war, the book is a reporter's primer on the enemy.
6659-history-of-king-charles-the-second-:
Jacob Abbott tells the life of Charles the Second with a strict vow: no tales dressed as history, no embellishment, no drift from truth as far as it can be found. His preface stresses that he used the best sources at hand and checked the annals written when the events themselves took place. Some error, he admits, is bound to slip into any history.

The narrative that follows covers the king's exile, return, court, and reign, in Abbott's plain, schoolroom style. Young readers were his first audience, but the tale holds for any reader who likes a straight story. History of King Charles the Second is a clear, honest introduction to a witty, troubled king.
666-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words beginning with P. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from P, the sixteenth letter, through Pa, a short form of Papa, and Paage, a toll for passage, and onward. Notes trace Latin, Greek, and Phoenician roots.

P is a letter of passages and payments: tolls, papers, and parcels fill its early pages, with plants and proverbs close behind. The entries show how prefixes like pa- and pre- built whole families of words. For a reader of old law, letters, or trade, this slice is a practical key.
66605-sarah-of-the-sahara-a-romance-of-n:
Walter Traprock wrote this spoof romance, published by Putnam in New York and London in 1923. Seventeen full-page illustrations dress it as a super-feature film of Traprock's imagining. Love at first sight opens the contents, and our first interview follows in the desert.

Into the great unknown, the wandering Wimpoles and love and lions fill the early chapters. A desperate predicament, an escape and sheik to sheik carry Sarah through the Sahara in jest. Traprock, a pen name of the publisher Putnam himself, sent up the sheik romances then sweeping the bookstalls with this deadpan travel tale.
66648-newshound:
Milton Lesser wrote this tale of the press of the days to come, first printed in a journal of such tales in July 1955. A note at its head states the twist of its world. The craft of news was a fine, split trade in the age two past our own. A good man of news, for one, told the deeds of the days to come in front of them. And he made them take place to fit his tale.

Darius McLeod leans back in his chair and watches the mayor sweat. His Honor pops a pill for his nerves twixt his lips, and gulps it down with no drink. His damp hands leave their wet print on the desk. He takes a clip from the sheet of that dawn from his coat. You men put me in this post, he tells McLeod.
66708-following-a-chance-clew-or-nick-ca:
Nick Carter tales fill the New Magnet Library set praised in these front pages. The blurb says one specialist wrote no other kind of fiction. His mind stayed fixed on new plots for his detective hero. Carter lands the crook behind bars at the end of each tale.

A long list names the best tales, from Wanted A Clew onward. Titles promise tangled skeins, bullion theft, and men of riddles as cases. The house urges new readers to try any one volume first. This volume holds Following a Chance Clew, or Nick Carter Lucky Find.
6681-sganarelle-or-the-self-deceived-hus:
Molière's one-act comedy from 1660, six months after the hit of Les Précieuses Ridicules, turns on a husband who thinks himself a cuckold. Sganarelle, or the Self-Deceived Husband, owes its first idea, some say, to an Italian farce never printed, so the debt cannot be proved. Old writers like Noël du Fail and Rabelais also fed the plot.

The joke is all in Sganarelle's own mind: he reads guilt into innocent acts and torments himself. Molière keeps the verse brisk and the farce tight, with no room for slack. Sganarelle is a short, sharp comedy of jealous fancy, still funny in its picture of a man fooled by himself.
6682-nets-to-catch-the-wind:
Elinor Wylie opens Nets to Catch the Wind with a poem on Beauty, warning that beauty is neither good nor bad, but wild as a gull's wings. Love her not too much, she warns, for that is even worse than calling her wicked. The set that follows runs from The Eagle and the Mole and Madman's Song to Wild Peaches, Velvet Shoes, and a Valentine.

Wylie's verse is taut, bright, and full of strange images, with a formal grace that never feels stiff. She writes of love, loss, and the natural world with a cool, clear eye. Nets to Catch the Wind is a fine, early modern poetry book, still sharp and lovely today.
6702-life-of-harriet-beecher-stowe-compi:
Charles Edward Stowe compiles his mother's life from her letters and journals, in a volume issued in 1890. Harriet Beecher Stowe herself opens with a note on why she wished to leave recollections behind, though failing strength had long held her back. Her son then lets her own words carry much of the tale.

From a New England childhood to Uncle Tom's Cabin and world fame, the letters show a writer, reformer, and mother at close hand. The life that emerges is busy, devout, and deeply human. Life of Harriet Beecher Stowe is a warm, first-hand biography, built from the author's own pen.
67101-the-north-americans-of-antiquity-t:
John Short wrote The North Americans of Antiquity, a study of the origin, migrations, and civilization of the old races of the continent. Harper of New York issued this third edition in 1882. A court and tower of the palace at Palenque, drawn after Waldeck, stands at the front.

The preface hails a new age of digging. Discoveries abroad, he says, turn American eyes to the rich fields at home. Explorers have lately worked the mound-works of the Mississippi valley and the cliff-dwellings of the West. Short argues that the mound-builders cannot be judged alone. Their civilization must be read beside the old races of Mexico and Central America. The age of American antiquity, he writes, is not all darkness: patient searchers are rolling up the curtain. General readers of 1882 got the mound-builder question argued whole.
67122-in-the-year-ten-thousand:
In the Year Ten Thousand, a tale by William Harben, is set in the year 10000 of our era. An old man of more than six hundred years walks with a boy through a great museum. The folk around them have fair forms and faces of a refined, spiritual cast.

The boy asks to hear of the Dark Ages, meaning our own time eight thousand years back. The elder leads him to a cabinet of time-worn books bound in solid gold. Only a few books survive, in the leading museums of the world, and the boy has never seen one. Men once spoke with their tongues, the elder explains, and wrote signs to swap thoughts. Mind-reading has since replaced all that, and speech itself needs explaining to the child.
67179-nimble-ike-the-trick-ventriloquist:
Nimble Ike, the Trick Ventriloquist is a ten cent tale by Old Sleuth, with rights held from eighteen ninety-four. It calls itself a tale of fun and frolic, and it opens in a top floor room of a big city tenement. An old man with bags of gold sits by a candle lit table. A bright lad of thirteen or fourteen kneels near him and begs for a share.

The old man refuses, since the boy was his pupil and has been paid in skill. Ike can throw his voice, work tricks, and speak three tongues, gifts the old man calls a fortune. Yet the old man saves all his gold for revenge, and the boy still does not know who his parents were.
67200-a-gringo-in-man-ana-land:
A Gringo in Mañana-Land is a travel book by Harry Foster, published by Dodd, Mead in 1924. Foster had written of a tropical tramp and a beachcomber in the Orient. His own photographs illustrate the journey. Seventeen chapters run from the Mexican border to Costa Rica. Bandits threaten the second chapter, in sleepy Hermosillo by the third. A chapter among the Yaqui Indians follows, with their Easter ceremony.

The west coast, the days of Carranza, and the Mexican capital fill the middle. Chronic insurrections get a chapter of their own. Guatemala, Salvador, and a revolution in Honduras come next. Where marines make presidents names the Nicaragua chapter. A long, long way to Costa Rica closes the road. Foster even bought a second hand car on the border for the trip.
67477-bee-keeping-for-the-many-or-the-ma:
Bee-Keeping for the Many is number three in the Manuals for the Many series, printed in London at the office of the Journal of Horticulture. Payne, its late author, wrote on the management of the common and Ligurian honey bee. This new edition, revised and enlarged by the journal's editors, reached its thirtieth thousand and sold for fourpence.

Contents cover the natural history of the bee, the situation of the apiary, and the choice of hives. Named designs include Payne's improved cottage hive, Neighbour's cottage and observatory hives, and the Stewarton hive. A bee keeper's calendar guides the year, making the little book a working manual for smallholders and cottage gardeners.
67841-the-emeryville-shellmound:
The Emeryville Shellmound is an archaeological report by Max Uhle. The University of California issued it at Berkeley in June 1907. It forms the first number of the seventh volume of its series. That series covers American archaeology and ethnology for the university.

The report describes excavations made in the spring of 1902. Professor Merriam of the university shared the direction of the digging. The contents open with early settlements and references to the region's mounds. The base and internal structure of the Emeryville mound are then examined. Its constituents — shells, bones, and fireplaces — receive separate treatment. Human remains, relics, and burials fill the heart of the first part. The age of the mound and its cultural stages close the general report. A second part catalogues the stone implements unearthed in the digging.
6803-algonquin-legends-of-new-england:
Charles Leland gathers Algonquin legends of New England, myths and folk lore of the Micmac, Passamaquoddy, and Penobscot tribes. A frontispiece shows Mik um Wess, the Indian Puck, in a red cap like a Norse goblin, scraped on birch bark by Tomak Josephs. Leland began collecting in the summer of 1882 among the Passamaquoddy at Campobello, expecting very little.

Surrounded by whites and converted to Catholicism, these few Indians yet kept scanty remains of old heathen lore, which Leland saved with care. The tales that follow are vivid, strange, and humane. Algonquin Legends of New England is a precious record of Native story, told close to its sources.
68170-dream-s-end:
Henry Kuttner wrote this tale of minds in peril for Startling Stories' July 1947 issue. Its blurb states the risk: Doctor Robert Bruno spends his own life force to cure a patient's madness. What he learns is how alone each human mind truly is.

The sanitarium was never quiet, the tale begins. Even at night a tense hush held, for the cycles of madness swing as sure as a merry-go-round. That evening Gregson, in Ward 13, slid down his curve and made trouble. Before the orderlies got him in a jacket, he broke the arm of a frozen patient. The man made no sound as the bone snapped. Bruno, chief of staff, waits in that hush.
6827-boy-scouts-of-the-air-on-lost-islan:
Gordon Stuart sends the Boy Scouts of the Air to Lost Island. The tale opens at dawn in Ring's back yard. Three boys kick dew off tall grass and peer toward cedars hiding the Fulton house. No light shows yet, grumbles the short, stocky boy; their friend is not up. Over the dam, a hopeless search, and Lost Island itself follow.

More thrills, a startling clue, a rescue, a voyage in the dark, and a mid-air miracle fill the chapters, with the Flying Eagle Scouts in the air. Stuart keeps the action brisk and the scout spirit high. Boy Scouts of the Air on Lost Island is a lively, early aviation adventure for boys.
68563-nappy-has-a-new-friend:
Nappy Has a New Friend is a picture story book by Inez Hogan, printed at New York in 1947. Hogan wrote a shelf of animal twin books and earlier Nappy tales. Nappy had chosen a pet, planted a garden, and wanted a dog. This book is a first edition, dedicated to Tommy Chandler.

Nappy shows off his airplanes to his friend the trashman. The trashman is collecting too, he says, collecting trash. Nappy rides with him to the town dump, and his dog Mut comes along. There Nappy finds another boy looking around, just as he is. Hogan tells the small adventure in short lines a beginning reader can manage alone.
6872-the-battle-ground:
Ellen Glasgow sets this novel in Virginia, where the Montjoy kin and their neighbors live out golden years before war breaks them apart. Dan and Betty grow up amid open doors, school days, and college talk, and the early books follow courtship, temper, and pride in a house proud of its name. Love scenes at firesides and on night roads sit beside the first signs of storm.

The later books carry the same people into the Civil War, with marches, battle, and the hard lot of women left behind. Ragged armies, cabins in the woods, and a long march home close the tale. The vanquished return to a place changed by guns and by loss, and try to live in peace again.
68733-the-kingdom-of-the-blind:
Kingdom of the Blind is a science fiction story by George Smith, from Startling Stories of July 1947. It opens in a laboratory, where Doctor Pollard, a psychologist, seems puzzled by his patient. A well dressed man sits asprawl in the chair before him in the first lines. Pollard asks whether he has never heard of James Forrest Carroll in the scene.

No, says the man, flatly, to the question put to him by the doctor. But you are James Forrest Carroll, Pollard tells him in reply on the page. The laboratory director shrugs and takes his leave of the hopeless case in the room. As with the others, he says, the case is almost complete amnesia, with memory completely shot. A man who is somebody, and knows nothing of it, is the seed of the plot that follows.
68737-a-climber-in-new-zealand:
Malcolm Ross wrote of climbs among the high snows of New Zealand. Edward Arnold issued the book in London in 1914, with photos by the author. Ross had led the New Zealand Alpine Club and wrote Aorangi and In Tuhoe Land. A note by Viscount Bryce opens the work with high praise.

Bryce calls the view of snows rising from the sea near Greymouth one of the finest on earth. Mount Cook, or Aorangi, tops the range at 12,347 feet. Snow lies far lower here than in the Swiss Alps at like height. Climbers and armchair travelers gain a full, fond guide to a grand range.
68749-peggy-in-toyland:
Peggy in Toyland is a children's story by Archibald Marshall, printed at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1920. Marshall also wrote Exton Manor and Sir Harry. The pictures are by Helen Barton. The story is dedicated to Kathleen Ann, and was begun for her mother. The chapters run past seventeen, from Peggy's surprising adventure to the battle and the close.

The first chapter introduces Peggy and some of her friends. A Dutch doll brings momentous news. Peggy arrives at the Royal Palace of Dolltown, and King Selim holds an audience. Then they all go to prison. Peggy and Wooden are released, and Peggy stays in a real dolls' house. The dolls talk it all over. Then come the escape, the pursuit, and Colonel Jim's attempt at a rescue.
68752-lives-and-exploits-of-the-most-not:
Silas Andrus and Son of Hartford published this gallery of rogues. Its title promises lives and exploits of the most noted highwaymen, robbers, and murderers of all nations. The matter is drawn from the most authentic sources and brought down to the present time. Claude Du Vall heads the contents, followed by Sawney Beane, Captain James Hind, the Golden Farmer, William Nevison, Jack Shepherd, Richard Turpin, James Maclaine, and Eugene Aram, among many more.

Du Vall's life opens the book: born at Domfront in Normandy, a miller's son raised to be a footman. He rode to Paris with returning horses and crossed to England at the Restoration. The lives are short, brisk, and moral only at the edges, with engravings throughout. Such collections sold crime as history, and this one ranges over two centuries of the road and the gallows.
68835-the-humour-of-ireland:
The Humour of Ireland gathers Irish wit from folk tale to stage comedy. Donoghue selected it, with introduction, notes, and a biographical index of authors. Walter Scott of London and Scribner of New York issued it in 1908. Oliver Paque drew the plates for this volume of the Humour series.

Old Irish tales open it: a demon of voracity exorcised, the Roman earl, goat skin fellow. Swift rhapsody on poetry and Steele letter from a liar follow in print. Farquhar, Sterne, Goldsmith, and Sheridan give the stage side of the wit. Bulls by Roche, Curran anecdotes, and Moore letters crowd the middle pages. Folk poems, riddles, and epigrams season the whole collection.
68963-a-short-history-of-the-norman-conq:
Edward Freeman wrote A Short History of the Norman Conquest of England. The Clarendon Press at Oxford put out this third edition in 1908. Freeman was late Regius Professor of Modern History at Oxford. Contents open with an introduction, then the English and the Normans. Early dealings between the two peoples take the third chapter.

The youth of Duke William and Harold, earl and king, follow. The two Harolds, the coming of Duke William, and the great battle come next. How William became king and won the whole kingdom fills the middle. His later wars and his rule of the land close the tale's body. Freeman told the same tale in five large volumes, he writes. This little book, a primer, tells it afresh and not as an abridgement. The conquest means far more than a crown changing hands, he holds.
69308-the-call-from-beyond:
The Call From Beyond is a tale of a lone flight to a far moon. Clifford Simak wrote it for a pulp book of the year 1950. Its hero is Frederick West, a man cursed with a strange gift. He holds a last truth with which no man can die.

West lands on the moon of Pluto, where no one lives or calls. A flash of light drew him down to the bare rock of that world. There stands a stack of glass jars, high and neat, in the dim light. The jars catch the far sun and break it in bright shards. No hand should have built such a thing in that waste of space. The stack may be a sign post, or the whim of a mad mind.
69395-the-quilt-of-happiness-creeping-je:
Kate Douglas Wiggin, author of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, published New England stories headed by Creeping Jenny, with copyrights running from 1901 to 1924. A frontispiece shows Rufus watching the dimple come and go in Jenny's cheek. Jenny Lane lives in a shabby little farmhouse on the Back Nippi road, the first story begins. The author's reading at Bixby Centre follows.

The quilt of happiness gives the volume its title. Matt Milliken's improvements close the contents. Wiggin's stories draw on her Maine childhood and kindergarten work. Nora Archibald Smith, her sister, held one copyright. Grosset and Dunlap reprinted the collection for the popular trade.
69435-rhoda-of-the-underground:
Florence Finch Kelly wrote this novel of love and risk for Sturgis and Walton of New York in 1909. Rhoda of the Underground carries plates by the Kinneys. She listens, with her hand clasped in his, stands as the front plate.

God's blessing lay in the sunshine, the tale opens, on green fields and gardens in bloom. The town sits quiet along the river, under kind warmth. Down at the steamboat landing it wakes to noise as the up-river boat comes in. Freight and folk pour off together. Farther back the maple streets stay still. Inside were a withered rose and a letter, one plate hints: a kept token drives Rhoda's tale of the hidden road.
69476-account-of-an-expedition-to-the-in:
Lady Mary Fox edited the Account of an Expedition to the Interior of New Holland. Richard Bentley issued the book in London in eighteen hundred thirty seven. A chain of lakes in far Australia opens the strange tale. A new settlement of the Southlanders grows on that shore.

Treaty and peace with the first folk mark the young town. Schools for their children and votes for senators come fast. A town named Bath rises with lit streets and rich feasts. Duels fill three whole chapters of law and heated talk. Court of honour and a band of women end that vice at last. Modes of voting, by ballot and by wealth, get weighed here. A prediction office logs prophecies for the state’s own use. The book dreams a whole new polity on a wild far shore.
69615-king-arthur-in-history-and-legend:
King Arthur in History and Legend is a small book of lore by W. Lewis Jones, a chair man of the English tongue at a Welsh seat of study. It stands in a set of small hand books of the lore of men put out by a great press of the old schools. The first print came in nineteen eleven, and a new print with small fixes in nineteen fourteen. A brief word at the front tells of the adds made at the back in that new form.

The list of parts gives the path of the book in full. First words lead in, then the most old tales of Arthur in writ. Then Arthur in Welsh tale and Welsh song, then the great false past lore man and the tale men who came past him.
69676-the-italian-alp-bee-or-the-gold-mi:
The Italian Alp Bee, or The Gold Mine of Husbandry gives short, plain rules for breeding Italian queen bees. The English text is a word-for-word rendering from M Hermann, kept close by design. Wrapper pages in front list improved hives for sale.

Those hives promise honey taken without killing the bees. Nutt's collateral box hive costs six pounds fifteen shillings, and a cottage hive one pound fifteen. The treatise itself teaches how to breed true, fruitful Italian queens. It also teaches how to multiply them by the hundred. Bee keepers who wanted the new Italian stock were the clear audience.
699-a-child-s-history-of-england:
Charles Dickens wrote this history of England for young readers, in plain, story-like prose. It runs from ancient Britain and the Romans through Saxon kings, the Norman conquest, and the long line of later monarchs. Each chapter takes a reign or an age and tells its chief events as a tale, with heroes, villains, and turning points.

Dickens speaks straight to children, praising good kings and blasting cruel ones, and he does not hide his views on power and pride. The book was meant to give the young a first, vivid sense of their country's past. It still reads as a lively, if partisan, tour of English history, and as a window on how Victorians taught that past.
69925-the-new-northland:
The New Northland is a volume by Gratacap, printed at New York in 1915. Sixteen designs by Albert Operti illustrate it. Its chief piece is Krocker Land, a romance of discovery. The title page names four makers for that romance, with the narrative by Alfred Erickson and editing by Azaziel Link.

Sixteen chapters carry the romance from the fiord to the sequel. The party reaches Point Barrow and crosses the ice pack. They meet a crocodilo-python, find the Valley of Rasselas, and enter Radiumopolis. A crater of everlasting light and a pool of oblation wait along the way. Goritz dies among the gold makers, and Erickson escapes. The book weds Arctic travel to pure invention.
69937-shakespeare-s-roman-plays-and-thei:
MacCallum wrote this study of Shakespeare Roman plays and their background. Macmillan printed it in London in 1910 with full contents. MacCallum taught modern literature at the University of Sydney then. Contents open with Roman plays of the sixteenth century first.

Appius and Virginia, French Senecans, and Wounds of Civil War appear. Shakespeare treatment of history takes the second part of the book. Plutarch, Amyot, and North stand as the plays ancestry sources. Julius Caesar gets long treatment on its place and its Plutarch debt. A Low German motto on love stands as the gift line to his dedicatee.
69990-a-month-in-switzerland:
A Month in Switzerland fronts press praise of its author's Egypt book. That earlier work treated Egypt of the pharaohs and the Khedive. The Spectator calls it thoughtful and near complete, the page quotes. Dilettante writers shun such hard problems, it says. The Literary Churchman calls it fresh and original. Mr Zincke's quick eye wins praise there.

Racy style and vigor of judgment mark him, it adds. The Guardian finds each chapter sharp on one topic. New light falls on old sights in his pages, it says. The Saturday Review praises his love of nature. Broad, deep sympathy marks his thought, it claims. Such review pages sold the new book on the old one's fame. A clergyman-traveler's bright Swiss month rode in on strong notices won among pharaohs and fellahin.
70086-sketch-of-the-reformation-in-engla:
Sketch of the Reformation in England is a work of church lore in a set of books of the faith. That set bore the name of a store house of the lore of the church. The host print bears the date of the spring of eighteen thirty seven at its head. Its first pages are not the work it self. They are words of praise for the set, wrote by church men of rank to its print house.

The print house voices its joy at those words in a note at the start. It is sure, that note says, that the known cast of their wells will win them all heed. The first of those words is from a chief church man of a west state. You are free to use my name, he says, in praise of that set.
70209-bird-in-hand:
Bird in Hand is a play in one act by Laurence Housman. Samuel French published it in New York and London at thirty five cents. Rights rest with Housman in the year 1916 by the caution page. Amateurs and professionals must seek leave before producing the play anywhere. Application goes to French at West Thirty Eighth Street in New York.

The persons are Professor Braintree, a famous scientist, and Miss Tuckey. Tuckey serves as his secretary in the study where it opens. Locum attends him as his medical man in the small cast. Elfrida is his granddaughter, the fourth person of the piece. Bird in Hand itself stands listed as a thing to be explained.
70267-the-condition-of-england:
The Condition of England, by C F G Masterman, was first published in 1909 in London. Masterman had also written on Tennyson as a religious teacher. He takes his motto from Ruskin, asking whether the nation is getting on, and if so, where it is going.

Ten chapters sort English life into groups and tests. Early chapters treat the spirit of the people, the conquerors, and the suburbans. Middle chapters treat the multitude, prisoners, and the countryside. Last chapters weigh science, letters, and faith as signs of progress. A final chapter warns of a false sense of safety. Readers get a sharp survey of Edwardian England, class by class, written from inside its own doubts.
7081-the-motor-girls-on-cedar-lake-or-th:
The Motor Girls on Cedar Lake opens with Cora Kimball welcoming Bess and Belle Robinson to camp, where talk turns at once to a new motor boat. Cora, the camp hostess, has just received the boat, and no boy stands ready to show her how to run it. Jack, expected to help, has not arrived, and Cora refuses to wait until evening to start her new craft.

Belle, her twin sister fears, may fall prey to white birches and want to paint pictures on bark. Cora fancies she will take to the pines, strong and dependable like big boys. The hermit of Fern Island waits in the title, promising mystery on the lake. The tale that follows mixes camp fun, motors, and a lakeside secret.
70814-after-world-s-end:
After Worlds End is a long tale of far science by Jack Williamson. It first ran in a pulp magazine in February of nineteen thirty nine. A front blurb asks if Earth men can beat a vast robot foe. One hero wakes from a long sleep cast by rays from the stars.

A dead man at a desk, hand clenched on a bright gem, opens the tale. His face shows youth and age at once, with deep grief in its lines. Cuts mar his frame in ways the finders can not yet place or name. A girl shut in a gem of black stone shares the hope of Earth. Wild odds pit frail men against a steel fiend for the world fate.
7095-malayan-literature-comprising-roman:
Malayan literature, translated into English for the first time with an introduction by Chauncey Starkweather, gathers romantic tales, epic poetry, and royal chronicles. The introduction calls the Epic of Bidasari easily the most charming poem of the collection, with all the absorbing fascination of a fairy tale. Readers glide into haunted palaces and beauteous gardens, through languorous nature into shadowy realms of the supernatural.

Sturdy bowmen and lithe lancers hurry in column, while mystic sentinels, djinns, demons, and spirit princes watch from another world. Starkweather praises a wealth of imagery and luxury of picturesqueness, shadowy, vague, mysterious, and entrancing. The volume opens Malay story and verse to English readers for the first time.
70979-the-riddle-of-the-rangeland:
Forbes Parkhill wrote The Riddle of the Rangeland, a novelette of the Wyoming mountains. The publisher's note says Parkhill lived in the West himself. His Ken-Caryl Case and other stories had already won him a name. The tale opens at the Red Rock ranger station. Sheriff Lafe Ogden, a long-barrelled revolver in his hand, knocks softly on the rough pine door. No answer comes.

The sheriff flings the door wide and stops short. Joe Fyffe, the forest ranger, lies face downward on the floor, crumpled and dead. Blood has dried round the edges where it spread beneath his arms. He has been dead some hours, shot, the men suppose. Young Otis Carr counted Fyffe a friend despite the ranger's silent, retiring ways. Parkhill builds a western murder mystery from that discovery: a dead ranger, an empty station, and a sheriff reading signs.
71152-a-lady-and-her-husband:
Lady and Her Husband is a novel by Amber Reeves of London. Putnam published it in New York and London in the year 1914. Eighteen chapters carry its study of a marriage in plain numbers. Chapter one opens on Rosemary looking round her mother's drawing room. The room charms her: gay, luxurious, and anxious to please all.

She feels sure her father must have planned that room himself. It reveals his mind: large, cheerful, excellent, and thorough in taste. Rosemary has chosen the room deliberately for an interview with her mother. She is going to tell her mother that she is in love. Shy of the poor lady's emotion, she fears a display there.
71258-celtic-scotland:
Celtic Scotland, a history of ancient Alban, is a large work on the early past of Scotland. It was printed at Edinburgh for David Douglas, with sellers in London, Cambridge, and Glasgow. The hosted copy comes from a later volume of the set. In a preface the author says the first volume went out of print, and that he revised the text with care for a new edition.

After long thought, he writes, he found nothing to alter in the views of early Scottish history set out in it. He confined himself to correcting plain mistakes and misprints. The work treats the Celtic centuries of Scotland, its kings, churches, and peoples, from records in Latin, Gaelic, and Welsh. Such histories rebuilt the distant past of the nation from charters and chronicles. This one stood as a standard account of Alban for scholars of its time.
71259-a-tour-through-holland:
Sir John Carr wrote A Tour Through Holland after traveling in the summer and autumn of 1806. His route ran along both banks of the Rhine to the south of Germany. Carr, of the Middle Temple, had already published The Stranger in Ireland and a tour round the Baltic. This Philadelphia printing dates to 1807.

The book is dedicated to John, Duke of Bedford, in a long letter praising his rule in Ireland. Carr lauds the Duke for going in person among the poor Irish peasantry and for trusting the laws over military force. The tour itself records what a well placed English traveler saw, heard, and judged in Holland and Germany.
71338-barotseland:
Barotseland: Eight Years among the Barotse is an account by Stirke, a native commissioner in Northern Rhodesia. John Bale published it in London. Sir Harry Johnston, once commissioner for Northern Zambezia, wrote an opening chapter. A photograph of Lewanika, late paramount chief of the Barotse, fronts the book. Stirke's preface thanks brother officials and a missionary friend for help. Photographers among his colleagues supplied the pictures.

Stirke stresses that the book is not official. No help came from the Administration, and the British South African Company did not approve it. He checked and rechecked his facts with care. Items lacking confirmation were cut, he says. The Barotse of his day were a mixed people, hard to describe with certainty. The book still offers, he holds, a fairly accurate picture. Eight years of residence stand behind its chapters.
71387-antiquarian-gleanings-in-the-north:
William Scott, of the Government School of Design at Newcastle, drew and etched a book of northern antiquities. George Bell of London sold it. Scott says in his opening note that the sketches began before any thought of print.

He bound himself to no one class of object. Some pieces were chosen for their tale, others for the rarity of their ornament. The first plate shows a nautilus cup set in gold, kept at Corby Castle. Scott calls it the finest of its kind he has seen. The second shows an ivory cup in gold, rich with pearls. Family lore ties it to a gift from Admiral Howard to Catherine of Aragon. Church work, plate, and old furniture fill the later plates.
71397-common-poisonous-plants-of-new-eng:
Common Poisonous Plants of New England is a short guide from the United States Public Health Service, issued in April nineteen sixty four. Heber W Youngken, dean of pharmacy at the University of Rhode Island, prepared the text. Joseph S Karas, head of the Poison Control Center at Rhode Island Hospital, helped as well. Photos came from Youngken. The price was thirty five cents from the Government Printing Office.

Short entries with photos treat one plant at a time in plain order. The list starts with the Amanita mushroom, baneberry, bittersweet, and bloodroot. It goes on to castor bean, foxglove, jimson weed, and lily of the valley. Poison hemlock and other New England risks close the run. Parents, teachers, and health staff can use the guide to spot risks fast.
7143-the-strange-cabin-on-catamount-isla:
Lawrence Leslie sends Max and his friends to the strange cabin on Catamount Island, opening with a dare from Herb Benson. Max must camp on the island, bad name and all, and stay a full week, though Benson doubts they have nerve even for the try. Contents promise Bandy legs in trouble, a sudden awakening, exploring the island, and what the ashes told Max.

The mystery of the cabin, an unwelcome discovery, and being watched from the shore follow, with the builder of the strange cabin, what happened on the second night, and a bold plan. Unseen perils hover near as the scheme works out, with unexpected allies and a last camp fire on the island. Leslie writes a boys camp mystery of dare, island, and secret.
71477-brave-bessie-westland:
Brave Bessie Westland is a story of Quaker persecution by Emma Leslie. The Religious Tract Society published the book at London. Leslie had written Audrey's Jewels and other tales for the young. Eight chapters carry the tale from a Quaker household to its close.

The story opens with Bessie hiding her small sisters in a cellar. Soldiers have taken their mother and father away for the faith. Bessie whispers that the Smithfield burnings are ended, to calm Dorothy's fears. Then a mob voice shouts down with the Quakers outside the door. Hands break furniture above while the girls cower in the dark. Bessie holds the door string and the children both. Leslie wrote of the suffering Friends of Charles the Second's reign for Sunday school readers.
71506-the-y-m-c-a-boys-on-bass-island:
The Boys on Bass Island, or The Mystery of Russabaga Camp, by Brooks Henderley, was copyrighted in New York in 1916. Henderley also wrote The Boys of Cliffwood in the same set. A front plate cries, steady now, keep her head straight into the wind. Twenty-nine chapters follow a Scout-like camp party through storms, losses, and a growing mystery.

Heads promise an invasion of pigs, a boy who had promised, and a surprise from a man named Nocker. On the island, things begin to vanish, nights bring strange events, and a wild man of the woods is suspected. A trap, a telltale footprint, and a pit that works clear the case. Henderley mixes camp craft, faith, and detection for boys.
717-chita-a-memory-of-last-island:
Lafcadio Hearn wrote this tale of Last Island, a pleasure resort off Louisiana that a great hurricane swept away. A small girl named Chita is found after the storm, alone among the wreck, and taken in by a Creole household. The book opens with the legend of the island, then follows Chita's rescue and her new life.

Hearn writes the Gulf coast with lush, musical prose, full of sea, heat, and Creole custom. Beneath the beauty lies the storm's terror and the fragility of a gay, careless world. The book is both a memorial to a lost place and a tender story of a child saved from the sea, told by a master of atmosphere.
71700-the-chronicles-of-fairy-land: Fergus Hume wrote the tales gathered as Chronicles of Fairyland, issued in a holiday line of juvenile classics with color pictures by Maria Kirk. The publisher's pages group it with George MacDonald's The Princess and the Goblin and Ouida's A Dog of Flanders, each in gilt cloth at a dollar and a half. The catalog copy gives the book's dress rather than its tales: octavo, decorated chapter headings, and color plates. Young readers got a fairy volume made to match the classics on the same shelf.
71936-pen-and-pencil-sketches-of-faro-e-:
Pen and Pencil Sketches of Faroe and Iceland is a travel book by Andrew James Symington. Fifty one illustrations engraved on wood by W J Linton picture it. An appendix holds translations from the Icelandic. The London edition is dated eighteen sixty two. A motto from Comus heads the book, on northern climes where day never shuts his eye. The volume is inscribed to the author's father in law, a Shetland doctor.

In his preface Symington says the greater part is a diary jotted down on the spot. It was written in the presence of the scenes described, he says. That keeps the freshness of first impressions for the reader, he hopes. The aim throughout is both to present pictures and to condense information, he adds. Frequent intercourse with Icelanders, in person and by letter, aided him.
72018-the-pilgrim-fathers-of-new-england:
Carlos Martyn wrote The Pilgrim Fathers of New England, a history from the American Tract Society. The New York book was entered for rights in 1867, at 150 Nassau Street. Martyn had written a life of John Milton and a history of the English Puritans. His preface cites Lord Bacon, who gave the highest earthly fame to builders of states. The Pilgrim Fathers, Martyn says, were members of that guild.

Their story, he holds, stands in the heroic age of America. Stoughton is quoted: no other state can boast such an origin. The tale is as true as it is beautiful, as authentic as it is sublime. The Forefathers built not for themselves or for posterity alone, Martyn adds. The career of the Pilgrims has been often painted, yet its interest never flags. The book gives the crossing, the colony, and the faith that bore both.
72061-in-the-great-white-land:
In the Great White Land is a tale of the Antarctic Ocean by Gordon Stables, printed at London and Glasgow by Blackie and Son. Stables also wrote The Naval Cadet and Crusoes of the Frozen North. A line from Coleridge about ice all around stands at the front of the book.

The tale is told in three books, from day dawn in the Arctic to a dash for the Pole. Chapter heads promise the ship's bears, first steps on the ice, a bright ice cave, and sledging on the tableland. Peril rules the last heads: fearful nights, hard suffering, and at last victory, with joy and sadness mixed.
72066-contraband:
Contraband is a novel by Clarence Budington Kelland, published by Harper and Brothers in 1923, alongside his Scattergood Baines and Sudden Jim. The setting is a small-town newspaper office whose owner, old man Nupley, has just died. His two printers, the veteran Tubal and the seventeen-year-old Simmy, have got out two issues alone and unaided since his death.

The opening scene is a dialect duet over the locked type form. The printers gossip about the heir who is coming to take over the paper: not the nephew they expected but a niece, and worse, a college woman. Simmy, who has thought deeply on such matters, declares that women have no business getting educated and should study cookbooks. Tubal, fifty come September and never married, shakes on a pact of bachelorhood. The comedy of the old hands awaiting their new mistress sets the novel's small-town machinery in motion.
72079-burden-the-hand:
Burden the Hand, a science fiction tale by Randall Garrett, ran in Infinity magazine in November 1958. A blurb at the head gives its hook in two lines. The clock was self correcting, so the plot of Van Ostrand was foolproof. Nikki Varden opens the tale staring down the barrel of a Lundhurst Twelve.

Her hands stay high above her head as she speaks to the men who hold her. Van Ostrand is big and fat, with sleepy eyes and an oily manner in the telling. The narrator says no one with half a brain could fall for that manner. A man who looks so much like a villain makes the mind reject the idea, he muses. That doubt is the trap the tale sets in its first pages.
72088-bomba-the-jungle-boy-on-jaguar-isl:
Bomba the Jungle Boy on Jaguar Island, or Adrift on the River of Mystery, is a boys' adventure by Roy Rockwood, with copyright in 1927 at New York. Rockwood also wrote the Great Marvel and Speedwell Boys books, and this is the fourth Bomba title in its list. A picture at the front shows Bomba dropped flat on the ground.

Chapter heads promise a blazing cabin, terrible jaws, a perilous crossing, and a skeleton. Bomba fights in the folds of a boa constrictor and faces trailing pumas and eyes that glare in the dark. The tale opens in storm, with rain in a pitiless torrent and thunder battering the hills, as Bomba's river journey turns to survival.
72156-through-england-on-a-side-saddle-i:
Through England on a Side Saddle is the diary of Celia Fiennes. Field and Tuer of the Leadenhall Press issued it in eighteen eighty eight. Fiennes rode through England in the reign of William and Mary. Mrs Griffiths, a kinswoman, wrote the first study of the diary here.

The study praises her close eye for manners and customs of those times. Towns, churches, and gentlemen seats are described in minute detail. Many seats she saw no longer exist, so her notes preserve them. She travelled on horseback or in her own equipage across many counties. The volume is given to the memory of the editor father.
72208-the-whirlwind:
The Whirlwind is a novel of the moor by Phillpotts, in three books. It came out at London in the first years of the last age, printed by a famed press of the city and a shire town. A front print shows its chief place, a farm house on the moor.

Its parts open with a man on a stone heap, then the farm it self. A stage of flops, kind words, and the keep of a great house fill the first book. A plain speech, a sharp word of blame, and a board meet join them. The price of a girl closes that book. First blood in a feud, the gates of dawn, and growth in thoughts fill the next.
72262-domestic-annals-of-scotland:
Robert Chambers wrote these domestic annals of Scotland from revolt to 1745. Chambers printed the book in Edinburgh and London in 1861. It follows two past volumes on Scotland from the Reformation. Chambers says the age is one of great transition in the land.

Rule shifts from harsh sway toward law bound government, he notes. Faith life softens, and taste for elegance and sport grows apace. Trade and work rise as pride and want give ground slowly. Chambers tells the change through home incidents told in the period words of the time.
72272-left-hand-right-hand:
James Schmitz wrote this science fiction story, printed in Amazing Stories in November 1962. Its headnote says men were tortured and killed while Earth scientists chatted pleasantly with the Tareeg, and asks whether they were traitors or waiting for the Ice Men.

Jerry Newland wakes on his bunk after being dead, in most practical respects, for the better part of three years. Troy Gordon tests him gently: names come back, but his work as courier pilot for the Cassa Expedition is gone again. They have been away from Earth three years and eight months, prisoners, and nobody else knows Newland is alive. A sign above the bunk coaches him to relax and take it easy. Readers get a slow-burn tale of damaged memory among the stars.
72398-the-right-hand:
The Right Hand: Left-Handedness is a study by Sir Daniel Wilson, president of the University of Toronto, printed at London in 1891. He dedicates the little volume to his grandson. The first chapter treats the hand itself. The hand, Wilson writes, is one of the most distinctive marks of man.

Without its special build man would be inferior to many other animals. The hand is the executive part of the arm by which man's capacity as the tool-user is set. It is the active agent of touch, the organ of the will, and the instrument that works with brain and heart. By it imagination is translated into fact. Later chapters treat the educated hand, palaeolithic dexterity, and the dishonoured hand, the left. Others handle the primitive abacus, the compass points, and handwriting. Wilson closes with theories in conflict and hand and brain.
72408-jupiter-found:
Jupiter Found is a science fiction story by Robert Young, from Amazing Stories of March 1963. Finlay illustrated the tale for the magazine in that issue. A blurb at its head says godhead can be more than a guilt complex in its theme. It can also be a sense of fulfilment that comes from the ability to create, it adds.

The tale opens on Jupiter, where a machine called 8M sinks a new shaft in the murk. He lowers his skip arm and scoops huge handfuls of iron ore into his blast furnace belly in the text. Around him swirls the greyish murk that passes for an atmosphere on that world.  A picture of himself of old at a roseate fireside flashes on his memory screen. Young robot, who remembers being a man, is one of his tender machines.
72418-the-truth-about-ireland:
The Truth About Ireland is a travel book by Alexander Corkey, printed with copyright in 1910. Its subtitle promises a trip through the Emerald Isle with an aeroplane. William Jennings Bryan wrote an introductory chapter on Ireland's bright future. Corkey dedicates the book to Wilbur and Orville Wright, conquerors of the air.

Nineteen chapters run from the beginning of the flight to the last day in Ireland. Corkey flies over Killarney, circles Londonderry, and alights at the Giant's Causeway. A flight with an Irish girl and days in Enniskillen and Dublin follow. Wicklow, the garden of Ireland, takes a chapter. The book mixes a new machine with an old country, seeing Ireland from above in 1910.
72516-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
The hosted file is the 1884 volume of Chambers's Journal with its index apparatus. Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art was a weekly. Chambers printed it at Edinburgh and London. A transcriber's table maps each issue to its pages. Number one ran from page 1 on the fifth of January. Each weekly number fills sixteen pages. The volume runs through the whole of 1884.

Such a table lets readers find a piece by its date. Bound volumes of the journal filled many home shelves. Its mix served the same public as its single issues. Tales, facts, and useful notes shared each number. The index form here is a modern helper for the text. It turns a year's weekly flow into a book. The journal was among the longest-lived of its kind. It taught and amused two generations of readers.
72520-annals-of-the-persecution-in-scotl:
James Aikman, who wrote a history of Scotland, compiled these annals of the Scots persecution. Hugh Paton printed the book at Edinburgh in 1842. Its span runs from the Restoration to the Revolution, years when faith and state tore at each other.

A plate at the front shows the Marquis of Argyle put to death in 1661. Book one runs from 1604 to 1660 to set the stage. Presbytery, the people's loved form of church rule, meets kings who first fight it, then bend. The Solemn League and Covenant, the fall of Hamilton, and the death of Charles fill the ground. Aikman tells how the stage was set for the hard years after 1660.
72627-observations-on-the-new-constituti:
Observations on the New Constitution is an Anti-Federalist pamphlet first printed at Boston in 1788, signed by a Columbian Patriot. This reprint is Old South Leaflets number 226, issued at Boston in 1955, with a prefatory note by Lawrence Towner. The pamphlet had its largest circulation in New York, in both pamphlet form and a newspaper series.

For many years the work was attributed to Elbridge Gerry, a leading Anti-Federalist. Towner explains that Mercy Otis Warren's own statement of authorship, in a letter of May 1788, gives her the honors instead. The note frames the era's problem: how to make government strong enough to survive, yet tender about individual life, liberty, and property.
72728-celtic-scotland:
Celtic Scotland is a history of ancient Alban by William Skene, the great Celtic scholar. Skene spent a life among Highland manuscripts, king lists, and church records of Scotland. His three volume work rebuilt early Scottish history from native sources at first hand. Alban is the old Gaelic name for the Scotland of Picts and Scots.

Footnotes in this text have been moved after each chapter and renumbered through the book. A lone letter with a macron survives in the transcription under a transcriber note. Tribes, saints, and the making of one kingdom from many fill the narrative. Historians still start from Skene when they enter Scotland first centuries.
72828-a-candle-in-the-wind:
Mary Imlay Taylor writes a home front novel in A Candle in the Wind, printed in New York in 1919. Taylor had writ The Impersonator and Caleb Trench. The book runs to thirty eight chapters of town and family life.

Diane is at her father's table with his guests when the tale starts. She hides the keen pain that the name of Overton wakes in her. The guest of honor is Arthur Faunce, young hero of a recent antarctic trek. New York has fêted him as the chief man left alive, raised up by the tragic death of Overton. Yet Faunce has come back to Mapleton at once, like a moth to the candle, the tale says.
72970-harebell-s-friend:
Harebell's Friend is a tale for children by Amy Le Feuvre, printed at London by the Religious Tract Society. Le Feuvre also wrote A Little Listener and Probable Sons. Eleven chapters carry the story, from a chapter called Not Wanted to one called Tom's Last Effort, with a runaway and a new uncle along the way.

The tale opens on a pier, where a small girl in a shabby waterproof stands watching the crowd. She has no parents, brothers, or sisters, and a district commissioner is bringing her home from the place where her parents died. Talk on the ship calls her a child bound to suffer, too full of feeling. Then a kind voice calls her little Harebell, and her face lights up.
73313-battleground:
Lester del Rey wrote this tale of doom in an alien culture. The story ran in Fantastic Universe in July 1954. A blurb asks just how wide Armageddon battleground may be. The hypercruiser Clarion cuts across space without going through it.

No stars, space, or time lie around the ship in transit. Great detectors follow an energy trail laid on the way out. Acting Captain Lenk studies his crew reflections in the port glass. Orders say survey all habitable planets on the line home to Earth. Jeremy the xenologist shrugs in the vote scene aboard the homeward bound ship here.
73357-no-star-s-land:
No Star's Land is a science fiction story by William Morrison. It ran in Fantastic Universe in July 1954. An editor's note praises Morrison as a master of the mistake story. Such tales show how foolish it is to confuse size with power. Here a spaceship lies marooned in free space between two blazing stars. A married couple, Jan and Karin, squabble as the ship drifts.

Karin declares that only a divorce can solve their quarrel. Jan answers that a court on Ganymede can grant one. Then he notices the ship has lost headway at half light speed. The star picture barely changes from second to second. They hang near two stars, each only millions of miles away. The teaser promises that a single atom can shatter a sun. Human smallness against cosmic giants drives the plot.
73463-the-girl-from-samarcand:
E Hoffmann Price wrote this story, printed in Weird Tales in May 1929. It opens in a New Orleans drawing room heavy with rich rugs. There Diane Clarke endures her guest's set question about them.

The rugs, Diane says, she married along with her husband Ham. He is a collector who fills the bathtub with milk to improve a little Bokhara's luster, and dares not let a maid touch the prayer-rug. She jokes that she has committed bigamy: the man was married to his rugs first, and she competes with a dozen favorites. Her friend Louise teases her for jealousy. The title points east, toward Samarcand and whatever the rugs conceal. Readers get Price's silky, sinister drawing-room weirdness.
73543-parish-life-in-medi-val-england:
Abbot Gasquet wrote on parish life in medieval England for the Antiquary's Books, first published at London in 1906 and reaching a second edition in 1907. Gasquet had written English Monastic Life. Passiontide, the office of the penitentiary, and the Lenten veil stand in a front picture. The parish opens the chapters, then the parish church in two long studies.

The parish clergy, the parish officials, and parochial finance follow. The parish church services, church festivals, and the sacraments fill the middle. The parish pulpit, parish amusements, and guilds and fraternities close the volume. A list of manuscript and printed authorities stands before the text. Pictures show a thurible found near Pershore, a pax, and a bracket with suspended dove and cover. Gasquet rebuilds the old English parish from records, rood loft to church ale, for general readers.
73620-the-island:
Richard Whiteing wrote The Island, or An Adventure of a Person of Quality, published by Longmans in London and New York in 1888. The narrator opens on a peak in the Pacific, at latitude twenty-five south, resting in the sounds of a summer noon. He hardly knows how he came there; last he remembers standing on the steps of the Royal Exchange in London.

His pocket diary shows a busy man's day: letters, coffee, an article for the Quarterly, and a tip about Turkish stocks. Chapters follow his flight, rescue, and settling down on the island. Then the book turns to government, arts, and laws, with a plot, a mission, and a village festival. Whiteing uses the castaway frame for a satire on English society and a sketch of a simpler commonwealth.
73678-a-trick-of-the-mind:
