A Trick of the Mind, by William Salton, ran in Fantastic in January 1958. The headnote says the average person uses about a tenth of his mind, and the rest lies dormant. Paul Donovan's whole brain suddenly went into action, it adds, and asks if a man can think his way out of jail.

Donovan sits at a bar and reaches for his martini glass. His hand stops in mid-air, rigid, and refuses to move. His whole body freezes while his mind seems to float above his head, watching in amusement. He orders the hand to obey with all his brain power behind the thought. The hand drops, but the glass slides across the bar of itself, rises to his lips, and pours. The glass then returns to its place while Donovan looks round in guilt.
73766-maori-folk-tales-of-the-port-hills:
Maori Folk Tales of the Port Hills is a set of tales of the Canterbury hills in New Zealand, told by James Cowan. It was put out in the early nineteen twenties by a house with shops in the chief towns of that land and in London. A note tells that some spellings stand as first printed.

A front print shows a map of the port and hills, and a photo shows the man who told the tales. The parts open with the views of the range, then take the Port Hills and their names. Maori names for each crag and pass are set out with their lore: hills of the rainbow god, a peak of a sky chief, and crags of sound steps. Old tales of ambush in the bush fill the next part.
73933-the-founding-of-new-england:
The Founding of New England is a history by James Truslow Adams. The Atlantic Monthly Press of Boston published it in 1921. A second impression followed in November 1922. A map of New England in 1640 illustrates the volume.

A saying of Lord Bryce on the historian's duty stands at the front. Truth, and truth only, is the aim, in that stern charge. The historian must record facts without favour to his own nation. The contents open with the American background and the staking out of claims. The race for empire and some aspects of Puritanism follow in turn. The first permanent settlement earns the fifth chapter of the book. The reassertion of imperial control leads toward the inevitable conflict. Loss of the Massachusetts charter closes the long colonial argument.
74256-children-of-no-man-s-land:
Children of No Man's Land is a novel by G B Stern, first published in London by Duckworth and Company in 1919. Stern had earlier written A Marrying Man and Grand Chain. The book is dedicated to Geoffrey Holdsworth. Its epigraph, from Ford Madox Hueffer, asks what love of one's land may be.

The poem answers that patriot love sleeps hidden for years. Then it takes the quiet heart like a wave and the whole soul like a tornado. The novel opens with Ferdinand Marcus urging that his daughter be let go and have a good time. Aunt Stella agrees that anything promises a change for a girl of twenty three. Behind the light opening stands the war's no man's land of the title. Stern writes of a generation caught between countries and loyalties in 1919.
74576-when-freemen-shall-stand:
When Freemen Shall Stand is a science fiction tale by Nelson Bond, first printed in Fantastic Adventures in November 1943. A headnote sets its stakes: Earth was conquered by Venus and her master, but the mysterious faces of Mount Rushmore became the gods that gave hope and fighting courage to beaten man.

The opening scene sits in a war time laboratory. Stephen Duane, a chemist now wearing lieutenant's bars, works with his assistant Chuck on a final experiment with a new gas. Duane hopes it might end the Second World War all of a sudden. A guard in a gas mask at an open door draws his sharp suspicion, and a barked German command tests the man's reflexes.
7460-how-sammy-went-to-coral-land:
Emily Paret Atwater, author of Tommy's Adventures, wrote this little volume for children spending time by the sea. The framing comes from a family holiday. Little Bob had been very ill in the spring, and the doctor ordered sea air and sea bathing to bring color back to his pale cheeks. Grandma, Bob, and Eleanor are all part of the seashore party.

Sammy's own tale carries the book. He goes out to see the world, escapes from a shark, and reaches Coral-Land, where the wonders of the sea unfold. Atwater mingles fiction with facts, drawing the natural history from Cooke's Toilers of the Sea and Hartwig's Denizens of the Deep. Young readers learn about coral and sea creatures while following a boy's adventure.
74683-a-dangerous-friend:
Emma Leslie wrote a moral tale for young readers about a boy named Tom and his three months in London. Leslie had written The Magic Runes and The Making of a Hero. Tom is about fourteen, the son of the village blacksmith. A letter from Uncle George opens the tale and sets Tom on his way.

In London a bad friend leads Tom toward theft and shame. Chapters ask if Tom was a thief, tell of an escape for his friend Bob, and call the fruits of sin apples of Sodom. The way of wrongdoers is shown as hard, as the chapter heads warn. The tale ends with a clear lesson on choice of friends.
74703-milly-s-errand:
Emma Leslie tells a shore tale in Milly's Errand, or Saved to Save, printed at Philadelphia in 1873. Martien made the book. A plate shows a boy running to a spar, where a child lies securely lashed to it. Eleven chapters carry the moral tale.

The brothers lead, then the little waif and the cottage home. The widow's death and God's messenger deepen the pathos. Rest for the weary, the doctor's kindness, and the doctor's story fill the mid run. Major Ferrers and a chapter headed Blessed Are the Meek close in on the conclusion. Chapter one opens on a sandy shore, where an old sailor raises his spy glass. Stormy weather is coming, he tells two stout boys with a donkey cart of sea weed. A ship in the offing had better tack for the harbor, he warns.
74710-celtic-scotland:
William Skene wrote Celtic Scotland, a history of ancient Alban, here in volume three. David Douglas put out this second edition at Edinburgh in 1890. Skene was historiographer-royal for Scotland. This third and last volume is named Land and People. A map shows Scotland with the ancient divisions of the land. A new edition was called for, and Skene took the chance to correct press errors.

This volume deals with the early land tenures and social condition of the Celtic inhabitants. Obsolete terms and old Celtic words crowd its pages, and breed mistakes of the press. Skene revised the text with great care in that view. He finds no material change to make in his views or conclusions. Those rest, he says, on years of careful research into a very obscure subject. A long Gaelic poem, with English facing it, stands in an appendix.
74742-here-and-beyond:
Here and Beyond is a book of six tales by Edith Wharton. Appleton published the work at New York and London in 1926, with decorations by Caswell. The stories had appeared in magazines in the years just before. The contents run from Miss Mary Pask to a tale named Velvet Ear-Pads.

The first story is told by a painter who has worked in Brittany. He delays a full year before he can speak of one night at Morgat. A fever in Egypt and a nervous collapse followed that night. Even writing of it was beyond him until rest cures in Switzerland rebuilt him. The opening sets the tale's air of dread held under plain telling. Other stories treat young gentlemen, a haunting, and a temperate zone household. Wharton's cool style governs tales of the seen and the unseen alike.
74822-our-trip-to-blunderland:
Jean Jambon wrote Our Trip to Blunderland, or a grand excursion to Blundertown and back, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1877 in its third thousand. Charles Doyle drew sixty pictures for the book. A preface in small capitals explains that the nursery has its share of the author's day. The tale was made to suit cooling times in other nurseries, as it had in his own.

A second note owns a debt to the maker of Queen Alice, hailed as Carrollus Primus. Three little boys, named Norval, Jaques, and Ranulf for the tale, have been reading of Alice's strange doings in sleep. Jaques wonders if he could get to sleep like her and walk through looking-glasses. Ranulf wants only to think it too, as Alice did.
74865-where-the-atlantic-meets-the-land:
Caldwell Lipsett wrote Where the Atlantic Meets the Land, a book of Irish tales published by Roberts Brothers in Boston in 1896. The contents promise a legend of Barnesmore Gap, a night of the Home Rule Bill, a border war, and a story called Orange and Green. A peasant tragedy and a pauper's burial stand beside lighter pieces.

The first tale, The Unforgiven Sin, opens on the rocks at Kilcross. Bella Sweeny, a maid at the big house, spends a holiday with Terry Gallagher, a groom, who does the honors of the scenery. They sit where black cliffs give way to sandy lowlands and a flat rock runs into the sea. Lipsett writes of the Donegal coast and its people with a local's ear for names, courtship, and feud.
74943-isles-of-the-sea-or-young-america-:
William Adams, who wrote as Oliver Optic, closed his second Young America Abroad series with a homeward voyage. The copyright dates from 1877. A preface calls the book the sixth and last of the series. It tells of the academy squadron on its way home across the Atlantic, and its title names the isles that fill the trip.

The young students call at Madeira, the Canaries, the Azores, and the Bermudas. One ship of the fleet pushes on to the Cape Verde Islands. At each stop the teacher of geography and history has his say, and the surgeon walks the shore with the boys. Tom Speers stands at the center of the story. Adams praises his high aims and firm purpose as the true marks of a young man. A long search at sea gives the tale its chief suspense.
75012-the-mystery-of-cabin-island:
The Mystery of Cabin Island is a Hardy Boys mystery by Franklin Dixon. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York in 1929. Walter Rogers drew the illustrations. The volume stands eighth in the series list printed up front. The Tower Treasure heads that list.

The contents promise a winter adventure. Ice-boating on the bay opens the tale. A strange note arrives early. Holiday plans bring the boys to Cabin Island. A man named Hanleigh watches them, unaware that he is watched himself. Stolen supplies and chicken thieves raise the stakes. A notebook and a cipher drive the middle chapters. The chimney hides the book's secret. Elroy Jefferson is pleased in the final chapter.
75051-borderland:
Borderland: A Country-Town Chronicle is a novel by Jessie Fothergill, published by Bentley in London in 1890. Fothergill had written The First Violin, Kith and Kin, and Probation. The book opens with a childhood chapter, then a first numbered chapter called Otho's Return. Magdalen and the neighbourhood, Langstroth's folly, and the faculty of close observation follow in the contents.

The human web of the town is sketched in the chapter titles. Gilbert's cautiousness, Gilbert's coup de théâtre, and the first-fruits of Gilbert's wisdom mark one thread. Michael, Roger, and Gilbert are grouped in another chapter, and three women in a later one. Otho's letter-bag, Eleanor, and thrust and parry fill the middle. The later titles grow quainter: brass pots and earthenware pipkins, how Crackpot was scratched, and how Ada solved her problem.
7520-snow-blind:
Katharine Newlin Burt, author of The Branding Iron, sets this novel in a snow country under a noon sun. The vast, flat land lies buried deep in snow, like a paper hoop rimmed by dark primeval forest, its surface shining with an unbearable brightness as of sun-struck glass. To the north, a single blunt mountain head breaks the horizon, and Hugh Garth drops down into the small space shoveled clear before his hidden cabin door.

Inside, a solid table stands in the center of the floor, and a woman sets heavy earthenware plates, nicked and discolored. She herself seems heavy and discolored, yet like the stove she has a dull glow. Burt writes the winter West as a place of glare, cold, and stubborn human warmth, where the snow blinds the eyes but not the heart.
75263-from-the-heart-of-a-friend:
From the Heart of a Friend is an anthology of sayings on friendship, chosen by Amy Addingley. Platt and Peck printed it at New York with copyright in 1910. Its preface opens with the name of friend itself, which quickens the pulse and warms the heart. Friendship, it says, is the most beautiful relationship in human intercourse.

The selections then speak in turn. Quarles advises judging a friend slowly, then receiving him joyfully and using him as one's very self. Landor says every eye turns to friendship in distress and in gladness alike. Lytton calls a good wife a man's best female friend. Emerson says a friend is one before whom he may think aloud. The little book suits a gift between friends.
75360-the-human-foot-and-the-human-hand:
The Human Foot and the Human Hand is a work of anatomy by Humphry, lecturer on anatomy and physiology in the University of Cambridge. Macmillan published it in 1861. The pages began as two popular lectures delivered in Cambridge, much enlarged for print but keeping the lecture form. The contents open with a complaint: most persons are strangely ignorant of the structure of their own bodies.

The foot comes first: the bones of the leg and foot, the peculiarity of the great toe, and the arch of the foot, more elastic in front than behind. Humphry compares man's leg with the horse's, and notes the calf as characteristic of man. The hand follows, with the dependence of hand on foot and the division of labour in the animal world.
75370-david-goes-to-greenland:
David Goes to Greenland is a boy's account of a voyage to the far north by David Binney Putnam. It came out in New York and London in 1926 from G. P. Putnam's Sons. A foreword by Captain Bob Bartlett stands at its front. The book is pictured from photos, with ornaments from drawings made for it by Kakutia, an Eskimo, at Karnah on Whale Sound. It is given to the author's mother.

The contents trace the trip in order. Off to Greenland stands first, then Through the Straits of Belle Isle and We Reach Greenland. Along the Greenland Coast, Upernivik and the Duck Islands, and Across Melville Bay stand next. Shipwreck and The Morrissey Repaired stand in the list, then Our First Narwhal and Our Eskimo Artist. Walrus Hunting and Across to Jones Sound close the run shown.
754-the-story-of-mankind:
Hendrik Van Loon wrote this history of the world for young readers, from early man to his own day. He tells the story in short, vivid chapters, with maps and drawings by his own hand, moving from Egypt and Greece through Rome, the Middle Ages, and the modern age. His voice is that of a lively teacher, not a dry scholar.

Van Loon links great events to the lives of ordinary folk and to ideas that changed the world, from writing to steam. The book won the first Newbery Medal and taught generations their first world history. It still charms as an old-fashioned, humane tour of mankind, even where later research has revised its facts.
75400-the-boys-of-columbia-high-on-the-d:
The Boys of Columbia High on the Diamond, by Graham Forbes, bears a copyright of 1911. The book is one of a set about the same school boys, with tales on the river, the gridiron, and the ice. Its short title is Winning Out by Pluck.

The first chapter takes the boys on the way to a baseball game, loud with school spirit. A warm start for the pitcher Coddling leads into a game worth seeing. A rally comes too late, and a thunderbolt hits the school soon after. Chapters treat a mark in clay, a plain talk with Bill Klemm, and a boy twice a prisoner. The close brings an uphill game won at the end, in true school-story style.
75418-ouroboros-or-the-mechanical-extens:
Garet Garrett's essay in the To-Day and To-Morrow series asks what machines are doing to mankind. Its title names the fabulous serpent that swallowed its own tail, an emblem, Garrett says, of man's old wish to get his desires by magic. The real story he tells is the quest since Adam to escape the doom of toil from the gate of Eden: in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.

Chapters treat the machine as if, the law of machines, the men who mind them or starve, and the paradox of surplus. Garrett argues that prayer, magic, and science have all aimed at the same plenty without drudgery. The book closes with dim vistas of a future the machine is still making.
75475-the-girl-he-left-behind:
Helen Beecher Long wrote a girls' novel copyrighted in 1918, drawn by R Emmett Owen, in her Do Something line. Long had written the Janice Day books, four volumes at a dollar twenty five each. A picture caption quotes a man leaving Miss Clayton to keep things straight here. Chapter one is titled So Perfectly Capable. A Comparison and a chapter called Dogfennel follow.

The girl left behind holds the home front during the first World War. Sully published the book at New York. Long's Janice Day heroine had already taught girls to do things. This wartime tale gives the same lesson under separation. Skiing appears in the early contents.
75823-by-beach-and-bog-land:
By Beach and Bog-Land is a volume of Irish stories by Jane Barlow, published in London by T Fisher Unwin in 1905. Paul Henry drew the frontispiece. An epigraph from Swinburne sings of the old green Irish land wrapped round by the sea. The stories are set among the poor of the west.

In the Winding Walk opens the contents. A Money-Crop at Lisconnel and The High Tide and the Man-Trappers follow. The Foot-Sticks of Slughnatraigh and Old Isaac's Biggest Haul keep the local colour thick. Crazy Mick and Widow Farrell's Wonderful Age close the visible list. Barlow wrote of bog and shore communities with a folklorist's ear. Her tales preserve the speech and hardships of Irish country people for English drawing rooms of the Edwardian years.
75901-elfin-songs-of-sunland:
Elfin Songs of Sunland is a book of children's verse by Charles Keeler, with decorations by Louise Keeler. The Live Oak Publishing Company of Berkeley, California, issued this fourth edition, the songs having first been copyrighted in 1904 and revised in 1914 and 1920.

Keeler dedicates the book in verse: elfin songs of sunland, frolicland and funland, little rhymes of child hours, wood elves and wild flowers, jingles of the forest green, all for little Merodine. The song list runs through a child's day and year. Come Away Children calls the troop out to play. Pieces follow on the hand-organ man, popping corn, the baker man, tops, and the kite. Then come the see-saw, soap bubbles, the brass band and the merry-go-round. The opening song makes the poet a piper: come away, children, frisk along with me, for there is sunshine and singing ahead.
76113-the-horror-in-the-burying-ground:
The Horror in the Burying-Ground, by Hazel Heald, ran in Weird Tales in May 1937. Its tag calls it a grim tale of a double burial in the old town of Stillwater. A short frame praises Heald's name with the magazine's fans, won by The Horror in the Museum and Winged Death. The tale starts on the old Stillwater road, used when the state road to Rutland shuts. Drivers hurry past one shut, still farmhouse on a knoll.

At the south edge of the town, a white-bearded half-wit haunts the old burying-ground and talks to those in the graves. The town itself rots: tower down, half its homes empty, life shrunk to Peck's store. Loungers there hint more than they say of the Sprague house. Horror fans get rot, hush, and a grave tale in whispers.
76247-how-joy-was-found:
Isobel W Hutchison writes a fantasy play in How Joy Was Found, from Frederick A Stokes of New York, copyrighted in 1917. The cast list is an allegory: Finn is Humanity, the Carpenter is Duty, the Tracker is Obedience, and the Gripper is Constancy. The Climber is Faith, a girl, and the Thief is Love, an old woman.

The Listener is Hope, a boy, and his puppy Bran is Joy, given to Hope for the present. Act one opens on the Green Isle, an earthly paradise across the western main, where the Big Young Hero sits among flowers. A girl sails in singing of harbors.
76250-on-the-borders-of-pigmy-land:
On the Borders of Pigmy Land, by Ruth B Fisher, was printed by Fleming H Revell at New York, Chicago, and Toronto in 1905. The tale starts at the start of 1900, when a steamer set seven missionaries down at Mombasa for far Uganda. Six were fresh to the dark continent. The Uganda Railroad bears them in.

Heads walk the land: Mengo, then Toro, the land of the Mountains of the Moon. Home life, royal life, women, and child life each get a full scan. Long tramps lead to the Albert Edward Lake and at last to the Pigmies, the Batwa, and a climb to the snows. Work in church, ward, and school closes the book. Mission fans get a bright, close view of new Uganda.
76532-gay-s-year-on-sunset-island:
Gay's Year on Sunset Island is a girls' adventure novel by Marguerite Aspinwall, copyrighted in 1926. The Goldsmith Publishing Company of Cleveland issued it. Gay Annersley, fifteen and an orphan, tells her own story. She lives in the sleepy New England village of Braeburn. Her aunt Mollie, her mother's twin, raised her from a week old. Uncle Charles and her cousins complete the household.

A surprise opens the first chapter and sends the family off. Planter's house, Rosemary's diary, and an exploring party follow. A night in the caves and Sir Henry Morgan's map raise the pirate strain. The map is stolen, and a boat called the Myra brings visitors. Dead Men's Inlet and Morgan's trail lead to the treasure hole. Captain Rawson returns before the lost treasure closes the tale.
76597-in-the-hollow-of-his-hand:
Hesba Stretton wrote In the Hollow of His Hand, issued in London by the Religious Tract Society. Stretton had earlier written Jessica First Prayer, Alone in London, and Bede Charity. Thirty two chapters fill the novel. A plate shows a man laying his hand on a woman heart. The tale treats faith under harsh rule, in Scotland and in Russia.

Chapter one treats the Scotch Covenanters, and chapter two treats the Russian Stundists. A boy reads by his sick mother bed in a clear, low voice with a foreign accent. He feels her feeble hands press his as he reads of sheep sent forth among wolves. Later chapters bring Father Cyril, a forwarding prison, and the great Siberian road. Exiles, a prison hospital, and a begging song show the cost of faith. The tale ends with rescue and a letter from Siberia.
76689-snow-blind:
Snow-Blind, a northern tale by Albert Treynor, opens with a radio call. Treynor had earlier written Hands Up, the title page notes. The book was printed in 1928 and came out in 1929. A Springfield station speaks to far posts of the Mounted Police. Its voice hunts Sergeant Buck Tearl at Port-o'-Prayer in the north.

Chapter heads sketch a hunt across snow and forest trails. A girl in handcuffs, an owl murder case, and lost loot appear. Lost tracks, night raiders, and a last-stand post fill the mid list. The call goes out to factors, whalers, and frost-bit police alike. Men at the edge of the Arctic hear that home voice nightly. The tale then drops into the white world those men patrol.
76820-the-history-of-the-norman-conquest:
Edward Freeman's History of the Norman Conquest of England is kept in volume one, third edition revised, printed at Oxford by the Clarendon Press in 1877. The full title adds its causes and its results. Freeman was a late fellow of Trinity College, and the title page piles his honours high, from learned societies at St Petersburg and Rome to the Historical Society of Massachusetts. The volume carries the preliminary history down to the election of Eadward the Confessor.

In his preface Freeman reports a thorough revision. He has added and corrected in detail wherever fresh matter or fresh light appeared, and improved the style, often putting a good English word where a stranger had crept in. One narrative point changed: on James Parker's arguments, he now holds that the murder of Sigeferth and Morkere at Oxford had been confounded with the massacre of Saint Brice.
76916-em-s-husband:
Mrs E D E N Southworth wrote a sequel to Em, by the author of Ishmael, Self Raised, and Lilith, published at New York by A L Burt. Chapter one, to the island, opens with verse from H Alford on a cliff bounded stream at summer noon. The pretty White Dove lay rocking at its moorings, the tale begins. She was gray outside and white within, and as clean as any little boat need be.

Old 'Sias hands his young passenger aboard and makes her comfortable in the stern. He loosens the chain and spreads the snowy sail. Southworth was America's bestselling novelist of the story papers. Her Em books ran through many Burt reprints.
76954-the-history-of-the-norman-conquest:
Volume two of Edward A Freeman's History of the Norman Conquest of England came from the Clarendon Press at Oxford in 1868. The volume covers the reign of Eadward the Confessor, the first stage of the struggle between Normans and Englishmen.

Freeman begins with Eadward's election and carries the story to his death, taking in the early years of William in Normandy as well. The fight in these years is political rather than open war, fought inside the English kingdom. Harold and William slowly emerge as the leaders of their two nations, though not yet as open enemies. The preface also maps the whole five-volume plan, from the causes of the Conquest to its results.
77109-a-journey-to-the-world-under-groun:
Klimius tells A Journey to the World Under-Ground, printed at London in 1742. Astley in Paul's churchyard and Collins at Salisbury sold the book. It is translated from the original. Contents open with the author's descent to the subterraneous world. His descent upon the planet Nazar follows in the second chapter.

The city of Keba, the court of the Potuan empire, and its people follow. Their religion, policy, and academy take chapters. A journey round Nazar fills a central chapter. Banishment and a voyage to a land of wonders come next. The rise of the fifth monarchy and the author's imperial dignity follow. A catastrophe, a return home, and an appendix close the tale. In 1664, after his Copenhagen examinations, the descent begins. Klimius gives a satire in the dress of a voyage within the earth.
77398-crimes-of-the-house-of-austria-aga:
Peabody edited Crimes of the House of Austria Against Mankind, in 1852. Putnam at New York put out this second edition that year. The charges are proved by extracts, the title page promises. Coxe, Schiller, Robertson, Grattan, and Sismondi supply the history. A history of the constitution of Hungary stands inside as well.

That Hungarian piece came out in May 1850, the title notes. The book opens on Schlegel's philosophy of history and its sophistry. The final cause of the universe, Schlegel would have it, built an empire. That empire was to be the bulwark of Christendom, he taught. Eighteen lectures in Vienna made that extraordinary course, the editor scoffs. Imperial authority alone could compel an audience to endure them, he adds. The imperial house challenges mankind to bring it to judgment, he holds. The extracts then arraign Austria century by century.
77457-the-machinery-of-the-mind:
Violet M Firth wrote The Machinery of the Mind. Dodd, Mead and Company issued it at New York in 1922. A G Tansley wrote the foreword. Twenty-four chapters fill the contents. Chapter One treats the body as the vehicle of mind. The growth of the nerve system follows.

How an idea enters the mind comes third. Upper and lower levels of mind get their own chapters. Complexes, instincts, and their diseases take the middle. Chapters on conflict, repression, and dissociation lead on. Dreams, phantasies, and delusions get a study. Chapters on treatment by mind close the course, with hypnosis among them. A plain tour of the new psychology, the book brought Freud-era terms to common readers.
77480-the-saga-of-silver-bend:
J E Grinstead wrote a western tale that ran in Argosy All Story Weekly in March 1929, in three weekly parts. Two riders haze cattle north toward Silver Bend. Dolly is a small, round faced singer with auburn curls. Old Sankey is long, lank, and thoughtful, with cold gray eyes. The two are side partners despite their differences.

Dolly sings the song of the Railroad Ranch as they ride. Sankey warns that killers across the river mean to cut the herd at the home round up. Silver Bend loops six miles deep, shaped like a bottle. Randy Ross, the head note says, must face death when war breaks loose.
77646-oberland:
Dorothy Richardson wrote a tale of a Swiss stay in her famed long set. Oberland first came out in London in 1927. Her set lists Pointed Roofs, Backwater, and Honeycomb ere it. The Tunnel, Interim, Deadlock, and Revolving Lights stand there too. The Trap stands just ere Oberland in that long chain of books.

A third porter fills her heart with hope in the first page. He bears a pile of soft head rests in his slow walk. Yet he goes on as deaf as the rest to her need. Her bags chain her feet as she dreams of a run and a tip. One yes or no is all she asks of the men there. Mind's fine film rules it.
77696-outward-bound:
Outward Bound is a play by Sutton Vane, printed at London in 1924. It was first produced at the Everyman Theatre, Hampstead, on 17 September 1923. Stanley Lathbury played Scrubby, Diana Hamilton played Ann, and Clare Greet played Mrs Midget. The scene is on board ship, and the time is the present.

Act one is in harbour in the morning, act two at sea the same evening, and act three about six days later. The curtain rises on a room that suggests rather than represents the lounge smoke-room of a small ocean liner. A bar stands on the right, a small writing table on the left. The centre door opens onto the deck, and behind it the liner railings can be seen. The colour of the sky arrests the attention at once: vague and almost nondescript.
77830-natural-history-lore-and-legend:
Hulme's Natural History Lore and Legend, issued by Bernard Quaritch in London in 1895, gathers quaint and bygone beliefs about the natural world from ancient and medieval writers. The subtitle warns that these authorities are of varying degrees of reliability.

The first chapter weighs how medieval naturalists worked: honest searchers, Hulme argues, whose science was bent by moral teaching, ready belief, and love of the marvellous. He draws on Pliny, Herodotus, Aristotle, bestiaries, and travel books from Marco Polo to Mandeville. Later chapters take up pygmies, men with tails, dog-headed peoples, mermaids, and werewolves. The book preserves a whole lost picture of nature, the one Europeans held before modern science remade it.
77852-country-rambles-in-england:
Country Rambles in England is a naturalist's journal with notes by the author of Rural Hours. Phinney of Buffalo published this American edition in 1853. A verse motto promises notes on plants, trees, birds, and insects. The preface starts from Gilbert White's Natural History of Selborne. No book like it had appeared since, the writer laments. That book kindled an ardent love of nature's ways early in life.

Constant observation of rural objects followed from that spark. Reflections arose and notes were made over many years. The journal gathers those notes into a country record. Susan Fenimore Cooper, the Rural Hours author, supplied the notes and additions. Her father was the novelist of the Leatherstocking tales. The English journal is the work of John Leonard Knapp. American readers got it framed by a kindred spirit.
77853-the-yangtze-valley-and-beyond:
The Yangtze Valley and Beyond is an account of journeys in China by Mrs. J. F. Bishop, known as Isabella L. Bird. It treats chiefly the province of Sze Chuan and the Man-tze of the Somo territory. The book came out in London in 1899 from John Murray, with a map and 116 pictures. It is given, with leave, to the Marquess of Salisbury.

A picture at the front shows Tibetan lamas masked for a rite dance. The contents open with a first chapter of a geographic kind, as the list begins. The dedication page states the author's deep respect for its man. It praises the noble and selfless work he has done for the British Empire, in her words. The book is a record of travel in west China by a famed woman traveler of her age.
78094-the-haunting-hand:
The Haunting Hand is a mystery novel by Roberts, published in New York in 1926. Its frontispiece shows Margot watching in terror as a small thin hand reaches from under her bed. The first chapter is called Movie Men and Mannequins. The tale opens in mid-October, with Margot Anstruther glad to live her days out of doors.

Chapter titles build the shivers: the grisly hand and the flame, a creature without a body, a midnight prowler, and a witness from the dead. Someone asks whose hand it is, and radium worth a king's ransom enters the plot. The book mixes the picture-studio world with ghost-story dread in the popular manner of the nineteen twenties.
78122-the-history-of-the-norman-conquest:
Volume three of The History of the Norman Conquest of England, by Edward Freeman, was printed at the Clarendon Press, Oxford, in 1869. Its subject is the reign of Harold and the interregnum. A Latin text from Deuteronomy about setting a king over the land heads the title page.

In his preface, Freeman explains a long delay: he waited for an accurate military ground plan of the battlefield of Senlac. He walked the ground in June with Captain James, and thanks the Duke of Cleveland for free access to the field within his private grounds at Battle Abbey. Companions at Stamford Bridge, talks with Professor Stubbs, and Bodleian checks all fed a battle account drawn from the original writers.
7843-the-happy-end:
Joseph Hergesheimer's The Happy End gathers stories written, he says, for one purpose only: to give pleasure, at the request of friends he had pleased. He dedicates them not to critics, middlemen, or academies, but, with a joke, to his grocer, who fed him in hard times.

Contents include Lonely Valleys, The Egyptian Chariot, The Flower of Spain, Tol'able David, Bread, Rosemary, Roselle, and The Thrush in the Hedge. The first tale opens in a rectory where a maid doubts a visitor's welcome. Warm, polished, and humane, the stories seek a happy end.
78473-reflections-of-a-beginning-husband:
Reflections of a Beginning Husband is a set of essays by Edward Sandford Martin. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in April 1913. Martin also wrote The Luxury of Children and Lucid Intervals before it. Eight chapters range from marriage plans to babies and to politics. Chapter heads promise details of living, commodities, and contentment in turn.

The first chapter opens with a letter that sets the comic tone. The writer and Cordelia wish to wed again, but not to be engaged. They ask leave to elope, as the more private and feasible way. Later chapters dine out, talk of schooling, and weigh the baby at home. Martin's voice is wry, urbane, and fond of the small ironies of wed life.
78499-the-royal-forests-of-england:
Charles Cox wrote on the royal forests of England in a book first published at London in 1905, with fifty three illustrations. The Greendale Oak of 1720 stands at the front. Cox gives the book to Richard Whitworth, chaplain of Newstead Priory and forty years vicar of Blidworth. Whitworth had a remarkable grip on the forest lore of Sherwood, Cox says, and skill as a ballad writer in the old lines.

Early forests, the forest courts, and the forest officers open the work. The beasts of the forest, agistments, hounds and hunting, and the trees follow. Later forest history leads into county tours: Sherwood, the High Peak, Duffield Frith, Dean, Essex, Windsor, and Sussex among them. Antiquaries and walkers get law, sport, and timber history in one full survey.
78721-with-the-lost-legion-in-new-zealan:
Colonel G Hamilton Browne, called Maori Browne and a late commandant in colonial forces, wrote a memoir of service in New Zealand, drawn by S Valda. He dedicates it to the officers and men of the Lost Legion. Their bones, he writes, lie in forgotten graves on fern ranges and in dense bush. They fell fighting for queen and flag.

Part one tells why he joined, his start, and his baptism of fire at Otapawa. Chapters cover bush whacking, the troopers, and how Maoris should be fought. Part two gives yarns of the Gate Pah, Te Kooti, and Ngatapa. The memoir is a veteran's record of the New Zealand wars.
78788-notes-on-the-cathedral-libraries-o:
Notes on the Cathedral Libraries of England, by Beriah Botfield, was printed at London in 1849. Botfield dedicates the notes to the Bishop of Ripon in warm terms. That bishop had been the instructor of his earlier years. He remained the friend of his maturer years, the dedication adds.

The preface grants that cathedral churches have been described and illustrated often. Little remains to be done in that direction, Botfield allows. The libraries chained above the stalls were another matter in his day. He tours the great collections of books kept in the cathedrals. Manuscripts, early printed books, and chained folios fill his notes. The book is a founding survey of England’s cathedral book rooms. Bibliophiles still start from Botfield on these shelves.
78796-the-crown-jewels-of-england:
The Crown Jewels of England is a book on the crown's own gems and gold. One writer kept the Jewel House in the Tower of London. The other was a scholar of old crafts and church lore. The book came out in 1919 in a fine, small run.

It is given, by leave, to the king on the throne at the time. Old books on crownings are listed at the front for the reader. They run from the days of the second Charles to late works. The seals of the realm are drawn from the seals as they stand. Care was taken to check each sketch with a known work on seals. The gems are thus shown with the weight of the house that guards them.
7882-the-life-of-kit-carson-hunter-trapp:
Edward S. Ellis's The Life of Kit Carson, hunter, trapper, guide, Indian agent, and colonel, opens by saying Carson's real worth was known only to close friends and careful students. More than his titles, he held mental and moral gifts that would have raised him in any calling.

Cast on the far western frontier as a youth, he won respect from tough, often lawless men through integrity, bravery, loyalty, quick judgment in danger, woodcraft, and daring leadership. As friend and counselor to Fremont the Pathfinder across the Rockies, Father Kit became a frontier legend.
78956-culture-s-garland:
Culture's Garland is a book of memoirs by Eugene Field, issued at Boston in eighteen eighty seven. Its subtitle calls it memoranda of the gradual rise of literature, art, music, and society in Chicago. Other western centres are named in a joking phrase as fellow ganglia. Julian Hawthorne wrote an introduction. A portrait shows the author at the age of thirty.

The preface argues that American humour has fallen to specialists. Each famous humorist keeps to his own line and never strays, it says. Field holds that humour means more than one man's comic oddity. It is the arch smile, half quizzical and half tender, with which human nature views its own follies. The introduction praises Field's name in journalism. His humour, it says, has a wider and loftier scope than the common run.
78970-local-color-in-loco-land:
Tuttle tells a tall, comic Western tale in the voice of Ike Harper, who watches two Eastern writers arrive by stage at Paradise. Orville Wellington Chatterton and William Burton Suggs have come West to live among plain folk and gather local color for a book on bold, rough life. Their guide is 'Dirty Shirt' Jones, who has one good eye and little patience.

Much of the fun comes from talk. The visitors use fine words for simple things, while Jones and Harper answer in dry Western speech. Suggs and Chatterton carry a small pistol and big plans, and their search for wild material sets up the clash that drives the story.
79060-from-england-to-iceland:
From England to Iceland is a travel record of a steamer trip north, fronted by the sailing bills of the Leith and Iceland Steam Shipping Company. Their first class screw steamer Camoens, of 1264 tons, ran in season between Granton and Iceland with mails and guests. First cabin fare was five pounds, or eight pounds for the round trip.

Ads for a guide to Iceland by Lock, with a large map of volcano sites, salmon rivers, and farms for night stays, fill the next leaves. Notes from a tourist on board the Camoens then tell of a calm day spent watching for the midnight sun. At the top of the run, some eight miles inside the Arctic ring, the sun sank red but would not set.

79221-local-option-in-loco-land:
Local Option in Loco Land is a western tale by W C Tuttle. Tuttle also wrote Dirty Work for Doughgod, his headnote says. The narrator rides with a partner called Dirty Shirt. They halt their burros to peer at a proclamation tacked to a tree beside the trail. The notice urges a vote for a man named Lindhardt Cadwallader Sims for sheriff. Defeat the demon rum, it adds.

The pair spell the notice out loud and sit down to figure its meaning. They are just getting over their yearly hunch that they know where gold lies, the narrator says. Such hunches take them away each spring, he explains. They return chastened, short on cash, and hairy of face. A sheriff named Scenery Sims, a former shepherd, is weighed in their talk.
79228-ernie-pyle-in-england:
Ernie Pyle's England pieces were gathered in this book, copyrighted in New York in 1941, and given to That Girl Who Waited. Contents divide the journey into parts. On My Way gives his qualms, the crossing, and a way station. All Quiet brings first impressions of a land at war. Most Hateful, Most Beautiful tells of a city ringed and stabbed with fire, a night stroll lit by war, and the landmarks.

The heroes are all the people, one part declares, with street scenes and the way of Wapping. Guns and bombers bring tea with sound effects and shop talk with the air force. The cave dwellers, an expedition to the north, and murder in the Midlands follow. A visit to Coventry after its blitz stands in the heads. Bombs do the damnedest things closes the parts, with a visit to the cartoonist Low and a good-bye to all that.
79557-malice-in-kulturland:
Malice in Kulturland is a satire by Horace Wyatt, with pictures, issued at New York in 1917. Its title twists a beloved children's book into a jab at Germany in war time, Kulturland being the land of German culture as its foes mocked it. The tale opens with a change, and with a sick girl. It was unlucky that Alice should fall ill as the summer holidays were about to begin, the narrator says.

One lovely day late in July she had a bad head and a hot tongue, and the doctor put her to her room. Dull days followed, with books and papers her only company. The papers held a long trial in France and speeches on home rule that she could not follow. Talk of civil war in Ireland filled the rest. From that sick room the satire takes its Alice into a Germany of nonsense and menace.
79570-mrs-mayo-s-second-husband:
Miller wrote a novel that opens at a deathbed, where Hunter Mayo lies told by his doctor to make his will. His young wife Elinor, worn with watch and grief, sits close by his side. Mayo thinks of how he won her from a score of suitors seven years past, and dread fills him.

Jealous love drives his last plea, that Elinor vow she will never wed again once he is gone. She starts at the words, with tears and a soft reproach in her eyes. The plea hangs in the air as the tale starts, and its cost drives the grief and strife to come.
79586-the-salvation-army-in-switzerland:
The Salvation Army in Switzerland is a plea for fair play by Josephine Butler, the English reformer. It was published in London in 1883, when the Army's work in Geneva was under attack. Butler takes up the question of legal justice for the new movement.

The chapters tell a tale of meetings closed and workers driven out. In Geneva the meetings were shut by decree. Miss Booth and Miss Charlesworth were expelled from the canton. Appeals went to the Geneva council and then to the federal council at Bern. In Neuchâtel a fine proclamation of free worship was soon dropped in practice. Meetings met with rowdy attacks, and private houses were stoned. Butler prints the petitions and the answers, and judges the case by them.
7963-the-eskdale-herd-boy-a-scottish-tal:
Mrs Blackford wrote this Scottish tale for young readers, following John Telfer, a boy who loses his parents and is taken up by Mr Martin, the local minister. Engaged as a herd-boy by Mr Laurie, John learns his work on the hills of Eskdale while the minister's daughter Helen learns her own lessons in perseverance and self-command. The chapters mix farm life, country excursions, and visits to neighbours' cottages.

The story teaches by example: honesty, patience, and steady effort are rewarded, while affectation and carelessness bring trouble. Its Border setting, with rustic manners, dogs, and moorland scenery, gives it charm beyond its moral. As an early children's book it shows how the nineteenth century liked to instruct its young readers, through adventure close to home rather than lectures.
79740-the-king-s-friend:
Robert Sulivan wrote a play in five acts, first performed at the Theatre Royal, Sadler's Wells, on May 21, 1845. He dedicates it to S Phelps, who played Henry the Fourth. Sulivan thanks Phelps for hints that adapted the play to the stage. He also thanks Mrs Warner, Phelps's managerial partner, for care and liberal spending in production.

The Marquis de Rosny is played by Mr H Marston, and the cast includes bravos named Vauteur, Bravache, and Poignard. Act one opens in Rosny's apartment at Mante. The marquis paces to and fro, suffering from recent wounds, while Maignan waits at a table to take dictation.
7981-synthetic-tannins-their-synthesis-i:
Georg Grasser, lecturer in tanning chemistry at the German Technical College in Brünn, wrote this technical book on synthetic tannins: how they are made, produced at industrial scale, and used. He builds on Emil Fischer's outline of the synthesis of natural tannins, then turns to the chemical industry. Notably the Badische Anilin und Soda factory at Ludwigshafen, which found ways to make production practical. No full list of synthetic tannins had yet been published.

The book serves tanners and chemists who needed a reliable survey of a fast-moving field. Its chapters move from laboratory synthesis to factory and finished leather, keeping the science tied to use. As a record of early twentieth-century industrial chemistry, it shows how a laboratory discovery became a working material.
8109-early-bardic-literature-ireland:
Standish O'Grady wrote this study of early bardic literature in Ireland, beginning from the monuments scattered across Europe: cromlechs and dolmens, great earthen tumuli, flagged sepulchres, and enclosures of tall pillar-stones. He argues that the makers of those works were not strangers but our own ancestors, and that out of their rude civilisation our own has slowly grown. Of that elder phase, he says, no record or tradition survives except through the bards.

The book introduces the Irish bardic tradition as the voice of a prehistoric world, carrying history in poetry. O'Grady, a key figure in the Irish literary revival, wrote to recover that heritage for modern Ireland. For readers interested in Celtic literature, it is a pioneering, romantic study, and a window onto how Ireland reimagined its past.
8537-lonesome-land:
B. M. Bower, author of Chip, of the Flying U, wrote Lonesome Land as a western novel, with four illustrations by Stanley L. Wood. Contents open with the arrival of Val, well-meant advice, a lady in a temper, the shivaree, and Cold Spring Ranch, as the hero enters ranch country and its rough customs.

Bower, the most popular western novelist of her day, writes of ranch life with humor and romance, and her heroines hold their own among cowboys. Readers get a classic western, brisk and good-humored, where a newcomer learns the land's ways. The novel suits fans of ranch fiction, and of Bower's Flying U world.
858-stage-land:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this comic guide to the world of the stage, as seen by the earnest student of the drama. He sorts stage folk into types: the hero, the villain, the heroine, the comic man, the lawyer, the adventuress, and the servant. Each type behaves by fixed rules that real life rarely follows.

Jerome mocks the gap between stage manners and common sense, with jokes on swoons, asides, and sudden fortunes. His dedication, to that retiring student of the drama, sets the teasing tone. The book delights theatre lovers, for it names every cliché they have laughed at, and it still reads as a witty tour of Victorian melodrama.
8659-sabbath-in-puritan-new-england:
Alice Morse Earle describes how Puritans in New England kept the Sabbath, from the meeting-house itself to the long services inside it. Chapters cover the plain building, the old pews, the seating order, the tithingman who watched sleepers, the icy winter cold, and the noon-house where families ate between sermons. Psalm books get close attention too, from the Pilgrims' book through the Bay Psalm Book and the Sternhold and Hopkins version.

Earle draws on old records, diaries, and church practice to show a day ruled by drums, horns, and shells calling people to worship. The book's charm lies in small, concrete detail: foot warmers, dog whippers, and children kept awake through hours of preaching. Readers gain a vivid sense of a stern but human Sunday, and of how much ordinary New England life bent around the church bell.
883-our-mutual-friend:
Charles Dickens wrote his last completed novel about John Harmon, heir to a fortune in dust heaps, who is supposed drowned on his return to London. The Boffins, his father's servants, inherit instead, and the tale follows their rise, the Wilfer family, and the river folk who found Harmon's body. Money, marriage, and murder intertwine.

Dickens fills the novel with rogues, lawyers, and schoolmasters, and with the Thames as a dark mirror of the city. Lizzie Hexam, Bella Wilfer, and Bradley Headstone carry a story of love and obsession. The book stands as a rich, sombre masterpiece, and a fitting close to Dickens's great career.
885-an-ideal-husband:
Oscar Wilde wrote this play about Sir Robert Chiltern, an ideal husband and rising statesman, whose past holds a secret sale of a state secret. Mrs Cheveley, a schemer with a letter as proof, blackmails him, while his wife, Lady Chiltern, holds him to a standard no man can meet. Lord Goring, the witty friend, must save the day.

Wilde's dialogue dazzles, but the play turns on forgiveness: Lady Chiltern must learn that ideals need mercy. First staged in 1895, the play was a triumph before Wilde's fall. It remains a brilliant comedy of politics and marriage, where wit and feeling share the stage.
8884-travels-in-syria-and-the-holy-land:
John Lewis Burckhardt, the late Swiss explorer, records his travels in Syria and the Holy Land in this 1822 volume. Published by the Association for Promoting the Discovery of the Interior Parts of Africa. The editor's preface hopes little apology is needed for an Asiatic volume from an African society: the Association, having secured a man of Burckhardt's education and talents. Spared neither time nor expense to teach him the language and manners of an Arabian Muslim so perfectly that his real character would escape detection in Africa's interior.

Burckhardt's Syrian journeys, made in that disguise and with a scholar's eye, describe Damascus, Palmyra, the Hauran, and the holy places with detail unmatched in his day. He died before publication, and his notes became a classic of exploration.
8887-marjorie-s-new-friend:
Carolyn Wells, author of the Patty books, writes Marjorie's New Friend, illustrated with scenes including Miss Hart holding a book and asking how many leaves it has. Contents move from a bothersome bag and a welcome Christmas gift, through merry Christmas and happy new year. To a tearful time, the going of Gladys, and the coming of Delight. A visit to Cinderella, a straw-ride, making valentines, Marjorie captive, and Miss Hart's help follow, with goldfish and kittens, a pleasant school, and a sea trip.

A valentine party, a jinks auction, honest confession, a visit from Gladys, and chessy cats close the year. Marjorie, a lively American schoolgirl, learns friendship, honesty, and kindness through small adventures rather than grand ones. Wells writes for young girls with humour and warmth, and the book belongs to the wholesome series fiction of its era.
8993-the-mysterious-island:
Jules Verne's novel, first put out in French in the 1870s, strands five men and a dog on a wild Pacific island after their balloon crashes. The castaways, led by engineer Cyrus Smith, have almost nothing, yet they build shelter, tools, and a small working world from scratch. A hidden hand seems to aid them at key turns.

Bit by bit they learn that Captain Nemo, the lone sea captain from Verne's earlier sea tale, has watched over them from his craft below the waves. The book pairs clear how-to detail with mystery and a final reveal, and it still stands as one of Verne's most loved tales of skill, hope, and survival.
9297-the-orange-yellow-diamond:
J. S. Fletcher wrote this detective novel in 1921 around an orange-yellow diamond and a pretty pawnbroker. Mrs. Goldmark's eating-house, a dead man, and a platinum solitaire open the case. Two letters, a Spanish manuscript, and a member of Parliament deepen it, with an inquest asking whose rings these were.

Melky intervenes, a back door opens, and a friend from Peebles calls for help. A private laboratory, a mortuary, and a five-hundred-pound note carry the plot to midnight secrets. Fletcher keeps clues fair and pace brisk. The novel is a solid golden-age mystery, neat and satisfying.
9332-georgie-s-present-or-tales-of-newfo:
Miss Brightwell wrote these tales of Newfoundland for children, under the title Georgie's Present. The book opens on a beautiful May morning, when George Green rises early for his birthday. Ten years old at last, he awaits his father in the breakfast parlor, eager for a whole holiday and a secret afternoon at Aunt Baker's.

Four chapters follow George's birthday gift and the tales it prompts, of Newfoundland life, sea, and shore. Brightwell, known for Annals of Industry and Genius, writes plainly for young readers. The book remains a charming Victorian gift book, warm and instructive.
9459-indian-legends-of-vancouver-island:
Alfred Carmichael wrote the text of these Indian legends of Vancouver Island, illustrated by J. Semeyn. His introduction warns that the unsophisticated native of British Columbia is almost a memory, leaving no monuments or ruins. Frame houses replaced old dwellings, and only slate carvings, stone hammers, and spear points remain as mementos.

Two tribes of the Alberni district, the Seshaht and Opitchesaht, anchor the tales, with winter villages on commanding sites. Carmichael preserves their stories with respect. The book remains a valuable record of coastal legend, and of a world already fading when it was made.
9503-seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-v:
Francis W. Halsey edited Seeing Europe with Famous Authors, a ten-volume travel set built from great writers' own pages. This second volume, part two of Great Britain and Ireland, tours literary shrines and famed scenes. Writers inside include Emerson, Hawthorne, Goldwin Smith, and Mrs. S. C. Hall. Each stop pairs a place with a pen that knew it well.

Stops include Stoke Pogis, Haworth, Gad's Hill, Rydal Mount, Stonehenge, Oxford, Cambridge, and Chester. The Eddystone Lighthouse and the home of the Pilgrim Fathers also appear. A reader gets a guided tour of Britain through its authors, rich in lore, and a fine way to plan a trip or to travel from an armchair.
9832-the-crimson-blind:
Fred M. White wrote The Crimson Blind in 1905, a mystery of voices, blinds, and hidden schemes. Chapters promise a voice in the darkness, a house of silent sorrow, and a medical opinion. Margaret sees a ghost, Rollo shows his teeth, and a man with a thumb returns. Hatherly Bell, Frank Littimer, and Enid cross the plot, with a crimson blind at its heart.

White builds suspense from whispers, figures, and a frame of picture, till the scheme works out. His prose favors brisk Edwardian thrills. A reader gets a lively, old-style mystery, full of blinds, bells, and a villain's patient plot.
9870-war-is-kind:
Stephen Crane wrote War Is Kind in 1899, a book of poems on war's bitter irony, with drawings by Will Bradley. The title poem tells a maiden not to weep, for war is kind, though her lover threw wild hands to the sky and his steed ran on alone. Drums boom, men born to drill and die march, and a field of corpses waits. A babe's father tumbles in yellow trenches, and a mother mourns her son.

Crane's short, sharp lyrics strip war of glory, praising slaughter only to damn it. The sea, a shell, and a splendid shroud close the images. A reader gets Crane's fierce anti-war verse, brief and haunting, from the poet of The Red Badge of Courage.
9948-the-banner-boy-scouts-afloat-or-the:
George A. Warren's 1913 scout story sends the Banner Boy Scouts afloat in search of the secret of Cedar Island. It opens with mysterious boxes and glorious news, then sets the boys cruising after laying in stores, ghost or no ghost.

On the swift Radway river they dodge snags and snares and get stuck fast in the mud. They read a water gauge, camp on Cedar Island, and find footprints in the sand, while a bursting meteor deepens the mystery. Warren writes brisk, earnest adventure. Young readers get boating, camping, and a ghost story that may have a plain explanation.
9983-wylder-s-hand:
J. Sheridan Le Fanu's novel, first published in 1864, opens with a narrator riding through the village of Gylingden carrying Mark Wylder's letter in his valise. Dinner parties at Brandon Hall follow, where Dorcas Brandon speaks and a London gentleman appears in Redman's Dell.

Captain Lake, a Persian magician's ring, and an ace of hearts deepen the mystery, as old secrets stir around the Brandon family. Le Fanu, master of the sensation novel, builds dread from drawing rooms and night walks. Readers get a slow, atmospheric puzzle of inheritance, villainy, and a hand reaching from the past.
9996-tis-sixty-years-since-address-of-ch:
Charles Francis Adams gave this Founders' Day address on January 16, 1913, taking as his text the words 'Tis Sixty Years Since. The phrase is the second title of Walter Scott's first novel, Waverley, which brought Scott fame when it appeared in 1814.

Adams, allotted a single hour, covers much ground in brief compass, looking back sixty years and more to the world that made Scott and his readers. His address suits listeners interested in history, literature, and the Adams family's long public life. Readers get a reflective talk on how a nation remembers its writers.
a-child-s-history-of-england:
Charles Dickens wrote this history of England for young readers, and the contents show its march reign by reign. It begins with ancient England and the Romans. It passes the Saxons and Alfred, then the Normans and the Conqueror. From there it goes through the Plantagenets: Henry the Second, Richard the Lion-Heart, John Lackland, and the long line of Edwards and Henrys.

Dickens tells each reign as a story of character — proud kings, wicked uncles, battles, and murders in towers — with his sympathies plainly engaged. He admires Alfred and Edward the First, scorns John and Richard the Third, and treats the Tudors and Stuarts at the same brisk pace, ending with the later Stuart kings. The history was written to be read aloud in a family, and its judgments are a novelist's, not a scholar's.
a-christmas-garland: Max Beerbohm parodies the great writers of his day in this Christmas garland. His pieces take off Henry James, Rudyard Kipling, H. G. Wells, G. K. Chesterton, Thomas Hardy, and Shakespeare among others. Each pastiche copies the victim's style while turning it to Christmas subjects. Beerbohm, himself a master stylist, makes imitation into a form of witty criticism.
a-daughter-of-the-land:
Gene Stratton-Porter opens in a small country church, where the minister takes his text: take the wings of morning. Outside, tall Kate Bates bends low along the footpath to keep her head below the windows. She is the youngest of a land-rich, cash-poor family, and the land that should have been her portion has gone to her brothers.

Twenty-eight chapters follow Kate through teaching, a contract quarrel, courtship, marriage, and the long work of winning a farm of her own, ending with blue ribbon corn. Chapter titles like Kate Takes the Bit in Her Teeth state her character plainly. Stratton-Porter writes farm life from inside knowledge, in praise of work and independence.
a-history-of-the-early-part-of-the-reign:
Charles James Fox's History of the Early Part of the Reign of James the Second, printed here in Cassell's 1888 National Library edition, is the great Whig orator's unfinished monument. Fox collected his materials in Paris in 1802, after the Peace of Amiens, and worked on the history in his last years. He died in 1806; the book appeared in 1808. It begins with his view of Charles II's reign and ends with Monmouth's execution in 1685, the early part only, as the title honestly warns.

Fox writes as a parliamentarian judging a king who meant to rule without parliaments. James's designs on the army and the law are traced from inside Whig memory. Sedgemoor and the Bloody Assizes end the fragment in tragedy. Readers get two books in one: a primary voice of English liberalism, and a history of 1685 written by the statesman who most feared its lessons being forgotten.
a-journey-to-the-western-islands-of-scot:
Samuel Johnson left Edinburgh on August 18, 1773, with James Boswell, to see the Hebrides he had long wished to visit, as his opening pages tell. This text follows the 1775 edition with the 1785 corrections. Johnson crosses the Firth of Forth to Inch Keith and works north along the coast before turning to the islands.

He records inns, roads, lairds, language, second sight, and the remains of the clan world after its breaking. Johnson judges schools, churches, and poverty with his usual force, and praises what earns praise. The book is travel writing of a high order: sturdy, curious, and full of sentences built to last.
a-knight-of-the-cumberland:
John Fox, Jr. wrote this short novel of the Cumberland mountains. That is the coal and feud country along the Kentucky and Virginia line. The narrator leads his small sister and a fashionable young visitor on horseback. The visitor is nicknamed the Blight. They cross the crest of the Big Black mountain. Their goal is country of moonshiners and feudsmen, where, he says, an older way of life still holds. The contents list eight chapters.

The visitors meet mountain customs head-on. They join a wild dog hunt. They pass a shooting scrape at close quarters. Election day counts as a great day. At last comes a tournament in the old style, where local men ride as knights. The Blight's presence tests both worlds. Fox made the Cumberlands his subject, and wrote the tale as both romance and report.
a-prisoner-in-fairyland:
A Prisoner in Fairyland is a 1913 novel by Algernon Blackwood, one of the most prolific writers of ghost stories in the history of the genre. Blackwood, also a journalist and broadcasting narrator, earned high praise from critics of the weird tale. Here he turns from ghosts to fairyland, and traps his hero among the fairies in an odd, gentle fantasy.

The mortal man dwells in the enchanted realm as a captive, and the story unfolds softly rather than as a tale of terror. Blackwood's gift was for atmosphere, for the thin border between the everyday world and a stranger one beside it. This novel applies that gift to fairyland, making captivity itself a dreamlike state the reader drifts through.
a-short-history-of-scotland: Andrew Lang writes this short history of Scotland, opening when Romans under Agricola crossed the border in the year 81. A magic mirror, he suggests, would show familiar hills above overflowing rivers. Thick oak and pine woods roaming with deer, elks, and boars covered land now arable, and lakes stood where fields of corn now stand. Clay and wattle huts, stockaded houses of tribal princes, and crannog villages on lochs held a people already far beyond the savage stage of culture.
a-wanderer-in-holland: Edward Verrall Lucas wanders in Holland in this volume, with twenty illustrations in colour by Herbert Marshall and thirty-four after old Dutch masters. The contents run from Flushing through sunrise on the Maas, Rotterdam, Gouda, Dort, Utrecht, and Scheveningen beach to Leyden, Haarlem's turf market, and Amsterdam's canals. Volendam, Alkmaar's cheese market, Hoorn, Enkhuizen, Harlingen, Kampen, Arnheim, Nymwegen, and Middelburg follow, with Vermeer, Steen, and Cuyp among the masters.
a-woman-of-the-world-her-counsel-to-othe: Ella Wheeler Wilcox, a woman of the world, counsels other people's sons and daughters in this 1904 volume, in a fourth impression of April 1910. Her letters address a law student of twenty-three, a Vassar girl, a bride on honeymoon, and a young woman facing the necessity to earn a living. A shop girl concerning her oppressors, a teacher of three years, and a would-be journalist receive counsel in turn. A former maid and a clergyman's son and daughter follow.
about-ireland: Elizabeth Lynn Linton writes about Ireland in this 1890 volume, apologizing for rushing into print on a subject she does not half know. She knows a little more than when she was an ardent Home Ruler, influenced only by sentiment and abstract principle. She hopes the process by which her own blindness was couched may clear the vision of others. Lay folk, she argues, must follow leaders their temperaments affiliate them to, since life is too short to examine every question from the beginning.
addresses-by-henry-drummond:
Henry Drummond's spoken addresses open with Love, the Greatest Thing in the World, his famous talk on the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians. He asks what the supreme good is, and answers against the common view: not faith, but love, is the greatest thing. The contents add Lessons from the Angelus, Pax Vobiscum, and First, an address to boys.

Later talks treat the changed life and dealing with doubt. Drummond, a Scottish scientist and evangelist, spoke to students across Britain and America, and his manner here is plain, warm, and direct. The love address alone was printed in huge numbers and carried his name around the world.
aesop-fables-townsend:
Aesop, a storyteller of ancient Greece, gave his name to hundreds of short animal fables. George Fyler Townsend translated the full body of tales into English prose. Foxes, hares, tortoises, and farmers crowd his pages.

Each brief story ends by teaching its lesson plainly. The tortoise beats the hare, and the boy who cried wolf loses his flock. Townsend's version became the standard English Aesop for generations of children. Adults still quote these morals without knowing their source. Few books so short have shaped so much everyday wisdom. Townsend's edition first appeared in 1867 and was reprinted many times.
afoot-in-england:
W. H. Hudson's Afoot in England opens by refusing guide-books, in a chapter that introduces his own. Hudson counts England's guides by the library and finds them never out of date, only superseded. On Going Back and Walking and Cycling state his method: slowly, on foot, returning. Seeking a Shelter and Wind, Wave, and Spirit follow.

Roman Calleva and a cold day at Silchester explore the buried Roman town under Berkshire fields. Salisbury and its doves, Whitesheet Hill, and Stonehenge with its tillage fill the Wiltshire chapters. In Praise of the Cow honours the animal of the downs. Hudson, the Argentine-born naturalist, walked England as an exile in love with a second home. His prose lingers where guide-books hurry: a road leading nowhere, an Abbotsbury swannery, a river followed for its own sake. The book is a classic of English walking.
after-london-or-wild-england: Richard Jefferies imagines England after London has fallen, as forest reclaims the land and people relapse into barbarism. The first part traces wild animals, woodland men, and invaders around a great lake, while the second follows life in this wild England. A landmark of speculative fiction, it asks what survives of civilisation when cities fail and nature returns.
algonquin-legends-of-new-england:
Charles G. Leland tells in his preface how the work began in the summer of 1882 among the Passamaquoddy at Campobello. He expected scanty remains of heathenism there. He found instead a whole mythology kept by oral tradition. His book gives the myths and folk lore of the Micmac, Passamaquoddy, and Penobscot tribes, as the title page states. A birch-bark frontispiece shows Mikumwess, the Indian Puck.

The contents center on Glooskap, the great hero: his birth, his making of elves, men, and beasts, his deeds, his family, and his battles with sorcerers and giants. Leland prints the tales with notes comparing Norse and other traditions. The collection preserved stories that might otherwise have been lost within a generation.
alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland:
Lewis Carroll wrote this children's novel about Alice, a girl who follows a waistcoat-wearing White Rabbit down a rabbit hole. She lands in a world that runs on nonsense and wordplay. The contents list twelve chapters, from the fall itself through the pool of tears, the caucus-race, and the mad tea-party, to a final trial over stolen tarts.

Alice grows and shrinks, argues with a Caterpillar, and meets the Cheshire Cat and the Mock Turtle. She also plays croquet with a flamingo under the Queen of Hearts, who orders heads off at every turn. Carroll plays with logic, verse, and riddles all through. The book's dream logic and puns made it a landmark of children's literature, read by adults as much as by children.
american-cookery-the-art-of-dressing-via: Amelia Simmons writes American Cookery, the art of dressing viands, fish, poultry, and vegetables, with the best modes of making pastes, puffs, pies, tarts, puddings, custards, and preserves. From imperial plum cake to plain cake, her recipes are adapted to this country and its ingredients. As the first American cookbook, it marks the birth of a national kitchen.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith begins a second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities with part eleven, again built from illustrations and page images of literary antiquities. The editor's note repeats the scanning caveat and points readers to the HTML file for the plates. A new sequence thus opens on the same visual terms as the first.

John Jay Smith's second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities continues in part twelve, a plate book of American antiquities. Text here is sparse because the original is images, and the editor directs readers to the HTML presentation for the full effect. The instalment extends the antiquarian survey into fresh material.

John Jay Smith offers part thirteen of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities, another gathering of facsimile plates. The note inside explains that few sections could be scanned as text, so the HTML file is the recommended route to the images. Viewed in sequence, the parts build a visual archive of American letters.

John Jay Smith's fourteenth part in the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities maintains the series' focus on reproduced pages and relics. The text file's thin content reflects the book's nature as a plate volume, a point the editor makes while pointing to the HTML edition. It serves best as a pointer to the richer visual original.

John Jay Smith continues the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities with part fifteen, presenting further plates of American literary antiquities. Scanning limits mean only a few passages appear as text, and readers are directed to the HTML file to see the plates. The instalment adds another sheaf of visual documents to the collection.

John Jay Smith's part sixteen of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities rounds out another set of illustrated antiquities. As before, the book lives in its page images, with the text file carrying only what scanning could rescue, and the editor's note pointing to HTML. The series as a whole preserves Americana in facsimile for later readers.

John Jay Smith's seventeenth part of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities adds another sheaf of plates to the antiquarian sequence. The text file again carries only the passages scanning could capture, with the editor's note sending readers to the HTML edition for the images. In order, the parts form a long visual survey of American historic papers.

John Jay Smith continues the second series with part eighteen of American Historical and Literary Curiosities, a volume of facsimile plates and page images. Because the original is pictorial, this text holds little continuous prose, and the editor points readers toward the HTML file. The instalment keeps the series' steady accumulation of Americana going.

John Jay Smith's nineteenth part in the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities presents more reproduced pages from the American past. The editor's note explains the thin text, a result of scanning a plate book, and recommends the HTML version for viewing. Each part stands alone, yet all belong to one antiquarian collection.

John Jay Smith offers part twenty-one of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities, another volume of page images and plates. Scanning rescued only a few text sections, so the editor directs readers to the HTML file for the full plates. The late parts of the series continue its work of preserving historic papers in sight.

John Jay Smith's part twenty-two of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities brings the sequence near its close with further illustrated antiquities. The text file, thin by the nature of a plate book, is accompanied by an editor's note pointing to the HTML edition. The volume completes another stage of the visual archive.
american-negro-slavery-a-survey-of-the-s: Ulrich Bonnell Phillips surveys American Negro slavery through the supply, employment, and control of Black labour under the plantation regime. The study examines how the system worked in economic and social terms, drawing on plantation records. Though later scholarship has challenged its views, the book long shaped historical debate on slavery.
an-account-of-some-of-the-principal-slav: Joshua Coffin gives an account of some of the principal slave insurrections, and others attempted, in the United States and elsewhere during the last two centuries. Addressed to the reader from New York, the work lists risings and plots with sober, abolitionist purpose. It is an early attempt to record Black resistance to slavery as history.
an-ideal-husband:
Oscar Wilde's play centers on Sir Robert Chiltern, a respected government official whose career rests on a secret from his youth. The cast list places the action in his London house and in Lord Goring's library. A visitor, Mrs. Cheveley, arrives holding proof of the old wrong and demands a price for her silence.

Four acts mix drawing-room wit with blackmail, a stolen brooch, and a friend who seems lazy but thinks clearly. Lady Chiltern must weigh the perfect husband she imagined against the flawed man she has. Wilde uses the plot to question public purity and private forgiveness, and the dialogue sparkles throughout.
ancient-poems-ballads-and-songs-of-the-p:
Robert Bell edited this anthology of the poems, ballads, and songs of England's rural poor, printed in London in 1857 as the title page shows. His subtitle states the sources: pieces taken down from oral recitation and transcribed from private manuscripts, rare broadsides, and scarce publications. The contents divide the harvest into poems, ballads, and songs.

The poems moralize on life, age, and death, with dialogues between an exciseman and Death and between husbandman and servingman. The ballads tell of Robin Hood, Lord Bateman, the blind beggar of Bednall Green, and Sir John Barleycorn. The songs praise the plough and the farmer's boy. Bell prints the material as literature worth keeping, with an introduction on its origins, preserving a working-class song culture that print was about to scatter.
anecdotes-of-painters-engravers-sculptor: Shearjashub Spooner gathers anecdotes of painters, engravers, sculptors, and architects, with curiosities of art, in volume three of three. The book collects lively stories of artists' lives, tricks, and masterpieces, drawn from his biographical history of the fine arts. It remains a browsable store of art lore for general readers.
angel-island:
Inez Haynes Gillmore opens Angel Island on the morning after a shipwreck. Five men lie bruised and speechless on a Pacific beach, haunted by the drowned. Frank Merrill, Honey Smith, Pete Murphy, and Billy Fairfax count their losses. No ship, no women, and no rescue are in sight.

The island's wonder arrives on wings: a company of flying women descends from the sky. The men fall in love with creatures who can leave whenever they choose. Courtship turns into a struggle over freedom, as the men plot to clip the women's wings. Gillmore, a feminist writer, built her fantasy as an argument. Angel Island uses a desert-island romance to ask who owns a woman's body and movement. Its serene prose carries a radical charge that still startles.
animal-carvings-from-mounds-of-the-missi: Henry Wetherbee Henshaw studies animal carvings from mounds of the Mississippi Valley, in the second annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology to the Smithsonian, covering pages 117 to 166. The paper describes carved pipes and figures, and what they tell of mound-builder art and belief. Henshaw's work remains a key source on Native American archaeology.
anne-of-the-island:
Lucy Maud Montgomery continues Anne Shirley's story in this novel, which opens with Anne leaving Green Gables for Redmond College. The dedication speaks to girls everywhere who wanted more about Anne. Forty-one chapters follow her college years: rooms at Patty's Place with friends, stories sold and rejected, proposals accepted and refused, and letters carrying news from home.

At home, Avonlea changes without her: Diana marries, old neighbors die, and Gilbert Blythe waits through Anne's confusion about what love should look like. A brief glamour with another suitor clears her mind. The final chapters bring degrees, weddings, and Anne's recognition of where her heart has been all along. The book balances campus comedy with a quiet growing-up.
at-the-back-of-the-north-wind:
George MacDonald's fairy tale appears here in an illustrated Children's Classics edition, marked as an eleventh impression. MacDonald tells of Diamond, a poor London boy who sleeps in a hayloft above the stable where his father works as a coachman. The North Wind visits him as a beautiful lady and carries him to the country at her back, where the dead children play.
