Diamond learns to drive from the stable men, sprawling tired across old Diamond, the horse he is named for. Between his flights with the Wind, he helps his struggling family and a little street girl. MacDonald blends dream journeys, city poverty, and gentle theology into a story about goodness that puzzled some child readers and charmed generations of others.
bede-ecclesiastical-history-england:
Bede, a monk of Jarrow in Northumbria, finished his Ecclesiastical History of the English People in 731. The translation here is the version revised from J. A. Giles's standard English text. Bede's history is the founding work of English history, and our main source for the island's conversion.

In five books he runs from Caesar's invasion to his own day. The heart of the work is the coming of Augustine's mission from Rome, the kings who accepted or refused baptism, and the saints of the young English church. Bede's care with sources and dates set a standard few medieval writers matched. The book made the English a people with a story.
beggars-bush-a-comedy-from-the-works-of-:
Beggars Bush, a comedy from the Beaumont and Fletcher folio, opens its plot in Flanders, where Wolfort has usurped the earldom. Gerrard, the rightful earl, lives disguised as Clause, king of the beggars, while his son-in-law Florez passes as Goswin, a rich merchant of Bruges. Bertha, called Gertrude, is the Duke of Brabant's daughter and Florez's mistress in the cast list's blunt terms.

Three knavish beggars — Higgen, Prigg, and Snapp — give the play its famous canting scenes, the beggars' bush itself being their trysting tree. A hunting speech in the middle reels off polecat, marten, and lucerne, stag and wild sounder, in a huntsman's brag. Fletcher builds romance on the double disguise: beggary as a kingdom in exile, waiting for one recognition scene to restore earl, daughter, and fortune together.
beyond:
John Galsworthy built his novel Beyond around Gyp, the daughter of retired lancer Charles Clare Winton, whose story opens at a registry office. Gyp has just married a foreign violinist her father calls the fiddler fellow, against his judgment and her own better knowledge. The marriage fails in the way Galsworthy marriages do: quietly, through temperament, selfishness, and the slow discovery that love was appetite.

What follows tests what a woman may claim beyond the rules. Gyp finds real love where the law and divorce courts of Edwardian England will not let her marry again. Galsworthy, who wrote The Forsyte Saga of property and marriage, here asks what fidelity means when the legal bond is the false one. The tone is tender and unsparing at once.
bowser-the-hound:
Thornton W Burgess wrote Bowser the Hound, copyrighted by Little, Brown in 1920, with pictures by Harrison Cady. Burgess dedicates the tale to the dog, the child's playmate and staunch ally. Old Man Coyote opens the plot by leading Farmer Brown's hound astray.

Bowser spends bad nights lost and hurt, while Blacky the Crow takes pity and flies for help. Reddy Fox dreams of chickens and gets drawn into the search. Verse tags head the chapters, in Burgess's Green Meadow manner. Bowser at last falls prisoner in a strange yard, and his great voice carries far. Blacky's wits, not Reddy's, do the real work of rescue. Young readers learn woods law: kindness counts, and mockery of the lost comes back on the mocker.
boy-scouts-of-the-air-on-lost-island:
Gordon Stuart's The Boy Scouts of the Air on Lost Island is a boys' adventure story built around flying, a dam and a mysterious island. Three boys wait at dawn in a back yard, watching for their friend Tod, while the sky lightens over the cedars.

Chapters promise a hopeless search, more thrills, a startling clue, a rescue, a voyage in the dark, and a mid-air miracle. The scouts patch their machine, the Skyrocket, and play a big game against rivals who trick them again and again. Stuart writes in the brisk serial manner of the period, and young readers who enjoy scouting tales with aeroplanes will find the pace unflagging.
brandes-main-currents-4-naturalism-in-en:
England's writers come under Brandes's eye in the fourth book of Main Currents, here in English, under the head of naturalism. He traces the turn toward plain truth in fiction and verse. A Dane's view of Victorian letters can startle English readers even now.

Brandes praises force and honesty while faulting prudery and cant. He sets English books beside French and German ones to test their worth. His judgments are bold, clear, and often still argued over. The volume shows how an outsider with wide reading could see a nation's writing more clearly than many of its own critics.
britannica-1911-aalesund:
Aalesund receives a port entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Norwegian seaport stands in Romsdal amt on two outer islands, Aspö and Nörvö, which enclose a fine harbour. Founded in 1824, it serves Söndmöre and the herring fishery as a chief station.

Steamers call between Bergen, Hull, Newcastle, Hamburg, and Trondhjem, and tourists pass through for the Jörund and Geiranger fjords. Ruins south of town are said to be Rollo's castle, Rollo being founder of the Norman dukes. The entry closes in grief: a gale-driven fire in January 1904 burned nearly the whole wooden town in one night. Few lives were lost, but aid poured in from Norway, Germany, and Britain. Its people counted 11,672 in 1900.
britannica-1911-abscond: Abscond is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word, from Latin abscondere, to hide or put away, as departing in a secret manner. Law narrows the sense: to remove from the courts' jurisdiction, or to hide so as to escape it. A person may abscond to dodge arrest for a crime, the entry states. Fraud supplies the other great case, flight meant to cheat creditors. Cross-references send the reader onward to Arrest and to Bankruptcy for the working detail.
britannica-1911-almond:
Almond is the fruit of Amygdalus communis, a plant of the rose family. It is closely allied to the plum and cherry. The entry opens with the word's tangled history. Greek, Latin, and Old French forms all played a part. In a plum, soft pulp clings to the stone. In the almond, a leathery coat covers the hard shell instead. That coat can be separated. The seed inside the shell is the edible kernel.

The tree seems native to western Asia, Barbary, and Morocco. It spread across the warm-temperate Old World. It ripens fruit even in the south of England. It flowers early in spring. The entry links that habit to its Hebrew name Shaked, meaning hasten. A passage in Jeremiah makes the same point. Trade varieties follow, with Jordan almonds from Malaga most esteemed. Notes on blanching sweet almonds for the table close the account.
britannica-1911-amsterdam-holland:
Water cuts Amsterdam into islands, and the likeness to Venice is often drawn. A half-circle outer canal guards the landward side, while four crescent canals inside it trace the old lines of wall and moat, and smaller canals cross them all. The city is Holland's chief, in North Holland province, on the south side of the Y, an arm of the Zuider Zee. Its name means the dam of the Amstel, the canalised river running through it to the Y.

Railways and canals tie it to every quarter, and 523,557 people lived there in 1900. The Dam square, old towers, churches, museums, markets, and industries are toured at length. History then runs from the medieval core through the Dutch Republic to 1810, when France ranked Amsterdam the empire's third town, after Paris and Rome.
britannica-1911-amsterdam-island:
Shipwreck and solitude give Amsterdam Island its human story. In 1871 the British frigate Megaera wrecked on its shore, leaving some four hundred people ashore for over three months. Longer still was Captain François Péron's stay: his memoirs tell of three years marooned on the island, from 1792 to 1795.

Also called New Amsterdam, the island is an extinct volcano in the Indian Ocean, rising 2,989 feet from the sea, empty of people and hard to reach. It lies about sixty miles north of St Paul Island, about halfway on the line from the Cape of Good Hope toward Tasmania. Anthony van Diemen found it in 1633, and France annexed it in 1893. Earlier sightings are weighed with care: Magellan's companions may have seen it in 1522, and a Dutch vessel, the Zeewolf, may have seen it in 1617.
britannica-1911-annapolis-maryland:
Annapolis is the capital city of Maryland. It is also a seaport. Anne Arundel county has its seat there. The United States Naval Academy sits there too. The Severn river flows past the city. Chesapeake Bay lies two miles away. Baltimore is twenty-six miles north. Washington is about the same distance west. Population in 1910 was 8,609.

The state house dominates the city centre. Its white dome rises 200 feet. Its cornerstone was laid in 1772. A colonial treasury building stands close by. Statues honour Taney and Baron de Kalb. Street names recall colonial days vividly. King George and Prince George both appear. Eighteenth-century residences survive in numbers. The Naval Academy was founded in 1845. The entry closes with colonial histories of the ancient city.
britannica-1911-arthurian-legend:
Arthurian legend covers the body of medieval tales around King Arthur. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica uses the French phrase Matière de Bretagne for the whole stock. Most texts in their known form date from about 1150 to 1250. Two key early works, by Nennius and Geoffrey of Monmouth, fall before that span.

Where the tales came from is the core dispute in the entry. One school credits Bretons in France who kept British tales alive. The other school credits Welsh bards who passed them to Norman poets. Names, lost poems, and thin proof on each side are weighed at length for the reader.
britannica-1911-auckland:
Auckland is a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a seaport of New Zealand. Auckland stands at the mouth of an arm of the Hauraki Gulf, capital of its province. Its population in 1906 was 37,736, or 82,101 with suburbs. Only six miles away lies Manukau harbour on the west coast.

The article paints the setting and the town. The gulf is studded with islands, and Rangitoto guards a fine harbour. The museum holds one of the best collections of Maori art. Suburbs spread across the inlet by steam ferry and among the hills.
britannica-1911-back-bond:
Back-Bond, or Back-Letter, is a Scots law term for a deed that qualifies the terms of another deed, or declares the purposes for which that other deed was granted. One paper thus limits or explains what a second paper seems to say on its face.

The entry's example makes the point concrete. A disposition may look absolute on its face, yet a back-bond can state the limited nature of the right actually held by the person receiving it. Put together, the two deeds amount to what England calls a deed of trust. So the back-bond is the private key to a public-looking grant, recording the true, narrower bargain behind it.
britannica-1911-baden-switzerland:
Baden is a town of Switzerland described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the canton of Aargau, on the left bank of the river Limmat, north-west of Zurich by rail. It is sought in the main for its hot sulphur springs. Tacitus names those springs, and they were in high vogue in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

The springs are held strong for cases of gout and rheumatism, and Swiss invalids crowd them. They lie a bit north of the old town, tied to it by a fine new road. Roman remains have been found in the gardens of the Kursaal. The town is a fair sight, with steep narrow streets and one gate left from its walls. The ruined castle of Stein, once a fort of the Habsburgs, crowns it on the west.
britannica-1911-baffin-bay-and-baffin-la:
Baffin Bay and Baffin Land are an arctic sea and island tract named for the explorer William Baffin, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. The bay is part of the long strait that splits Baffin Land from Greenland. It spans from about 69 to 78 degrees north in latitude. From its north end, sounds and channels link it to the polar sea and to the island groups of the far north.

Baffin explored the bay in full in 1616, the text notes. Its coasts are for the most part high, steep, and deeply cut in by the sea. The sea is frozen for the greater part of the year. Yet lanes of open water along the coasts can be sailed from early June to late September in most years. The bay is noted in the head as a centre of northern sea trade and hunting.
britannica-1911-bagelkhand:
Bagelkhand is the subject of a region entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a tract of country in central India made up of native states. The chief state was Rewa, with eleven smaller states and estates beside it. The whole agency sat under an agent for central India.

The entry gives the total area and the population count for nineteen hundred one. That count had fallen over the prior ten years, a drop the entry links to famine. Poor rain in the mid eighteen nineties led to famine, and drought struck again a few years later. The agency itself was set up in March eighteen seventy one.
britannica-1911-balfour-francis-maitland:
Francis Maitland Balfour (1851–1882) was a British biologist, younger brother of Arthur James Balfour. Born at Edinburgh, he found at Harrow a master, George Griffith, who backed his love of natural science. At Trinity College, Cambridge, he took second place in the Natural Science Tripos of 1873.

Lectures on embryology by Sir Michael Foster turned Balfour toward animal morphology, the study of animal form and growth. Work at the Naples zoological station won him a fellowship at Trinity in 1874. The 1911 Britannica entry highlights his monograph of 1878 on the Elasmobranch fishes, which shed new light on how organs such as the urinary and nervous systems develop in vertebrates.
britannica-1911-band:
Band is a word for something that binds or fastens one thing to another: a cord, a rope, or a tie. Bookbinders use the straps that fasten sheets to the back of a book. The word is a variant of bond, from the Teutonic stem bindan, to bind, and bend comes from the same root.

Other senses fill the 1911 Britannica entry. In building, a band is a flat frieze running round a tower or wall, often with bold mouldings and carved circles or shields. The two small linen strips worn at the neck in legal, clerical, and academic dress are called bands, survivors of the falling collar of the 17th century. Later parts treat further uses of the word.
britannica-1911-barere-de-vieuzac-bertra:
Bertrand Barère de Vieuzac (1755–1841) was a member of the French National Convention, born at Tarbes in Gascony on 10 September 1755. His surname came from a small fief of his father, a lawyer at Vieuzac, and he kept it long after feudal rights were renounced in August 1789. He began practice as an advocate at Toulouse in 1770.

Barère won a name as an orator and a flowing essayist, and Bigorre sent him to the states-general in 1789. In the Assembly he was known less as a speaker than as a journalist, through his paper the Point du Jour. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, follows the career that made him, in its opening words, one of the most notorious members of the Convention.
britannica-1911-barren-island:
Barren Island, a volcanic island in the Bay of Bengal, gets a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The island is roughly circular and about two miles across. An outer rim rises between 700 and 1000 feet, and inside that rim stands a central cone reaching 1015 feet. The whole mass rises steeply from water about 800 fathoms deep.

Volcanic activity is the other fact the entry records. The cone was active during the years from 1789 to 1832, a span of more than four decades. After 1832 it had gone quiet, and the entry describes it as dormant since that time. Readers get the island's shape, heights, depth of surrounding sea, and active dates, with no claim that the volcano had finished for good.
britannica-1911-barry-sir-redmond:
Sir Redmond Barry (1813–1880), a British colonial judge closely tied to Melbourne, Australia, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of a major-general from County Cork, he was educated in Kent and at Trinity College, Dublin, and called to the Irish bar in 1838. He emigrated soon after, stayed briefly in Sydney, and then settled in Melbourne, the city that shaped the rest of his life and career.

Law came first, then public building of another kind. Barry became Victoria's first solicitor-general in 1851, later a supreme court judge and acting chief-justice. Knighted in 1860, he represented the colony at exhibitions in London and Philadelphia. His lasting mark, the entry stresses, was education. He founded the University of Melbourne in 1853 as its first chancellor. He also led the public library, gallery, and museum, and pushed government to spend heavily on learning.
britannica-1911-bartlett-paul-wayland:
Paul Wayland Bartlett (1865– ), an American sculptor born in New Haven, Connecticut, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He was the son of Truman Bartlett, an art critic and sculptor. At fifteen he went to study in Paris under Frémiet, modelling animals at the Jardin des Plantes, the city's botanical garden and menagerie. He won a medal at the Paris Salon of 1887, an early mark of standing in the French art world.

Public monuments dominate the list of his works. Named pieces include The Bear Tamer in New York and the equestrian Lafayette in Paris, presented by American schoolchildren. Strong figures of Columbus and Michelangelo for the Congressional Library in Washington are also listed. The Ghost Dancer, a Dying Lion, an equestrian McClellan for Philadelphia, and a Joseph Warren for Boston are also listed. The entry adds his remarkable bronze patinas of reptiles, insects, and fish.
britannica-1911-basin-stand:
Basin-stand is a piece of furniture described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a small stand, usually carried on three legs and most commonly made of mahogany or rosewood, made to hold a wash-hand basin. Before fixed plumbing in bedrooms, such a stand was a room's washing place. It was a standard article of furniture through much of the eighteenth century.

Two sizes served two purposes. The smaller stands were used for rose-water ablutions, light washing with scented water, or for the operation of powdering the hair. The larger ones carried sockets for soap-dishes, holding the soap within reach of the basin. Those larger stands were the direct predecessors of the ample modern wash-hand stand. Both kinds were often very elegant, and were widely used in their period.
britannica-1911-bathory-sigismund:
Sigismund Báthory (1572-1613) was prince of Transylvania, nephew of Stephen Báthory. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes he was chosen prince while still a boy. A regency ruled for him until he came of age in 1588. He then broke with old policy toward the Turks at once.

He joined a league of Christian princes against the Porte instead. That bold shift caused fear and a demand for a fresh oath at home. He crushed his foes and won great victories in 1595. At Giurgevo he destroyed the army of Sinan Pasha that year. He later gave up the throne, tried to retake it, and died at Prague.
britannica-1911-bazard-amand:
Amand Bazard (1791–1832) was a French socialist born at Paris. He helped defend Paris in 1815, then held a minor post in the prefecture of the Seine. Around 1820 he drew friends into the Amis de la vérité, from which a French form of Carbonarism grew, with Bazard at its head.

A failed rising at Belfort broke the society, and Bazard turned from politics to social change. He joined the school of Saint-Simon, wrote for Le Producteur, and lectured in public on its teaching from 1828. A quarrel with Enfantin over the freeing of women left him near alone, and he died in July 1832.
britannica-1911-bechuanaland:
Bechuanaland is the subject of a country entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name comes from its inhabitants, the Bechuana. It was a country of British South Africa on the central tableland that stretches north to the Zambezi. The Orange river bounds it on the south, with German territory to the west.

In land and people the region enjoys almost complete unity, the entry says. Politically it was divided into distinct parts. British Bechuanaland had become part of Cape Colony in eighteen ninety five. Its area and population are both given. The northern part formed a separate protectorate, treated next in the entry.
britannica-1911-beck-jakob-sigismund:
Jakob Sigismund Beck (1761-1840), a German philosopher, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Danzig, he was educated at Konigsberg. He became professor of philosophy first at Halle, from 1791 to 1799, and then at Rostock. His life's work was the criticism and explanation of the doctrine of Kant.

In 1793 he published a guide that drew the heart out of Kant's critical writings, long used as a handbook of the system. The article sets out his reading of Kant. Where Kant speaks of things in themselves as if they stood in time, space, and cause, Beck says the words are a popular dress for the sake of clarity. The true meaning, he held, is idealism: of objects outside the mind's awareness, knowledge is impossible. Matter itself is built up by an original act of the mind.
britannica-1911-belfast-ireland:
Belfast is a city and county borough, the capital of the province of Ulster. It is the county town of county Antrim in Ireland. Its people numbered 349,180 in 1901. Belfast is a port of the first rank, set where the river Lagan runs into Belfast Lough. It lies on the north-east coast of the island, 112 miles north of Dublin by rail. Three railways have their end stations there, and boats run on set lines to Liverpool and other ports of Britain.

The city is built on silt and on land won back from the sea. Most of it stands no more than six feet above the mark of high water. For a long time that low site left it open to floods and to waves of disease. Care in drainage at last made the place sound for health.
britannica-1911-ben-lomond:
Ben Lomond is a mountain in the north-west of Stirlingshire, Scotland, near the east bank of Loch Lomond. It rises 3,192 feet, about nine miles from the head of the loch. Granite, mica schist, diorite, porphyry and quartzite make up its rocks, the quartzite gleaming white at a distance like snow.

Grass covers the hill to the top, and climbers favour it, coming from Rowardennan, Inversnaid or Aberfoyle. The summit view runs north to the Grampians with glimpses of Ben Nevis, west to Jura, and south to Arran and Tinto Hill. Eastward it reaches as far as Edinburgh Castle and Arthur’s Seat, which gives the climb its fame.
britannica-1911-bend:
Bend is really three words wearing one spelling. From Old English bendan comes a bending or curve, as in the bend of a river, or the ribs, the “wales,” of a ship. From bindan, to bind, comes the sailor’s bend, a knot, as in the cable bend or the fisherman’s bend.

From Old French bende, a ribbon, heraldry takes its bend: a diagonal band across a shield, running from the dexter chief to the sinister base. Tanners use the word too, for the half of a hide after the thin parts are trimmed away. Bend-leather, from that half, is the thickest and best leather for soles.
britannica-1911-bergschrund:
Bergschrund is a German word, from Berg, mountain, and Schrund, a cleft or crevice. It names the gaping crack found near the top of a snowfield or glacier, close against the rock wall. The split runs roughly parallel to the rock face at the glacier basin’s upper edge.

The crack opens because the glacier, settling downward, pulls its whole mass away from the mountainside. It can run down to the solid rock beneath the ice. At its bottom lie blocks of ice and chunks of rock torn from the wall and floor by the glacier’s lower part. For climbers the bergschrund is often the last hard step before the rock of a high peak, though the entry stays with the crack’s cause and shape.
britannica-1911-berkeley-england:
Berkeley is a market town of Gloucestershire, England, near the river Severn in the Vale of Berkeley. It counted just 774 people in 1901 and stands on a gentle rise in rich pasture country. The vale’s dairies make the famous cheese called “double Gloucester,” and the town trades in coal, timber, malt and cheese.

Dr Edward Jenner, pioneer of vaccination, was born at Berkeley in 1749 and lies buried in its handsome church. South-east of the town stands Berkeley Castle, one of England’s noblest baronial castles and one of the few still lived in. The manor gave its name to the great Berkeley family, and the Berkeley Ship Canal joins Gloucester to the docks at Sharpness, dodging the hard upper Severn.
britannica-1911-berry-charles-ferdinand:
Charles Ferdinand, Duke of Berry (1778–1820), was the younger son of Charles X of France. He was born at Versailles. At the Revolution he left France with his father. He served in the army of Condé from 1792 to 1797. He then joined the Russian army. From 1801 he lived in England for thirteen years. There he married Anna Brown, an Englishwoman.

The marriage was cancelled in 1814 for political reasons. The 1911 Britannica entry then follows his return to France. Louis XVIII made him commander in Paris during the Hundred Days. In 1816 he married a Neapolitan princess, Caroline. A saddler named Louvel stabbed him at the Paris opera in February 1820. His widow's later plots and secret marriage close the article.
britannica-1911-berthoud-ferdinand:
Ferdinand Berthoud (1727–1807) was a Swiss chronometer-maker, born at Plancemont in Neuchâtel. He settled in Paris in 1745. There he won a great name for the excellence and accuracy of his chronometers. Those instruments, used to find longitude at sea, had to keep near-perfect time. He became a member of the Institute in Paris. He was also a fellow of the Royal Society of London.

This short 1911 Britannica entry names one book among his works. It is Essais sur l'horlogerie, published in 1763, a treatise on clock and watch making. Berthoud died in 1807 at Montmorency, in Seine et Oise. His nephew Louis Berthoud (1759–1813) succeeded him in the business. The entry gives no list of his inventions or patrons. It rests on his reputation for precision.
britannica-1911-birjend:
Birjend is the capital of Kain, a sub-province of Khorasan in Persia. It stands at 32 degrees 53 minutes north and 59 degrees 10 minutes east. Its height above the sea is 4,550 feet. The population is about 25,000 people. The town lies 328 miles from Meshed by the direct road. A fertile valley running east and west holds the town. Barren hills, the Kuh i Bakeran range, bound that valley on the south.

The Khusp river runs through the valley but is generally dry. Water supply for the town and its 70 or 80 villages is very scanty, the 1911 Britannica entry stresses. A ruined fort stands east of the town at a hill's foot. Birjend holds six good caravanserais, a college, and some mosques. Post and telegraph offices opened there in 1902. The entry is a compact gazetteer note on a dry Persian valley town.
britannica-1911-birmingham-england:
Birmingham, England, is a great industrial city in the north-west of Warwickshire. The 1911 Britannica article, one of the longest city pieces in the volume, gives 522,204 people in 1901. It lies 113 miles north-west of London, served by three railway companies. The town stands on New Red Sandstone in the valleys of the Rea and Tame feeders. Ground rises from 200 to 600 feet across the site. The Lickey hills skirt it to the south-west.

The article works through site, history, government, churches, and trades in deep detail. Birmingham's metal trades and workshops anchor its fame as a manufacturing metropolis. Suburbs spill into Staffordshire and Worcestershire beyond the county line. Riots mark its history at points, including church-and-king mobs and the Murphy riots of 1867. Long lists of local histories, from Hutton in 1783 onward, close the piece. It is a full civic portrait, not a gazetteer note.
britannica-1911-bishop-auckland:
Bishop Auckland is a market town in County Durham, England, 11 miles south-south-west of Durham city. Several North Eastern railway branches join at the town. Its urban district held 11,969 people in 1901. The town stands beautifully on a height near where the Wear and Gaunless rivers meet. The parish church lies a mile off, at Auckland St Andrew. That fine cruciform church was once collegiate, mostly Early English in style.

The palace of the bishops of Durham stands at the town's north-east end. It is a spacious, splendid, if irregular, pile on five acres, set in a park of 800 acres. Bishop Anthony Beck first chose the site under Edward I. Up the Wear stands tiny Escomb church, massively built and thought to date from the 7th century. Its stones include Roman work from nearby Binchester fort. Collieries and iron works employ most of the town's workers.
britannica-1911-blantyre-nyasaland:
Blantyre was the chief town of the Nyasaland protectorate in British Central Africa when the entry was written. It stands about 3000 feet above the sea in the Shiré Highlands, 300 miles by river and rail north-north-west of the Chinde mouth of the Zambezi. About 6000 Africans and 100 whites lived there.

Scottish missionaries founded the town in 1876 and named it after David Livingstone's birthplace. It housed the head offices of the main trading firms and mission bodies in the protectorate, and the trans-continental telegraph line passed through it. Its pride was the Church of Scotland church, a red brick building mixing Norman and Byzantine styles, built wholly by local labour and fronted by an avenue of cypress and eucalyptus trees.
britannica-1911-blantyre-scotland:
Blantyre is a coal parish in Lanarkshire, Scotland, a few miles south-east of Glasgow, with 14,145 people in 1901. Its name is Gaelic for the warm retreat. High Blantyre, Blantyre Works, Stonefield, and smaller villages make up the parish, and coal mining was carried on across the whole district.

Blantyre Works is remembered as the birthplace of David Livingstone (1813–1873) and his brother Charles, who both worked as piecers in a local cotton mill as boys. The entry notes the scant remains of Blantyre Priory, founded late in the 13th century, on the Clyde opposite Bothwell Castle. Stonefield, the largest place in the parish, was given over wholly to mining, and rail links tied the villages to Glasgow.
britannica-1911-blashfield-edwin-howland:
Edwin Howland Blashfield (born 1848) was an American painter known for large wall decorations in public buildings. Born in New York City, he studied in Paris under Bonnat. He joined the National Academy of Design in 1888. He began with genre scenes. Later he turned to decorative work praised for fine, soft colour.

His murals filled domes and halls across the country. The entry lists work at the Chicago Exposition of 1893. It names the Library of Congress dome in Washington and the Minnesota capitol. It names the Baltimore court-house too. New York sites run from the Waldorf-Astoria ballroom to the Vanderbilt and Huntington houses. With his wife he wrote Italian Cities (1900) and edited Vasari's Lives. He led the societies of mural painters and of American artists.
britannica-1911-bolton-edmund:
Edmund Bolton (born 1575, still living in 1633) was an English historian and poet of Catholic faith. By his own account he was born in 1575, schooled at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, and later lived at the Inner Temple in London. In 1600 he gave poems to the collection England's Helicon.

As a follower of the duke of Buckingham he won a small post at the court of James I. His plan for an English academy won the king's favour but died with him. Bolton wrote a life of Henry II for Speed's Chronicle, dropped because his sympathy for Becket showed his faith too plainly. His key works are Hypercritica, a short critical essay rich in notes on living writers, and Nero Caesar (1624), a study of depraved monarchy.
britannica-1911-bond:
Bond, in English law, is a duty taken on by deed, and the entry sets out how such an instrument works. The giver of the bond, the obligor, binds himself to pay money, or to do or not do some act, and backs the promise with a penalty. A condition is added to undo the bond if the duty is met.

That undoing clause is called the defeasance. The sum secured is usually half the penalty named. A full model money bond is printed, with blanks for names, dates, and sums, followed by its condition for payment of £1000 against a £2000 penalty. Later pages treat the kinds of bonds, how they are enforced, and how the penalty could be claimed or relieved in court.
britannica-1911-bonner-edmund:
Edmund Bonner (about 1500–1569) was bishop of London under the Tudors, remembered for his part in the Marian persecution. The entry opens with a quarrel over his birth: Strype printed a detailed account making him a natural son, which a contemporary disputed on weak proof. He was schooled at Broadgates Hall, Oxford, and took degrees in civil and canon law.

Ordained about 1519 and a doctor by 1525, he became Wolsey's chaplain and was with the fallen cardinal at Cawood. Passing into Henry VIII's service, he was sent to Rome in 1532 to block the king's case in the papal court. At Marseilles in 1533 he delivered Henry's appeal from the pope to a general council. Later pages trace his embassy work, his bishopric, his fall under Edward, his return under Mary, and his death in prison.
britannica-1911-bridgend:
Bridgend is a market town in southern Glamorganshire, Wales, standing on both sides of the river Ogwr, from which its Welsh name Penybont-ar-Ogwr is drawn. The urban district held 6062 people in 1901. Rail puts it 165 miles from London on the Great Western trunk line, with a branch toward Barry.

Farming trade fills its market, but coal gives the town its weight. The mining valleys of the Llynvi, Garw and the two Ogwr streams meet about 3 miles north and drain through Bridgend as their natural outlet. Local work includes joinery, a brass and iron foundry, a tannery, a brewery, brick-works and stone quarries. Ruined castles at Newcastle and Coity, the county lunatic asylums at Angelton and Parc Gwyllt, and a parish formed only in 1905 complete the picture.
britannica-1911-brighton-england:
Brighton is a borough of Sussex, England, and one of the best-known seaside resorts in the United Kingdom, 51 miles south of London by rail. Its people numbered 123,478 in 1901. Easy reach from the capital is named as the chief cause of its fame, and the town climbs the seaward slope of the South Downs in mild, sheltered air.

The sea front runs nearly 4 miles from Kemp Town in the east to Hove in the west, facing the English Channel. Inland the town, Preston included, spreads some 2 miles. Channel currents push shingle eastward, and the sea once ate at the shore. A massive sea wall, begun about 1830, 60 feet high and 23 feet thick at its base, at last held it back. Churches, the old parish church of St Nicholas with its Norman font. The pulpit once held by the preacher F. W. Robertson from 1847 to 1853 fill out the survey.
britannica-1911-bristol-england:
Bristol is a city and seaport of England, chiefly in Gloucestershire but partly in Somersetshire, 118 and a half miles west of London, with 328,945 people in 1901. The river Avon, marking the county boundary, runs confined between hills through a narrow valley floor where the old city core rests, reaching the Severn estuary 8 miles below.

Between city and channel the valley pinches into a gorge crossed at one stride by the famous Clifton Suspension Bridge. Above Bristol the hills close in again at Keynsham, leaving the city in a basin-like hollow some 4 miles across that spreads up northern heights. Railways fill the account: the Great Western from London, a link to South Wales by the Severn tunnel, outports at Avonmouth and Portishead. A Midland trunk line north through Gloucester, Worcester, Birmingham and Derby, both companies sharing one central station.
britannica-1911-bristol-rhode-island:
Bristol is the shire-township of Bristol county, Rhode Island, about 15 miles south-south-east of Providence, forming a peninsula between Narragansett Bay on the west and Mount Hope Bay on the east. It covers 12 square miles and held 6901 people in 1900, rising to 8565 in 1910, with ferries and two railways linking it outward.

Mount Hope, 216 feet high on the eastern side, commands fine views, while the gently rolling land suits farming, above all onion growing. The chief village, also Bristol, is a port of entry with a deep, roomy harbour, makes rubber and woollen goods. Is famed for yacht building: America's Cup defenders Columbia and Reliance came from the Herreshoff yards there. At the close of King Philip's War in 1676, Mount Hope Neck, the beaten sachem's seat, passed to Plymouth Colony, and the township followed in 1680.
britannica-1911-brunetiere-ferdinand:
Ferdinand Brunetiere (1849–1906) was a French critic and man of letters born at Toulon on 19 July 1849. Schooled at Marseilles and at the Lycee Louis-le-Grand in Paris, he aimed at teaching and sat the examination for the Ecole Normale Superieure but failed. The war of 1870 barred a second attempt. Private tuition and literary criticism became his path instead.

Successful articles in the Revue Bleue brought him to the Revue des Deux Mondes, first as contributor, then secretary and sub-editor, and finally in 1893 as principal editor. In 1886 he was made professor of French language and literature at the Ecole Normale, a singular honour for one who had not passed through the academic mill. He presided over conferences at the Sorbonne. The Legion of Honour came in 1887 and the Academy in 1893.
britannica-1911-bundelkhand:
Bundelkhand, a tract of Central India, is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica with two senses of its bounds. In the past sense it takes in five British districts of the north. In the rule sense of the day it is held to a set of native states under one state desk. Those states and lands past count are named with their sum of area and of folk.

The folk count of nineteen hundred and one past one million three hundred thousand in sum. That count shows a fall of more than a tenth in ten years. The text lays that fall to the work of years of dearth. The chief states of the set are named in a row of eight. A rail line of a great firm cuts the north of the tract.
britannica-1911-burke-edmund:
The 1911 Britannica article on Edmund Burke (1729-1797) profiles the British statesman and political writer. It calls his one of the greatest names in political literature. Burke was never tried in a post of supreme power. He was not the most effective speaker of his age. He was not its most original thinker either.

The article argues that no one matched his blend of gifts. He used broad ideas to judge the problems of the day. He stayed close to the details of practical politics. He was also a master of fine prose. The account then turns to his early life. He was most likely born at Dublin in 1729. His father was a Protestant attorney. His mother was a Catholic. He was schooled at Ballitore from 1741.
britannica-1911-bute-island:
Bute is the most key isle, though not the largest, of the group that forms a Scots county in the Firth of Clyde. It lies south west of a port town and a long sail from Glasgow. A thin bent strait parts it from the main land on two sides, and a broad sound parts it from a sister isle south.

The 1911 Britannica entry gives its area and its run from point to point. Its width shifts much from bay to bay of its cut coast. Piers stand at four shore towns, but one town is in truth the port for the whole isle. Steam boats link that port by rail and sea to a chain of Clyde towns, with boats at all hours of the day.
britannica-1911-campion-edmund:
Edmund Campion, an English Jesuit who lived from 1540 to 1581, gets a full life story in the 1911 Britannica. Born in London and schooled at Christ's Hospital, he greeted Queen Mary for the city's scholars in 1553. At Oxford he became a fellow of St John's College and won fame as a speaker. Queen Elizabeth heard him in 1566 and held him in regard.

Doubts on faith beset him, and he left Oxford in 1569 for Ireland. Hunted there for popery, he fled to Douai and joined the Roman Church. He became a Jesuit at Rome in 1573 and worked at Brünn, Vienna, and Prague. In 1580 he came back to England in disguise and preached in secret to Catholics. His book of ten reasons against the Anglican Church caused a stir in 1581, and he was seized at Lyford.
britannica-1911-capefigue-jean-baptiste-:
Jean Baptiste Honore Raymond Capefigue is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Capefigue was a French historian and writer of lives who lived from 1801 to 1872. He was born at Marseilles. At age twenty he went to Paris to study law, but soon left law for the press. He edited and wrote for many papers in Paris.

The article says his royalist views colour all his works. He preached the divine right of kings and found kind words even for flawed courts. He wrote lives of queens and royal women of France and other lands. His histories range over the whole span of French history. A national library list holds seventy seven works by him in many volumes. The text judges that his haste hurt both his truth and his judgment, despite his wide access to state papers.
britannica-1911-carlisle-england:
Carlisle is a city of Cumberland, in northern England. It is the county town of that shire. It stands 299 miles north-north-west of London. The Scottish border lies only 8 miles north of it. Its population in 1901 was 45,480. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the city. Carlisle lies on the south bank of the river Eden. Two tributaries, the Caldew and the Petteril, join there.

The suburb of Stanwix stands across the Eden to the north. A handsome bridge of 1812–1815 joins it to the city. The rivers at Carlisle are not navigable. A canal to Port Carlisle, opened in 1823, failed. It was converted into a railway in later years. Silloth, 21 miles away, is the nearest real port. Carlisle is one of Britain's great railway centres, though. Lines from England and Scotland meet at its stations. The article covers its castle, cathedral, trades and history.
britannica-1911-carrel-jean-baptiste-nic:
Jean Baptiste Nicolas Armand Carrel (1800–1836) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French publicist born at Rouen, the son of a well-off merchant. He studied at the college of Rouen and at the military school of St Cyr. His bold, upright, and independent temper marked him out, and he joined the army as a sub-lieutenant with deep admiration for Napoleon's generals.

Carrel took a secret part in the failed Belfort conspiracy, and when war with Spain broke out in 1823 he resigned and escaped to Barcelona. There he joined the foreign legion and fought against his old comrades until the legion surrendered near Figuières. A council of war condemned him to death, but a flaw in the process saved him, and he was acquitted and freed. With his soldiering over, he moved to Paris and trained as a writer under the historian Augustin Thierry.
britannica-1911-cartwright-edmund:
Edmund Cartwright (1743–1823) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English inventor born at Marnham in Nottinghamshire. He studied at Oxford, took a fellowship at Magdalen, and published poems before settling as a country clergyman at Goadby Marwood in 1779. In 1784 his attention turned by chance to the problem of weaving by machinery.

The result was the power loom, patented in 1785 and improved under later patents in 1786 and 1787. His weaving factory at Doncaster failed and passed to his creditors in 1793, and a Manchester mill using his machines was burned in 1791. He also patented a wool combing machine in 1789. The entry shows a clergyman poet whose invention reshaped textile work while bringing him little profit.
britannica-1911-castell-edmund:
Edmund Castell lived from 1606 to 1685 and was an English orientalist. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Tadlow in Cambridgeshire, his birth place. At age fifteen he entered Emmanuel College at Cambridge as a youth. He soon moved to St John's for the sake of its fine library. His great work was a lexicon in seven tongues of the east.

That book, the Lexicon Heptaglotton, came out in the year 1669. He spent eighteen years on it, at sixteen hours a day by his claim. Fourteen helpers worked with him at a cost that ruined him. He spent some twelve thousand pounds and sank into deep poverty. In 1667 he was jailed for debts his brother had left him.
britannica-1911-chase-salmon-portland:
Salmon Portland Chase (1808–1873) was an American statesman and jurist, and the start of his life is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Cornish township, New Hampshire, on the thirteenth of January 1808. His father died in 1817, when the boy was nine. Salmon then spent some years in Ohio with his uncle, Bishop Philander Chase.

The uncle was a pioneer bishop of the Protestant Episcopal Church in the West. Chase graduated at Dartmouth College in 1826. He studied law at Washington under William Wirt, the attorney general. He was admitted to the bar in 1829 and moved to Cincinnati in 1830. There he soon won a strong place at the bar. He also published an annotated edition of the state laws, a work long used as a standard.
britannica-1911-chatham-england:
Chatham is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a port and borough of Kent, England. It stands on the right bank of the Medway, 34 miles east south east of London by rail. Its population in 1901 was 37,057. To the west it joins Rochester and to the east Gillingham, so the three boroughs form one town of over 110,000 people. Apart from the dockyards and fortifications, the entry finds few objects of interest.

St Mary's church opened in 1903 on a site that bore a church in Saxon times. St Bartholomew's chapel belonged to a leper hospital founded in 1070 by Bishop Gundulph, one of the first in England. An almshouse founded in 1592 by Sir John Hawkins for decayed seamen still stands. The Chatham Chest, a fund begun by Hawkins and Drake in 1588, was merged into Greenwich Hospital in 1802. Statues honour General Gordon and Thomas Waghorn. Brickyards, lime kilns, and flour mills work in the district.
britannica-1911-christmas-island:
Christmas Island is a British possession in the Indian Ocean, held under the rule of the Straits Settlements. The 1911 Britannica article places it about 190 miles south of Java. It is shaped like a square with hollowed sides, some twelve miles long and nine miles wide. No man had lived on it before the first settlers came in 1897. Thick forest of great trees then covered the whole island.

The settlement at Flying Fish Cove holds some 250 souls, of European, Sikh, Malay, and Chinese stock. Roads have been cut and clearings farmed. The island is the flat top of an undersea mountain that rises more than 15,000 feet. Its own height above the sea tops one thousand feet. Three terraces step down from a central plain to the shore cliff. Rich beds of phosphate of lime give the island its trade worth.
britannica-1911-clermont-ferrand:
Clermont-Ferrand is a city of central France, capital of Puy-de-Dôme, 113 miles west of Lyons on the Paris-Lyon railway, with 58,363 people in the commune in 1906. It sits on an eminence at the western border of the fertile plain of Limagne. Hills surround it on three sides, with the Puy-de-Dôme standing out among the mountains behind. Since 1731 it has joined the two towns of Clermont and Montferrand.

Old Clermont streets by the cathedral are narrow and sombre, bordered by old houses built of lava. Boulevards divide them from the modern quarters of the joined city. The cathedral, a Gothic edifice begun in the 13th century, was completed only in the 19th under Viollet-le-Duc. Its stained glass runs from the 13th to 15th centuries. A Crusades monument with a statue of Pope Urban II stands in the square.
britannica-1911-cockburn-sir-alexander-j:
Sir Alexander James Edmund Cockburn (1802–1880) rose to be lord chief justice of England. He was born on 24 December 1802, of old Scottish stock. His father served Britain as envoy to the state of Columbia. His mother came from a French family. Birth and schooling gave him strong French, of use all his life.

He read at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, and became a fellow there. He entered the Middle Temple in 1825 and was called to the bar in 1829. Work on the western circuit came slowly at first. Lord John Russell made him solicitor-general in 1850 and attorney-general in 1851. The entry praises the care he gave to every case, great or small. No counsel or suitor, it says, left his court unheard.
britannica-1911-coney-island:
Coney Island is an island about nine miles south-east of the south end of Manhattan, on the south shore of Long Island. Bays, a tidal creek and broad salt marshes split it from the main shore. It lies within the Borough of Brooklyn in New York city. The island is the west end of a chain of sandbars near 100 miles long.

The island itself runs about five miles long. Its width runs from a quarter mile to one mile. Rail lines, electric lines and summer steamboats all serve it. The entry calls it the most popular sea resort in the United States. Four districts mark its length. Sea Gate, at the west end, holds summer homes and a yacht club house. West Brighton draws the crowds with side-shows, booths and dance halls. Luna Park and Dreamland stand there. Brighton Beach and Manhattan Beach lie east.
britannica-1911-contraband:
Contraband is a term of trade and war law treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In broad use it means traffic that the law forbids. As contraband of war it means goods that folk of neutral states may not supply to a side at war. The word comes from French roots for against a proclaimed ban.

In practice such goods fall in two kinds. The first kind serves war at once, as arms and gear for fleets and armies do. The second kind can serve war or peace, and is banned only by its use or its goal. Jurists and states still clash on what goods fall in each class. They clash too on goods bound first for a neutral port but meant at last for a foe. The article tells of the Hague talks that sought a shared rule.
britannica-1911-cormon-fernand:
Fernand Cormon is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French painter born in Paris in eighteen forty five. Three masters trained him in the craft of paint in his youth. He rose to lead the ranks of history painters in modern France.

The entry notes his early taste for stark scenes of blood and death. One famed work shows a first man in flight from a divine curse. Hall panels for a town house trace birth, death, wedlock, and war. Stone age tales held his brush for years of work in a row. A state cross of honour came to him in eighteen eighty.
britannica-1911-cornwall-england:
Cornwall is the far south west county of England, bound by two seas. Its county entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Atlantic bounds it north and north west, and the Channel south. Devonshire lies to its east, and the Scilly Isles belong to it.

No county in England holds a stronger sense of self than Cornwall. That mark shows in trade, past events, names, lore, and the land itself. The county forms a long cape, seventy five miles from end to end. The Tamar river forms most of its border with Devon in the east. High moors and broad hills form the spine of the Cornish cape.
britannica-1911-cortland:
Cortland is a city and the county seat of Cortland county, New York. It stands in the centre of the state, on the Tioughnioga river, where its east and west branches join. Its people numbered 9,014 in 1900 and 11,504 in 1910. Two railways serve the city, the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western and the Lehigh Valley. The Franklin Hatch library stands in Cortland, as does a state normal and training school opened in 1869.

The city is a noted centre of making. Its works turn out wire, wire-cloth and netting, cabs, carriages and waggons, iron and steel, and wall-paper. Dairy supplies, corundum wheels, and clothing are also made there. The worth of its factory output rose by near half between 1900 and 1905. The town was first settled in 1792 as part of Cortlandville. In 1900 the village of Cortland was chartered as a city.
britannica-1911-crowland:
Crowland, or Croyland, is a market town in Lincolnshire, England, in a low fen district on the river Welland. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 2,747 in 1901. A house of monks was founded there in 716 by King Aethelbald. It honoured Saint Guthlac, a young noble turned hermit who had lived on the isle. Danes burned the abbey in 870, and fire struck again in 1091. A fine Norman abbey rose in 1113.

What stands now is the ruined nave and the tower arch. The great west front, of Early English date, is the finest piece left. The north aisle is restored and serves as the parish church. A strange bridge with three arms still stands in the town. It spanned three streams, now covered, and its three paths meet at a point in the middle. Royal charters kept its rights for near eight hundred years.
britannica-1911-crown-land:
Crown land in Britain meant land held by the king as king. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces how that estate grew and how control of it changed over time. Early kings held a private estate, palace lands, and rights over folkland. By the Norman Conquest those strands had merged into one crown estate.

Later kings gave much of the land away to friends and favorites. Parliament then stepped in and set firm limits on such grants. George III gave up his own claim to the income for a fixed civil list payment. Later law put the lands under named boards with set powers to lease, sell, and swap land.
britannica-1911-cumberland-england:
Cumberland is the most north-western county of England, bounded by Scotland, Northumberland, Westmorland, Lancashire, and the Irish Sea. Its area is 1,520 square miles. The south holds about half of the Lake District, with Scafell Pike, at 3,210 feet the highest mountain in England. Derwentwater, Wastwater, and Ullswater stand among its lakes. Valleys run out from the fells to a flat coastal belt, widest on the Solway Plain.

The Eden valley parts the Lake District from the Pennine face, where Cross Fell rises to 2,930 feet within the county. Salmon fisheries enrich the Eden, and trout fill many streams and lakes. The long entry works through geology, rivers, and the county's antiquities in turn. A heavy list of authorities closes the survey, from Ferguson's History of Cumberland to the Victoria County History. The whole is a full county portrait of land, water, and past.
britannica-1911-cumberland-maryland:
Cumberland is a city in Maryland and the county-seat of Allegany county, on the Potomac river about 178 miles west of Baltimore. Its population grew from 12,729 in 1890 to 21,839 in 1910. Five railways serve it, and the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal ends there. The city sits about 635 feet above the sea, shut in by high hills. A deep gorge called the Narrows cuts those hills to the west as a natural gateway.

Coal mined nearby drives Cumberland's large trade, and in 1905 it ranked second among Maryland's manufacturing centres. Iron, steel, bricks, flour, cement, silk, and leather lead its products, and factory output rose over half between 1900 and 1905. The city owns its water-works and electric light plant. First settled in 1750, the place gained Fort Cumberland in 1754, which Braddock occupied the next year. It was laid out in 1763 and chartered as a city in 1850.
britannica-1911-cumberland-rhode-island:
Cumberland is a township of Providence county, Rhode Island, in the north-east of the state, with the Blackstone river along most of its west border. Its area is 27.5 square miles, and its people rose from 8,090 in 1890 to 10,107 in 1910. Many villages crowd its borders, from Cumberland Hill and Diamond Hill to Valley Falls. The land is mostly hilly and rocky. Granite, limestone, and some coal, iron, and gold are found there.

That mineral wealth won Cumberland the name of the mineral pocket of New England. The Blackstone and its branches give strong water power. Cotton goods, silk goods, and horse-shoes lead its manufactures, whose value grew faster than in any like town in the state. William Blackstone, the first lasting white settler in Rhode Island, built his Study Hall there about 1635. The township was formed in 1747 from the old Attleborough Gore and named for William Augustus, duke of Cumberland.
britannica-1911-cummerbund: A cummerbund is a band worn round the waist. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the word from the Hindustani kamar-band, a loin band. Eastern health lore holds that the head should stay cool and the stomach warm. The turban guards the head from the sun. The cummerbund guards the belly against shifts of heat and cold. In India it is made of many folds of cloth. The cloth is muslin or a bright dyed stuff.
britannica-1911-curll-edmund:
Edmund Curll, who lived from 1675 to 1747, was an English bookseller born in the west of England. The 1911 Britannica article says his parents were of humble rank. He was apprenticed to a bookseller at Exeter, then set up in London on his own. He made his name by staged quarrels in the papers. His part in a set of court poems in 1716 sparked a long feud with Pope. Pope took his revenge in the Dunciad.

Curll grew famed for coarse books, till his name stood for print filth itself. Twice he was called to the bar of the House of Lords. In 1725 he was convicted of obscene print, and in 1728 he stood an hour in the pillory. In forty years he put out a vast range of books. A list of them counts 167 works of high standard, most free of his taint.
britannica-1911-dee-scotland:
The Dee, a river of Aberdeenshire in Scotland, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It flows east from the Cairngorms to the North Sea at Aberdeen. It rises in the Wells of Dee on Ben Braeriach. That spring stands 4,061 feet above the sea. The river drops fast in its first few miles. Burns from the flanking hills feed its upper course.

With its side streams it drains a thousand square miles. The course runs about ninety miles in all. It is swift and rough for the first half. Below Aboyne it broadens and slows. Near Aberdeen its channel was reshaped to add dock room. The article praises the beauty of the Braemar stretch. About two miles above Inverey it cuts a narrow gorge. There it forms the falls known as the Linn of Dee. The river is one of the finest salmon streams in Scotland.
britannica-1911-dortmund:
Dortmund is the chief commercial town of the Prussian province of Westphalia, standing on the Emscher 50 miles east of Dusseldorf. Its people grew from 57,742 in 1875 to 175,292 in 1905, and since the old walls came down in 1863 the town has turned modern. Old churches remain, the Reinoldikirche with its stained glass and the Marienkirche with an eleventh-century nave, and the restored thirteenth-century town hall holds the antiquarian museum.

The town's real weight is industrial: it sits in the great Westphalian coal basin with iron ore beds beside it. Steel rails, mining plant, wire ropes and machinery lead its output, with great breweries and a corn and timber trade behind them. The article recalls its Hanseatic supremacy and its passage to Prussia in 1815.
britannica-1911-elland:
Elland is an urban district in the Elland parliamentary division of Yorkshire, England, standing on the river Calder south of Halifax. Its population in 1901 was 10,412. The church of St Mary is built in the Decorated and Perpendicular styles. Cotton mills, woollen factories, and ironworks employ the town's working people. Flagstone quarries at Elland Edge and fire-clay works add to its industry.

Elland Hall, though almost rebuilt, keeps alive the memory of a fierce family feud. The Ellands feuded with the Beaumonts of Crosland Hall, whose site can still be traced nearby. A nephew of Sir John Elland met death in 1342 at the hands of a Beaumont kinsman. Sir John took vengeance on that house and on the allied houses of Lockwood and Quarmby. The children of those families were raised to avenge their parents, and after many years they succeeded, cutting off Sir John Elland and his heir.
britannica-1911-enfield-england:
Enfield is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a market town in Middlesex, England, eleven miles north of London Bridge. The article gives the town's people as 42,738 in 1901, up from 31,536 ten years before. It stands on the west slope of the Lea valley, on two rail lines, with rows of workers' homes reaching toward the river.

The piece notes the villas of men whose work lies in London and the hands employed at the Royal Small Arms factory at Enfield Lock. It describes the church of Saint Andrew, part old and part later work, with its tombs and brasses by the market place. Enfield Palace, the grammar school founded in 1557, and the New River all get a mention. The entry shows a country town fast turning into a London suburb.
britannica-1911-exeter-england:
Exeter is the county town of Devonshire, 172 miles west-south-west of London, with 47,185 people in 1901. The old city rides a broad ridge rising steeply from the Exe's left bank. The castle crowns the ridge on a great British earthwork, now laid out as a promenade. High Street and Fore Street are narrow and picturesque, lined with houses of the 16th and 17th centuries.

The cathedral, though not among England's largest, is praised as unmatched in beauty and detail. Apart from its Norman transept towers, the work is Decorated, from about 1280 to 1369. Inside, one unbroken roof spans nave and choir, with a minstrels' gallery and Bishop Stapeldon's throne of about 1320. Scott restored the whole between 1870 and 1877. The city's woollen trade, begun under Elizabeth, once exported over half a million sterling a year, second only to Leeds, but died out by the early 1800s.
britannica-1911-fabre-ferdinand:
Ferdinand Fabre (1830-1898) was a French writer of novels set in the south of France. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him from Bédarieux in Hérault to Paris and back. Raised by his uncle, an abbé, he trained for the priesthood at first. A strong inner turn in 1848 led him away from that path.

His first novel, Les Courbezon (1862), dealt with country priests in the Cevennes. That theme ran through most of his later work. Books such as L'Abbé Tigrane and Mon Oncle Célestin drew praise for their close and fair portraits of clergy life. He later served as curator of the Mazarin Library.
britannica-1911-falkland:
Falkland is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a royal burgh of Fife in Scotland. The town, with 809 people in 1901, stands at the north base of East Lomond hill, twenty-one miles north of Edinburgh. It looks old-world, with many ancient houses still standing. Its trades are linen weaving and brewing, and it has few public buildings besides the town hall.

What lends the place its fame is the palace of the Stuarts. The site was a hunting tower of the Macduff earls of Fife. There Albany had the heir to the throne, David, duke of Rothesay, starved to death in 1402. The tower was rebuilt as a palace under James the Third and finished in 1538, and it became a favourite summer home of the Stuart kings.
britannica-1911-ferdinand: Ferdinand is a royal name shared by many kings and princes of Europe in this 1911 Britannica entry. In Spanish the name takes the form Fernando or Hernando. In Italian it takes the forms Ferdinando or Ferrante. Its old German root is read as brave in the host. The entry sets a clear order for the men who bear the name. Emperors come first in that list. Kings of Naples, Portugal, and Spain come next, with more lines to close.
britannica-1911-fife-scotland:
Fife, a sea-girt county of Scotland, is surveyed in a shire entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Firth of Tay bounds it north and the Forth bounds it south. The North Sea washes its east shore for mile on mile. Perth, Kinross, and Clackmannan shires close its west side in land. Five isles, from May to Inchgarvie, belong to the county roll.

Its ground runs to just over five hundred square miles in all. The Lomond Hills are its chief heights in the south-west part. West Lomond tops seventeen hundred feet above the sea at its peak. The Eden is its longest stream at twenty-five miles of flow. Trout crowd its high waters, though weirs bar the salmon run. The Leven drains its great loch east to the Forth.
britannica-1911-fogelberg-benedict-erlan:
Benedict Erland Fogelberg (1786-1854), Swedish sculptor, was born at Gothenburg on 8 August 1786. His father, a copper-founder, backed his early taste for design and sent him to Stockholm in 1801 to study at the school of art. There he fell under the influence of the sculptor Sergell, who passed on his own love of antique art and natural grace. Fogelberg worked hard at Stockholm for years, though his instinct for severe beauty rebelled against the rococo taste then ruling the city.

A government pension in 1818 let Fogelberg travel. He studied a year or two in Paris, under Guerin and then the sculptor Bosio. In 1820 he reached Rome, the dream of his life, and spent most of his remaining years there in steady work and close study of the art of the past. In 1854 the king called him home to Sweden, where he was received with honour, as the entry closes his career.
britannica-1911-franz-josef-land:
Franz Josef Land is an Arctic archipelago east of Spitsbergen and north of Novaya Zemlya, running from about 80 to 82 degrees north. Its glacier-covered islands rise to about 2400 feet, and their main rock is basalt pushing through the ice near the shore. Bear and fox are the only land mammals, though the bird life drew scientific interest.

Julius Payer, with the Austrian ship Tegetthof beset in the ice, first saw the land in August 1873 and reached Cape Fligely at 82 degrees 5 minutes north. Leigh Smith charted the south coast in 1881 and 1882. The Jackson-Harmsworth party worked from Cape Flora from 1894, and there Jackson met Nansen in June 1896. The duke of Abruzzi wintered in Teplitz Bay in 1899, and his sledge party reached 86 degrees 33 minutes north the following spring.
britannica-1911-fredegond:
Fredegond (died 597) was a Frankish queen who rose from serving-woman to wife of King Chilperic I. At her urging he put away his first wife Audovera and strangled his second, Galswintha, sister of Queen Brunhilda. Chilperic married Fredegond in 567, and her hold over him proved ruinous to his house and realm.

She pushed him into war with Austrasia and procured the murder of the victorious King Sigebert in 575. His sons by Audovera all died tragic deaths while she fought to secure the throne for her own children. Two sons died in infancy, but a third lived to reign as Clotaire II. After Chilperic death in 584 she governed the western kingdom for the boy, plotted against Childebert II, beat Theudebert at Laffaux, and died in 597.
britannica-1911-frederick-maryland:
Frederick is a city and the county-seat of Frederick county, Maryland, on Carroll Creek, 61 miles by rail west of Baltimore. Its population was 10,411 in 1910. Rich Monocacy valley farmland surrounds it, with Catoctin Mountain west and Sugar Loaf Mountain south, and most buildings are brick or stone.

The Maryland school for the deaf and the Woman College of Frederick stand here. Francis Scott Key and Roger Brooke Taney lie buried in Mount Olivet cemetery, where a monument honours Key. Canning works and makers of flour, bricks, brushes, leather goods, and hosiery drive the trade. Germans settled the place in 1733, named for Frederick Calvert of the Baltimore family. Braddock prepared his ill-fated march here in 1755, and Whittier poem Barbara Frietchie later made the city famed in the Civil War.
britannica-1911-gavelkind:
Gavelkind, in the 1911 Britannica, is a land-tenure custom tied chiefly to Kent, where all land is presumed held by it until the contrary is proved. More exactly, it is socage tenure subject to the custom of gavelkind. The entry sets out its six chief peculiarities in order.

A tenant may grant his land away at fifteen, may always leave it by will, and loses nothing by felony: 'the father to the bough, the son to the plough.' If he dies without a will, all sons share equally, not the eldest alone. A widow's dower is one half, not one third. The entry traces gavelkind to before the Conquest, when it was the general custom, later displaced by primogeniture. Irish gavelkind, a tribal form, is set apart at the close.
britannica-1911-gazaland:
Gazaland is a district of Portuguese East Africa, running north from the Komati river at Delagoa Bay to the Pungwe river. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it a well-watered, fertile country. It is also named as one of the chief recruiting grounds for labour for the Transvaal gold mines.

The name comes from Gaza, a Swazi chief of Chaka's time. His son Manikusa welded refugee clans into one tribe, the Matshangana, and by 1836 mastered the country as far as the Zambezi, taking the Portuguese posts. The entry follows his son Umzila, who ceded the land south of the Manhissa to the Portuguese yet held the north in independence until about 1884. A rival figure, the Goanese prazo-holder Gouveia, closes the account.
britannica-1911-gensonne-armand:
Armand Gensonné (1758–1793) was a French politician born at Bordeaux on the 10th of August 1758, son of an army surgeon. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him from the bar to the Legislative Assembly as deputy for the Gironde in 1791. Speaking for the diplomatic committee, he backed Brissot's line against the court.

He moved two bold steps: charging the king's brothers in January 1792 and declaring war on the king of Bohemia and Hungary that April. In the Convention he attacked the Paris Commune and, at the king's trial, voted death while backing an appeal to the people. He presided over the Convention in March 1793 and shared the Girondist fight against the Mountain. Named on the arrest list of the 2nd of June, he was tried in October and guillotined on the 31st, meeting death with calm.
britannica-1911-gibson-edmund:
Edmund Gibson, who lived from 1669 to 1748, was an English churchman and legal scholar. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from Bampton in Westmorland to Queen College at Oxford. In 1692 he brought out a valued edition of the Saxon Chronicle with Latin text. Notes on Quintilian and a large new edition of Camden Britannia followed fast.

Archbishop Tenison made him chaplain and keeper of his library in 1694. He then held parish and cathedral posts at Lambeth and in Surrey. Church rights and the powers of Convocation drew much of his thought in that age. The entry shows a scholar whose books served both church and law.
britannica-1911-glenalmond:
Glenalmond is a glen in Perthshire, Scotland, to the south-east of Loch Tay. It takes in the upper two-thirds of the course of the Almond river. That stretch runs for twenty miles. For most of its length the glen runs east by south. At Newton Bridge it turns sharp to the south-east for three miles. There it narrows so much that the pass is called the Small Glen.

Past the pass the glen widens and runs east to Trinity College, a well known public school. One spot is held by local lore to be the grave of Ossian. A Roman camp's remains lie near Buchanty. The high ground at the head of the glen is crowned by Ben Chonzie, 3,048 feet high. The district east of Buchanty is said to be the Drumtochty of Ian Maclaren's tales.
britannica-1911-gmund:
Gmund is the subject of a town entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town lies in Germany in the realm of Wurttemberg. It stands in a rich vale on the river Rems. A fine bridge spans the river at that point. Old walls with towers ring the town. Its count in 1905 was just under nineteen thousand souls. Old churches stand among its old houses and halls.

Clocks and watches were the chief goods made there. Work in silver goods was also strong in the town. Trade in corn, hops, and fruit kept its market busy. Schools for trade and drawing served the town youth. Walls first rose round the town in the early 1100s. It won town rights from Frederick Barbarossa. It stayed a free town of the empire till 1803. In that year it passed to Wurttemberg for good.
britannica-1911-gosse-edmund:
Edmund Gosse, an English poet and critic born in 1849, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in London, son of a noted zoologist of the same surname. In 1867 he became an assistant among the printed books of the British Museum. He moved in 1875 to a translator's post at the Board of Trade.

Gosse was later librarian to the House of Lords and a Cambridge lecturer in English letters. The article praises his work in bringing foreign writing home to English readers. His Northern Studies dealt with the letters of Holland and Scandinavia. He translated Ibsen's Hedda Gabler and, with Archer, the Master Builder. He also wrote a life of Ibsen and edited the English works of Björnson. Norway thanked him with a knighthood of its order of St Olaf in 1901. His own verse fills several volumes listed at the close.
britannica-1911-gotland:
Gotland, an island in the Baltic Sea that belongs to Sweden, is surveyed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It runs about seventy five miles long and no more than thirty wide, with the mainland some fifty miles off. With small islands near it, Gotland forms a district of its own for rule.

The island is a flat shelf of limestone, low in height, with steep coasts edged by tall free standing pillars of rock. Some streams run part of their course below ground, and caves are not rare. Old marshy moors had been drained and put to crops by the time of the entry. Less than half the land was under forest. Barley was the chief grain, sent to breweries on the mainland, and sugar beet was grown and worked in beet sugar plants on the island. Sheep and cattle were also raised.
britannica-1911-grand-island:
Grand Island is a city and county seat of Hall county in Nebraska. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the Platte river in that state. It lies about 154 miles west of Omaha on the plain. Its count grew from 7,554 in 1900 to 10,326 in 1910. Three rail lines meet and serve the growing prairie city there.

The town stands on a slope above the broad flats of the Platte. Rich farm land of great yield spreads round it on all sides. Two colleges teach youth there, one Baptist and one for business. A state home for old soldiers and sailors dates from 1888. Grand Island does a large wholesale trade and runs a horse market.
britannica-1911-gravesend:
Gravesend, a river port and market town of Kent in England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the right bank of the Thames, across from Tilbury Fort. In 1901 it held just over twenty-seven thousand people. The town runs for two miles along the bank, up a low rise to Windmill Hill.

The old low town is a maze of narrow streets, while the new high town is broad and fine. Steamboat piers from the days of gay river trips still line the front. London folk crowd there for day trips and for the summer, and yachts fill its reach. Shrimp fishing is a chief trade, with boat yards, iron works, and brewers in the town. Fruit and greens grow round it for the London market.
britannica-1911-greenland:
Greenland, Danish Gronland, is a large continental island, the greater part of it within the Arctic Circle and the whole arctic in character. The 1911 Britannica opens its long article with the island's isolation. No land joins it to Europe or America, though submarine ridges link it to Iceland, the Faeroes and Scotland, and to Baffin Land across Davis Strait.

Only a narrow strait parts its far north from Ellesmere Land. The entry maps its seas with care: the North Atlantic and the Greenland Sea to the east, Denmark Strait toward Iceland, and Davis Strait and Baffin Bay to the west. Northward the bay narrows into Smith Sound, Kane Basin, Kennedy Channel and Robeson Channel. From that geography the article moves to the ice cap, the coasts, the Norse and Danish settlements, and the exploration of the interior.
britannica-1911-greensand:
Greensand, in geology, is a name applied to three distinct parts of the Cretaceous system, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article sorts them out. They are the Upper Greensand, the Lower Greensand, and the Cambridge Greensand at the base of the Chalk. Early English geologists coined the term for sandy rocks. Such rocks often show a green colour from tiny grains of the mineral glauconite.

Until the fossils were closely studied, the upper and lower beds were much confused. The article then confines itself to the Lower Greensand. Fitton examined that formation in detail and proposed a new name for it in 1845. The name was revived in 1885, since the sands often lose their green tint as the iron turns red and brown. The formation is typically seen in the Weald, the Isle of Wight, and Dorset.
britannica-1911-grindal-edmund:
Edmund Grindal (c. 1519–1583) rose through the Elizabethan church. He served in turn as bishop of London, archbishop of York and archbishop of Canterbury. Born at Hensingham in Cumberland, he was a farmer's son. He studied at Cambridge and became a fellow of Pembroke Hall in 1538. He later served as a chaplain to Edward VI.

Under Mary he fled abroad to Strassburg and then Frankfurt. There he tried to settle disputes among the English exiles. The fight was over how far reform should go. Returning in 1559, he helped revise the liturgy. Yet his scruples over vestments and church government set him apart. He also shrank from punishing Puritans harshly. He founded a free school at St Bees. He left money for the poor of several places.
britannica-1911-halifax-england:
Halifax is a borough in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the town and its buildings. It lies in a bare, hilly district on the small river Hebble, near its meeting with the Calder. Its people rose from 97,714 in 1891 to 104,936 in 1901.

The entry notes the town is mostly modern, though a few fine old houses remain. It picks out the town hall, finished in 1863 to the designs of Charles Barry. It also names the parish church of Saint John the Baptist, with its tall western tower and fine old woodwork. All Souls church, built in 1859 to designs by Gilbert Scott, is praised as a good sample of his work.
britannica-1911-hamilton-scotland:
Hamilton is a burgh of Lanarkshire, Scotland. Its population in 1901 was 32,775. It stands near the junction of the Avon with the Clyde. Glasgow lies about ten miles north-west by road. Two railway companies serve the town. The town hall is Scottish Baronial, with a 130-foot clock-tower. Queenzie Neuk, where Queen Mary rested before Langside, is a noted spot.
