Cotton, lace and embroidered muslins are manufactured there. Carriage-building and market gardens also employ people. The district is famed for its apples. Real prosperity rests on coal and ironstone. The surrounding field is Scotland's richest mineral ground. Hamilton palace stands just east of the town. Its portico pillars are each a single stone block. The palace grounds cover nearly 1,500 acres. Cadzow Castle's ruins lie nearby. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hamilton, Scotland entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hand:
Hand is a word common to the Teutonic languages. German Hand and Gothic handus are its kin. It names the terminal part of the human arm. The fingers and palm make it up. Some animals have prehensile limbs called hands too. Transferred uses of the word fill most of the account. Hand can mean charge, authority or agency. Phrases like at first hand show that range.

From the hands' position it also means direction. Right hand and left hand come from that use. A given hand symbolises marriage and oaths. Labourers and ships' crews are called hands. So is a person of special skill, an old parliamentary hand. Clock pointers and card deals take the name too. As a measure a hand equals four inches. It survives only in measuring horses. The hand of glory, a hanged man's dried hand, closes the entry.
britannica-1911-helmund:
The Helmund is a river of Afghanistan, about 600 miles long. It is identical with the ancient Etymander. Only the Kabul river rivals it in importance there. It exceeds the Kabul in both volume and length. It rises in the Koh-i-Baba west of Kabul. Its infant stream parts the Unai and Irak passes. No European followed its next fifty miles. Below Girishk it becomes a mountain river no longer.

At Girishk the Herat to Kandahar route crosses it. Forty-five miles lower the Arghandab joins it. Then it runs 300 to 400 yards wide and 9 to 12 feet deep. Even in the dry season it never lacks water. In Seistan it turns north for 70 to 80 miles. It ends in the Seistan swamps by various mouths. Its shifting bed caused repeated frontier squabbles. Persian Seistan, once highly cultivated, is now barren waste.
britannica-1911-herold-louis-joseph-ferd:
Louis Joseph Ferdinand Herold, a French musician who lived from 1791 to 1833, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Paris, he was the son of a skilled pianist. After his father died, he entered the Paris conservatoire in 1806 and studied under Catal and Mehul.

The entry follows his win of the grand prix de Rome in 1812 for a cantata on the Duchess de la Valliere. He then spent years in Italy, writing a symphony, chamber works, and his first stage work, shown at Naples in 1815. Back in Paris, he worked with Boieldieu in 1816 and won favour with his first French opera in 1817. Many stage works followed in quick order.
britannica-1911-hickeringill-edmund:
Edmund Hickeringill (1631–1708) was an English divine who lived an eventful life across the Commonwealth and the Restoration. A junior fellow of Caius College, Cambridge, in 1651–1652, he joined Lilburne's regiment as chaplain. He then served in the ranks in Scotland and in Swedish service, and rose to captain in Fleetwood's regiment. For a time he lived in Jamaica, and published an account of it in 1661.

That same year he was ordained by Robert Sanderson, bishop of Lincoln, having passed through shades of belief named Baptist, Quaker and Deist. From 1662 until his death in 1708 he was vicar of All Saints', Colchester. A vigorous pamphleteer, he clashed with Henry Compton, bishop of London, and paid heavy damages for slander in 1682. He made a public recantation in 1684 and was shut out of his living from 1685 to 1688. His career ended with a conviction for forgery in 1707, a year before his death.
britannica-1911-hill-rowland:
Rowland Hill (1744–1833) was an English preacher, born at Hawkstone, Shropshire, in 1744. Educated at Shrewsbury, Eton and St John's College, Cambridge, he scandalized his friends by preaching before taking orders, fired by Whitefield's example. In 1773 he took the parish of Kingston, Somersetshire, where crowds flocked to his open-air services.

With inherited wealth Hill built Surrey Chapel in London in 1783, keeping always to the forms of the Church of England. His powerful voice and bold manner fitted rude audiences, and Southey ranked his delivery with Kean's. He helped found the Religious Tract Society, the British and Foreign Bible Society and the London Missionary Society. His Village Dialogues (1810) reached a 34th edition by 1839.
britannica-1911-hill-sir-rowland:
Sir Rowland Hill (1795–1879), author of the penny postal system, was born at Kidderminster in 1795. A younger brother of Matthew Davenport Hill, he was named after Rowland Hill the preacher. A spinal complaint kept him lying down as a child, and he passed the time repeating figures aloud to huge totals. At school his gift for mathematics was plain.

At twelve Hill was helping teach mathematics in his father's Birmingham school, and later he chiefly ran it. His system for educating boys in large numbers, printed in 1822, left as much power as possible with the boys themselves. It worked so well that the head master never used his veto in six years. As an educationist he ranks beside Arnold of Rugby. His lasting fame rests on the penny post.
britannica-1911-hinterland:
Hinterland is the subject of an entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The German word means the land behind. It names the region that lies behind a coast or a river line. It can also mean a country that relies on another region for its trade.

In plain physical use words such as interior or back country are more common. Yet the term gained a sharp political sense in the eighteen eighties. Germany claimed rights in the land behind parts of the African coast it had seized. That claim became known as the doctrine of the hinterland. The entry explains how far that claim was said to reach.
britannica-1911-hippolytus-greek-legend:
Hippolytus, in Greek legend a son of Theseus and Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons, is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a famed hunter and chariot driver, dear to Artemis. His stepmother Phaedra fell in love with him. When he refused her, she hanged herself and left a letter that blamed him falsely.

Theseus drove his son out with curses and called on Poseidon to destroy him. A sea monster rose as Hippolytus drove by the shore at Troezen. The horses bolted, and he was dragged in the reins till he died. One tale from Epidaurus says Asclepius raised him back to life at the plea of Artemis. At Troezen girls cut a lock of hair for him before marriage.
britannica-1911-holy-island:
Holy Island, or Lindisfarne, is an island in the North Sea, 2 m. from the coast of Northumberland. Its population was 405 in 1901. At low water flat sands join it to the mainland, crossed by a track marked with wooden posts and passable for vehicles. The island measures 3 m. east to west and covers 1,051 acres, sandy and barren in the north, fertile in the south.

Rabbits, fish, oysters and farm produce are exported. At the south-west angle stands the fishing village, now a summer watering-place, with a harbour sheltering small vessels. The island takes its name from the monastery St Aidan founded there, restored in 1082 as a cell of Durham. Aidan chose Lindisfarne in 635 as the head of his new diocese, and St Cuthbert was among its bishops. In 793 the Danes landed and burnt the monastery. The castle, on a basalt rock east of the village, dates from about 1500.
britannica-1911-hoyle-edmund:
Edmund Hoyle (1672–1769) was the first systematizer of the laws of whist, and the author of a book on games. He was born in 1672; his parentage and birthplace are unknown, and few details of his life survive. For some time he lived in London, and partly supported himself by teaching whist. For his pupils he drew up a Short Treatise on the game.

That treatise passed hand to hand in manuscript before Hoyle printed it, entering it at Stationers' Hall in November 1742. Hoyle's laws stayed authoritative until 1864, when the Arlington and Portland clubs adopted new rules that slowly replaced them. He also published rules for several other games, and his book on games has passed through many editions. The weight of his name survives in the phrase according to Hoyle, still used for settling any point by the book. The short entry is drawn from the whist article's ground.
britannica-1911-huber-ludwig-ferdinand:
Ludwig Ferdinand Huber (1764–1804) was a German author, born in Paris on the 14th of September 1764. His father, Michael Huber, did much to spread the study of German literature in France. The family moved in his infancy to Leipzig, where the boy was carefully taught modern languages and literature, inclining most to those of France and England.

At Leipzig Huber grew intimate with Christian Gottfried Körner, the poet's father. At Dresden he became engaged to Dora Stock, Körner's betrothed's sister, and fell in with Schiller, one of Körner's staunchest friends. In 1787 he was made secretary to the Saxon legation at Mainz, and stayed until the French occupation of 1792. There he took up the cause of the family of his friend Georg Forster, who had gone over to republican views. The account follows his later work as a writer and editor in Stuttgart and Ulm.
britannica-1911-ipswich-queensland:
Ipswich, a coal town of Queensland, is placed in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Bremer River, west of Brisbane by rail. In 1901 its folk came to over eight thousand in count. Rich farm, mine, and workshop lands spread round its streets. Coal crops out on the river banks at the town's edge.

That coal takes but light labour to dig from the ground. A woollen mill, saw mills, and foundries give work in town. Great rail workshops stand at North Ipswich by the lines. Settlers first built on the site in the year 1829. The town took its charter of rule in the year 1860. Its name keeps the bond with the old Ipswich of England.
britannica-1911-james-i-of-scotland:
James I (1394-1437) was king of Scotland and a poet, and his captivity opens an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of King Robert III, he was born at Dunfermline in July 1394. After his elder brother David died in murky circumstances, his father resolved to send James to France for safety.

The entry tells how English sailors seized the boy on the way, and Henry IV refused to ransom him. On his father's death in April 1406 James became king in name only, while his uncle Albany ruled Scotland and showed no haste to free him. Held first in the Tower of London, he was moved to Nottingham and Evesham, and his schooling went on under able tutors.
britannica-1911-james-ii-of-scotland:
James the Second, king of Scotland who lived from 1430 to 1460, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was the sole living son of James the First and was born on October 16, 1430. He was crowned at Holyrood in March 1437, soon after his father's murder. His mother and great lords held power while he was a boy.

His youth was marked by fierce strife between the Douglases and the Crichtons. James wed in July 1449 and took up the rule himself. In 1452 he called the great earl of Douglas to Stirling and stabbed him on a charge of treason. War with the Douglases broke out at once. By 1455 James had won and seized their lands.
britannica-1911-james-iv-of-scotland:
James the Fourth, king of Scotland, who lived from 1473 to 1513, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of James the Third, and the nominal head of the rebels who beat his father's troops at Sauchieburn in 1488. When his father was killed there, James became king.

He took a path quite unlike his father's with the nobles, and he was warm and open with his low born subjects, among whom he liked to wander unknown. Few Scots kings won such broad love, the entry says, or reigned with so little strife at home. Crowned at Scone days later, he took an active hand in rule. A small rising was soon put down, and a nobles' plot to hand him to Henry the Seventh came to nothing. Henry still sought peace and thought of a marriage match.
britannica-1911-james-v-of-scotland:
James the Fifth, king of Scotland, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He lived from 1512 to 1542. He was the son of James the Fourth. He was born at Linlithgow in April 1512. He became king when his father was killed at Flodden in 1513.

The regency was held first by his mother, Queen Margaret. After her second marriage, in August 1514, it passed to John Stewart, duke of Albany. The boy's minority was then torn by constant quarrels. One faction, led by the earl of Angus, favoured England. The other backed France under Albany. The queen-mother and the nobles fought to gain the king's person. Each side sought to hold the boy, and so to hold power. The text notes that England did not press its win at Flodden. The scene is a kingdom ruled through a child.
britannica-1911-jind:
Jind was a native state of India in the Punjab, and the 1911 Britannica entry gives its size, people, and rule in compact form. It ranked among the Cis-Sutlej states. Those states came under British sway early in the eighteen hundreds. Its land lay in three split tracts set amid British districts, and its folk grew grain and cotton for sale.

The entry notes goods made there, from gold and silver work to leather, wood ware, and cloth. It then tells the line of its chiefs, Sikh rajas famed for their loyalty to the British. In the Mutiny year the raja took the field first and fed troops bound for Delhi. Two towns close the piece, old Jind and the new seat at Sangrur.
britannica-1911-john-of-england:
John (1167–1216), king of England, was the youngest son of Henry II by Eleanor of Aquitaine, born at Oxford on the 24th of December 1167. Lacking lands granted to his elder brothers, he was nicknamed Lackland. His father still planned great things for him: a Savoy marriage scheme, the earldom of Cornwall in reserve, a Gloucester heiress as bride, and the lordship of Ireland in 1177.

Sent to govern Ireland in 1185, he came home within months in disgrace, having offended loyal chiefs and failed to guard the settlers. In 1189 he joined Richard and the French king in the plot against his dying father. Under Richard he was loaded with lands and income yet barred from the regency during the crusade. He then worked against the chancellor Longchamp and plotted to secure England for himself. The long entry follows his reign to its end and closes with a guide to the record sources.
britannica-1911-jurien-de-la-graviere-je:
Jean Baptiste Edmond Jurien de la Gravière (1812–1892) was a French admiral, son of an admiral who had served through the Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars. He was born on the 19th of November 1812 and entered the navy in 1828. He was made commander in 1841 and captain in 1850, and in the Russian War he commanded a ship in the Black Sea.

He became rear admiral in December 1855. In 1859 he led a squadron in the Adriatic and sealed the Austrian ports with a close blockade. In October 1861 he took command in the Gulf of Mexico, and two months later led the expedition against Mexico, rising to vice admiral in January 1862. In the war of 1870 he held the Mediterranean fleet. He died on the 4th of March 1892. He was also a full writer on naval history, most of whose works first appeared in the Revue des deux mondes.
britannica-1911-kean-edmund:
Edmund Kean (1787–1833) was an English actor, born in London on the 17th of March 1787. His father was probably Edmund Kean, an architect's clerk, and his mother was an actress, Ann Carey. In his fourth year he first appeared on the stage as Cupid in Noverre's ballet of Cymon.

As a child his liveliness and cleverness made him a general favourite. But the harsh facts of his lot, and the lack of firm handling, bred self reliance with wayward ways. About 1794 kind persons paid for his schooling, and he mastered his tasks with striking ease and speed. Finding the restraint unbearable, he shipped as a cabin boy at Portsmouth. He found he had traded one bondage for a harder one. He then feigned deafness and lameness with such skill that he fooled even the doctors.
britannica-1911-kerguelen-island:
Kerguelen Island, Kerguelen's Land, or Desolation Island, is an island in the Southern Ocean, southeast of the Cape of Good Hope and southwest of Australia, nearly halfway between them. It lies between about 48 and 50 degrees south. Its greatest length is about 85 miles, but its area is only about 1400 square miles.

The island is mountainous throughout, and from the sea it can look like a run of jagged peaks. Ridges and mountain masses are parted by steep sided valleys. They run down to the sea and form deep fjords, so that no part of the interior is more than 12 miles from salt water. The chief summits are Mount Ross at 6120 feet, Mount Richards at 4000, and Mount Crozier at 3251. The coast is deeply cut, and the fjords on the north, east, and south form well sheltered harbours.
britannica-1911-khokand:
Khokand is a town of Russian Asia in the province of Ferghana, and its own article follows other town entries in the hosted text. The 1911 Britannica entry places it on the rail line from Samarkand to Andijan. It held more than eighty six thousand people in 1900. The town sits in a rich watered oasis at some height above the sea.

Harsh winters and hot summers mark its climate, and rain is scant each year. A citadel stands inside a wall near twelve miles round, with garden suburbs beyond. Broad streets, large squares, and a handsome bazaar show its modern face. The old palace of the khans draws note for its fine form.
britannica-1911-kustenland: Küstenland, meaning coast-land or littoral, is a common name for three crown-lands of Austria: Görz and Gradisca, Istria and Trieste. Together they cover 3084 square miles and held 755,183 people in 1900. The three lands are joined for some purposes of government under the governor of Trieste, and the legal and financial officers of Trieste also hold authority over the whole littoral.
britannica-1911-ladybrand:
Ladybrand is a town of the Orange Free State, 80 m. E. of Bloemfontein by rail, with another railway running to Natal by way of Harrismith. Its population in 1904 was 3862, of whom 2334 were whites. The town sits pleasantly at the foot of the flat-topped Platberg, about 4 m. W. of the Caledon river, which parts the province from Basutoland.

It is the centre of a rich arable district and has a large wheat market. It is also a health resort: the nearness of the Maluti Mountains keeps the climate bracing even in the summer months, November to March. Coal and petroleum are found in the neighbourhood. The town is named after the wife of Sir J. H. Brand, president of the Orange Free State.
britannica-1911-laporte-roland:
Roland Laporte, a Camisard leader known as Roland who lived from 1675 to 1704, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Mas Soubeyran in the Gard. He was the nephew of a Camisard chief shot in 1702. Roland himself then led a band of a thousand men.

He shaped his band into a drilled army with stores, arms depots, and hospitals. For bold acts and fast moves he was second just to Cavalier. He called himself general of the children of God and spread fear from Nimes to Alais. In 1704 he cut a Catholic regiment to pieces at Fontmorte. Sold out to his foes, he was shot that August while he fought his captors.
britannica-1911-lebuf-edmond:
Edmond Leboeuf is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Leboeuf was a marshal of France, born at Paris in 1809. He passed through the Ecole Polytechnique and the school of Metz. He won his spurs as an artillery officer in the Algerian wars.

By 1852 he was a colonel, and at the siege of Sebastopol he led the guns of the first French corps. Promotion came fast: general of brigade in 1854 and of division in 1857. In the Italian war of 1859 his artillery work at Solferino helped win the day. He later served as aide-de-camp to Napoleon the Third. In 1866 he handed Venetia over to Victor Emmanuel for France. On Marshal Niel's death in 1869 he became minister of war and reformed the War Office with vigor.
britannica-1911-limburg-holland: Limburg is the smallest province of Holland and the farthest south-east. Gelderland bounds it north and North Brabant north-west. Belgian Limburg and Liége lie south. Germany lies east. Its ground covers 850 square miles. The count of 1900 gave 281,934 people. The Meuse runs along its south-west edge, then through its north. The Geul and the Roer feed that river. Maastricht is the capital. Roermond names the second of its two parts.
britannica-1911-ludlow-edmund:
Edmund Ludlow, who lived from about 1617 to 1692, was an English parliament man and a soldier of the civil war. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Maiden Bradley in Wiltshire. He read at Trinity College, Oxford, and entered the Inner Temple in 1638. When war broke out he joined the life guard of Lord Essex. He fought at Worcester and at Edgehill. In 1643 he held Wardour Castle till a stout defence failed.

Ludlow rose as a horse officer and fought at Newbury and Basing House. In 1646 he took his father's seat in parliament and joined the republican party. He helped drive Pride's Purge in 1648. He sat among the judges of the king and signed the death warrant. In 1651 he went to Ireland as a horse general. There he all but finished the conquest of the island by 1652.
britannica-1911-magellan-ferdinand:
Ferdinand Magellan, who lived from about 1480 to 1521, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The entry calls him the first circumnavigator of the globe. He was born at Sabrosa in northern Portugal and came from the lower ranks of the Portuguese nobility. As a boy he served as a page to Queen Leonor.

The article follows his early years at sea in the service of King Manuel. He sailed for India in 1505 with the first Portuguese viceroy in the East. He was wounded at Cannanore in 1506 and again at the battle of Diu in 1509. He helped build a fort at Sofala and joined a voyage meant for the Spice Islands. Those years set the stage for his later westward voyage.
britannica-1911-mahaffy-john-pentland:
John Pentland Mahaffy, an Irish scholar of the classics born in 1839, is covered in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born in Switzerland on July 12, 1839. He was schooled in Switzerland and Germany, then at Trinity College, Dublin. There he held the chair of ancient history.

Mahaffy is shown as a man of great range who printed many works. His books on the Silver Age of Greece became standard guides in the field. Titles list histories of Greek letters and of Greek social life, and a work on the empire of the Ptolemies. He also rendered a Kant study into English and wrote a full study of Kant. He edited the Petrie papyri in three volumes.
britannica-1911-maiwand: Maiwand is a village of Afghanistan, fifty miles north-west of Kandahar, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is chiefly notable for the defeat of a British brigade under General Burrows by Ayub Khan on 27 July 1880, during the second Afghan War. Burrows advanced to Maiwand and attacked, but the Afghans, some 25,000 strong, outflanked his force. Of 2,476 British troops engaged, 934 were killed. The rout forced Sir Frederick Roberts to make his famous march from Kabul to Kandahar.
britannica-1911-mallow-ireland:
Mallow is a market town and spa in County Cork, Ireland. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on the Blackwater river, north of Cork city. Its people numbered 4,542 in 1901. Rail lines branch there toward Kerry and toward Waterford. The town owes its wealth to a fine valley ringed by hills. A warm spring there was held good for weak health. A spa house with baths was built in 1828.

Works in the town make mineral water and condensed milk. Corn mills and tanneries add to its trade. The parish church dates from 1818, with bits of an older church beside it. James the First gave the town its charter. Its old name, Magh Allo, means plain of the Allo. A Desmond castle once guarded the ford at the river. Mallow is also a hub for salmon fishing on the Blackwater. The air is very mild.
britannica-1911-malone-edmond:
Malone, Edmond, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an Irish Shakespeare scholar. Born in Dublin on the 4th of October 1741, he was a barrister's son. He read at Trinity College in Dublin and joined the Irish bar in 1767. His father's death in 1774 left him with means to live.

He then moved to London and mixed in its art and letter circles. He was a close friend of Doctor Johnson and Sir Joshua Reynolds. He helped Boswell check and proof the Life of Johnson for print. His own great work was on the order of Shakespeare's plays. That study came out in 1778 and is still largely held true. More parts on the plays and the old stage came after.
britannica-1911-margaret-queen-of-scotla:
Margaret Tudor, who lived from 1489 to 1541, was queen of Scotland. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica makes her the eldest daughter of Henry the Seventh. She was born at Westminster in November 1489. Talks to marry her to James the Fourth of Scotland began before she was six. The match was meant to buy off James's backing of a pretender. The wedding took place at Edinburgh in August 1503.

A treaty of lasting peace came with the marriage. Her father's meagre dowry soured ties between the crowns anyway. The entry paints her whole later life as one long intrigue. She swung between factions, now for England, now against it. She was crowned in March 1504. Of her children, only the son born in 1512 lived. He became James the Fifth on his father's death at Flodden.
britannica-1911-mayo-smith-richmond:
Richmond Mayo-Smith, an American economist who lived from 1854 to 1901, is given a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Troy, Ohio, he was educated at Amherst and at Berlin and Heidelberg. In 1877 he became assistant professor of economics at Columbia University, and from 1883 he held the chair of political economy and social science there till his death in November 1901. 

He gave himself above all to the study of statistics, and he was known as one of the foremost authorities on that subject in his day. His works include books on emigration and immigration, on sociology and statistics, and on statistics and economics.
britannica-1911-melbourne-england:
Melbourne is a market town in Derbyshire in England, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It lies 8 miles south of Derby, on the Midland railway line. Its count in 1901 was 3,580 souls in the town. It stands in an undulating district on a small southern branch of the Trent. That river lies about 2 miles away from the town.

The church of Saint Michael is a fine example of Norman work in the text. It has a nave with clerestory, chancel, and aisles, and three towers in all. Melbourne Hall, a building of the time of William the Third, stands in formal Dutch gardens. The domain was owned at an early date by the bishops of Carlisle, who obtained the manor in 1133. Trades of the town are silk making and boots and shoes.
britannica-1911-middelburg-holland:
Middelburg is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Middelburg is the old capital of the province of Zeeland in Holland. It stands in the middle of the island of Walcheren. A ship canal and rail line link it to Flushing. By 1903 its people numbered just over nineteen thousand. Many fine old houses recall its wealth up to the end of the seventeen hundreds.

The article praises its town hall, built near 1512, with a tall square tower. Statues of the counts of Zeeland and Holland adorn its front. Inside lie the city archives and rich old collections. The old abbey, founded in 1150, now houses the provincial council. It holds fine old tapestry and hosted royal guests in past times. Churches in the town hold monuments to counts and to admirals lost in war with England.
britannica-1911-mull-island:
Mull, the largest isle of the Inner Hebrides in Scotland, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. Its count in 1901 was 4,334 people. The Atlantic bounds it on the west and south, and sounds and firths bound the rest. Its area is near 367 square miles, at most twenty seven miles long.

Sea lochs cut deep into the coast of Mull, and fresh lakes lie inland. Its chief peak, Ben More, rises to 3,185 feet. Most rocks are of fire origin, with basalt cliffs that hold arches and caves. Sheep and cattle are raised, and grain and potatoes are grown. The damp air suits grazing more than crops, the piece notes.
britannica-1911-normanton-queensland: Normanton is a town in Queensland, Australia, noted in a brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on the river Norman, east of the Gulf of Carpentaria. In nineteen oh one it had just over eight hundred folk. It is the centre of a district that ranks among the chief sheep and cattle farming districts of the colony. It is also the outlet for goldfields and copper mines inland. A rail line ends there, and large meat packing works stand in the town.
britannica-1911-north-holland:
North Holland, a province of the kingdom of Holland, is mapped in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies between the North Sea and the Zuider Zee. South Holland and Utrecht bound it on the landward side. Its people passed one million in 1904, and its area runs to 1070 square miles.

The province takes in the Frisian islands of Texel, Vlieland, and Terschelling. Wieringen, Marken, and Urk in the Zuider Zee belong to it as well. The land falls into three parts by nature. Foreshore and sand dunes come first, then inner dunes and geest grounds. Low fens and clay lands form the third part. The dunes form the great wall that keeps the sea at bay. No inlets pierce that coast, so trade towns are absent from the sea board, Ymuiden aside.
britannica-1911-northampton-england:
Northampton is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the county town of Northamptonshire, England. The town lies 66 miles north west of London, mainly on the north bank of the river Nene, and its people grew from 75,075 in 1891 to 87,021 in 1901. Main roads meet near the centre in a broad market place. A fountain stands there on the site of the old cross, burned in the great fire of 1675 that levelled much of the town. Of seven old parish churches four remain.

Among them, All Saints was rebuilt after the fire under its kept Decorated tower, and St Peter's, near the old castle site, shows a fine Norman interior. The town's staple trade is the making of boots and shoes on a very large scale, and its schools rest on a free grammar school founded in 1552.
britannica-1911-norwich-england:
Norwich, the county town of Norfolk, England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands one hundred and fourteen miles north-east of London. The census of 1901 counted 111,733 people there. Three stations serve the city.

The city lies in the valley of the Wensum, just above its meeting with the Yare. The ancient city sat inside a deep bend of the smaller river. Its walls, built across fifty years from 1294, ran four miles in circuit. Only fragments of those walls and their twelve gatehouses now remain. The suburbs long ago burst far beyond that ring. The castle stands high on its mound above the town. Only its early Norman keep survives, long used as a prison. In 1894 the keep was fitted out as a museum and art gallery. The cathedral, founded in 1096, lies on low ground below.
britannica-1911-ormond:
Ormond, a village and winter resort in Volusia County in Florida, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits on the Halifax river, an arm of the Atlantic that runs along the east coast of Florida, south of Saint Augustine by rail. Its people numbered 595 in 1900 and 689 in a state census five years later.

The Halifax river region is famed for its fine oranges and grapefruit. The hard Ormond Daytona beach, about two hundred feet wide at low tide and some twenty miles long, gives rare scope for driving, motoring and cycling. Tournaments of a Florida automobile association were held on it each year. The old King's Road, built by the English in the seventeen hundreds, had been improved for automobiles near the town. West of Ormond stand the ruins of an old sugar mill, most likely from the late seventeen hundreds.
britannica-1911-paddington-england:
Paddington is a north-western borough of London, England, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its streets and its past. It is bounded by Hampstead, Marylebone, Westminster, and Kensington, and held 143,976 people in 1901. The best houses stand in Bayswater, near Kensington Gardens and Hyde Park.

The entry traces the main roads, from Bayswater Road along the park to Edgware Road and Harrow Road. The name Paddington does not appear in Domesday, and the land belonged early to Westminster Abbey. In the eighteenth century its rural scenery drew artists, and open country could still be found there in the middle of the nineteenth.
britannica-1911-paris-legend:
Paris, also called Alexandros, is in Greek legend the son of Priam, king of Troy. His mother was the queen of Troy. Before his birth she dreamed she bore a firebrand. Seers read the dream to mean her child would wreck his land. So the babe was left on Mount Ida to die.

The 1911 Britannica entry tells how herdsmen saved him and raised him among them. Grown fair and strong, he was known at last and taken back by his kin. His byname came from his brave guard of the herds. The entry then sets the famed choice of Paris. Three goddesses vied for a prize for the most fair, each with a bribe of her own. He chose the one who pledged him the most fair woman in the world.
britannica-1911-penrith-england:
Penrith is a market town in Cumberland, England. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica mixes its trade, halls, and one famed cup. It stands in a valley near the river Eamont. Three rail lines meet there, and its 1901 count topped nine thousand.

Breweries, tanneries, and sawmills work beside farm trade. The town lives chiefly off the land around it, though. Ruins of a castle raised against the Scots still stand. A grammar school refounded by Queen Elizabeth serves the town. Nearby Eden Hall holds a treasured enamel cup in a leather case. Songs say fairies left that cup at a well in the park. Its loss or breakage would end the luck of the hall. The manor changed hands from Scots kings to great earls over time.
britannica-1911-peterborough-england:
Peterborough is the subject of a city entry in the 1911 Britannica. The city lies in Northamptonshire in England. It is built along the river Nene on its north side. It stands on the west edge of the Fen country. Four rail lines served the city at that time. Its count in 1901 was just under thirty one thousand souls. The great church of Saint Peter rules the city view.

That church is the third to stand on its site. Danes burned the first church in the year 870. Fire took the second church in the year 1116. The present church was begun the next year. It took one hundred and twenty years to build. It was blessed for use in the year 1237. Eight spans of work can be traced in its walls. Later windows were set with care to keep its unity.
britannica-1911-pond:
John Pond, an astronomer royal of England, is the true subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The head first closes the life of a composer and a note on cloaks. Then the Pond life starts in full and runs to the end. Pond was born in London about 1767, son of a rich trader. He entered Trinity College, Cambridge, at the age of sixteen.

Ill lungs broke his course and sent him to live abroad. In 1800 he settled near Bristol to fix star places with fine tools. His 1806 proof of a shift in a Greenwich wall tool changed practice. New star circles came to the Royal Observatory from his work. He rose to head that post and joined the Royal Society.
britannica-1911-pound:
Pound is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its first subject is the enclosure where stray or seized animals are held. Cattle kept in a pound stay there until their owners redeem them. The holding acts as a pledge, pressing the owner to settle a debt or repair damage done.

The entry lists the cases in which animals may be impounded. They may be distrained for rent, or seized while doing harm on another's land. Strays may be taken up, and beasts may be seized under legal process. A pound belongs to the township, village, or manor where it stands. Its keeper must receive whatever is offered to his custody. A statute of 1554 fixed rules for driving seized cattle to a nearby pound. The same law set the keeper's fee at fourpence.
britannica-1911-prince-edward-island:
Prince Edward Island is a province of the Dominion of Canada, and its rocks and soils open the account in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The province lies between set lines of latitude and longitude in the Gulf of St Lawrence region. The base rock formation is Permian in age. Outliers of Triassic rock also occur in places.

Coal seams are thought to lie below the Permian beds. Those seams sit too deep to be of practical value, the entry judges. The rocks are soft red sandstone with a mica content, and shales. Irregular beds of brownish red conglomerate run through them. Those beds hold pebbles of white quartz and other rocks. Beds of hard dark red sandstone occur with the shales as well. Bands of reddish brown conglomerate show at many points across the island.
britannica-1911-queensland:
Queensland is a state of Australia given a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It fills the whole north-east of the continent, with the isles in Torres Strait. Torres Strait and the Gulf of Carpentaria bound it on the north, and the Pacific Ocean bounds it on the east. Its area is near six hundred and seventy thousand square miles.

Its coast runs three thousand miles, and the state is twelve hundred and fifty miles long. With so long a shore it is rich in ports on the Pacific side. The article names them in turn, from Brisbane on its river to Cooktown and Thursday Island in the far north. The still Inner Passage, inside the Great Barrier Reef, favours the ports of the north-east. Brisbane was founded in 1826, but settlement was held back till 1842.
britannica-1911-queenstown-ireland:
Queenstown is a seaport and naval station in county Cork, Ireland, on the south side of Great Island in Cork Harbour. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 7,909 in 1901. The town climbs a steep slope above the harbour in terraces of wide streets and fine houses. Its mild air draws guests in summer and winter alike. Before the American war it was a small fishing village named Cove of Cork.

Queen Victoria landed there in 1849, on her first visit to Ireland, and the town took her name. Forts guard the harbour mouth, and a state dockyard fills three islands near by. A dry dock and a deep basin serve the fleet. Mail steamers for America call at the port. Troops embark there, and the admiral's flagship lies in the harbour.
britannica-1911-reading-england:
Reading is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town in England. It is the county town of Berkshire. It lies west of London on the Great Western railway. A count from 1901 gives it 72,217 people. It is a key junction on that rail system. Lines south link it to two other rail companies. The Kennet and Avon canal ties it to Bath and Bristol. The Thames gives it wide links by water as well.

The town lies in the flat valley of the Thames. It stands on the south bank, where the Kennet joins. Its people more than doubled in thirty years. That growth gives the town a modern look. Its old churches have been much restored and rebuilt. Greyfriars church was once a friary church of the town. After the friaries fell, it served as hall, workhouse, and gaol. It came back to church use in 1864.
britannica-1911-remand:
Remand is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In English law, a remand is the sending of a prisoner back to custody by a court's order. The word comes from a Latin term for sending back. The prisoner returns to the very custody from which the court received him.

The entry works through the main cases. A man who seeks release by habeas corpus and fails is remanded to the custody he challenged. A court trying a case can remand the accused during any break in the hearing. In a preliminary inquiry, a prisoner not freed on bail may be held for up to eight days. Further remands can follow until the inquiry ends. Then the accused is discharged, freed on bail, or sent to prison to await trial. The piece gives the plain rules of a step every criminal lawyer knows.
britannica-1911-ribot-theodule-armand:
Théodule Armand Ribot, born in 1839, was a French psychologist. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Guingamp. He taught from 1856 and entered the École Normale in 1862. In 1885 he lectured on experimental psychology at the Sorbonne. Three years later he took the chair of that subject at the Collège de France. His thesis on heredity became his best known book.

That book gathers many cases of traits passed down in families. It stresses the bodily side of mental life and skips the spiritual. His study of current English psychology showed his leanings. He also rendered Herbert Spencer's work into French. Short books treat diseases of memory, of will, and of personality. Others cover attention, feelings, and the passions. The entry lists a shelf of works in steady reprint. His name anchors the lab study of mind in France.
britannica-1911-robert-i-king-of-scotlan:
Robert the First, called the Bruce, king of Scotland, born in twelve seventy four, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of the seventh Robert de Bruce, earl of Carrick by right of his wife. He was the eighth in the male line from a Norman baron who came with the Conqueror.

When the Maid of Norway died in twelve ninety, his grand sire claimed the crown of Scotland. That claim ran through a daughter of a great earl of the old line. A rival claim ran through the elder daughter of that same earl. The men of Edward the First chose the rival. The place of birth of the Bruce is not known for sure. It was most like a castle of his mother on the coast of Ayr.
britannica-1911-robert-ii-king-of-scotla:
Robert the Second, king of Scotland, is a royal life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was called the Steward, and he lived from 1316 to 1390. He was a son of Walter, the steward of Scotland, and of Marjorie, daughter of King Robert the Bruce. He was born on the second of March 1316.

In 1318 the Scottish lords ruled that if Bruce died with no sons, the crown should pass to this grandson. The birth of a son to Bruce in 1324, the later King David the Second, put that off for near forty-two years. When the child David took the throne in 1329, the Steward rose fast in state affairs. He led Scots troops at Halidon Hill in 1333 and, with the earl of Moray, was picked as regent while David found safety in France. The two men soon quarrelled, and Robert ruled alone.
britannica-1911-robert-iii-king-of-scotl:
Robert the Third, who lived from about 1340 to 1406, was king of Scotland. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls him a ruler in name only. He was the eldest son of King Robert the Second. His parents wed after his birth, which cleared his claim.

A horse kick crippled Robert in about 1387. His brother took charge as guardian of the realm in 1389. Robert took the throne in 1390 and changed his name from John. That first name recalled a hated past king of Scots. Real power stayed with his brother all the same. In 1399 his son Rothesay was made lieutenant of the kingdom. Rothesay died in strange ways at Falkland in 1402. English hands seized the younger prince in 1406, and Robert died weeks later.
britannica-1911-rock-island:
Rock Island is a city in Illinois, seat of its county, on the east bank of the great west stream. It faces a town in Iowa past two spans. Fast runs in the stream stretch past the town for miles. Its count of folk in nineteen ten was past twenty-four thousand.

Four rail lines serve the town, and a cut joins the great stream near by. An isle of rock in the stream holds a state arms works, the most weighty in the land for small arms and gun gear. Trade by boat and rail is large. Wood, farm tools, flour, and glass lead its trades.
britannica-1911-roermond:
Roermond is a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Roermond is a town in the province of Limburg, Holland, on the right bank of the Maas where the Roer flows in. It is a rail junction. The count of 1900 put its people at more than twelve thousand. Its old walls have been pulled down and in part made into fine walks.

The town is the seat of a Roman Catholic bishop. Its finest building is the Romanesque minster church of the early thirteenth century. The church first served a Cistercian nunnery and has been much restored. The cathedral of St Christopher bears a tall tower topped by a copper figure of the saint. The old bishop's palace is now the courthouse. Woollen, cotton and silk cloth, paper, flour and beer are made in the town.
britannica-1911-rohilkhand:
Rohilkhand is a tract in the United Provinces of India, named for the Rohilla tribe. The 1911 Britannica article says the name in its full sense covers the modern division of Bareilly. That division has an area of 10,720 square miles. It is used as a common second title for the division. Six districts make it up: Bareilly, Bijnor, Budaun, Moradabad, Shahjahanpur, and Pilibhit.

The count for the division in 1901 was 5,479,688 people. State power over the princely state of Rampur runs through the commissioner of the division. The short entry gives no more than these bounds, names, and counts. It points the reader to the Rohilla tribe itself for the human tale behind the name.
britannica-1911-rosamond:
Rosamond, known as the Fair, who died about eleven seventy six, is the subject of a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the mistress of King Henry the Second of England. She is thought to have been the daughter of Walter de Clifford.

The proof for her birth is thin, the entry warns. It rests on a note in a roll from the reign of Edward the First. Henry kept the link hid for some years. He owned it in the open only when he shut up Queen Eleanor. Rosamond was buried at Godstow, before the high altar. Her body was later moved on the orders of the Bishop of Lincoln. Tales of poison and of a maze at Woodstock came from later writers.
britannica-1911-rossland:
Rossland, a city in the Kootenay district of British Columbia, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. The city was set up in 1897, and its count in 1907 was 4,033 people. It sits in a valley seven miles west of Trail on the Columbia River. It lies eight miles north of the line with the United States.

Rail lines link Rossland to Trail, the Arrow Lakes, and towns in Washington state. The city owes its growth to rich beds of iron and copper ore that carry gold near by. Its best known mines are the Le Roy, Centre Star, and War Eagle. Power and light come from Bonnington Falls.
britannica-1911-rostand-edmond:
Edmond Rostand, a French dramatist, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in April eighteen sixty nine, he was the son of a prominent journalist of Marseilles. His first play, a burlesque, was produced at the Theatre Francais in eighteen ninety four. That debut opened a rapid rise on the Paris stage.

His second piece drew its motive from the tale of the troubadour Rudel and the Lady of Tripoli. Sarah Bernhardt created the lead role in that play. She also played the lead in his biblical drama a few years later. The entry traces a young playwright whose works drew the greatest actress of the day.
britannica-1911-round:
Round is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a word of shape and use. The word comes from Old French and Latin roots for circular. As a noun, the word has several specific applications. It names the rung of a ladder in one use. It names the rounded bar between the legs of a chair. It also names the circuit of the watch in a fortress.

That watch patrols the sentries of a camp or town. From that use comes the beat of a policeman. The full course at a game of golf is a round too. Old dances called rounds set dancers in a circle or ring. They were popular in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Later the name went to dances in two lines. For the round in music, the entry points to canon.
britannica-1911-rutland-england:
Rutland is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a midland county of England. It is the smallest county in all England. Its area is given as 152 square miles. Lincolnshire bounds it on the north and east. Leicestershire bounds it on the north and west. Northamptonshire lies along its south east side. The surface rolls in pleasant ridges of high ground. Those ridges run east and west across the county.

Rich valleys lie between the ridges of Rutland. The chief of them is the vale of Catmose. That vale sits in the Oakham district of the county. North of it rises a tableland with wide views. The vale keeps its old fame for rich soil. The poet Drayton praised that soil in verse. The north west is also home of the Cottesmore hunt. A royal forest once covered much of the county. Patches of that forest still exist in places.
britannica-1911-saargemund:
Saargemund is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a town of Germany. In French the town is called Sarreguemines in the text. It stands where the Blies and the Saar rivers join as one. The town count for 1905 is 14,932 folk.

Its works make faience, plush, velvet, leather, and china ware goods. It is a chief store place for boxes made near the town. Most of those boxes are snuff boxes made in great bulk. The town began as a Roman settlement in old times. It won civic rights early in the thirteenth century of our era. In 1297 it was ceded to the duke of Lorraine. It passed to France in 1766 and to Germany in 1871.
britannica-1911-sable-island:
Sable Island is the subject of a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. The isle belongs to Nova Scotia in Canada. It is made of loose sand that shifts with wind and wave. It runs about twenty miles long and one mile wide. A lake about ten miles long lies inside it. Sand bars at each end stretch far out to sea. The isle had no port and was prone to fog.

More than two hundred wrecks were known on its shores. That toll gave it the name of the grave of the Atlantic. From 1873 Canada kept lights and a rescue post there. Those steps cut the risk by a large share. The isle keeps shrinking as sand is worn away. Trees and grass were set to bind the sand. Wild fruit grows there in summer. A breed of wild ponies has lived there for years.
britannica-1911-sand:
Sand is what rocks and minerals become when they are ground down by natural or man-made forces. Such products sort by grain size into gravels, sands, and muds or clays. Grains too fine to feel, about a thousandth of an inch wide, make a mud or clay. Grains as large as peas make a gravel. Sands can be even in grain when a soft flow of water or a steady wind has sorted them.

More often, sands shift much in the size of their grains and in the stuff they are made of. The great source of natural sand is the work of air, frost, rain, and plants on the faces of rocks. Those forces break rock down to a fine powder. In other words, sands are as a rule the yield of wear on rock at the surface of the earth.
britannica-1911-sauerland: Sauerland is a hilly district of Germany, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in Westphalia, between the Sieg and the Ruhr rivers. To the south the Sieg parts it from the Westerwald. To the north the Ruhr parts it from the coal lands of Ardey. The land is a well wooded plateau of old rock, cut by deep valleys with tracts of heath. In 1911 it was already a place that walkers and tourists liked to visit.
britannica-1911-shetland:
Shetland, or Zetland, is a group of islands forming a county of Scotland, and a survey entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes Britain's most northerly possession. The archipelago counts over a hundred islands and islets, north-east of Orkney, between the Atlantic and the North Sea. It covers about 551 square miles.

The entry names Mainland as the chief island, with Yell, Unst, and Fair Isle among the others of note. The land is uneven, rising to 1,475 feet, and most inland scenery is bleak, treeless peat and boulders. The coast, by contrast, is grand, with sheer cliffs over 1,000 feet high, and shores so cut by inlets that no spot lies more than three miles from the sea.
britannica-1911-sigismund:
Sigismund, who lived from 1368 to 1437, was emperor and king of Hungary and Bohemia. The 1911 Britannica entry traces a life shaped by crowns, pledges, and long wars. He was a son of the emperor Charles the Fourth and was raised at the Hungarian court. He wed Maria, heir to Hungary and Poland, in 1385 and was crowned king in 1387.

His bride was seized by rebels and freed with Venetian help in 1387. To raise funds he pledged Brandenburg to a cousin and fought nine years for his throne. Foes in the south backed a rival king from Naples. Only in 1395 did his ally Garay crush that revolt for good.
britannica-1911-sill-edward-rowland:
Sill, Edward Rowland is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American poet and teacher. He was born at Windsor, Connecticut, on the twenty-ninth of April 1841 and died in 1887. He graduated at Yale in 1861 as class poet. He then tried business in California.

In 1867 he entered the Harvard Divinity School but soon left it for a post on the New York Evening Mail. He taught in Ohio towns for some years, then became head of Oakland High School in California. From 1874 to 1882 he was professor of English literature at the university of California. Failing health drove him back to Ohio in 1883. He spent his last years on writing, much of it unsigned, for the great magazines. He died at Cleveland on the twenty-seventh of February 1887.
britannica-1911-sind:
Sind is a region article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a former province of India. Sind is the most northerly part of the presidency, with an area of 53,116 square miles and a population in 1901 of 3,410,223. It takes in six districts, from Karachi to the Upper Sind Frontier, together with the native state of Khairpur. It differs widely from the rest of the presidency in land, climate and custom.

The article then describes the land itself. Sind proper is the central plain watered by the Indus, between the Kirthar hills and the Thar desert. The Indus flows south in a bed raised by silt, shifting its course often. The article compares Sind to Egypt: as Egypt depends on the Nile, so Sind depends on the Indus.
britannica-1911-south-portland:
South Portland is the subject of a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. South Portland is a city in Cumberland County in Maine. It stands on Casco Bay, split from Portland by an arm of the bay. A ferry and four bridges link the two cities. By 1910 its people numbered near seven thousand five hundred. The Boston and Maine railway serves the city.

The article notes the state school for boys seated in the city. At Spring Point stands Fort Preble, set up in 1808 as a coast defence post. At Portland Head stands Fort Williams. City works include steel rolling mills and railway car shops. Ship building is also carried on, with goods such as marine hardware and varnish. South Portland was part of Cape Elizabeth until 1895. Its city charter, granted that year, was accepted by voters in 1898.
britannica-1911-south-shetland:
South Shetland is a chain of isles on the rim of the far south zone, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica maps it in brief. The chain lies south east of Cape Horn by about five hundred miles. A strait splits it from a tract of lands with more than one name. The chief isles are named from west to east in a row of eleven.

One isle of the chain is marked as of pure fire birth. On its south east side a gap six hundred feet wide leads in. That gap gives way to a lake in a fire cup, near round in form. Men in past years told of steam that still rose from vents in the isle. A great north rover found no sign of fire work on its face when he came.
britannica-1911-st-amand-mont-rond:
St-Amand-Mont-Rond is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a place in central France, in the department of Cher. The town stands some thirty-nine miles south of Bourges, on the rail line to Montlucon. A count in 1906 put its people at 7,711. It sits at the foot of the hill of Mont-Rond, on the right bank of the Cher.

The article points out a church that mixes the round-arched and Gothic styles, plus several old houses. Near by stand the fine chateau of Meillant, built from 1500 to 1510. The abbey of Noirlac also stands near, with a twelfth-century church. The town grew up round a friary founded in the seventh century by Saint Amand. Its ruined hill fort later held out for the great Conde during the Fronde, falling after a siege of eleven months in 1652.
britannica-1911-st-johns-newfoundland:
St Johns is the capital of Newfoundland, on the east coast of the island. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it the most easterly city of America. It stands just 1,700 miles from Queenstown in Ireland by sea. The town climbs rising ground on the north side of its harbour. That harbour is landlocked and hid from the open ocean swell.

Its mouth, called The Narrows, is guarded by two high hills. Signal Hill and South Side Hill flank the tight sea gate. The gap runs some 1,400 feet wide and then pinches to 600. Ships of the largest tonnage can enter at all states of tide. The town all but owns the whole trade of the island.
britannica-1911-stamford-england:
Stamford, a market town in Lincolnshire in England, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. A small part of the town lies in the next shire. It stands on the river Welland, at the land edge of the fen country. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was eight thousand two hundred and twenty nine.

The town stands in fair view on the steep banks of the river. It is of the top rank for old remains. It once held church halls for fourteen parishes in all. Six of those stand now. One church was built at the end of the twelve hundreds. It holds a tower of one style and a spire of the next. A rich wool merchant paid for the spire of a second church. A third church was rebuilt in full on an old site.
britannica-1911-staten-island:
Staten Island, which forms the borough of Richmond in New York City, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is also Richmond county, the far south county of the state of New York. The Narrows split it from Long Island to the east. Kill van Kull splits it from New Jersey to the north.

Counts show fast growth. The roll rose from about fifty one thousand in eighteen ninety to near eighty six thousand in nineteen ten. A ferry links the island to Manhattan, five miles off, and to Perth Amboy in New Jersey. A fast rail line runs along the north shore and the south east side. Tram lines and fine drives add to the links. The entry gives a firm base on place, growth, and travel for the island.
britannica-1911-stephen-king-of-england:
Stephen, king of England, who lived from about 1097 to 1154, is profiled at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a grandson of William the Conqueror through his mother Adela. His uncle, Henry the First, raised him in favour and gave him lands and knighthood. By marriage he gained the county of Boulogne.

Barons had sworn to accept the Empress Matilda as heir after Henry. When Henry died, Matilda was abroad, and Stephen crossed the Channel at speed. He claimed his oaths had been forced and won backing in London. The church, the barons, and the pope in time backed his crowning. Two charters of liberties won goodwill at first. But barons soon used his weak hold to demand rich grants. The entry traces how that loose grip shaped his reign.
britannica-1911-stigand:
Stigand died in 1072 and was archbishop of Canterbury in England. The 1911 Britannica life first notes him in the year 1020. He was then chaplain to King Canute and later to his son. After Canute died he seems to have advised the widow Emma. In 1043 he was made bishop of Elmham in the east.

In 1047 he moved to the see of Winchester in the south. He backed Earl Godwine in his clash with Edward the Confessor. In 1052 he helped make peace between earl and king that year. That same year he took the archbishopric when Robert was outlawed. Pope Leo and his heirs refused to own him as rightful holder.
britannica-1911-stipend:
A stipend is a fixed payment made at set times, or a salary for services. The word is used most of all for the income of a church post. It also names the salary paid to any minister of religion in a parish. In Britain a paid magistrate appointed by the Crown is called a stipendiary. Such magistrates serve in set boroughs on the home secretary's advice.

The Latin root joins words for a gift of coins and for weighing out payment. That Latin word was applied first to the pay of the Roman army. From that use it came to mean military service itself in set phrases. A phrase in Tacitus counts campaigns by the stipends a man had earned. The word also meant a tax or impost, payable in money.
britannica-1911-stoliczka-ferdinand:
Ferdinand Stoliczka lived from 1838 to 1874 and was an Austrian student of fossils. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Hochwald in Moravia, his birth place. He was born there in May 1838 and schooled at Prague. He took his doctorate at the university of Vienna in time. Teachers there urged him toward geology and the study of fossils.

As early as 1859 he sent Vienna a paper on freshwater shells. Those shells came from Cretaceous rocks of the north east Alps. In 1861 he joined the Austrian Geological Survey as a staff man. Next year he was made palaeontologist to the survey of India. At Calcutta the Cretaceous fossils of south India were placed in his hands.
britannica-1911-sudbury-england:
Sudbury, a market town mainly in Suffolk, England, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Part of the town lies in Essex. It stands on the river Stour, which boats can use up to the town. In nineteen oh one it had just over seven thousand folk.

Three old churches stand out, each with carved wood work of note. One holds a fine oak pulpit from fourteen ninety. A school set up in fourteen ninety one is also named. Old half timber houses line some streets. Coconut matting is a chief trade good. Silk work came from London in the last century, and horse hair weaving began then too.
britannica-1911-taylor-rowland:
Rowland Taylor (died 1555) was an English Protestant martyr born at Rothbury in Northumberland. He took minor orders at Norwich in 1528. He took law degrees at Cambridge in 1530 and 1534. He took up reformed views and became a chaplain to Cranmer in 1540. In 1544 he was given the living of Hadleigh in Suffolk.

Taylor preached a noted sermon at St Paul's Cross in 1547. He went on to posts at Rochester, Canterbury, and Exeter in the next few years. He seems to have backed the cause of Lady Jane Grey. Days after Mary was named queen in July 1553, he was put in custody. Set free, he fought the return of the Mass with the backing of his parish. That stand led to his arrest again in 1554.
britannica-1911-thalberg-sigismond:
Sigismond Thalberg, a German pianist and composer, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Geneva in eighteen twelve, he was taken to Vienna as a boy. There his schooling was completed under the care of Count Dietrichstein. He first played as a pianist at Prince Metternich's house in eighteen twenty six.

The entry follows his rise from first works to wide fame. His first piece came out in eighteen twenty eight, a work based on airs from Euryanthe. By eighteen thirty his success was firm, and Liszt was his only rival. He was named a court player to the emperor of Austria. Shows in Paris and England won praise for his touch.
britannica-1911-thames-new-zealand:
Thames, a seaport and gold-mining centre in New Zealand, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in North Island, at the mouth of the river of its name. The Firth of Thames, a deep inlet of the Hauraki Gulf, fronts the town. The census of 1906 counted 3,750 people there.

The town unites the old settlement of Grahamstown with two suburbs under one council. Steamers reach Auckland in forty-two miles among the islands of the gulf. The railway takes a far longer, roundabout route to the same city. Foundries, shipbuilding yards, and sawmills line its good harbour. Its sea fisheries send much of their catch to Auckland. Inland, gold-bearing ground supports mining towns along the river. Te Aroha, up that river, draws visitors to its hot medicinal springs as a health resort.
britannica-1911-thornhill-england:
Thornhill is an urban district in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies two miles south of Dewsbury, served by three rail lines. Counts from nineteen o one put its people at just over ten thousand.

The church of Saint Michael keeps an old chancel with side aisles. Its tower is in the Perpendicular style, while the nave is modern build. Fine tomb stones mark the old Savile family inside the church. Glass bits from the fifteenth century fill the east window with colour. Most townsfolk work in wool mills and in shoddy and carpet trades.
britannica-1911-thornhill-scotland:
Thornhill, a village in Dumfriesshire, Scotland, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands in the parish of Morton in Nithsdale, fourteen miles north of Dumfries by rail. Its population in 1901 was 1,132. The village sits amid tree clad hills, watered by the river Nith and smaller streams.

The entry names the parish church in the village, plus a library and a natural history museum. In the museum grounds stands a statue of Richard Cameron, the covenanter. Weekly sales of livestock matter to the place, and a farm show is held each September. Three miles away stands Drumlanrig Castle, a seat of the duke of Buccleuch. Built of red sandstone from 1679 to 1689, it cost its builder a vast sum.
britannica-1911-torrington-england:
Great Torrington is the subject of a town entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town lies in Devonshire in England on the Torridge. It stands on a hill above a wooded vale. Three bridges cross the river at that point. The count in 1901 was just over three thousand souls. A mayor and a small town board ran the place. Gloves were the main goods made there in large scale.

Flour, butter, and leather work are named as the next trades. The past of the town goes back to Saxon times. It held a market in those early days. Lords, charters, and fairs fill the long past notes. In the civil war it was besieged and forced to yield in 1646. A fire in 1724 burned the town books.
britannica-1911-valencia-ireland:
The 1911 Britannica article on Valencia describes an island off the south-west coast of Ireland. It lies in county Kerry. It forms the southern horn of Dingle Bay. The island is about seven miles long and three miles broad. The strait to the mainland makes a fine natural harbour. It is deep enough for large vessels.

The town of Knightstown stands on the island. It holds the buildings of a telegraph company. From Valencia the steamer Great Eastern first laid a cable to Newfoundland in 1866. Four cables cross the Atlantic from the island. Its weather reports warn London of Atlantic storms first. The island once exported fine slate. Its cliff scenery is grand. Its plant life is rich and almost tropical.
britannica-1911-vinland:
Vinland, a land on the eastern coast of North America, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Norsemen visited and named it early in the eleventh century. The name means Wineland, from the wild grapes found there. The article builds its case first on a German writer, Adam of Bremen.

Adam had visited the Danish court and heard King Svend speak of the land. The king told of wild grapes fit for very good wine. He also told of grain that grew there unsown, in plenty. The article calls Adam's passage the one sure mention of Vinland in a medieval book outside the northern world. It also warns that Adam placed the land amid Arctic ice and gloom. Its worth lies in backing the Icelandic tales of the voyages.
britannica-1911-wakefield-england:
Wakefield, a city in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands on the river Calder, mainly on the north bank, 175 miles from London. Its people numbered 41,413 in 1901. Several railways serve it through two stations, in pleasant rolling country at the edge of the industrial district.

A fine bridge of eight arches crosses the Calder. On it stands the chapel of St Mary, a rich Decorated structure 50 feet long. Its endowment is ascribed to Edward the Fourth, in memory of his father, who fell at Wakefield in 1460. The bishopric of Wakefield was formed in 1888, mostly from that of Ripon. The cathedral church of All Saints stands on a very old site. It was almost wholly rebuilt in the early fourteenth century and consecrated in 1329.
britannica-1911-ware-england:
Ware is a market town in Hertfordshire, England, set on a river north of London. A branch rail line serves it. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its town count at the turn of the age. Its church is a cross shaped work in two late Gothic styles. It is built of flint and stone.

The entry walks the church part by part. It names a choir said to be the work of a great lady of the royal house. It names a side chapel and a nave of five bays. It notes a squat tower with battlements, and a rich font. A modern great house west of town stands on the site of an old friary. The town hall holds a book room and a hall for talks. The entry ends with the famed Great Bed of Ware, named in a play.
britannica-1911-weissenburg-am-sand:
Weissenburg am Sand is a town in Bavaria in the Middle Franconia tract of Germany. It sits in rich low land at the west foot of high hills, south west of Nuremberg. Its count of folk in nineteen five was just past six thousand. Old walls and towers still ring the town.

Two churches in the old pierced style and a town hall of the same style are named. A spring with baths draws guests, and a Roman fort has just been found near by. An old fort on a hill looks down on the town. Trades run to fringe, bricks, beer, and cloth.
britannica-1911-wermund:
Wermund is a short 1911 Britannica article on an ancestor of the Mercian royal family. He was a son of Wihtlaeg and the father of Offa. He seems to have reigned in Angel. His story is kept by Danish historians, above all Saxo Grammaticus.

By those tales, his reign was long and happy. Its good fortune was marred in time by the raids of a warlike king, Athislus. Athislus slew Frowinus, the governor of Schleswig, in battle. The death was avenged by Frowinus's two sons, Keto and Wigo. Yet their fighting two against one man was held a national disgrace. Only the later single combat of Offa wiped that stain away. The article also notes a guess about who Athislus really was. Tale and history meet in this brief life from the age of legend.
britannica-1911-westmorland:
Westmorland, a county in the north-west of England, is mapped in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Cumberland, Durham, Yorkshire, and Lancashire bound it on all sides. It touches the sea at the Kent estuary in Morecambe Bay. The entry splits the shire into four zones by their height and form.

Wild moor in the north-east climbs to near two thousand eight hundred feet. A third of the Lake District lies in the west of the county. Helvellyn and other famed peaks stand in that tract. The Vale of Eden forms a lower third zone, and low hills round Kendal make the fourth. Uplands cross the mid line of the county from end to end. The Pennine chain walls its east side for its full length.
britannica-1911-william-i-king-of-englan:
William the First of England, called the Conqueror, opens a long royal life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in ten twenty seven or ten twenty eight, he was the base born son of Duke Robert of Normandy. His mother was the child of a tanner at Falaise. When Robert died on a holy trip in ten thirty five, the boy took the duchy. Three of his guards were slain in years of wild strife that came next.

By age twenty he had crushed a revolt with help from King Henry of France. Wins at Alencon and Domfront made his hold firm by ten forty nine. A trip to England in ten fifty one may have won him a pledge of the throne from Edward. His match with Matilda of Flanders in ten fifty three strengthened that claim.
britannica-1911-william-ii-king-of-engla:
William the Second is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The hosted text opens with the tail of the article on his father, William the First. It then turns to William the Second himself, called Rufus. He lived from about 1056 to 1100 and was king of England. He was the third son of William the First and Queen Matilda of Flanders.

The article says Rufus was born some years before the conquest of England. His exact birth date is not known. He seems to have been his father's favoured son and stayed often in his company. Yet he was kept, like his brothers, from any share in ruling England or Normandy. A quarrel with Rufus sparked his brother Robert's first break with their father. Rufus bore arms on the royal side in that civil war.
britannica-1911-william-iii-king-of-engl:
William the Third, king of England and prince of Orange, born at the Hague in sixteen fifty, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the only son of William the Second of Orange. His mother was Mary, daughter of Charles the First of England. He was born eight days after his father's death.

His father had tried to seize full power and failed. On his death the post of stadtholder was done away with. Power passed to John de Witt and the Holland party. William grew up among foes, with a great name but little real power. He learned to hide his feelings behind a cold face. In sixteen seventy two France invaded Dutch land, and the folk turned to him for help.
britannica-1911-william-iv-king-of-engla:
William the Fourth, king of England who lived from 1765 to 1837, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the third son of George the Third, born at Buckingham Palace in August 1765. In 1779 he went to sea as a midshipman. The next year he sailed under Rodney and fought off Cape St Vincent, and he saw plenty of service in the rest of the war.

That service gave William a strong liking for the sea. After the war he travelled in Germany and was entertained by Frederick the Great. He passed for lieutenant in 1785 and was made captain the next year. Tired of his station, he sailed home without orders and was punished. In 1789 he was made duke of Clarence. When war came in 1793 he wanted active work but got no command.
britannica-1911-woburn-england:
Woburn is a market town in Bedfordshire, England, described in this 1911 Britannica article. It lies in a hollow of a northern spur of the Chiltern Hills, in a well wooded area, about fifty-one miles north-west by north of London. Its people numbered 1,129 in 1901, and there was some farm trade, with a little straw plaiting and lace making.

West of the town lies Woburn Park, the grounds of Woburn Abbey, the seat of the dukes of Bedford. The abbey began as a Cistercian house in 1145, though only scant remains show in the mansion that rose on its site. Henry VIII granted the lands to John, Lord Russell, in 1547. The mansion, begun in 1744, holds a fine collection of paintings and other works of art.
britannica-1911-wolowski-louis-francois-:
Louis François Michel Raymond Wolowski, French scholar of trade and lawmaker, was born in Warsaw in 1810 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was schooled in Paris but went back to Warsaw and joined the revolt of 1830. The new Polish leaders sent him to Paris as secretary to their legation.

When the revolt was crushed, he settled in Paris and became French in 1834. In 1833 he founded a review of law and court rulings. His pen poured out works on trade and finance. He set up the first Crédit Foncier in France in 1852. In 1864 he became a teacher of the study of trade at the Conservatoire. He sat in the national assembly in two spans and backed free trade and a two metal money standard.
britannica-1911-woodstock-england:
Woodstock is a market town and borough in Oxfordshire, England, north west of London. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it at the end of a branch rail line and gives its town count at the turn of the age. A small river in a steep, fine vale splits the town into New and Old Woodstock.

The entry lists the church, town hall, and almshouses, each with its date and style. Farm work feeds the town, plus an old trade in leather gloves that dates to the fifteen hundreds. It is ruled by a mayor, aldermen, and a council. The piece then turns to the manor, granted for all time to a famed duke after a great win in war, and to the grand house raised there.
britannica-1911-worcester-england:
Worcester, a church city and the chief town of its shire in England, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river Severn, west north west of London. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was forty six thousand six hundred and twenty four. Two rail firms serve it, and branch lines run to three towns from its stops.

The city lies in the main on the east bank of the Severn. That river is broad and calm at this point. The main part of the town lies on a ridge that runs with the banks. A mayor, a set of elder men, and a set of town men rule it. Its area is past three thousand acres. The great church stands in fair view close to the river.
britannica-1911-wound:
Wound is the subject of a medical entry in the 1911 Britannica. The word names a break in the soft parts of the body. Its root links to old words for strife and pain. Bruises are wounds where the skin is not broken. In loose tissue the swell and stain show most. Blood in the tissue causes that stain of skin. Its hues shift from dark purple through green to yellow.

A large pool of blood in tissue has its own name. Cold wet cloths are the chief cure for a bruise. The blood is most often soaked up on its own. If rot threatens, a cut must drain the place clean. Open wounds fall in four kinds in the entry. Cut, torn, pierced, and shot wounds are those kinds. Each kind is told apart by its edge and depth. Risks and cures for each kind follow in turn.
britannica-1911-yarkand:
