Yarkand is the chief town of the main oasis of Chinese Turkestan, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes the oasis and its waters. The town stands on the Yarkand-Darya river, 3,900 feet above the sea. The settlements of the oasis fill the south-west corner of eastern Turkestan. They are scattered along the many rivers that run down from the Pamir, the Karakoram, and the Kuen-Lun mountains.

The Kashgar oasis bounds it on the north, and desert parts it from Khotan on the south-east. The Yarkand-Darya and its glacier-fed tributaries bring plenty of water into the desert. Countless canals carry the water to fields that spread in a broad belt of loess at the mountain foot. In the foothills rich pastures rear goats, yaks, camels, sheep, and cattle.
britannica-1911-zeeland:
Zeeland is a province of Holland, bound by Belgium to the south and the North Sea to the west. South Holland lies to the north and North Brabant to the east. The province covers 690 square miles and held 227,292 people in 1905. Zeeland is made of the delta islands at the mouths of the Maas and the Scheldt. The Scheldt splits in two arms, the Western Scheldt and the Ooster Scheldt. A strip of main land, Zeeland-Flanders, forms part of the province too.

The islands are named in the article: Schouwen and Duiveland, St Filipsland, Tolen, North and South Beveland, and Walcheren. The past of each island is a tale of loss and gain in the fight with the sea. They were built up by slow heaps of mud in a shallow bay, cut off from the sea by dunes.
britannica-1911-zululand:
Zululand is a land in the south east of Africa, the north east part of Natal. It spans a wide tract from the Tugela stream to the edge of a realm past the sea. Its coast runs past two hundred miles on the warm sea. North it meets small tracts and a free realm.

The land is part of the hill and flat high ground that falls to the sea from a great chain. Sand hills clothed in brush mark the shore. Past them a low plain holds wide lakes, the most big near thirty-five miles long. Hills and high flats take up the rest, some dense with woods.
building-a-state-in-apache-land:
Charles D. Poston set down how Arizona came to be, drawn from his pieces in the Overland Express, dated 1894. Part one tells how the land was won. San Francisco in the early 1850s opens the tale. A house at Stockton and Washington, called the Government Boarding House, held senators and high staff.

Night talks in its parlor, over a bottle of Sazerac, turned on a new treaty with Mexico. More land was the aim, though no sharp want drove it. The treaty of 1848 had left a flaw in the line, and a road south was the true prize, as the tale goes on to show. Poston's own hand in the work gave him the tale from inside. Land, law, and Apache ground form the stakes of the whole.
castle-richmond:
Castle Richmond, by Anthony Trollope, is his Irish novel of the great famine, presented here in a 1906 edition with an introduction by Algar Thorold. Thorold reports that Trollope wrote it in 1861, long after leaving Ireland, and judges the plot mechanical and the characterization weak, with one great exception. The book's value, he argues, is documentary: graphic famine scenes observed carefully and, on the whole, impartially.

The exception is Abe Mollett, an unscrupulous blackmailer drawn, Thorold says, with real art and a hunter's loving preoccupation. Around the castle and its family, Trollope sets landlords, priests, and parsons against starvation in County Cork, and the introduction notes that his priest comes off a better man than his parson. Modern readers often come to this novel for exactly what its introducer praised: a major novelist testifying, from memory and conscience, to a catastrophe England preferred to forget.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-croy:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Croyland, or Crowland, describes a Benedictine monastery in Lincolnshire, sixteen miles from Stamford. Ethelbald, King of Mercia, founded it early in the eighth century in memory of St. Guthlac.

Danes destroyed the house and slaughtered its community in 866. After refounding under King Edred it burned again in 1091, was rebuilt by Abbot Joffrid, and burned once more in 1170 before rebuilding under Abbot Edward. Thereafter Croyland prospered almost unbroken to the Dissolution, richly endowed by visitors to Guthlac's shrine and secure in its fenland isolation. The entry names its notable abbots, including Ingulphus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-mori:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Morimond describes the fourth daughter of Cîteaux, in Champagne. Odelric d'Aigremont and Adeline de Choiseul founded it in 1115, with Arnold as first abbot. Arnold, its first abbot and a member of one of Germany's noblest families, was long counted a column of the Cistercian Order.

Through Arnold's zeal Morimond grew rapidly, planting colonies across France, Germany, Poland, Bohemia, Spain and Cyprus. Celebrated foundations included Ebrach in 1126, Holy Cross in 1134, and Aiguebelle in 1137, and by the late eighteenth century Morimond counted nearly seven hundred daughter houses. Briefs from popes also placed Spain's military orders under Morimond's spiritual jurisdiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-absalon-of-lu:
Absalon of Lund, also known as Axel, was a famous Danish prelate born in 1128 at Finnestoe in Seeland. He died at Soroe's Benedictine monastery on 21 March 1201, the house his father founded. A graduate of the University of Paris, he taught briefly at Ste. Genevieve's school. Roskilde gained him as bishop in 1158; Lund gained him as archbishop in 1178, with primacy over Denmark and Sweden, and eventually he served as papal legate.

In that office he laboured for the final extirpation of paganism in Scandinavia, notably on Rugen, its last stronghold. He held great political influence under King Waldemar I and Canute VI. At his request Saxo Grammaticus composed his sixteen books of Danish history, and the fourteenth book carries a tribute to Absalon himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Ribe, with twenty-nine deaneries and 278 parishes, covered Ribe, Vejle, and Ringkjobing, with part of North Schleswig. Saint Ansgar founded its first church in 860. Saint Rembert served it, and heathens destroyed it after his death in 888. It rose again toward 948, when Saint Leofdag, first Bishop of Ribe, was consecrated by Archbishop Adaldag of Hamburg.

Leofdag is said to have been martyred by heathens at Ribe. Until the death of his third known successor Vale, who ruled from 1044 to 1059, the bishops of Ribe, Schleswig, and Aarhus wandered Jutland on missionary tours. In 1060 Jutland was divided into Ribe, Aarhus, Viborg, and Vestervig. Bishop Thure, from 1125 to 1134, began the Cathedral of Our Lady, finished under Elias, from 1142 to 1166, who founded the chapter in 1145. Radulf, an Englishman, brought Leofdag's relics to the cathedral, though Leofdag was never formally canonized.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-galla:
Antoine Galland, a French scholar of the East born in 1646, gave Europe its first Arabian Nights. Poor after his father's early death, he won patrons who sent him to study at Noyon and Paris. At twenty-four the French ambassador took him east, where he learned Turkish, Persian, and Arabic.

As king's antiquary in the Levant, he gathered coins, inscriptions, and manuscripts for France. In 1709 he took the chair of Arabic at the College de France. His translations ranged from Indian fables to Ottoman and Persian histories, and his Nights, drawn from Arabic tales, made him famous far beyond scholarly circles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auckland:
Auckland is a diocese covering the Auckland provincial district of New Zealand, with its islets and the Kermadec Group, an area of 21,665 square miles. Its story opens in 1835, when Pope Gregory XVI erected the Vicariate Apostolic of the Western Pacific. He chose Jean Baptiste Francois Pompallier as its first vicar. Pompallier reached Hokianga in January 1838 with Marist fathers, at a time when fewer than one hundred white Catholics lived in all New Zealand.

Marist missions to the Maori people grew fast despite hostile rumors spread by Wesleyan trader-missionaries. By April 1846 about five thousand Maori had been baptized, with many more preparing. Pompallier moved his base to Auckland in 1845, and Auckland and Wellington were later split into separate sees. April 1906 figures close the entry: twenty-nine parochial districts, seventy-nine churches, about five thousand Catholic Maori, and two thousand six hundred children in Catholic schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basutoland:
Basutoland is a mountainous district of South Africa, a prefecture apostolic of 10,293 square miles. It is bounded by the Orange River Colony, Natal, and Cape Colony, with Maseru as chief town. About 700 whites and 309,000 natives live there, ruled by native chiefs under a British Resident Commissioner. The climate is healthful, cold in winter, rainy in summer, and the country has neither railways nor proper roads.

Annexed to Cape Colony in 1871 and a Crown Colony from 1884, it became an independent prefecture on 8 May 1894. The Oblates of Mary Immaculate, present since about 1862, founded Roma, its first mission, that same year. Its first prefects were Monginoux, Baudry, and Cenez, all Oblates. Droughts, locusts, and few priests hamper evangelization, though a settled population keeps missionaries close to their flocks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bequests-for-:
Bequests for Masses in England receive a long legal history in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Before the Reformation, gifts of land or money for Masses were valid, save where mortmain laws barred gifts to religious houses. Tenure by divine service even bound land to prayers for the dead, and great wills of the age are full of such gifts.

The break came with the Chantries Act of Edward VI, which dissolved chantries and cast doubt on requiem Mass bequests ever since. Later statutes and court cases, including the Superstitious Uses Act, narrowed what testators could leave. The entry traces that long legal shadow from medieval piety to modern trust law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-ferdi:
Blessed Ferdinand, Prince of Portugal, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Portugal in 1402, sixth son of King John I and Philippa of Lancaster, he died at Fez in Morocco in 1443. Sickly from youth, bodily weakness never hindered a spirit and intellect of remarkable quality, the entry says.

His mother had nursed a martial spirit in her sons, giving each a sword on her deathbed for widows, orphans, and country. Ferdinand joined the disastrous Tangier expedition of 1437, was left hostage for Ceuta, and died in captivity rather than see the city surrendered. The entry presents a prince-martyr of Portugal's crusading age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-louis:
Louis Allemand, Cardinal and Archbishop of Arles, became the leading voice for council supremacy over the pope at the Council of Basle. Born near Belley about 1380, he rose through papal service to become Bishop of Maguelonne in 1418, Archbishop of Arles in 1423, and cardinal in 1426.

At Basle he headed the party that deposed Eugenius IV and elected Felix V, whom he consecrated and crowned in 1439, while also tending plague victims and promoting the Immaculate Conception decree. After Felix resigned in 1449, Nicholas V restored Allemand's dignities, and he died in 1450, venerated as Blessed from 1527.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-univ:
The plan for a Catholic University of Ireland took shape at the Synod of Thurles in 1850. Reviving true learning mattered for the well-being of Irish Catholics, and lay students needed higher schooling on Catholic lines. They kept away from the Queen's Colleges, where religion had no official recognition. Pius IX had suggested it, and Louvain offered an inspiring example.

The Holy See approved it in 1852, funds poured in, and property was bought in Dublin. John Henry Newman became rector. He took his oath of office at Pentecost in 1854. The university's work began that November under statutes sanctioned by Rome, with papal authority to grant degrees. The hierarchy, acting through a committee, governed the institution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-bro:
An entry on the Christian Brothers of Ireland, an institute founded at Waterford in 1802 by the merchant Edmund Ignatius Rice. After two centuries of penal laws, a Catholic could not legally school his children as Catholics, nor could a teacher take up the work. The ignorance and misery of Waterford's Catholic boys moved Rice to act. Bishop Hussey backed him, and in 1800 he gave his fortune and his life to the cause.

Rice opened his first school in 1802, and young men soon joined him; the citizens built them a monastery in 1803. Houses followed at Carrick-on-Suir, Dungarvan, and Cork, where the bishop summoned citizens to gain the same benefit in 1811. Dublin gained a community in 1812, and by 1907 ten Dublin communities taught over 6,000 pupils in primary and secondary schools, orphanages, and industrial schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cleveland:
The Diocese of Cleveland, established on 23 April 1847, covers the part of Ohio north of the southern limits of ten counties from Columbiana to Van Wert. Its territory spans thirty-six counties and 15,032 square miles. The first missionaries in Ohio were Jesuit Fathers Potier and Bonnecamp, coming from Quebec in 1749 to evangelise Hurons along the Vermilion and Sandusky Rivers.

Two years later Father de la Richardie joined them from Detroit and settled part of the Hurons near present Sandusky, building a chapel, Ohio's first place of Catholic worship. These Hurons took the name Wyandots on leaving the parent tribe. Drawn into the French and Indian War and then Pontiac's conspiracy, they saw the Jesuits unjustly forced out in 1752, Potier the last among the western Hurons. No systematic mission work followed until 1795, when Father Edmund Burke came as chaplain at Fort Meigs near Maumee, serving there until February 1797.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commissariat-:
Gregory Cleary's entry defines a Holy Land commissariat in the Order of Friars Minor. It is the district assigned to a commissary gathering alms for Palestine's Holy Places, kept by the Friars Minor. More narrowly it means the convent where that commissary lives. Always a friar, he takes office by letters patent from the minister general. Each year he sends the minister an account of alms received. Those alms may never, without express leave of the Holy See, go to other ends, however pious.

Bishops' annual collections reach Jerusalem's custos through their district commissary. Forty commissariats stood across the Christian world. Naples, founded when Robert of Anjou redeemed the Holy Places from Egypt's sultan, ranks as the oldest. Seven served English-speaking lands. The United States commissariat sits at Washington's Mount Saint Sepulchre, with new houses in California and Saint Louis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Ernest Salmon's entry covers the Congregation of Saint Edmund, founded in 1843 by Jean-Baptiste Muard at Pontigny, France, for popular missions. Members also give themselves to parish work, youth education in seminaries and colleges, direction of pious associations, and foreign missions. The motherhouse stands at Pontigny, but since the expulsion of religious orders the superior general lives at Hitchin, England.

In the United States the congregation holds two houses. Swanton, Vermont, hosts a missionary house and apostolic school training young men for priesthood and religious life. Winooski, Vermont, holds a college with twelve fathers, eight scholastics, and one hundred pupils. Short as the entry is, it maps a missionary congregation's French roots, English exile, and American classrooms in a single compact sketch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-damaraland:
A mission entry describes Damaraland, the middle part of German South-West Africa between latitudes 19 and 23 south. From the Atlantic coast the traveller crosses a 42-mile sand belt of giant dunes. Next come ninety miles of barren desert with bare mountains. Then Hereroland proper rises to 7,000 feet, and finally the rolling Omaheke plain runs toward the Kalahari. Rain is scarce, and only cattle-raising thrives.

Its peoples were the Hill Damara, about 20,000 original possessors robbed of pastures by the invading Herero, and the Herero themselves, Bantu immigrants of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Down to modern times the Damara lived among the Herero as slaves, but sided with Germany in the Herero rising and improved their lot. Catholic missions, schools, and the region's peoples are surveyed in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-didymus-the-b:
Didymus the Blind of Alexandria was born about 310 and lost his sight at the age of four. Yet in time he ranked among the best-read scholars of his day. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he learned by listening, turning over at night what readers had read aloud by day. In time he seemed to have written it all on the pages of his memory.

Saint Jerome called him not the blind man but the Seer. Saint Anthony told him to rejoice in a spiritual sight shared with saints and apostles. The entry surveys his biblical commentaries and his place among the teachers of Alexandria. It also weighs which works are truly his, giving a vivid life of learning without eyes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dietrich-gres:
Dietrich Gresemund was a German humanist born at Speyer in 1477. His father, a court physician to the Elector of Mainz, gave him a thorough classical schooling. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that by 1493 the youth was already linked with Wimpfeling and Abbot Trithemius. In 1494 he printed his first work, and Trithemius praised him as a youth who had outstripped many grown men, even doctors.

Gresemund studied medicine at Speyer like his father and moved in the learned circles of Mainz. He died there in 1512, only thirty-five years old. The entry gathers the scant sources for a short life that still shows how early German humanism prized Latin letters and new learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-education-of-:
Blindness and its teaching are the subject of this long survey, which opens by noting that organised schooling for blind pupils dates only from 1784. Drawing on census figures, it puts the share of blind people at about one in five hundred in Asia. In Africa the share is about one in three hundred. In Europe it is about one in eleven hundred. In all, it reckons near two and a half million blind people alive in the world.

Heat, glare, snow light, and disease help explain why blindness clusters in hot lands and near the poles. The entry then traces teaching methods. These include raised print, the Moon system, and Braille, with its dots read by touch. It surveys schools and workshops country by country, and notes Catholic care for blind pupils. Readers get both the scale of the need and the slow craft of meeting it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ermland:
Ermland, or Ermeland, is a district of East Prussia and an exempt bishopric. Saint Adalbert of Prague, dead in 997, and Saint Bruno of Querfurt, dead in 1009, converted the heathen Prussians of this region to Christianity. Two centuries later Teutonic Knights and Cistercians brought civilization into the land as well. In 1243 the possessions of the Teutonic Knights were divided into the dioceses of Culm, Pomesanien, Ermland, and Samland.

Albert of Suerbeer, a Cologne man and former Archbishop of Armagh in Ireland, was appointed Archbishop of Prussia. In 1251 he chose Riga as his see, confirmed by Alexander IV, who in 1255 made Riga metropolitan over the four dioceses. It was not until 28 August 1251 that the first actual bishop was consecrated. Anselm of Meissen, also a Teutonic Knight priest, was consecrated at Valenciennes by the papal legate Pietro of Albano.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-established-c:
The Established Church of Scotland dates from August 1560. In that month the Scottish Parliament decided that the Protestant Confession of Faith should be the established, and only authorized, creed of the kingdom. Papal jurisdiction fell to the same Parliament's abolition, and hearing or celebrating Mass drew a death penalty under its ban. Yet appointing or maintaining the new clergy got no provision from it.

December 1560 brought the first General Assembly, and there the First Book of Discipline won approval. Doctrine, worship, the election of ministers, and their generous support from the confiscated revenues of the ancient Church all fell under its legislation. Ten districts divided Scotland, each with a travelling superintendent who instituted ministers and set the Church in order. A scheme for popular and higher education, much praised, was sketched by the Reformers, but they never carried it out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-finland:
Finland was then a grand duchy of the Russian Empire, a land of lakes and forests. Its people, about 2,900,000 souls, were chiefly Finns, with Swedish settlers on the coasts. Christianity came from both east and west: Russian missionaries reached Karelia, and Erik of Sweden crusaded in 1157. An independent church order grew under Bishop Thomas, whose see later moved to Åbo.

The last Catholic bishop resigned in 1523, and Gustavus Vasa pressed Lutheranism on the land. By the sixteenth century's end the Catholic Church in Finland had ceased to exist. Under Russian rule from 1809, Catholics regained the right to exist, but numbered only about 1,000 souls. Most Finns belonged to the Lutheran National Church, in four dioceses with 512 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-patri:
Francis Patrick McFarland, born at Franklin, Pennsylvania, on 16 April 1819 and dead at Hartford, Connecticut, on 2 October 1874, was the third Bishop of Hartford. His parents, John McFarland and Mary McKeever, had emigrated from Armagh, and from childhood he leaned toward the priesthood. After teaching in a village school he entered Mount St. Mary's College, Emmitsburg, graduated with high honours, stayed on as teacher, and was ordained at New York by Archbishop Hughes on 18 May 1845.

Hughes set him to teach at St. John's College, Fordham, but McFarland longed for parish ministry and made missionary journeys among scattered Catholics. After a year he became pastor at Watertown, New York, then in 1851 at St. John's, Utica, where seven years of saintly labour won notice as far as Rome. He declined the vicariate of Florida in 1857, was elected Bishop of Hartford, consecrated at Providence in 1858, and resided there until his diocese was divided in 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-rene:
Francois-Rene de Chateaubriand, born at Saint-Malo in Brittany on 4 September 1768 and dead at Paris on 4 July 1848. He was a French writer whose Genius of Christianity helped restore Catholic imagination after the Revolution.

When the monarchy fell he sailed for America on 8 April 1791, and the wilderness gave his poetic mind inexhaustible imagery. But on Louis XVI's arrest at Varennes he felt duty-bound to serve imperilled royalty, returned to France on 2 January 1792, married, and emigrated. He joined Conde's army, was wounded and left for dead before Thionville, and escaped to England in 1793. There he lived in abject misery in London until 1800, returning under an assumed name. His Genius of Christianity, published in 1802, made him famous at once, winning him a Rome embassy secretaryship from Bonaparte and a place in the French Academy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-free-church-o:
The Free Church of Scotland broke from the established Church in 1843 over who should control the Church's own life. Known since 1900 as the United Free Church, it counted more than half a million of Scotland's Presbyterians by 1908. The entry traces a long fight over patronage, the right of private patrons to name parish ministers.

Scottish Presbyterians had claimed freedom from civil meddling since 1560, but the 1712 act restored private patronage. The Assembly's Veto Act of 1834 let congregations refuse an unwanted presentee, yet civil courts struck it down in the Auchterarder case of 1838. After a Ten Years Conflict, the evangelical party walked out in 1843 rather than yield the Church's spiritual freedom to the state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-garland:
Garland means a wreath of flowers or evergreens once worn at baptism, weddings, funerals, and solemn processions. The earliest sure baptismal garland comes from seventh-century Alexandria, where the priest crowned the newly baptized after communion. The custom lingered there into the eighteenth century. A Gallican phrase about the baptized and crowned in Christ likely speaks in metaphor instead.

Bridal crowns began with pagan Greeks, passed to Romans, and by Chrysostom's day crowned Christian couples as victors over fleshly temptation. The Greek Church keeps the rite with silver crowns. Funeral wreaths first honored virgin martyrs, then all martyrs, and in England maids' garlands hung above graves into recent times, notably in Devon and Cornwall. Clergy too wore rose garlands in procession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-of-tre:
George of Trebizond, a Greek scholar born in Crete in 1395, carried Greek learning into Renaissance Italy. Named for his family's Trebizond origin, he arrived about 1420, before Constantinople's fall, and swapped lessons with Vittorino da Feltre at Mantua, Latin for Greek. After Venice and Florence he reached Rome, where Eugenius IV gave him a leading professorship at the restored university in 1431.

Nicholas V prized him as a translator of Ptolemy and Eusebius, but arrogance and quarrels with Bessarion, Gaza, and Poggio drove him to Naples. His former pupil Paul II restored him as papal abbreviator, yet fresh quarrels followed. Siding with Aristotle against Plethon's Plato, he lost Bessarion's friendship, whose reply counted 259 errors in his translation of Plato's Laws. He died resenting obscurity in 1486.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greenland:
Greenland is an island stretching from within the Arctic Circle south to about 59 degrees north latitude, between 20 and 75 degrees west longitude. Roughly triangular with its apex pointing south, it is bounded by the Arctic Ocean, Smith Sound, Baffin's Bay, Davis Strait, and the Atlantic. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a land of ice, fiords, and hard winters.

The interior is a plateau rising toward the east, with peaks above 13,100 feet. Immense ice fields launch glaciers to the sea. Only the southwestern valleys and south-facing hills grow vegetation, and farming is out of the question, though lettuce and cabbage thrive comparatively well. Ivigtut, outside Siberia, is the only known source of kryolite, used in making aluminum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guitmund:
Norman Benedictine Guitmund, later Bishop of Aversa, defended the doctrine of Transubstantiation against Berengarius of Tours in the eleventh century. A pupil of Lanfranc at Bec alongside St. Anselm, he refused a bishopric from William the Conqueror in 1070 and boldly called the Norman conquest of England robbery.

Between 1073 and 1077 he wrote his dialogue treatise On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist, answering Berengarius point by point. His account of how Christ is present stays unclear, and he treats the decay of the species as a trick of the senses. Taking the name Christianus in Rome, he was made Bishop of Aversa by Urban II in 1088 and died there between 1090 and 1095.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-helinand:
Flemish-born poet and chronicler Hélinand, born at Pronleroi about 1150, won Philip Augustus's favour as a worldly courtier before turning Cistercian at Froidmont about 1190 and becoming a model of piety. Whatever hours monastic duty left, he gave to study, preaching after ordination, and writing, and Beauvais honours him as a saint on 3 February.

Surviving works fill a large stretch of Migne. There are twenty-eight sermons in neat Latin steeped in pagan poets and Fathers, two ascetic treatises, a letter recalling a renegade monk, and a passion of Theban Legion martyrs. A world chronicle to 1204 follows, its early part lost and its history too uncritical for much weight. A French poem on death survives in only four broken stanzas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-harland:
Henry Harland, a novelist born at St. Petersburg in 1861 to New England parents, studied theology briefly at Harvard and spent a year in Italy, returning a Catholic at heart. Rising at four before his day's work at the Surrogate's Court, he wrote As It Was Written and a Jewish trilogy signed Sidney Luska, a name he later wished forgotten. In London from 1887 he wrote stories collected in Mademoiselle Miss, Grey Roses, and Comedies and Errors.

Harland founded The Yellow Book in 1894 with Aubrey Beardsley. It made both men lions of the hour until failing health ended it in 1897, the year he and his wife entered the Church. His later novels, The Cardinal's Snuff Box, The Lady Paramount, and My Friend Prospero, are pervaded by Catholic faith. A physician gave him two years at thirty; he lived fourteen fruitful ones, dying at San Remo in 1905.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-ii-king:
Henry II, king of England from 1154, was born in 1133 to Matilda, daughter of Henry I, and Geoffrey Plantagenet, from whom he inherited Anjou, Touraine, and Maine. Knighted at sixteen, ruler of Normandy and Anjou at eighteen, husband of Eleanor of Aquitaine at nineteen, he forced Stephen to terms at twenty and took the crown a year later. With his chancellor Thomas Becket he crushed feudal resistance, surrendered castles, and reorganized the exchequer and royal justice, reforms later embodied in the Assizes.

Prosperity broke on his quarrel with Becket, raised to Canterbury in 1162. Henry's attack on the jurisdiction of church courts produced the Constitutions of Clarendon, six years of persecution. Becket's murder in 1170, followed by Henry's barefoot penance at the martyr's shrine in 1174. The rebellions of his sons, probably stirred by Eleanor, embittered his closing years. He died on 6 July 1189, a king whose legal reforms outlasted his personal tragedies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hucbald-of-st:
Hucbald of St. Amand was a Benedictine monk, born in 840 and dead in 930 or 932, whose birthplace is unknown. He entered the order at St. Amand near Tournai and added music to his studies, then completed his general and artistic education at St. Germain d'Auxerre. By 883 he taught at St. Bertin, and with Rémi d'Auxerre he restored the old church singing schools in the diocese of Reims in 892.

Hucbald worked to improve neumatic notation, which showed melody's rhythm but left intervals to tradition. After trying Greek notation again, he invented the Dazia signs, which mark intervals and church modes plainly. Those signs proved clumsy and never won lasting favour, so he later fixed the scale's intervals with lines and the Latin alphabet's first letters, a step toward modern notation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-iceland:
Iceland is a North Atlantic island, counted with Europe by population and history though really part of America. It lies between set northern latitudes, separated from the New World by the ice-bound Strait of Greenland. Much indented by fjords on northern and western shores, it covers about forty thousand square miles, only two-fifths of it habitable.

From a barren, rocky plateau averaging two thousand feet high rise glaciers, broad summits, and volcanic mountains such as Hecla and Oeraefa. Those peaks have belched lava and mud to great havoc in eruptions like those of 1783, 1845, and 1873. Earthquakes are frequent, rivers short but full, and inland lakes many. The climate is oceanic, with moderate temperature swings and frequent fogs, and the entry goes on to Iceland's people, history, and church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ireland:
Ireland, set in the Atlantic west of Great Britain, is surveyed here on the encyclopedia's largest scale, from its coasts to its saints. At most it is 302 miles long and 174 miles wide. It covers 32,535 square miles in four provinces and thirty-two counties. Its center is a level plain ringed by coastal mountains. Many rivers and bays cut it. Its climate is mild yet very moist. Its soil suits farming and pasture better than mining.

Ancient names — Ierna, Juverna, Hibernia, Ogygia, Inisfail — open a history that runs through early kings, missionaries, Norse raids, Norman conquest, and later centuries of penal law and revival. Geography, peoples, church organization, schools, and literature each get their section. Readers find a whole country in one entry, written just before the political upheavals that would soon reshape it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-sirmo:
Scholar Jacques Sirmond ranked among the greatest of the seventeenth century. He was born at Riom in Puy-de-Dôme in October 1559. He died at Paris on 7 October 1651. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1576. In 1581 he became professor of classical languages at Paris. There he counted St Francis de Sales among his pupils. Called to Rome in 1590, he served sixteen years as private secretary to Superior General Aquaviva.

During those years he spent leisure moments studying antiquity's literary and historical treasures. He kept close ties with learned men then at Rome, including Bellarmine and Baronius. He helped Baronius compose the Annales. In 1608 he returned to Paris. In 1637 he became confessor to King Louis XIII. His first literary work appeared in 1610. From then until life's end, almost every year saw a new publication. The entry presents a Jesuit antiquarian at Europe's scholarly center.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-allemand: Jean Allemand, a French priest and scholar of Eastern languages born in 1799 and dead in 1833. He taught Scripture at the Roman Seminary and served as a consultor and censor in Rome. He also edited a journal of religious science. His known writings defend purgatory against an English critic and warn against Champollion's reading of Egyptian hieroglyphs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste-Antoine Ferland, a French-Canadian historian born at Montreal in 1805 and dead at Quebec in 1865, spent his youth gathering notes on Canada's past before he ever wrote a book. Ordained in 1828, he served country parishes, then directed studies and later led the college of Nicolet.

Ferland turned to print only near forty, answering a rival church history in 1853 and publishing notes on Quebec parish registers. Named professor of Canadian history at Laval in 1855, he gathered fresh papers in France and drew large crowds to his public lectures from 1858 to 1862. Those lectures, printed as his Course of Canadian History, fixed his name as a founder of the field.

Jean-Baptiste Marchand, a Sulpician priest born at Verchères in 1760 and dead at Sandwich, Ontario, in 1825. He led Montreal College and then served the Hurons at Detroit for nearly thirty years. Ordained in 1786, he joined the Montreal Sulpicians in 1788. He soon headed their college, then Saint Raphael's.

In 1796 Marchand succeeded to the Huron mission at Assumption parish opposite Detroit, now Sandwich. A bishop's first recorded visit there in 1801 confirmed some five hundred people, and an assistant came, though he was recalled in 1806. Marchand laboured on mostly alone, tending a frontier flock through war, change, and distance from Quebec.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jocelin-de-br:
Jocelin de Brakelond, a late-twelfth-century English chronicler, was the Bury Saint Edmunds monk. His abbey history under feeble Abbot Hugh and energetic Abbot Sampson gave Carlyle material for the second book of Past and Present. Entering the abbey in 1173, Jocelin learned under novice-master Sampson, who made him chaplain and constant companion when he became abbot in 1182.

Jocelin served as chaplain to 1188, guest-master a decade later, and almoner in 1212, last heard in April 1215 advising Abbot Hugh II on manors. His chronicle runs from 1173 to 1202, including Henry of Essex's tale, and was first edited for the Camden Society in 1843, the edition Carlyle used. Shrewd, kindly, and plainly truthful, Jocelin won Carlyle's warm praise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-almond:
John Almond was a Cistercian monk counted among the confessors of the faith under Elizabeth I. A native of Cheshire, he had been a monk in Henry VIII's reign. The name of his abbey is not known. His fate during and after the suppression of the monasteries cannot be traced.

His closing sufferings are known from an account printed by Foley. It tells of an aged priest worn down by imprisonment, left in Hull Castle to pine away under revolting neglect until his death on 18 April 1585. The supplementary process of the English martyrs included his case. It stands as a stark example of what Elizabethan prisons did to Catholic priests who would not conform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-england:
John England was the first Bishop of Charleston and a leading voice for Catholic emancipation in Ireland and America. Born at Cork in 1786, he entered Carlow College in 1803 and preached to crowded congregations. He founded poor schools from which the Presentation Convent grew, and was ordained in 1809. His pen and tongue assailed the Veto measure of 1814, and next to O'Connell his influence was greatest in the agitation for emancipation.

Consecrated Bishop of Charleston at Cork in 1820, he refused the customary oath of allegiance to Britain. He reached Charleston that December to find a diocese of three states with Catholics scattered in little groups. He built up churches, schools, and a seminary, and edited a diocesan paper. He defended the Church in public controversy until his death at Charleston in 1842, leaving a model of an American bishop in a missionary age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-garland:
John Garland was an English poet and grammarian who spent most of his life teaching in France. Born in England, he studied at Oxford under John of London, one of Roger Bacon's masters, then was fostered in France, a land he cherished above his birthplace. He studied at Paris, and grammar and belles-lettres were his subjects at Toulouse and later at Paris.

Reaching Toulouse near the close of the Albigensian war, he wrote about 1229 an epithalamium for the Virgin. He also wrote his epic On the Triumphs of the Church, celebrating crusading victories and the crushing of heresy. Back in Paris by 1234, he composed a poem on accent in over fourteen hundred hexameters and a poem on the liturgy. He also wrote schoolbooks in verse: glossaries, a grammar compendium, lists of homonyms, a rhetoric, and a collection of versification examples. He took his name from Paris's Rue Garlande.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-olivie:
Joseph Olivier Briand was the seventh Bishop of Quebec and a second founder of Canada's Church. Born at Plérin in Brittany in 1715 and ordained in 1739, he secretly left home to follow Bishop Pontbriand to Canada. As vicar-general he ran the diocese during the siege of Quebec in 1759 and tended the dying at Ste-Foy in 1760.

After the British conquest, Briand judged that allegiance must change and worked to secure the Church under London. Consecrated at Paris in 1766, he won the Quebec Act of 1774, which let Catholics hold public office and confirmed religious freedom. He declined clergy gifts for his support and lived at the Quebec Seminary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kaiserwilhelm:
Kaiserwilhelmsland was the German portion of the island of New Guinea, some 460,000 square miles with about a million inhabitants. The first Catholic missionaries arrived in August 1896, three priests and three brothers, and twelve stations soon lined a coast some four hundred miles long. The little mission steamer Gabriel linked them. An apostolic prefecture set up in 1896 passed to the Society of the Divine Word.

By 1909 the mission counted twenty-two priests, seventeen lay brothers, and twenty-nine sisters, though no native priests yet, and a cathedral, St. Michael's at Alexishafen, was already planned. Thirteen parochial schools taught six hundred pupils, and some 1,960 baptisms had taken place since the start. Language was the great difficulty: about 120 pupils at St. Michael's spoke twenty-five different tongues. Adults also learned trades like carpentry, smith-work, boat-building, and tailoring, in hopes the mission might one day support itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lincoln-engla:
The diocese of Lincoln was founded by St. Theodore of Canterbury in 678, when he moved the Lindiswaras out of Lindisfarne's diocese. The bishop's first seat was at Sidnacester, now Stow, until in 870 the Northmen burnt St. Mary's church, and eighty years passed with no bishop.

But this stood in the extreme corner of what was England's largest diocese. The Norman bishop, Remigius of Fécamp, chose Lincoln for his cathedral after the Council of 1072 ordered bishops into walled towns. In 1185 the earthquake damaged the cathedral, and when St. Hugh became Bishop of Lincoln the next year he rebuilt it from the foundations. The nave rose during the next half century, when Robert Grosseteste was bishop. In 1255 St. Hugh's choir came down for the Angel Choir, designed to hold his shrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-francoi:
Louis Wolowski was a Polish-born French jurist and economist, born at Warsaw in 1810 and dead at Gisors in 1876. His father served the provisional government of the Polish rising of 1830, and sent the young Louis to Paris as a legation secretary. The family settled there, and Louis became a French citizen in 1836.

His Revue de legislation et de jurisprudence, founded in 1834, built his name, and a chair of industrial law at the Conservatory of Arts and Crafts held him for thirty-two years. Elected to assemblies in 1848, 1849, and 1871, he shaped finance, backed the Credit Foncier land bank, defended bimetallism and free trade, and helped limit child and women's labour in 1871.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-legrand:
Louis Legrand was a French theologian and Sorbonne doctor, born in Burgundy in 1711 and dead at Issy in 1780. After St. Sulpice he taught at Clermont, joined Saint-Sulpice in 1739, and took his Sorbonne doctorate in 1746, later directing studies at St. Sulpice.

No major Sorbonne judgment, it was said, passed without his counsel. He drafted the condemnation of Rousseau's Emile, praised as learned, exact, and clear, though Rousseau's genius outlived it. He also framed censures of Marmontel's Belisaire and Berruyer's history, and spared Buffon's Epoques after the author's retraction, winning esteem from both writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lund:
Lund is an ancient Catholic diocese in Scania, now the capital of that former Danish province, set on wooded heights eight miles from the Sound and twenty-four east of Copenhagen. Its university holds about 200,000 volumes and over 2,000 manuscripts, beside schools, observatory, gardens, museum, and hospitals.

Its Romanesque cathedral, crypt from the eleventh or twelfth century, was restored between 1833 and 1878, and St. Peter's alone survives of thirty medieval churches. In the Middle Ages Lund stood as metropolis of Denmark, yet fire, war, and Swedish destruction in 1452 wore it down. Ceded to Sweden in 1658, it regained life only with its university, founded in 1666.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maitland:
Maitland was a diocese in New South Wales, named for the chief settlement on the Hunter River. It began as a bishop's title in 1848. William Henry Davis then became coadjutor to Archbishop Polding of Sydney. It became a residential see only in 1865, alongside Goulburn and Bathurst.

James Murray, once secretary to Cardinal Cullen, was consecrated at Dublin on 14 November 1865. He took possession on 1 November 1866. His territory was wide at first, then trimmed in 1887 at his own request. The diocese then ran from Camden Haven to Red Head, west to Wollar and Cassilis, over about 12,000 square miles. Among some 150,000 people, 30,000 Catholics, mostly Irish, were served by 40 priests in twenty districts. Thirty convents, schools for about 4,000 children, a Redemptorist house at Waratah, and Australasia's only Catholic institute for deaf mutes completed the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maryland:
Maryland was one of thirteen English colonies that became original states of the American Union after the 1776 Revolution. It covered 13,327 square miles, 3,386 of water, with 1,275,434 people in 1906, of whom 37.1 per cent claimed church membership: 23.7 per cent Protestant, 13.1 per cent Catholic, and 0.3 per cent others. Baltimore, chief city, grew nine per cent in 1900 to 1910, reaching 558,485.

George Calvert, converted to Catholicism in 1625, withdrew from office with son Cecilius and sought a colony, and on 25 March 1634 Jesuit Andrew White's Ark and Dove party celebrated landing. The colony's genial climate, fertile soil, liberal plantation terms, and security drew settlers, but Richard Ingle's 1644 raid, aided by Claiborne, struck at the Catholic colony. In 1649 the Assembly passed the celebrated Toleration Act. Puritan usurpation later made Catholics suffer greatly, and a 1692 Act of Religion enforced England's penal laws in the colony.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mind:
Mind, in Greek nous, Latin mens, German Geist or Seele, and French ame or esprit, has been used in a variety of senses in English. The corresponding terms in other languages show a similar want of fixity. Aristotle reports that Anaxagoras, compared with other early Greek philosophers, seemed like one sober man among drunken men. He introduced nous, mind, as the efficient cause of the universe's general order.

Aristotle himself, treating the soul, identifies nous with the intellectual faculty, conceived as partly active and partly passive. The article then examines mind and consciousness, the origin of mental life, mind and matter, and mind and mechanism. It sets scholastic teaching against modern materialist and mechanist accounts of thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moritz-von-sc:
Moritz von Schwind, born at Vienna in 1804 and dead at Munich in 1871, was a painter of inexhaustible invention. He was a leading ornament of the Munich school, above all a draughtsman and painter of small detail. He made little pictures harmonious in colour and composition. Romantic by nature, he deepened that bent in the studio of Ludwig Schnorr von Carolsfeld and through his Catholic schooling.

After a journey to Rome, fresco work at Karlsruhe and a short stay at Frankfurt, he reached Munich in 1847. There Cornelius strongly influenced him. His spirit recalls the minnesingers, Eichendorff and Brentano. His material was nature and life, above all child life, lyrically conceived in watercolour. He prized religious painting, and at the Wartburg castle he painted fine frescoes of the works of mercy and the life of Saint Elizabeth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-zealand:
New Zealand, formerly a colony, became a Dominion by royal proclamation in September 1907, remaining under British sovereignty. It consists of three main islands, North, South or Middle, and Stewart, plus smaller groups. Those groups are Chatham, Auckland, Campbell, Antipodes, Bounty, Kermadec and Cook Islands, with half a dozen atolls beyond the Cook Group. Its total area, 104,751 square miles, runs about one-seventh less than Great Britain and Ireland.

Good grazing land has made it a great wool, meat and dairy country, with considerable farming, excellent timber, and valuable though little developed minerals. Volcanoes mark the North Island's centre, Ngauruhoe erupting in 1909, and the North Island holds the boiling geysers, said to be the world's oldest except one group. The entry covers the islands' peoples, towns, government, and the Catholic Church's dioceses, missions and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-newfoundland:
Newfoundland, a British North American colony of 42,734 square miles, is bounded north by the Strait of Belle Isle, separating it from Labrador. It faces the Atlantic east and south and the Gulf of Saint Lawrence west, between 46 and 51 degrees north and 52 to 59 degrees west. It was North America's first portion discovered by European voyagers.

The Cabots sailed from Bristol in 1497, landing on 24 June, Saint John the Baptist's festival, in the harbour they named Saint John's, its name to this day. Seeking new lands, power, wealth and territory, they also sought the Gospel's spread and heathens' conversion. They brought priests and missionaries, Augustinians or Black Friars, so Mass was surely celebrated on those shores in 1497. Portuguese, French and English settlement, fisheries, and the Catholic Church's growth follow in the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-newport-engla:
Newport in England is a diocese named for Newport, a town of about 70,000 at the Usk's mouth in Monmouthshire. Before Pius IX restored hierarchy in England in 1850, the old Western District had since 1840 split into two vicariates. The northern one, twelve Welsh counties with Monmouthshire and Herefordshire, was called the Vicariate of Wales.

When an Apostolic Brief of 29 September 1850 divided the country into dioceses, six South Welsh counties with Monmouthshire and Herefordshire became Newport in England and Menevia. Menevia, Latin for Saint David's, signalled two future dioceses. Its first bishop was Thomas Joseph Brown, Benedictine, who had ruled the Vicariate of Wales for ten years. In March 1895 Leo XIII split off five South Welsh counties into a new vicariate, leaving Newport as Glamorganshire, Monmouthshire and Herefordshire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oliver-almond: Oliver Almond, an English priest and writer educated at Rome from 1582 to 1587 and at Valladolid. He worked as a missionary in England and gave a precious chalice to the English College at Rome. Foley thought him brother of the martyr John Almond, but Gillow showed that link probably mistaken, and Gillow conjectures Oliver wrote The Uncasing of Heresies, printed around 1623.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-berlan:
Pierre Berland was Archbishop of Bordeaux from 1430 to 1457, born in the Médoc in 1375. Of humble birth, he studied humanities at Bordeaux and canon law at Toulouse only through friends' generosity. Ordained priest, he served as the archbishop's secretary, canon of St. Andrew's, and pastor of Soulac before his own elevation. Education absorbed him: he founded Bordeaux University and endowed St. Raphael's College with twelve scholarships for poor students.

His archbishopric sat delicately inside the Hundred Years' War, Guyenne favouring England while Joan of Arc's martyrdom and Henry VI's Paris coronation as King of France repelled him. Twice he travelled north to moderate his suzerain, failed, and transferred his allegiance to Charles VII, helping bring the whole province under the French crown as the war ended. Old and infirm, he resigned in 1457 and died soon after, honoured still: St. Andrew's tower of 1440 bears his name, Pey Berland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-bertra:
This entry covers two French cardinals named Pierre Bertrand, uncle and nephew. The elder, born at Annonay in 1280, studied and taught law at Avignon, Montpellier, Orléans, and Paris, rose high in Parliament, the King's Council, and the Queen's Chancery, then took orders. He became Dean of Puy, Bishop of Nevers, then of Autun, and cardinal under John XXII in 1331.

His best title to fame is defending the Church's rights at the 1329 Conference of Vincennes and in writings like his Libellus against Pierre de Cugnières. He founded charities at Annonay and Paris's Collège d'Autun for fifteen poor students. The younger Bertrand, born at Colombier in 1279, followed the same path to Nevers, Autun, and Arras, became cardinal in 1344, served Avignon's popes on delicate missions, and crowned Charles IV emperor. Both died at Montaud priory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plegmund:
Plegmund was a Mercian hermit who became Archbishop of Canterbury under King Alfred. He spent his early life as a hermit on an island near Chester that took his name, Plegmundham, now Plemstall. His fame for piety and learning drew Alfred to summon him to court to help with the king's literary work.

Chosen archbishop in 890, he travelled to Rome for the pallium, the woollen band of office, from Pope Formosus. When Formosus' acts were condemned in 897 and the condemnation confirmed in 905, Plegmund's own position grew doubtful. In 908 he returned to Rome, and the next year he consecrated seven bishops in a single day, five for Wessex, before his death in 914.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poland:
Poland covers the former kingdom that stretched across the western Sarmatian Plain and the northern slopes of the Carpathians. Its area was about 435,200 square miles, twice the size of Germany, and its name likely comes from pole, the Polish word for field or plain, the mark of its landscape. Until 1772 it was bounded by the Baltic, Russia, Tatar lands and Hungary, Bohemia, and Prussia.

Its rivers run north to the Baltic, the Oder, Vistula, Niemen, and Düna, or south to the Black Sea, the Dniester, Bug, and Dnieper. Farming always led its industry. The entry divides the kingdom into its historic lands, from Great Poland and Masovia with Warsaw to Silesia, Pomerania, Volhynia, and Podolia, each with its chief cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prebend: A prebend is the right of a chapter member to his share of a cathedral's revenues. The word also means the share itself. In a wider sense it marks any slice of cathedral revenues set aside to keep the clergy tied to it, even those outside the chapter, in semi prebends. Prebends count as benefices and follow the same laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-providence-rh:
The Diocese of Providence covers the whole State of Rhode Island, and this encyclopedia entry traces its story from the first Masses on its soil to its early twentieth-century shape. It was erected on 17 February 1872, at first taking in part of south-eastern Massachusetts as well, until that district became the Diocese of Fall River in 1904. Catholic worship first appeared in the colony in late 1780, when French chaplains with Rochambeau's army said Mass openly at Newport and Providence.

Bishop Harkins, consecrated on 14 April 1887 in the still unfinished Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul, dominates the later pages. A lover of order and method, he organized the diocese and made its charities his own, above all the orphan asylum begun in 1851. By the entry's count, sixty-one parishes stood in Providence county against eighteen small ones in the state's other four counties, a picture of a strongly Catholic little state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhode-island:
Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, one of the thirteen colonies, is the smallest state in the union, at 1,054 square miles. It takes in the Island of Rhode Island, Block Island, and the lands around Narragansett Bay. It is bounded by Massachusetts to the north and east, the Atlantic to the south, and Connecticut to the west. The 1910 census counted 542,674 people, and Providence, the capital at the bay's head, counted 224,326 as the industrial centre of a wealthy, dense district.

Long chiefly a manufacturing state, Rhode Island drew many Canadian Catholics after the Civil War, and in recent years Italians and Poles in great numbers. Its Catholic population counts about 65,000 Canadians and French, 40,000 Italians, 10,000 Portuguese, 8,000 Poles, and 1,000 Armenians and Syrians. A government report on religious bodies puts Catholics at 76.5 per cent of Providence, served by 199 priests in the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-i-kin:
Richard I of England, later famed in song as Coeur-de-Lion, or the Lionheart, reigned while spending most of his life outside England. Born at Oxford in 1157, the second son of Henry II, he was raised among the southern French lands of his mother, Eleanor of Aquitaine. He was made Duke of Aquitaine before he was sixteen. As a young prince he joined his brothers in revolt against their father, then made peace and waited for the crown.

King from 1189, he won renown for knightly daring and for his part in the Third Crusade, yet the entry stresses how little he governed England itself. It follows his campaigns, his captivity in Germany on the way home, his ransoming, and his death from a wound in France in 1199. Readers meet a warrior king whose legend, the article suggests, owes more to later minstrels than to his own subjects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richmond:
The Diocese of Richmond is a suffragan see of Baltimore. It covers most of Virginia and part of West Virginia. This entry traces its story from the first Spanish landings to its organization in 1820. Richmond was erected on 11 July 1820, originally embracing Virginia and the territory that later became the Diocese of Wheeling. Its extent, measured at over 31,000 square miles in Virginia alone, is set out county by county.

Colonial beginnings came long before the diocese itself. In 1526 Lucas Vasquez de Ayllon led a Spanish party of 600 to the James River. Dominicans said Mass in a chapel, only the second Catholic place of worship on American soil. Fever killed Ayllon, and the settlement failed within a year. A Jesuit mission on the Rappahannock in 1570 ended in the martyrdom of its members. From these fragile starts, the entry follows Catholic life in Virginia down to the diocese's formal founding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roermond:
Roermond is a diocese in Holland, suffragan of Utrecht, covering the province of Limburg. In 1909 it counted 332,201 people, among them 325,000 Catholics, with a chapter of nine canons, fourteen deaneries, 173 parishes, and 197 churches with resident priests. Its institutions included a seminary at Roermond and a boys' preparatory seminary at Rolduc. They included about seventy primary schools, two gymnasia, and schools for philosophy and theology. There were thirty-five higher schools for girls, sixty charities, forty-five men's houses with 2,400 members, and 130 convents with 3,900 sisters.

The see was erected in 1559 under Philip II, when the Netherlands dioceses were reorganized after long talks with the papacy. Roermond, its bounds fixed in 1561, became suffragan of Mechlin. The reorganization met fierce opposition from bishops who lost territory, abbots whose abbeys were absorbed, and a fast-growing Calvinism. Its first bishop, Lindanus, consecrated in 1563, could not take up his duties until 1569 and later retired amid revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-margare:
Margaret of Scotland, queen to Malcolm III, was born about 1045 and died in 1093. Daughter of the exiled prince Edward and granddaughter of Edmund Ironside, she reached Scotland after a storm drove her family's ship north while they fled the Norman conquest. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows an English princess who became a Scottish queen.

Marriage, delayed by her wish to enter religious life, took place between 1067 and 1070. As queen she poured her energy into reforming church practice, founding religious houses, and caring for the poor, while raising children who would shape both Scotland and England. The entry weighs what can be known against what rests only on tradition, and shows why she stayed a beloved figure long after her death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scotland:
Scotland, as the term is now used, covers the whole northern part of Great Britain, divided from England by the Cheviots, the Tweed, and smaller streams. It spans about 30,000 square miles, 292 miles long and 155 broad, mostly mountainous, with only a quarter of its land cultivated. Its great entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with geography before history.

The Grampians form the chief range, Ben Nevis the highest hill at 4,406 feet, and rich coalfields run east to west along the Forth and Clyde. The climate runs colder and, except on parts of the east coast, wetter than England's. Romans called the land beyond Forth and Clyde Caledonia, its people later Picts, and the country Pictland, until the name Scotland came into use. The entry then follows church, clan, and crown through the centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shrines-in-gr:
This entry is a gazetteer of sanctuaries of Our Lady and of the saints across England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland. In England it moves from Abingdon, where Saints Edward the Martyr and Dunstan encouraged pilgrimage, to Canterbury and Caversham. At Coventry, Leofric and Godgifu founded a splendid abbey church in 1043. Images plated with silver and rich offerings from queens and kings recur through the list.

Scotland and Ireland add their own sanctuaries. They run from Our Lady of Loreto at Musselburgh, destroyed by reformers, to Dublin, Muckross, Navan, and Trim. Trim, the most celebrated Irish shrine, saw its image publicly burnt in 1539. Shrines of saints follow, above all Thomas Becket at Canterbury. His gold-plated tomb drew pilgrims from across Christendom until Henry VIII despoiled it. Edward the Confessor, Patrick, Wulstan, and Gilbert of Sempringham stand beside him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siam-thailand:
Siam, the land of the White Elephant and country of the Muang Thai, the Free, lies in the southeast corner of Asia between French and British possessions. It stretches some 1,130 miles north to south and covers about 242,580 square miles, near the size of Spain and Portugal together, divided into 41 provinces. Its people, estimated between six and nine million, include a third Siamese, a quarter Chinese or of Chinese descent, and Burmese, Cambodians, Laotians, Malays, and Europeans besides.

The Siamese are praised as polite, hospitable, and light-hearted, skilled as goldsmiths, painters, and carvers, living under a perpetual summer on rich rice and pepper harvests. The entry's second half is mission history. A vicariate came in 1662, the Paris Foreign Missions took charge in 1669, King Phra-Narai welcomed the missionaries, and later persecutions in 1729, 1755, and 1764 tested a church that kept growing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sigismund:
Sigismund, King of Germany and Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, was born at Nuremberg on 15 February 1361 and died at Znaim in Bohemia on 9 December 1437. Second son of Emperor Charles IV, he was betrothed to Maria, eldest daughter of the King of Hungary and Poland. During his elder brother Wenceslaus's reign, he pressed his claim to Hungary after its king died, and on 31 March 1387 he was crowned King of Hungary.

In 1389 he had to defend his new kingdom against the Turks, after Sultan Murad I crushed the Serbian kingdom at Kosovo. Murad's son Bayezid beat a Christian army under Sigismund at Nicopolis. Bohemian clergy and nobles rebelled against Wenceslaus's favorites in 1389, backed by Sigismund and Jost of Moravia. When electors deposed Wenceslaus as emperor in 1400, he named his brother imperial vicar for Germany and governor of Bohemia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-somaliland:
Somaliland, the triangular territory at the north-eastern tip of Africa jutting toward Socotra, is the subject of this wide-ranging entry on land, people, and exploration. Bounded by the Gulf of Aden, the Indian Ocean. And the hills of Harrar and Shoa, it covered about 356,000 square miles with roughly a million inhabitants. And Greek sailors once knew it as the country of aromatic gums.

Exploration began with sixteenth-century Portuguese in Ethiopian service, stalled for centuries, and resumed in the nineteenth with Burton and others, yet knowledge stayed patchy. Harsh climate, dry soil, poor transport, and hostile inhabitants, the entry says, made it one of the least welcoming places on earth. And its frank, period tone is itself part of the historical record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alcmund:
St. Alcmund, or Alchmund, was bishop of Hexham, dying in 781, and this entry admits that almost nothing of his life is known beyond the veneration he drew. Hexham's church, founded by St. Wilfrid, had become an episcopal see, and Alcmund, succeeding as bishop in 767, lived in remarkable piety until his death on 7 September 781, buried beside St. Acca outside the church.

Two and a half centuries later, after Danish ravages had erased all memory of his tomb. The saint reportedly appeared in a vision, bidding a Hexham man tell Alured, sacrist of Durham, to translate his body. Alured found and exhumed the remains, pocketed one bone for Durham, and found the shrine immovable until the bone was restored, a tale the entry tells with straight-faced charm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-brigid-of-:
St. Brigid of Ireland, incorrectly known as Bridget, was born in 451 or 452 to princely ancestors at Faughart near Dundalk in County Louth. She died on 1 February 525 at Kildare. This entry follows a girl who refused many offers of marriage, took the veil from St. Macaille as a nun, and settled with seven other virgins at Croghan Hill's foot, but moved thence to Druin Criadh in the plains of Magh Life.

There, under a large oak, she erected her famous convent of Cill-Dara, the church of the oak, now Kildare. It is exceedingly difficult to reconcile the statements of Brigid's biographers. The Third, Fourth, and Fifth Lives agree in assigning her a slave mother in the court of her father Dubhthach, an Irish chieftain of Leinster. Probably the most ancient life of Brigid, by St. Broccan Cloen, who is said to have died on 17 September 650, is metrical in form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-clair-augu:
St. Clair Augustine Mulholland was born at Lisburn in County Antrim, Ireland, on 1 April 1839. He died at Philadelphia on 17 February 1910. This entry follows a boy who emigrated to Philadelphia with his parents while still young. His youthful tastes inclined him to military affairs, and he became active in the militia ranks. At the Civil War's outbreak he was commissioned lieutenant-colonel of the 116th Pennsylvania Volunteers, attached to Meagher's Irish Brigade, and later made its colonel.

He was wounded in the Irish Brigade's famous charge up Marye's Heights at Fredericksburg on 13 December 1862. At Chancellorsville on 3 and 4 May 1863, he led his regiment and distinguished himself by saving the Fifth Maine Battery's guns, abandoned to the enemy. For that, general orders complimented him, and Congress awarded him the Medal of Honor. In that campaign General Hancock gave him command of the picket line, and he covered the army's retreat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-clement-of:
St. Clement of Ireland, also known as Clemens Scotus, was born in Ireland towards the middle of the eighth century. He died perhaps in France, probably after 818. This entry follows a man not to be confounded with Claudius Clemens. About 771 he left for France. An Irish monk of St. Gall wrote his Acts, dedicating them to Charles the Fat, and says Clement and his companion Albinus, or Ailbe, arrived in Gaul in 772, announcing himself as a vender of learning.

So great was their fame that Charlemagne sent for them to his court, where they stayed some months. Ailbe was then put in charge of a monastery near Pavia, but Clement was asked to stay in France as master of a higher school. These events may have taken place in winter 774, after Charlemagne had been in Italy. Clement was regent of the Paris school from 775 until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-louis-bert:
Louis Bertrand, Dominican missionary of the New World, sailed for America in 1562 and reaped a harvest his canonization process celebrates. Born at Valencia on 1 January 1526 to Juan Bertrand and Juana Angela Exarch, he was related through his father to Vincent Ferrer, the Dominicans' great wonder-worker. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 9 October 1581.

His boyhood showed none of the prodigies that often forecast heroic sanctity. Early he conceived becoming a Friar Preacher, and despite his father's efforts to dissuade him, he took the Dominican habit at Valencia's St. Dominic convent on 26 August 1544. After probation, in which he outshone associates as an ideal religious, he professed himself bound to perfection's life. Grave, apparently humourless, yet gentle and sweet, he won all he met. Landing at Cartagena, he entered a missionary career of extraordinary fruit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-osmund:
Osmund, bishop of Salisbury under William the Conqueror, helped draw up Domesday Book before he built a cathedral and a liturgy. A Norman of exalted standing, said to be son of Henry, Count of Séez, he came to England with his uncle the king. He served as chancellor and sat among the chief commissioners for the great survey. Lanfranc consecrated him bishop of Sarum in 1078.

His diocese joined Dorset, Wiltshire, and Berkshire at Old Sarum, a fortress hill rather than a city. There he raised a cathedral and compiled the Sarum use, the order of worship that shaped English liturgy for centuries. Present at the great assembly of 1086 that accepted Domesday, he died in 1099. His feast is kept on 4 December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stipend:
In canon law, a stipend is the fixed payment that supports a cleric. This entry explains how that support took shape across the centuries. It starts with the Latin roots of the word, a weighed-out gift or wage, then looks at early practice, when clergy often lived by a trade.

Paul the tentmaker set that pattern. Over time, tithes from the faithful became the main support. Bishops and councils pressed for them, and Charlemagne made them compulsory. Later sections sort out benefices, endowments, and the Mass offering, which gets full treatment here. Readers gain a compact history of how the Church paid its priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-wigand:
Three saints named Wigand appear in the Roman Martyrology, and this entry keeps them apart. The first, bishop and martyr kept on 1 April, succeeded Domnio at Salona before 312, and his body was brought from Dalmatia by John IV in 640. His relics lie in the Lateran baptistery, which shows him in mosaic.

The second, a youth of fifteen kept on 18 May, died with ten companions under Decius at Camerino in 254. He is patron of Camerino and Fabriano, pictured as a Roman knight with banner and sword. The third, an abbot kept on 13 October, came from Berri in the later fifth century, joined the monks of St Martin of Tours, and was soon elected abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-switzerland:
Switzerland, the Confederatio Helvetica, is a confederation of twenty-two cantons in central Western Europe, three of them split into half-cantons. Covering 15,976 square miles and named for Schwyz, one of the founding cantons, it divides physically into Alps, central region, and Jura. The Alps run 170 miles in a straight line from Mont-Dolent to Piz Mondin, and Monte Rosa, at 15,217 feet, is the highest peak.

Four river basins drain the country. The Rhine runs to the North Sea, the Rhone to the western Mediterranean, and the Po to the eastern Mediterranean. The Inn runs through the Danube to the Black Sea, and the first three meet at the Gotthard watershed. Great lakes rim the Alps and Jura, from Geneva and Constance to Lucerne, Lugano, Maggiore, and Zürich. The long entry then treats history and church affairs, with a wide bibliography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-heliand:
Old Saxon poetry retelling the Gospel takes centre stage here, in the oldest complete work of German literature. Its name means Saviour. A Latin preface published by Flacius Illyricus claims Louis the Pious ordered Old and New Testament renderings into Saxon, so his subjects might know Christianity better. A Cottonian fragment found by Junius before 1587 began modern study.

Hickes printed extracts in 1705, and Eckhart identified the poem in 1720. Schmeller's full edition of 1830, from a Munich manuscript, gave the work its title. Poetic craft, Gospel harmony, and Saxon warrior imagery make the Heliand a bridge between heroic song and Christian teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-irish-in-:
Irish emigrants across the world, beyond Ireland itself, fill this vast survey, opening in the United States. Irish Catholics stood in Virginia before 1633, and Irish names thread the records of Jamestown and later colonies, though exact first landings stay conjectural. Jesuit Father Andrew White's voyage in the Ark and Dove brought a storied company to Maryland.

Later sections sweep through Canada, Australia, South America, and the Continent, tracking soldiers, priests, labourers, and merchants. Numbers, parishes, and public men mark each settlement's growth. For readers tracing the Irish diaspora, the entry gathers a scattered history into one long, rich narrative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trebizond:
An Armenian Catholic diocese on the Black Sea, named for the trapezium shape of its site. A Greek colony from Sinope founded in the eighth century before Christ, it passed through the kingdoms of Armenia and Pontus to Rome. Pompey declared it a free city and Hadrian gave it an artificial harbour.

In 1204, when Latins took Constantinople, a Comnenus prince proclaimed himself Emperor of Trebizond. He founded a Greek empire that lasted some two and a half centuries. The entry also lists eighteen Greek bishops, from Domnus at Nicaea in 325 to Dorotheus, who signed the union decree at Florence in 1439.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-twiketal-of-c:
Twicetal, also called Thurcytel or Turketul, was a tenth-century English churchman of royal blood. He died in July 975. He is said to have served as chancellor to three kings: Athelstan, Edmund, and Edred. The entry warns that this claim rests on a doubtful source and must be taken with care. In 946 he left court life to become a monk at Croyland Abbey, a house wrecked by Danish raids and sunk in ruin and want.

Chosen abbot, he gave the abbey six of his own manors and raised it back to a flourishing state. He counted St Dunstan and St Ethelwold among his friends and shared their reforming spirit for English monastic life. The entry sorts honest evidence from invention, leaning on Ordericus Vitalis. It sets aside a long fanciful life printed under the name of Ingulf, a fourteenth-century forgery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-almo:
John Almond was an English priest and martyr born about 1577 who died at Tyburn on 5 December 1612. His childhood passed at Allerton near Liverpool, his birthplace, and at Much Woolton. His boyhood and early manhood were spent in Ireland, until at twenty he went to the English College at Rome. There he crowned his course brilliantly with the Grand Act, a public defence of theses covering all philosophy and theology.

Cardinals Baronius and Tarugi, who presided, warmly congratulated him. The account of his death calls him a reprover of sin and a good example. It praises his ingenious and acute understanding, his sharp conceits and answers, his modesty, and his courage and readiness to suffer for Christ. Arrested in 1608 and again later, he was tried for his priesthood and suffered at Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-ho:
Thomas Holland was a Lancashire Jesuit executed at Tyburn in December 1642. Born at Sutton in 1600, he studied at St-Omer and Valladolid, then entered the Jesuit novitiate at Watten in Flanders and was ordained at Liège. A skilled linguist, he spoke French, Spanish, and Flemish, and proved adept at disguise on the English mission.

Arrested on suspicion in a London street in October 1642, he was tried at the Old Bailey for being a priest. No firm proof was offered, but his refusal to swear that he was not a priest brought a guilty verdict. Crowds flocked to him in prison, where he heard confessions and said Mass. His brethren called him a library of piety, and he was allowed a long speech and prayers before he was hanged.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-i:
William Ireland, alias Ironmonger, was a Lincolnshire-born Jesuit executed at Tyburn in January 1679. Educated at St-Omer, he joined the Society at Watten in 1655, served for years as confessor to the Poor Clares at Gravelines. Was sent to the English mission in 1677 as procurator, or business manager, of the province.

Arrested in person by Titus Oates on the night of 28 September 1678, he was charged with plotting to kill the king at a Jesuit meeting the previous August. A journal he kept in Newgate gives a day-by-day account of where he was away from London from 3 August to 14 September. One woman's claim that she had seen him in Fetter Lane on 20 August outweighed that alibi. After two reprieves he was executed with layman John Grove, who protested their innocence at the gallows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-widukind:
Widukind was a Saxon leader and head of the Westphalian nobility, the moving spirit of Saxon struggles for independence and heathen faith. Frankish accounts, coloured by national feeling, give only an outline of his character. After Charlemagne's victory in 777 he fled to Denmark, judging opposition useless for the moment. When Charlemagne went to Spain in 778, Widukind returned, trusting Saxon love of independence.

Organized a war of revenge: Saxon hordes plundered the middle Rhine region and threatened Fulda, so monks fled carrying St Boniface's remains, until a Frankish army defeated them at Laisa. Hatred turned against churches and priests and Willihad, first Bishop of Bremen, abandoned his mission for a time. Charlemagne's terrible punishment of four thousand Saxons at Verden on the Aller strengthened the national party. Widukind again fled to Denmark before persuading northern Elbe people and Frisians to join the revolt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zululand:
Zululand is the South African territory between 28 and 29 degrees south latitude, inhabited by the Zulus or Amazulus of the Bantu family. Early in the nineteenth century the Zulus were a small tribe of barely two or three thousand souls. Ten years later they could field 100,000 warriors and devastated much of South Africa, terrorizing Boers and British settlers alike.

This transformation came from the military genius Tchaka, the Zulu Napoleon. Succeeding his father in 1810, he joined Dinghwiswayo, King of the Umtewa, introduced military discipline, and incorporated conquered tribes' young men into his army. By 1818 his conquerors had exterminated or subjugated all neighbours except the Umdwandwe under Zuidi. Zuidi captured and killed Dinghwiswayo but was in turn overcome by Tchaka, whose power was then unchallenged. His empire in 1820 stretched from Delagoa Bay to the Saint John River, embracing Natal, Zululand, Swaziland, Tongaland, and part of the Transvaal.
children-of-the-whirlwind:
Leroy Scott wrote Children of the Whirlwind, a novel that opens on a shabby street near New York's East River. Maggie Carlisle grows up around the pawnshop kept by the Duchess, a shriveled old woman wrapped in rumor. Larry Brainard begins life on the same hard streets. Scott warns early that unpromising beginnings can hide strong souls.

Crime, prison, and the pull of old companions shape Larry's path. Maggie faces her own temptations in a world of easy money. Their stories cross as each tries to escape the whirlwind of the title. Scott mixes underworld detail with a belief in reform and second chances. Readers get a serious popular novel of New York poverty, punishment, and the slow work of starting over honestly.
chita-a-memory-of-last-island:
